title: Benny and Paula Clark building custom homes in Lewisport
description: Benny and Paula Clark Homes by Benny Clark is one of Owensboro's most pre
content:
Benny and Paula Clark Homes by Benny Clark is one of Owensboro's most prestigious custom home builders. Husband and wife team, Benny & Paula Clark, build people their dreamhomes, including step-free homes, and are celebrating their 49th anniversary this year. They have around 550 projects under their belt, and have recently completed a 'forever home' for a couple in downtown Lewisport. 'A couple wanted to re-invest in downtown Lewisport,' Benny said, 'so we built them their forever home, which is a step-free home.' Many with mobility challenges are choosing step-free homes in order to stay and live at home and not have a need for living in an assisted facility, he said. 'They want to live in their own homes,' Benny explained, 'so we have floor plans with an open concept and the bathrooms are easier to use, etc.' Benny started looking into home building many years ago. 'When I got out of the service,' he said, 'I came back to Owensboro and started working for Anderson's Department Store downtown in display and advertising and all of the sudden I started painting and remodeling. I joined the Home Builders Association of Owensboro and became president. I went on to become President of the Home Builders Association of Kentucky, and then sat on the Board of Directors in Washington, D.C. for 30 years. So my education is on-the-job training. We were in subdivisions for a long time in Owensboro – Lake Forest and the Summit Golf Course Community, we helped start all that and other subdivisions. And, we had furnished model homes with plans you could choose from. Since getting out of subdivisions, we now do site-built houses on people's land or building lots. We have built several in Hancock County and Ohio County.' Pricing Benny's wife, Paula, a Hancock County native, runs the program at their office in Owensboro in Accounting and Interior Design. Their clients really appreciate her expertise in design. She explained that since all of their homes are custom-designed to each individual client, that the cost of their homes range in pricing depending on how upscale the client wants to go on appliances, flooring, and other amenities. 'You can pretty well start at $185 per heated square foot,' she said, 'and we have them that are at $245 and $255 a square foot. Let's say for a 2,500 heated square foot home in the custom home market today, that would run anywhere from $460K to $475K based on the selections and what each client wants, but in that also is a very large oversized 2-car garage, covered porches, sidewalks, patios, parking aprons, etc.' The Clark's 3-Step Design Program Benny said that the Clark's 3-Step Design Build Program works great with helping their clients with their budgets and what their ideal plan is for their dream home. 'The first budget is – what does their land cost? The second budget is infrastructure – what does your infrastructure cost? Do you have a sewer tap? Are you on a septic tank? Do you need your lot or land cleared? Do you need a construction driveway? Are utilities available? Is Kenergy for power, or a gas company? Are you on a propane tank? Water company? All of that is calculated into the infrastructure budget,' he said, 'and a typical infrastructure budget for
most people is going to start around $20K to maybe $25K.' It could cost in the $6K range or up to clear a lot in the country, for example, and a septic tank could cost up to $8,500. In contrast, infrastructure cost would be much less for a lot in a downtown area such as in Hawesville or Lewisport. Building Near Floodplains 'We have to be careful that when people buy lots or land that there's not a high water table area,' Benny added, 'and that they're not in a floodplain. The house we just finished in Lewisport touched on a floodplain so we made an application to the state and had an engineer come over and set a benchmark. We built the house a foot and 6 inches above the floodplain so there's no flood insurance and we documented that and put it on record so these guys are safe. It's just a matter of calculating on what you're doing.' Benny and Paula are building another step-free custom home for a client in Lewisport on Pell Street next. 'We already built him the home he's in but he wants to upscale and downsize,' Benny said. 'He wants all of the amenities but yet he wants it step-free. He wants to age in place, and he wants full-service care to come to him. He doesn't want to ever go to full-service care so if we put this plan together it will be a universal design for an aging in-place, step-free environment and he can live there with full-service care. We help people in that way.' Interest Rates 'People building a custom home,' Paula said, 'they realize – there's an old saying in the mortgage industry, it's: ‘You marry the cost and you date the rate.' Because rates always fluctuate. So they look at it as – if it's their time to build and they want to build then they'll build now, and when rates drop they'll refinance. A lot of times when the rates start coming down a lot, material pricing goes up. So it ends up being a wash, but you are better off while material pricing is down to go ahead when interest rates are a little higher to build because you can always re-fi that interest rate.' Benny added, 'On interest rates, our National Homebuilders in Washington, D.C., I'm a past board member and life senior member with that group, and they're saying we're going to have 2 clicks down on interest rates starting this spring so you're probably going to see that. The good news now is building material and costs are held, and now is the time to build when material costs, etc., are at a lower level and not worry about interest rates. It will continue to fall between now and November because this is a presidential election year.' Homes by Benny Clark is located at 4775 Shell Drive in Owensboro, and the phone number is (270) 929-0581. Visit their website at: https://www.homesbybennyclark.net By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Anne Higgins shares creative kitchen tips, important lesson for cooks
description: Just the thought of spring gets Anne Higgins, owner of of Willow & Pine Market, excited to organize spaces and get creative…especially in the kitchen. 'As a military family, we've moved a lot and I've…
content: Just the thought of spring gets Anne Higgins, owner of of Willow & Pine Market, excited to organize spaces and get creative…especially in the kitchen. 'As a military family, we've moved a lot and I've had to organize a variety of kitchen spaces…small, large, and everything in between,' Anne said. 'I tend to be a bit of a maximalist. I love kitchen gadgets, tools, and utensils! Let me share with you some of my spring cleaning tricks to help keep my kitchen tidy and functional. I begin by sorting through every single drawer and cabinet…throwing away broken and damaged items…eliminating unnecessary duplicates…and paring down to only those items that I really use.' Best practices – quality products 'A good way to reduce clutter in your pantry and kitchen is to buy utensils and appliances that serve dual functions. Another best practice is to buy quality products that won't have to be replaced quickly. Dreamfarm is one of my favorite brands. Their utensils are durable and can be used for multiple tasks.' Quality kitchen towels 'Don't hang on to faded, old towels when there are so many pretty options available!! Quality towels make all the difference when cooking, baking, and cleaning up. They can also add a touch of color and personality to your kitchen. I love using Geometry towels! They are made from recycled materials, are super absorbent and are fast drying! I also love to display Crown Linen Designs hand towels which are beautifully embroidered and made from high quality linen. Once you have cleaned out and organized, move everything off the countertops, give them a good cleaning, and begin to add some seasonal touches.' Get creative! 'Before purchasing anything, try decorating with your favorite serving pieces instead. Prop up your favorite platter in the corner…fill a mixing bowl with fruit…display candles and other small items on a special cake stand. I have so many wooden utensils (because I'm a maximalist!) that I store them next to my cooktop in a larger planter! Be creative and showcase your special things'! Important lessons 'One of the most important lessons a cook learns is 'everything in its place' – to streamline organization and enable efficiency. Seamless integration of carefully selected everyday essentials will ensure an at-home chef is set up for success in the kitchen! Come see us at Willow & Pine Market, for your everyday essentials in downtown Owensboro, 126 West 2nd Street.' By Anne Higgins – vimeo.com/812876867

title: Hancock schools needs volunteers to help with Junior Achievement program
description: This month's HC Cha
content: This month's HC Chamber Breakfast Speaker – Ohio Valley Program Manager for Junior Achievement (JA) of West Kentucky Chelsey Chaney. The guest speaker at this month's Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Breakfast on Tuesday, was Ohio Valley Program Manager for Junior Achievement (JA) of West Kentucky Chelsey Chaney. Due to a lack of volunteers in Hancock County, there were 3 JA programs available to HCHS students last fall and they did not get to have them! So if you're thinking of volunteering, it will be greatly appreciated. 'Junior Achievement is the largest non-profit organization in the world that's dedicated to giving young people the knowledge and skills they need to own their economic success, plan their future and, basically, get ready for being an adult,' Chelsey said. 'Our programs teach financial literacy, work-readiness and entrepreneurship. There is a major need for volunteers in Hancock County. More teachers are requesting our programs than ever. Right now, we have the ability to do 30 programs in Hancock County. Last year we did 15, so we have more of a need for those volunteers but not enough of a volunteer pool to get these kids the programs that would help them be successful in life and in the future. Owensboro has a lot more programs in a lot more grade levels than we are able to provide to Hancock County right now and that is why it's so important for us to get those volunteers so that we can get Hancock County the same things that Owensboro is getting. There's no reason that Daviess County should have it and Hancock County not have it.' Volunteer Training 'Anybody can be a volunteer. All you have to do is care,' she said. 'We have guidebooks in all of our programs that will guide you through every step of everything that you need to do. It even prompts you on what to say, so you can't do it wrong. You don't have to have any previous classroom or presentation experience in order to be able to lead one of these programs. You're not just given materials and thrown into a classroom where you'd have to figure it out yourself. I will train you and we provide all of the materials for each activity. The guidebook will walk you through, step by step, on what you're supposed to do. Of course, we like for volunteers to put their own spin on it. If you see something that you think would benefit the students in your class more, adjust it to whatever you need to. Make it more fun if you see a way that it could be more fun. As you go in a couple of times, you're going to get to know the kids and what works best for them, and what they know and what they don't know. I've volunteered with 19 classrooms in over 9 counties since I've been with JA, about a year and 3 months. One of the schools I've volunteered in most is my son's school. I am known by a ton of students as 'Miss JA'. They'll see me and run up and hug me. It really is fun and is also a good way, especially in those middle and high school classrooms, to be able to talk to the students about your career. Those of you who work in Hancock County, you want to keep having employees in Hancock County and these are the next generation. It's an opportunity for you to talk to them about what your work life is like and what it would be like to work for your company as well. It's not just a win-win because it's fun, it's a win-win because it can help Hancock County in the future.' HCHS Chelsey emphasized the need for volunteers at Hancock County High School saying, 'There is a JA Personal Finance Program that is 5 sessions of 45 minutes. We have one more volunteer needed.' HCMS She said there are now JA programs back at HCMS for 6th & 8th grades. 'The 6th grade program teaches about finding your career path and what works for you. The 8th grade program teaches more about branding yourself to employers and what your skills are,' she explained. 'It helps them develop both their idea of what their interests are and how they can relate to a job later on.' NHES & SHES She continued saying, 'We've also had kindergarten, 1st & 2nd grade programs. All of our programs build onto each other and that's why I would like to see us have programs in every grade level in Hancock County one day. Everything builds on the next thing. The kindergarten program teaches about ourselves and what jobs we can do, even around the house. The 1st grade program teaches about our families, what jobs they do and how they contribute to the community. In the 2nd grade program, they learn a little about taxes and what they go to. They have to do a job and get paid. You pay them and then turn around and take their (tax) money back, and 2nd graders are so shocked by that. Then, we talk about how that money goes to contribute to the government, public schools, libraries, roads, and all of those types of things. In the 3rd grade program, we talk about our city and how the community contributes to the city, what we can do to make the city better and entrepreneurship – planning a business, making a business plan and all of those things. We do have a 5th grade program and we've already had volunteers at both NHES and SHES this year. That is more global-based – what things we get from other countries and how we get those things.' Chelsey handed out flyers with descriptions of the classes JA offers in HC. 'If you choose to volunteer,' she said. 'You schedule those directly with the teachers so it is on dates that work for your schedule. Aside from the middle & high school, most of the teachers don't specify a time and usually you get to pick so it makes it a lot easier. Kindergarten and 1st grade are only 30 minutes long – 5 sessions for 30 minutes. The middle school programs, right now, are 6 sessions of 45 minutes. The only high school program we have left is 5 sessions of 45 minutes.' Volunteers Encouraged HC Chamber Executive Director Tina Snyder told about some of her JA teaching experiences in hopes of encouraging others to volunteer saying, 'This year, I volunteered in a 1st grade classroom at NHES. It was SO fun. I emailed the teacher and asked if I could do 5 days in a row in one week (instead of one day for 5 weeks in a row). They looked forward to seeing me every day. It was a lot of fun so if you're having second thoughts – don't. Just do it; you won't regret it. It was definitely a rewarding experience. There are 7 or 8 of us here in the County that do this on a regular basis. I say just go for it!' Sign-Up! If you are interested in volunteering, please contact Chelsey Chaney at (270) 314-5287. You can call or text to request a volunteer application form which can be filled out and returned online, or you can email Chelsey at: Chelsey.Chaney@JA.org. The next step is some training that you can do in Owensboro or online, then you will be connected with the educator at the school where you'll be volunteering to coordinate the day(s) and time(s) you'll be teaching. The teaching materials for each program are provided. For further information, follow the West KY JA Facebook Page and check out the website: westky.ja.org. Junior Achievement of West Kentucky is located at 123 W 4th Street, Suite 301 in Owensboro. The office phone number is: (270) 684-7291. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hancock wins big at new home track
description: Wyatt Emmick clears the barrier on his way to victory in the 110 meter hurdles during the Hornets' win at the new HCHS track. Hancock County hosted a track meet at the school's new track and field…
content: Wyatt Emmick clears the barrier on his way to victory in the 110 meter hurdles during the Hornets' win at the new HCHS track. Hancock County hosted a track meet at the school's new track and field complex and both Hornet teams defeat McLean County during a very exciting event. The HCHS girls team won by a team score of 52-31. The boys won 92-21. 'It was a great meet,' HCHS coach Wes Meserve said. 'It was a lot of fun watching our kids do so well.' Girls results Tessa Walls won both the girls' 100 and 200 meter dash events. Walls took the 100 with a time of 14.1 seconds, with Nahomy Yanez second in 14.8. Walls won the 200 in 30 seconds flat. Izzy Ross was second in 31.2, Yanez third in 32.7 and Jayda Meserve fourth in 33.00. Meserve won the 400 meter dash in 1:14. Juliana Nevitt took second in the 800 meters in 3:19. Lyla DeJarnette was third in 3:22 and Alivia Bernardi fourth in 3:26. McLean's Aubree Davis won in 2:59. DeJarnette won the 1600 in 7:11. Nevitt was second in 7:15 and Bernardi third in 7:17. McLean won the girls 4×800 meter relay in 12:31. Hancock was second in 12:39. Runners were Nevitt, Ross, DeJarnette and Bernardi. Hancock's Addy Harrison won the high jump uncontested. Her best clearance was four feet. Yanez won the long jump with a leap of 12–07 feet. Harrison was second at 11–03. Ross won the triple jump uncontested. Her best distance was 29–03.5. McLean's Ragan Brown took the shot put event at 20–10. Sydney Weatherholt was third with a throw of 16–10.5. 'We knew the girls would struggle a little because our numbers are down, but they still came out with the win,' the coach said. 'Our girls have a lot of potential.' Boys results The HCHS boys team was dominate during the meet. 'Our goal was to win everything except maybe triple and high jump, but we ended up winning the triple and were second and third in high jump,' coach Meserve said. 'We had so many really good performances.' Christian Yanez won the boys 100 meter dash in a very close race. Yanez's time was 11.5 while teammate Ben Baker finished in 11.6. Matthew Carroll was tied for third at 11.7, Mekhel London sixth at 12.5, Julius Girten seventh at 13 seconds, Camden Toler eighth in 13.5 and Logan Mooneyham ninth in 13.9. Baker won the 200 meters in 24.3 seconds. Carroll was second in 26 flat, London third in 26.4, Girten fourth in 27.1, Toler fifth in 27.4, Ashton Vogt seventh in 28.6, Ethan Heavrin eighth in 28.9 and Mooneyham ninth in 29.1. Cooper Jones won the 400 meters in 55.6 seconds. Noah Henson was third in 1:04, Heavrin fourth in 1:05 and Henry Proctor fifth in 1:11. Henson won the 800 meters in 2:26.1 while Max DeJarnette was a close second in 2:26.9. Hunter Stephens third in 2:27.4, Emmitt Meserve fourth in 2:27.9, Proctor fifth in 2:39 and Eli Swihart eighth in 2:59. Meserve won the 1600 with a comeback sprint to the finish line. Meserve's time was 5:23, with Stephens second in 5:25. Swihart was sixth in 6:32. Wyatt Emmick won the 110 meter hurdles in 16.6 seconds. Wyatt cruised to victory in the 300 hurdles with a time of 44.8 seconds. Hancock County won both the 4×100 and 4×800 meter relays. Runners were not listed. McLean took the high jump while Eli Embry was second at five feet. Vogt was third at 4–10. Jones won the long jump with a leap of 18–05. Yanez was third at 17–01.5 and Embry fourth at 15–06. Embry won the triple jump with a distance of 32–10. Meserve was third at 32–04. Meserve's jump broke the HCMS record. Alex Basham won the shot put with a throw of 45–05 feet. James Singleton was third at 37–10, Lawson Ward third at 29–08.5, Jameson Domerese fifth at 25–08, Jameson Boarman sixth at 23–02.5, Jack Ryal eighth at 19–02.5, and Andrew Owens ninth at 17–01.5. Basham won the discus with a throw of 95 feet. Ward second at 84–00, Singleton third at 83–05, Boarman fourth at 61–11, Domerese fifth at 61–08.5, Ryal sixth at 56–07, and Owens eighth at 46 feet. By Steve Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Fluoridated Water
description: The tooth decay prevention benefits that studies show fluoride having on children's teeth only occur when it has been applied directly to the teeth, not when it is consumed. When water is fluoridated…
content: The tooth decay prevention benefits that studies show fluoride having on children's teeth only occur when it has been applied directly to the teeth, not when it is consumed. When water is fluoridated (added to the public drinking water) it has been proven to cause health problems in children and adults so why is it added? A Harvard study shows that fluoridated water is linked to cancer risks and risks for lower IQ in children. Only 5 percent of the world continues to fluoridate its water supply. Fluoride in the water supply is banned or restricted in many other nations across the world, among these are: China, Austria, Belgium, Finland, Japan, Israel, and parts of Africa. According to the Fluoride Action Network, only 5 countries in Europe still fluoridate their water supplies and in varying percentages – one percent of Poland, three percent of Serbia, eleven percent of Spain & the U.K., and 73 percent of Ireland. In 2015, the recommendation in the U.S. was lowered for the amount of fluoride in the water. It had been 0.7 to 1.2 mg parts per million (ppm), and was changed to no more than 0.7 ppm. Ask yourself: Why did they lower it? And, ask yourself this: Why are citizens able to research, gather enough information to support the fact that fluoride in the public drinking water supply is causing health problems, present the data to their city/county officials and have it removed? That is actually happening more increasingly in communities all over the U.S. and Canada. It recently happened in Union County, North Carolina. The Board of Union County Commissioners voted and passed a ban of fluoride from a portion of the county's water supply due to the irrefutable evidence that was presented to them by the concerned public. Over-fluoridated water has been proven to cause dental fluorosis – staining teeth with a yellow/brown coloring. And, since we know that the studies that show it helping prevent tooth decay are only when it is applied directly to the teeth, then why would we be drinking it? Using it in the water supply to prevent dental cavities really is absurd. In less fluoridated water, only an extremely low percentage of the fluoride touches the teeth when you drink it and then it goes into your body and gets deposited in the tissues of your liver, heart, brain, bones, kidneys, thyroid etc., and can cause serious damage. A study revealed that drinking fluoridated water can cause diminished kidney & liver function in adolescents (published by The Mount Sinai Hospital on August 8, 2019). Pregnant women who drank more fluoridated water had children with IQ points that were 3 or 4 points lower than the average by ages 3 and 4. This was published several years ago in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) Pediatrics. These are only 2 of many studies that you can find through researching. If your water is fluoridated, invest in a filtration system for the entire house, or install shower and faucet filters separately. For drinking water, filtered spring water may be the ideal solution. Why invest in a shower filter? Because your skin is the largest organ in your body and bathing/showering in fluoridated water (along with the other questionable additives in the public water supply) will result in the absorption of those chemicals into your skin, and thus into your bloodstream. Then, your body will have to do something with it because is does not belong there and it can set-up/get deposited in organs and cause health problems, just as when it is consumed. Be Well and God Bless You. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: New weather Siren at Commonwealth brings total up to 15 county wide
description: There are 15 total functioning weather sirens now installed in Hancock County that have replaced all of the older sirens in the county. The sirens were delivered in late February and the cost, after…
content: There are 15 total functioning weather sirens now installed in Hancock County that have replaced all of the older sirens in the county. The sirens were delivered in late February and the cost, after the help of grants, was around $55K, shared between Hancock County Fiscal Court and Commonwealth Rolled Products. Testing vs. Actual Emergency The weekly siren tests are at noon every Friday, and last 30-60 seconds. In the event of severe weather, a severe thunderstorm or tornado warning for example, the sirens will go off for a full 3 minutes. Of the new sirens installed, there are those that replaced 3 inoperable sirens in the southern part of the county in Roseville and Easton, as well as one at Commonwealth. Director of HC Emergency Management Kyle Veach said, 'This is just a great partnership between one of our local industries and the HC Fiscal Court to provide safety for our community during severe weather, as well as the employees of Commonwealth. We hope to see partnerships like this continue, and to grow this partnership that we have right here.' Commonwealth Health Manager Parvin Phillips, HC Emergency Management Director Kyle Veach and Terry Dossett, McLean County Emergency Mgmt. Director. Around the middle of last year, a collaborative effort began to get Commonwealth approved to have a weather siren on the property. Veach and others were able to get the state's approval through some grants and funding, along with Commonwealth's contribution to the project to get the weather siren put onsite at the plant, which is connected to Hancock County Dispatch. Commonwealth Health Manager Parvin Phillips said that with the total workforce of 1,150 employees and with the fact that on any given day there could be approximately 400 onsite, the threat of a weather emergency is always present. Tornados and severe thunderstorms could put the plant in jeopardy as well as the safety of their employees. Siren at Commonwealth – Heard within 2-mile radius The weather siren has been installed at the plant, it's functional and is going to provide another level of safety for the people onsite and the surrounding community. According to the test that was ran recently, the siren at the plant can be heard over 2 miles away, which is an added benefit to the community as a whole to alert citizens of the potential that severe weather could be present. When the weather sirens are activated, there are secure places for employees to ride out the storm in safety, Phillips added. There are over a dozen spots, designated 'muster points' onsite, where they have tornado shelters installed inside the plant. Based on the operations and some of the intricacies of what they do at the plant, it could be detrimental to just stop and walk away, he said. They don't have the luxury to always do that, so all employees are educated annually. They do emergency preparedness training this time every year, and review the designated muster points, share information with all of the employees and make sure they know where to go in the event of an emergency. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Joseph 'Sonny' Bickett
description: Joseph 'Sonny' Bickett, 82, of Reynolds Station, died Saturday, March 23, 2024, at Ohio County Healthcare.
content: Joseph 'Sonny' Bickett, 82, of Reynolds Station, died Saturday, March 23, 2024, at Ohio County Healthcare. He was a Navy veteran, was a retired foreman from the Paper Mill and he trained thoroughbreds. He was a wonderful husband, father and grandfather. He was an avid golfer and loved UK basketball. Sonny was preceded in death by his parents, Leo and Mable Bickett; and sisters, Helen Brown and Betty Edwards. He is survived by his wife of 40 years, Cathy Bickett of Reynolds Station; children, Stacy (Randy) Bickett of New York, Stephanie Young of Texas, Travis (Craig) Snyder of Atlanta, Georgia, Joey (Jenny) Snyder of Owensboro, Dannielle (Daren) Sanders of Reynolds Station and Daniel Bickett of Louisville; grandchildren, Sterling Simpson, Hayden, Sam and Garrett Sanders and Emma and Liam Bickett; and sisters, Mary (Bob) Rummage of Owensboro and Ruby (Doug) Taylor of Lewisport. Funeral services are 11:00 a.m. Wednesday, March 27, 2024, at Geary Funeral Home, Fordsville, with burial in Newton Springs Cemetery. Visitation will be 4:00 – 8:00 p.m. Tuesday and after 9:00 a.m. Wednesday at the funeral home. Condolences may be made at gearycares.com.

title: Tindle goes the distance in Hornets 4-3 win
description: Brock Tindle fires a pitch during Hancock County's 4-3 win over Henderson County at Vastwood Park Tuesday. The senior hurler pitched a complete game. Brock Tindle pitched a complete game and the…
content:
Brock Tindle fires a pitch during Hancock County's 4-3 win over Henderson County at Vastwood Park Tuesday. The senior hurler pitched a complete game. Brock Tindle pitched a complete game and the Hornets defeated Henderson County 4-3 at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown Field Tuesday.
'Brock comes out everyday and competes and we saw that tonight. He commanded all game,' HCHS coach Brad Keown said. The Colonels plated a run in the first inning before Hancock County answered with a run in the second. Louden Fluharty got the Hornet offense going with a double and Tindle followed with a base hit. Fluharty later stole home and the score remained tied at 1-1 until the fifth. Kolby Keown drew a walk then advanced to second base on a catcher's error. Keown moved to third on a wild pitch and Jacob Shultz walked and stole second. Dec Lewko was intentionally walked to load the bases and up came Jack Roberts. Roberts delivered a deep fly ball that enabled Keown to tag up and score. With the Hornets now leading 2-1 with runners at the corners, Jordan Payne smacked a 2-out base hit that brought home Shultz. Carson Clark followed with a ground ball and the Colonels threw the ball away. Lewko scored on the play and the Hornets led 4-1. 'We got a couple of runners on base and put some pressure on them. The tail end of our line up did what they needed to do then Jack delivered on a hard shot to center. Jordan was struggling at the plate tonight then he smacked one up the middle and showed why he's leading the team in batting average,' the coach said. Henderson County fought back and plated two runs in the sixth. The Colonels were aided by two Hornet errors, but Tindle battled and got the final two batters out on strikes. Tindle finished off the game with a big strike out in the seventh and the Hornet celebrated the
victory! Tindle got the win while allowing three runs (one earned) on six hits, with seven Ks and two walks over seven complete innings. 'We had Brock down to the wire on pitch count, but he never let down from the first to the last inning. That's the best part about him. You couldn't see that he was ever getting tired and that's what senior leadership looks like,' Keown said. Clayton Brown took the loss on the mound for Henderson County. The Hornets had just three hits, but they were timely and they ran the bases aggressively. Payne was 1 for 3 with one RBI, Fluharty was 1 for 3 with a double, and Tindle was 1 for 3. Clark and Roberts had one RBI each while Lewko, Keown and Shultz all scored one run each. Fluharty, Shultz, Clark and Lane Dixon all stole one base each. By Steve Wimmer

title: Gold Star Family of Sgt. Edward R. Basham Honored
description: A tribute was made to Hancock County's Gold Star family who lost their father, United States Marine Corps Sergeant Edward R. Basham, at the KSDAR (KY Society Daughters of the Revolution) Luncheon held…
content: A tribute was made to Hancock County's Gold Star family who lost their father, United States Marine Corps Sergeant Edward R. Basham, at the KSDAR (KY Society Daughters of the Revolution) Luncheon held on Friday, March 29th, on Vietnam Veterans Day. Sgt. Basham's children, Maurine Basham Kahl, W. Lloyd Basham, Gloria Basham Pennington, Mildred Basham Hilley and Mona Basham Poole each received a ribbon, pin and certificate. Lloyd gave a thank you speech for the tribute to his family and for the memorialization of his father saying, 'I appreciate you guys having this. I really do believe that our community today in Hancock County as a whole is a great community to be in. It's a great community to raise your family in. It's also a great community that will come together in situations where, if you need help, you can find it in Hancock County. I appreciate each and every one of you. Thank you.' Sgt. Edward R. Basham Sgt. Edward R. Basham lost his life while serving in the Vietnam War during an ambush on December 11th, 1966. He and Cpl. Ernie W. Rosser both lost their lives while headed to Company D, 1st Battalion, 7th Marines Combat Base, in a M54 5-ton 6×6 cargo resupply truck pulling a water trailer. The other 4 marines in the truck were wounded. Sgt. Basham also served in the Korean War. Former USMC Sgt. Don Lorraine was Basham's squadron leader in Korea. 'I am sure Ed was as brave in Vietnam as he was in Korea,' Sgt. Lorraine said in a remembrance. 'He survived with honor, two of the bloodiest battles of the Korean War, E Berlin, Boulder City, only to lose his still young life in another ‘Hell Hole' called Nam. There are many I have forgotten, but Eddie will always be remembered not only for his bravery but his dry sense of humor. He was just a great kid. God, we were all kids.' Gratitude Can Never Be Enough Judy Gore, Regent of Yellow Banks Chapter Daughters of the American Revolution, welcomed all in attendance on this emotional day. She thanked all of Edward R. Basham's family members who attended, as well as those who could not attend. 'Gratitude for their service and sacrifice can never be enough,' she said. Cathy Mullins, Music Teacher at Whitesville Elementary, sang the National Anthem. Hancock County Students presented the Posting of the Colors, and HCHS Choral Student Preston Blanton sang a patriotic song. Vice-Regent of Yellow Banks Chapter DAR Debbie Owens spoke on the Vietnam War. A Proclamation was read by Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts, Jr., and Donn Wimmer, Hancock Clarion Editor, was a guest speaker. The KSDAR invited all Vietnam Era veterans to attend the luncheon held at the Hawesville Methodist Church. All Vietnam Veterans were honored and the luncheon was made possible by a collaborative partnership between HC Yellow Banks Chapter of Kentucky, The National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution, Hawesville Methodist Church, HC Public Libraries, HC Fiscal Court, the Vietnam War Commemorative Committee, Gold Star Families of the U.S., citizens and veterans of Hancock County and the Edward R. Basham Family. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hancock County Public Libraries are a Huge Asset to the Community
description: This week is National Library Week and was celebrated at the two outstanding Hancock County Public Libraries (HCPL) in Hawesville and...
content:
Members of the Hancock County Public Library staff: from left: Kasia DeMauri, Susan Taylor,Sherry Hagman, Amber Bridges, Molly Ramsey, Shiloh Johnson, Amanda Powers, Gale Johnson, Kelley Richardson, Patrick Burk, and Director Tina Snyder.
Members of the Hancock County Public Library staff: from left: Kasia DeMauri, Susan Taylor,Sherry Hagman, Amber Bridges, Molly Ramsey, Shiloh Johnson, Amanda Powers, Gale Johnson,
Kelley Richardson, Patrick Burk, and Director Tina Snyder.
This week is National Library Week and was celebrated at the two outstanding Hancock County Public Libraries (HCPL) in Hawesville and Lewisport in various ways.
HCPL Director and Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Tina Snyder spoke at the Hawesville Library on Tuesday morning, April 9th for this month's Chamber Breakfast sponsored by the libraries. Tina has done a phenomenal job as director over the libraries for over 20 years now. She began with HCPL in 2000 and started serving as director in 2003.
There are approximately 2,509 people with active library cards in Hancock County, according to the data for the 2022/2023 fiscal year, as well as 28,483 items that were checked out. There were 3,444 people who enjoyed being able to access the libraries' computers over that one-year timespan and 260 free programs were provided. There were 22,553 who visited the libraries, 31,587 books & movies were checked out, and there were 11,091 uses of the Wi Fi as well.
Library Services HCPL offers many services and programs. By having a library card, you have access to over 50,000 titles, and that number is always growing. There are various titles available to listen to in audio book form, free downloadable audio books & e-books, book clubs that meet the fourth Tuesday of the month, Bookmobile services, free children's programs, computers with internet access, free printed copies & color copies, free fax service, laminating, an overhead projector available for checkout, fiction titles, non-fiction titles, book request orders, large print books, 7-day checkout bestselling & new books, and over 7,000 DVDs to choose from for checking out, just to name some of the many services available to you at HCPL.
Enthusiastic and energized, our HCPL team members are ready to help you! Pictured left to right: Molly Ramsey, Teen Librarian; Gale Johnson, Circulation Clerk; Amber Bridges, Children's Librarian; and Susan Taylor, Bookmobile Librarian.
Helpful Tips You can check out books from HCPL anywhere in the world as long as you have an internet connection. Titles will automatically return themselves on the due date and no action is needed on your part. If a book is returned before you finish, you can check it out again and 'Libby' will remember your place!
Did you know that you can check out up to 20 items at a time? Digital books are not unlimited in quantity so there may be holds on the book you want. Just tap the calendar icon on the website to see the estimated wait time.
You can also place a hold on an item that is checked out and you'll be notified when it's your turn. There is NO LIMIT on magazine checkouts. Also, the time listed beside earbuds is the total playing time for audio books.
Hawesville Library The first public library in Hancock County was housed in a small room in a building across from the HC Courthouse in June, 1954. Then, in 1965, was relocated into the Boling Building on Main Cross Street in Hawesville.
Members of the state library met with HC library board members in 1966, explaining that unless the county voted on a tax to provide funding to maintain it, that there would be no more state funds available. A petition was circulated and in March of 1967, a special taxing district was established; The library receives 91 percent of its operating budget through this.
A 2-story, 5,500 square-foot library building was then built in downtown Hawesville in 1968, on land donated by Father C.P. Riney and the Immaculate Conception Church parish. That served as the main library for 41 years. In June of 2011, the main library was relocated to its current location at 1210 Madison Street.
The newly constructed 10K square foot Hawesville Library opened in May, 2012. There is a large meeting room/programming space, study room, family restrooms, children's area, teen space, modern space, staff office area and storage. Since the grand opening, the number of library cardholders has grown. The community enjoys tons of programs that are offered, and Hancock County citizens appreciate the free fiber internet that is available.
Many improvements were recently made at the Hawesville location, including re-upholstered furniture, a brand new circulation desk and freshly painted interior walls. Tina said they were 'super excited' about the modifications they were able to accomplish there.
Former and current HCPL Board members and building committee members celebrated the payoff of the Hawesville Branch Library construction loan with a note burning in January of this year. The total cost of construction was $2.3M, and the final bulk payment in the amount of $363,446.49 was made on December 28th, 2023.
In 2012, the first payment was made on the loan for the Hawesville Library construction project, and the last payment was actually not scheduled until 2051. However, they were able to make that final payment early, and all with only one tax increase on the taxpayers.
The Main Hancock County Public Library in Hawesville
Lewisport Library The newest addition to the HCPL system is the Lewisport Branch Library. The grand opening/ribbon cutting was held on June 26th, 2021. They have already begun making payments on the loan for the construction, but are not allowed to make a principal-only payment on it for 5 more years so they have opened a CD at Independence Bank for $125K, so it can start gaining some interest. They expect to pay off the loan early, just as the Hawesville Library loan was.
The City of Lewisport applied for a Community Development Block Grant through GRADD that helped with the building of the new library in Lewisport. Mayor Chad Gregory and Tina Snyder were instrumental in making the project happen for this second location.
The Lewisport Branch Library
HC Librarians The county's library system currently has 12 employees, and they all rotate throughout the system. This exceptional team of librarians help people find what they're looking for and go above and beyond to serve the community.
Shiloh Johnson, circulation clerk, and Kelley Richardson, branch manager, pose for a photo during 'Library week' Tuesday. The Lewisport branch of the Hancock County Public Library is a wonderful place to visit.
Bookmobile The HCPL Bookmobile makes both public and private stops, and has nearly a thousand books, DVDs, CDs and audiobooks available to check out. If you see it parked in any public place, it is open and ready for business. (*Wi Fi is available 24/7 at each of the library locations. The Bookmobile also serves as a Wi Fi hotspot when parked.)
If you would like the bookmobile to visit your location, or if you have questions or special requests, please call Susan Taylor at (270) 927-6760 or (270) 295-3765.
Book Club Two book clubs are offered at HCPL on the fourth Tuesday of each month. There is a 10 a.m. club at the Lewisport Library, and a 5:30 p.m. club at the Hawesville Library. If you'd like more information, please call Kelley Richardson at (270) 295-3765.
Locations & Numbers The Hawesville Branch Library is located at 1210 Madison Street, and the phone number is: (270) 927-6760. The Lewisport Branch Library is located at 400 2nd Street, and the phone number is: (270) 295-3765.
Hours of Operation Hawesville Library hours are: Mon.-Wed. – 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Thurs. – 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., Fri. – 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Sat. – 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and closed on Sundays.
Lewisport Library hours are: Mon. – 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Tue. – 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., Wed.-Fri. – 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Sat. – 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and closed on Sundays.
Website, Pages & Email The HCPL website is available 24/7. You can look to see when your items are due and also put items on hold that you'd like to check out. Please visit: www.hcplky.org, which also includes a full list of detailed services that the libraries offer. The Facebook and Instagram pages can be found by typing in: @hancocklibky. If you have any questions, you can call either branch of the library, or email the staff at: hcplky1@gmail.com.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Fiscal Court Reports On Several Issues
description: Director of the Hancock County Emergen
content:
Director of the Hancock County Emergency Management Agency Kyle Veach reported at the HC Fiscal Court Meeting on Monday that the Ohio River is expected to rise above flood levels. The flood gates were raised Monday morning in Hawesville with the expectation of excess rain over the next few days.
Veach said installation of the county's new sirens and digital radios is going well. 'Hopefully, the weather will stay good where they can keep installing. While the schools were on spring break, everything went good,' he said. 'They were actually able to move faster than they thought they would.
The new command post we started in the last couple of weeks is moving forward. They're starting on the building. The doors will be installed on the 22nd.'
Ohio River Flood Update
Ohio River Flood Update A Cannelton Locks and Dam Operator said the 3-day predicted forecast for the lower gate, (for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, April 12th), is 39.6 on Wednesday, 40.3 on Thursday, and at 38.8 on Friday.
'We're going to be dropping out,' he said. 'I don't know if we're going to see that 40.3 because we're dropping out just a little bit now (as of early Wednesday morning). All of the locks above us are already dropping down.
What we documented and observed here yesterday (Tuesday, April 9th) at 2 p.m., we made a 39.4 on our lower gates. That was the highest that we got on our lower gates. We've been dropping out since. I don't see any river bumps; I don't see us coming back up. We'll be dropping all the way down. It looks like we'll be dropping out to 33 feet by Sunday . That's what it's showing right now.
dropping out to 33 feet by Sunday. That's what it's showing right now. We usually go by what we see on the National Weather Service and what we get from the locks above us. It should show all of the locks on up the Ohio River (on the National Weather Service site – https://www.forecast.weather.gov/.)
Senior Services Report
Senior Services Report 'We are going today (Monday) to the botanical gardens for the eclipse party,' HC Senior Services Program Director Lona Morton said. 'I will be attending the Optimal Aging Conference at the end of the month, the 21st-23rd. We've been busy shuffling around supplies. We're thankful for the HC Road Dept. crew for helping us find a home for everything. We have an extra round table and chairs. I gave 2 to Emergency Management. They're staying in the county and being dispersed that way, since we have the new ones.'
Special Tour at Jeffreys Cliffs
Special Tour at Jeffreys Cliffs Wednesday, April 24th is a Special Tour Day at Jeffreys Cliffs, from 9 a.m.-3 p.m.. It will be open to everyone and volunteers will provide ATV vehicle transportation back the main trail for anyone to see the forest, cliffs and the large Morgans Cave rock shelter. Lona says the seniors who would like to go on that trip again, or those who missed the opportunity last time will be able to enjoy it that day.
Road Dept. Report
Road Dept. Report HC Road Dept. Supervisor Dave Tindle said the crew are all set with mowers for now. One of the new mowing tractors was delivered and they are going to make sure everything is working well with that. The second one should arrive in June or July.
Occupational Tax Report
Occupational Tax Report The occupational tax report was approved by the court. 'It looks like as of today, $3,628,999,' Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts reported. 'That's down from $4,581,221 this time last year. It's down about $950,000.'
Treasury Report
Treasury Report County Treasurer Melissa Johnson's report was approved by the court. 'As of this date, $9,455,518,' Roberts said. 'Last year this time it was $9,092,994.'
Economic Report
Economic Report HC Industrial Foundation Director of Economic Development Mike Baker reported, 'The activity at the Lewisport Industrial Park – we're seeing some renewed interest there, not only with folks that are there but we've had some interesting conversations with some potential people that are looking at that, so word is getting out; That part of the county is starting to grow.
Some of that inquiry is related to the distilling industry and the associated industries that go along with not just storing whiskey but barreling and distilling whiskey. We're continuing to be excited about the potential down there.'
Contour Fabrication & Mechanical, Inc. (CFM) are in the process of buying the additional land in Lewisport Industrial Park to start the next part of their business, Baker said. 'They're very busy and have a lot of lines in the water, if you will,' he said. 'There's a lot of excitement with what they're doing there. They just started doing some work over at the new Pratt Paper plant in Henderson.
Crescent Paper Tube made the decision to unionize with the United Steel Workers. We'll watch that and see how that develops. I think that's probably the smallest plant that we've seen become part of the Steel Workers.
Unemployment – January was 4.8. January last year was 4.6. Typically, what happens at the end of the year, the new year starts and more people that haven't been looking for work start filing their papers and looking, etc. Unemployment for February is 5.3. Daviess County is 5.2. Ohio County is 7.1. Breck County is 5.9, and Henderson is 4.9. Kentucky is 5.1 and the U.S.A. is 4.2.
A lot of times what we'll see is that if you get a big contractor project happening at one of our plants and that project gets completed, those construction workers might get laid off for a week and then they'll go file and that might bump our numbers a little bit, but there's nothing fundamentally happening that affects our employment; It's just a seasonal trend.
The big news, last week, was the Century green smelter that was announced. The Dept. of Energy granted Century a $500M grant to build a new, environmentally-friendly smelter. We don't know the exact cost of the new smelter. I've been told it could be as high as $4 Billion to $5 Billion dollars. There's a lot of discussion left to occur. It sounds like it may be a little premature. Obviously, the question is, would Hancock County have a shot at that? We're talking to the Century officials and doing everything we can to stay on their radar for that.
There's a lot of discussion happening at both Frankfort and Chicago, where Century is headquartered, and at Northeast Kentucky. There's some speculation that the old Brady site was going to be a new aluminum mill a few years ago that never materialized, that that could be what they're looking at. The timing on it – it would probably be 2030 before anything is seen. We'll have to watch and see how that develops.'
Roberts said, 'Century made it pretty clear to me that we're (Hancock County) not going to be considered on that. The Hawesville location is not being considered at all for that project. Western Kentucky isn't being considered for this facility. The Northeast site is what they're looking at.'
Baker added, 'People have asked if they can't just retro-fit this smelter. It's not going to happen. A green smelter is most likely going to be hydro-electric. Can you imagine the solar panels it would take to power a 400 megawatt smelter? They're looking elsewhere for this; You're right.
The other part of that, though, is Century has assured me that that smelter would not replace Hawesville or Sebree and that they still officially plan to re-open Century if the conditions are right. We don't know what those conditions would have to be. We haven't seen any movement on that yet but that's what their official position is so we'll take them at their word.
There's definitely a need for a new smelter. We're down 4 smelters that are open, and only 2 of those are operating at full strength. And, there's going to be a continued need for that aluminum. There's probably 25 smelters operating in the United States. There were 10 or so in the Northwest because that's where a lot of water – a lot of those smelters were powered there, but electrical rates still shut those down. That industry has just almost disappeared from this country.'
The Clarion Editor Donn Wimmer, Hancock County Airport Board Member for many years, added that the HC Airport is buying land from Century for a new 10-bay hangar. 'This will add three different buildings for planes,' Donn said. 'The first two, which hold 10 each (equaling 20 planes), are full. We have a long waiting list so we've decided to build another hangar that will hold 10 more airplanes. Some of the bays may be larger, for larger aircraft to park there.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Joey Taylor
description: Joseph Roberts 'Joey' Taylor Jr., (85) passed away on April 12, 2024 in Lewisport surrounded by family. He was born on Sept. 17, 1938 to Joe and Catherine Taylor in Lewisport. Joey was raised on a…
content:
Joseph Roberts 'Joey' Taylor Jr., (85) passed away on April 12, 2024 in Lewisport surrounded by family. He was born on Sept. 17, 1938 to Joe and Catherine Taylor in Lewisport. Joey was raised on a hard scrabble farm in the Muddy Gut bottoms of Hancock Co. where his parents bestowed on him and his four siblings the perfect mixture of good ol' country fun and a strong work ethic.
One of the things Joey was most proud of was enlisting in the United States Marine Corps after graduating from Lewisport High School. He served his country for three and a half years, aboard an aircraft carrier as support throughout the Mediterranean Sea and stationed in Okinawa, Japan.
While on leave, Joey met the love of his life, Clara Jeanette Newton. They married on Aug. 12th, 1960 and spent 60 blissful years together until Jeanette's passing on Oct. 4th, 2020.
Joey had a zest for life that was hard to equal. He never met a stranger and would talk to anyone about anything. He loved to quail hunt and continued that endeavor through the early 1990's. More than the hunting itself, Joey loved to train the bird dogs and had several top-quality English Setters during his hunting career. Joey also loved to fish. On any warm day he and Jeanette could be found on some of the local waters trying to catch their limit. They always caught enough to have several family fish fries every summer.
Joey and Jeanette raised three sons on the same plot of land that Joey grew up on and spent his life. They instilled the same mixture of fun and work on their sons.
Joey worked for several years at Olean Tile Co. in Lewisport before making a transition to Commonwealth Aluminum in Lewisport where he retired from. He made lifelong friends at both facilities. Besides his parents, Joey was preceded in death by his wife, Jeanette, his brothers Ledrew and Mike, and his daughter-in-law Becky Taylor.
He is survived by his sons Chris, Tim (Denna) and Pat (Tammy); grandchildren Amber Snyder (Ben), Jacob Taylor (Brianne), Cain Taylor, Jared Taylor (Lauren) and Paige Taylor. He also leaves behind 12 great-grandchildren to carry on his legacy.
Services will be held at 11 am on Monday, April 15, 2024 at Gibson & Son Funeral Home, Lewisport Chapel with burial following in Lewisport Cemetery with Military Honors. Joey's family will be greeting friends on Sunday from 2 pm until 6 pm and on Monday from 9 am until service time at the funeral home. Memorial contributions may be made to 4-H Shooting Sports. Share your memories and condolences with his family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Domtar Earth Choice Committee Upcoming Earth Day Events
description: There are some fun upcoming activities that Domtar is hosting in support of Earth Day this year that you won't want to miss! Their 2024 Earth Day theme is 'Planet vs. Plastic'. Domtar's Earth Choice…
content:
There are some fun upcoming activities that Domtar is hosting in support of Earth Day this year that you won't want to miss! Their 2024 Earth Day theme is 'Planet vs. Plastic'. Domtar's Earth Choice Committee organizes these activities with a focus on community engagement and they are centered around literacy, sustainability and wellness.
Domtar EHS & Engineering Administrative Assistant and Earth Choice Committee Member Kristin Rapp said, 'We try to tie that into the events that we do, such as the upcoming Jeffreys Cliffs hike, along with the new Poster Contest and the 5K for Autism Awareness.'
The Earth Choice Committee is made up and led by all Domtar employees who are able to participate actively in various earth-friendly events that they plan in the community each year. All of Domtar's mills have a committee that provides activities and events for their individual communities.
2nd Annual Big Foot Hunt & Hike at Jeffreys Cliffs On Saturday, April 20th, the Domtar Earth Choice Committee, in support of Earth Day, is having their 2nd Annual Big Foot Scavenger Hunt & Hike at Jeffreys Cliffs, from 9 a.m.-11 a.m. Everyone is encouraged to come out and attend this fun event and hike!
'We had a really good turn-out last year,' Kristin said. 'I'm hoping that the weather is going to be nice and that we can have a really good turn-out this year.'
Before last year's hike, committee members were brainstorming about fun ways to get the community to come and hike at the Cliffs, and that's when they came up with the fun idea for the 'Big Foot Hunt' theme.
They are hoping to have someone dressed up as Big Foot to greet hikers this year, and there will be a Nature Scavenger Hunt with small door prizes awarded. There will be a variety of small giveaways at the entrance of Jeffreys Cliffs, Kristin said.
'We plan on having a wheel that you spin,' she said. 'It's especially fun for the kids. They can spin it and maybe win something cool. Additionally, we'll have some giveaways like frisbees, seed packets, snacks, water, and Domtar Big Foot-themed stickers, etc., that people are free to take.'
Jeffreys Cliffs is located at KY 1406 in Hawesville. The event is open to all members of the community, and any donations will benefit Jeffreys Cliffs.
First Annual Domtar Planet vs. Plastic Earth Day Poster Contest Domtar provided Emilie Young's 4th & 5th Grade Art Class students at North Hancock Elementary with poster boards and markers. They've been working on their posters for a couple of weeks, and the theme is: 'Planet vs. Plastic', which is Domtar's 2024 theme. Bookmarks and seeds will be given to all student participants.
'We went with NHES because it would just provide a smaller number of entries this first year,' Kristin said. 'This is the first year we've done something like this in a really long time. Next time we do this, whether it be for Earth Day or another themed activity, we would probably try to go with South Hancock Elementary, or include both schools.
We're hoping to pick up the posters by Friday, April 19th, and go through them and choose the winners. We're awarding the top three, and we'd really like to display the posters at the Jeffreys Cliffs Big Foot Hike if we can make that happen.' (* The winning posters will be featured in an upcoming edition of The Clarion.)
Tiny Library Installed at Jeffreys Cliffs Did you know that Domtar's Earth Choice Committee purchased and installed a Tiny Library at Jeffreys Cliffs just a few weeks ago?! 'We've already been filling it up with family friendly books,' Kristin said. 'People have already been taking from it, which is what it's for. We plan to keep it as stocked as we can throughout the year.
We're really excited about it. We were excited that it is already being utilized. The goal for us, is we were trying to put a lot of family friendly, nature-themed books in there. If they're coming to hike, they probably like that kind of stuff.
I don't think there would be an issue with people who either want to return books that they've taken from it, or if they have gently-used, family friendly books that they wanted to put in there. If it could just be utilized, and if that includes other people coming and donating to it that would be perfectly fine. So far, all of the books have been purchased by Domtar. That is the plan, is for Domtar to keep it stocked.'
Domtar Book Drive Domtar has an Annual Book Drive from December-January and donates the books to a local library. 'We had already donated those books from this year before we had purchased the Tiny Library,' she said, 'but moving forward we may even use some of those donated from the mill to go in there and use it for that as well.
We do really well at our Book Drive for the mill. Those drives are Domtar employee led also. In 2023, we donated to the Hancock County Public Library and this year we donated to the Perry County Public Library. We put a lot of focus into Hancock County because that's where the mill is and where a lot of our employees are from, but even the surrounding areas, we try to do things where we can.'
Domtar Glasses Drive Domtar has partnered with the Lions Club and they are going to provide some collection boxes to be set-up around the Hawesville mill in various departments so that employees can bring in their old eyeglasses that they no longer use. Those will then be recycled through the Lions Club.
Earth Day at the Mill All employees at the Hawesville mill were given white oak tree saplings last week to take home and plant. 'A lot of people take them home and plant them on their property,' Kristin said. 'Sometimes they'll give them away to other people that might prefer to plant them. They really enjoy getting the trees.
Last year, we gave out small dogwood bushes. It went over well, but we were trying to mix it up and do something this year that will be a little bigger. A white oak will live a really long time. We also give out literature regarding Earth Day and recycling.'
River Sweep Employee volunteers go to the river bank on the Domtar property to clean up litter/waste once a year, and this year's River Sweep is scheduled for May. 'For the River Sweep,' she explained, 'it is for Domtar employees only because it is on Domtar property. It is totally volunteer. All supplies are furnished by Domtar and at the end of the work day we all just go out and pick up and clean up what we can until the next year.'
2024 Autism Awareness 5K Kristin said Domtar does plan to do the Autism Awareness 5K again this year. Last year's 5K Run & Walk was held in downtown Hawesville on October 21st. All of the proceeds were matched by Domtar and donated to Autism Advocates of Hancock County.
Biodegradable Products Domtar announced last year that they would be investing $51 million into upgrading equipment at the 50-year-old Hawesville mill. They are repurposing one of the 2 paper machines (pulpers) to produce fiber-based, biodegradable products such as earth-friendly 'plastic' bags. This project is still in the works but there are no updates available yet, Kristin said. The conversion is a long process and takes time.
Domtar Paper Company celebrated 175 years of business last year, with around 6,400 employees in over 50 countries. The Hawesville mill employs approximately 400 employees. They produce 600,000 tons of fine, specialty paper each year.
If you'd like to apply for a position at Domtar, go to Domtar.com, and complete the application process. There are computers available to use at the HC Career Center, the KY Career Center and the public libraries. Domtar is located at 58 Wescor Road in Hawesville.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Tim Cecil new county fair board president
description: We are non-profit and everything we make goes right back into the Hancock County Fair. The Board Members are all volunteers. We use any monies collected and put in the bank for the work needed on the…
content:
We are non-profit and everything we make goes right back into the Hancock County Fair. The Board Members are all volunteers. We use any monies collected and put in the bank for the work needed on the grounds, water bill, electric bill, insurance for the grounds, gas and any supplies needed for the buildings and for ribbons, trophies and things of that nature.
We apply for grants when we can to build new things, or maintenance for any existing buildings. If needed, we have to hire plumbers, contractors, etc., to fix what we can't. They usually give us a discount or offer free labor, but hardly ever is it totally free.
New Board Officers Voted-in at HC Fair Board April Meeting The Hancock County Fair Board Members would like to announce the change of officers, effective immediately. Tim Cecil was successfully voted in as HC Board President during April's meeting. Greg Wettstain, former President, will step down from the position, however, will remain an active member.
After accepting the resignation of Scott Basham, Kyle Hodskins was voted in as Vice-President. Both Cecil and Hodskins have been active members for many years. They have a great reputation for working well together, making this combination a successful one!
Paula Powers will remain as Treasurer of the Board, as well as Karen Colbert, Secretary. Debby Hurst will take on a new role as Co-Secretary, becoming the advocate for the public concerning fair issues.
The Officers and Board Members have a close bond and work well together as a team, making it a strong beginning for a great 2024 Fair Year! We look forward to serving the residents of Hancock County and call it an Honor to be a small part of this great community! -See ‘Ya at the Fair!
2024 HC Fair The 2024 Hancock County Fair, held at the HC Fairgrounds in Hawesville, will be Wednesday, July 31st-Saturday, August 3rd. More details will be provided about this year's events in The Clarion as the date gets closer
By Hancock County Fair Board Co-Secretary Debby Hurst

title: Lady Hornets blank Breck 10-0 at Vastwood Park
description: Four Lady Hornet softball players received honors after last week's All 'A' Classic 3rd region tourney. From left, Jordyn Waltrip, Layni Roberts and Lily Roberts were all named to the All-Tournament…
content:
Four Lady Hornet softball players received honors after last week's All 'A' Classic 3rd region tourney. From left, Jordyn Waltrip, Layni Roberts and Lily Roberts were all named to the All-Tournament Team, while Kylie Westerfield (injured) made the All- Academic Team.
Lily Roberts threw a 1-hitter and hit a home run and Audrey Carnes went 4 for 4 during a 10-0 win for the Lady Hornets over Breckinridge County on Tuesday at Vastwood.
The outcome was in doubt for a long while as both teams played solid defensively.
The Lady Tigers did not have a base runner until the third inning, but Hancock County was also scoreless through three.
Roberts was averaging two strike outs per inning and Carnes was smacking line drives. The freshman led off the fourth with a hit and Ella House followed with a liner, but the ball was caught and the next two Lady Hornet batters hit fly ball outs.
Ava Riggs and Jordyn Waltrip led off the fifth inning with line drive singles. Madyson Higdon was hit by a pitch and the bases were loaded. Baylee Estes was also hit by a wild pitch and the Lady Hornets were on the scoreboard, leading 1-0.
Carnes continued her hot streak and made the score 3-0 when she ripped a double to left field. House followed with a 2-run hit and Roberts took the first pitch and sent it over the fence in center field. The 2-run homer put Hancock County ahead 7-0. Waltrip came up again and doubled in a run to give the Lady Hornets eight runs in the frame.
Roberts struck out the side in the sixth before Ansley House hit a walk-off 2-run double to end the game via run rule.
Roberts allowed no runs on one hit, with 12 Ks and one walk in six innings on the mound. Ashlyn White took the loss for Breck.
Carnes was 4 for 4 with a double and two RBI, Waltrip was 2 for 3 with a double and one RBI, Roberts was 1 for 3 with the home run and two RBI, Ella House was 1 for 3 with a double and two RBI, Ansley House was 1 for 1 with a double and two RBI, Estes was 1 for 3 with one RBI and two runs scored, Riggs and Layni Roberts both went 1 for 3. Aubree Mosby scored a run. Riggs, Waltrip and Carolina Jones all stole a base.
By Steve Wimmer

title: HCHS track teams fifth at Apollo meet
description: Christian Yanez leaps for distance during the long jump competition at HCHS. The HCHS track teams competed in a 9-team meet at Apollo High School in Owensboro Tuesday. Both Hancock County girls and…
content:
Christian Yanez leaps for distance during the long jump competition at HCHS.
The HCHS track teams competed in a 9-team meet at Apollo High School in Owensboro Tuesday. Both Hancock County girls and boys teams placed fifth.
Ben Baker won the boys 200 meter dash with a time of 23.76. Christian Yanez was sixth in 24.15, Wyatt Emmick ninth in 24.36, Matthew Carroll 16th in 25.13, Mehkel London 17th in 25.24, Kaleb Helm 29th in 26.33, and Camden Toler 30th in 26.47.
Alex Basham won the shot put event with a throw of 46–06.5 feet. James Singleton was fifth at 39–03.5, Lawson Ward 10th at 34–10.5, Aiden Thrasher 13th at 33–02.5, Drake Haycraft 25th at 28–02.5, Jameson Boarman 27th at 27–08.5, and Jameson Domerese 29th at 27–01.
Basham was second in the discus with a throw of 122–03. Singleton sixth at 106–06, Ward 20th at 85–05, Haycraft 23rd at 80–03, Boarman 26th at 77–05, and Domerese 27th at 76–06. Kolyn Cruz of Daviess won at 130–08.
Olivia Coomes placed fourth in the 100 meter hurdles in 19.92. Owensboro Catholic's Mallary Bailey won in 17.43.
Eli Embry was third in the boys 110 hurdles in 22.1 seconds. Max DeJarnette was fifth in 23.04 and Ashton Vogt sixth in 23.12. Webster County's Malakai Orcutt won in 18.79.
Naholy Yanez was 15th in the girls 100 meter dash in 14.44. Addy Harrison was 23rd in 15.55 and Nevaylyn Merry 24th in 15.65. Analea Sanders of Apollo won in 12.63.
Baker ran fifth in the boys 100 meters in 11.6 seconds. Cooper Jones was 10th in 11.81, Emmick 18th in 12.06, Carroll 24th in 12.27. Conner White of Daviess won in 11.13.
Lyla DeJarnette was 12th in the 1600 meter run in 6:54, and Juliana Nevitt 17th in 7:14. Mallory Raines of Daviess County won in 5:45.
Noah Henson was 19th in the boys 1600 in 5:27, and Jacob Shultz was 28th in 5:40. Brice Nelson of Webster County won in 4:34. Izzy Ross was fifth in the girls 400 meter dash in 1:08. Jayda Meserve 15th in 1:13, Yanez 17th in 1:15, and Alivia Bernardi 25th in 1:21. Bentlei Stallings of Daviess won in 1:06.
Baker was fifth in the boys 400 in 55.01. Carroll ninth in 56.94, Emmick 13th in 59.18, Henry Proctor 25th in 1:03.1, Landon Hodges 27th in 1:03.9, and Emmitt Meserve 28th in 1:04. Lacon McKinney of Henderson won in 52.89.
Vogt was ninth in the 300 hurdles in 50.77. DeJarnette 10th in 51.65, and Embry 11th in 53.65. Tyreese McCombs of Henderson won in 44.56.
Nevitt was 17th in the girls 800 in 3:12. DeJarnette was 21st in 3:15, and Bernardi 24th in 3:21. Lucy Spaw of Daviess won in 2:24.
Jones was 10th in the boys 800 in 2:22, Hunter Stephens 15th in 2:24, and Hendrix Van Cappellen 23rd in 2:32. Preston Glassco of Webster won in 2:04.
Ross was 13th in the girls 200 dash in 30.16, Tessa Walls 15th in 30.29. Analea Sanders of Apollo won in 26.98.
Meserve was seventh in the girls long jump with a leap of 13–03. Yanez ninth at 12–07.5. Tyleah James of Daviess won at 14–02.75.
Jones was sixth in the boys long jump with a leap of 19–01, and Yanez was seventh at 19 feet. Connor White of Daviess won at 21–06.
Ross was fourth in the girls triple jump with a distance of 27–11. Emily Bertke of Apollo won at 31–05.25.
Addy Harrison was third in the girls high jump with a height of 4–06. Aubrey Ezell of Catholic won at 4–10.
Baker was sixth in the boys high jump at 5–02. Julius Girten was 14th at 4–10 and Vogt was 15th at the same height. Kamden Walters of McLean won at 5–08.
Apollo was the girls team winner with 124 points Hancock County was fifth with 21 points. Henderson was the boys team winner with 115 points. HCHS was fifth with 56 points.
By Steve Wimmer
