title: Tennis team comes from behind to beat Breck
description: Lukas Anderson lines up a background shot during a match with Breck County here Friday. The HCHS boys tennis teams came from behind to win 3-2 over Breckinridge County at Vastwood Park Friday. 'I'm…
content:
Lukas Anderson lines up a background shot during a match with Breck County here Friday.
The HCHS boys tennis teams came from behind to win 3-2 over Breckinridge County at Vastwood Park Friday.
'I'm not sure how we pulled this one out being down 0-2. Tyce (Boling) and our doubles came through,' HCHS coach Dan Hopkins said.
Lukas Anderson lost 5-8 to Roman St. Clair in #1 singles action, and Alex Madden fell 4-8 to Will Lewis.
Tyce Boling won 8-0 over Kaleb Dubree and Van Reska defeated Dubree in a junior varsity match. Kyle Anderson and Tre London tied the match with an 8-4 doubles win over Brayden Garrett and Aaron Drake. The Hornets secured the win when Preston Blanton and Caleb Ewing won 8-6 over Elliot Tapp and Landon Critchelow.
'Shout out to Preston who wasn't going to give up and Caleb who showed great courage. We're now 5-4 on the season,' Hopkins said.
Ella Chappell sprained her ankle during warm-ups and was forced to forfeit her match with Amelia Reed.
Chiara Landes battled tough but fell 8-9 to Cecelia Oquendo, and Ruchi Patel lost 1-9 to Abby Martin.
Audree Morris and Kylie Bowlds took the lone win for HCHS when they defeated Maylee Noor and Amber Rogers 8-6 in doubles action.
'Pray for Ella who badly hurt her ankle just before the match began. Our doubles team of Audree and Kylie are on a roll,' the coach said.
Edmonson County The Hornet boys team won 4-1 over Edmonson County Tuesday at Vastwood Park. The Wildcats only had two players, but their #1 Brayden Johnson is the best in the region, according to HCHS coach Dan Hopkins.
Johnson defeated Hancock's Lukas Anderson 6-1, 6-0.
Caleb Ewing won 8-2 over Adin Gates, while both doubles matches were won by forfeit. 'I thought Lukas played pretty well, but they don't have much else. Caleb won easily,' the coach said.
The Lady Hornets fell 0-5 to Edmonson.
Chiara Landes lost 4-8 to Addison Blaining, Kylie Bowlds lost 4-8 to Riley Monroe and Audree Morris lost 1-8 to Chaney Browning. Ruchi Patel fell 4-8 to Sydney Herron in a JV match.
The doubles matches were forfeited by Hancock.
'We had several close matches, but they were just a little better.'
By Steve Wimmer

title: Coach Jody Hamilton Celebrates 1,000 Wins
description: Legendary Kentucky Coach Jody Hamilton, of Hawesville, is in his 39th year of coaching and has just hit 1,000 career wins as a...
content:
Seen here in the front row are Coach Jody Hamilton's 5 grandchildren (l to r): Josey, Wiley, Kennedy, Ruth & Rowdy, celebrating his 1,000 wins as a high school baseball coach at the OCHS Aces game on Saturday. In the back row (l to r) are: Wade & Neena Gaynor, Jody & Denise Hamilton, and Casey & Alix Hamilton.
Legendary Kentucky Coach Jody Hamilton, of Hawesville, is in his 39th year of coaching and has just hit 1,000 career wins as a high school baseball coach.
Jody went out of retirement in 2018 to coach at Owensboro Catholic High School, and on Saturday, April 20th, the OCHS Aces beat the Union County Eagles 12 to 2 during their home game, tipping his total wins to a thousand.
'We played well,' he said. 'It was fulfilling that we did finally top that thousand. My wife, Denise, has been here all this time with me. It is an honor and it's been a great privilege coaching the players that I've had. I've had some great parents and great administrators. It's just been a lot of fun.'
Jody & Denise, moved to Hawesville from Owensboro in 2020, along with their daughter and her husband, Neena & Wade Gaynor. They purchased land together and built their houses near each other.
Jody started coaching in 1983, right out of college, at Raceland-Worthington Independent Schools in Northeastern Kentucky. 'I was there until 1986,' he said. 'It is a small school, a lot like Owensboro Catholic. We had about 250 kids, Grades 9-12.
Then I went to Boyd County High School in 1987, and I was there until 2002. I guess that's where we really got started as far as having success in building (athletic) programs. We won the State Title in 2001.'
In addition to his many years of baseball coaching, he coached football for 6 years, basketball for 7 years and golf for 4. He was also Athletic Director at West Jessamine County High School, near Lexington.
He played baseball while attending high school in Ashland, KY, mostly outfield and some pitching. 'I went from there and played at Morehead (MSU),' he said. 'And, from there I played in the Yankee Organization, for a real short time. Then I got into coaching.'
Jody's wife, Denise, is a retired English teacher. They are blessed with 2 grown children, Casey and Neena, and 5 grandchildren. Casey Hamilton and his wife, Alix, have 3 children: Kennedy, Ruth & Rowdy (twins). Neena & Wade Gaynor have two children, Josey & Wiley.
Casey is Jody's Assistant Baseball Coach at Owensboro Catholic High School. Jody said it's been a great opportunity to be able to spend more time together and work together at what they both love.
'Casey was in college baseball, coaching for nearly 15 years,' Jody said. 'He moved to Owensboro and was coaching at Kentucky Wesleyan College, and that's where he met Alix. Now he's coaching with me.
The connection with Wade (a Hancock County native) came through Casey. Casey and Neena were roommates in college and Casey played baseball at Western Kentucky University with Wade.'
Casey coached at Western after graduating, and Neena moved to Lexington for her nursing career. She visited often and that's when she and Wade starting dating and then later married. Wade is the Market President for Hancock County at Independence Bank and Neena is a published author.
Jody & Denise are very happy with their move to Hawesville and love being close to their children and grandchildren. 'We enjoy just being this close to Josey and Wiley, and now that Casey is back, we have all the grandkids within 25 minutes of each other,' he said, 'it's a real pleasure. They're a lot of fun.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Oden granted Probation
description: Connie Jean Oden, of Hawesville, was indicted on December 22nd, 2022 on the charge of second-degree manslaughter, and was also charged with tampering with physical evidence. She plead no
content:
Connie Jean Oden, of Hawesville, was indicted on December 22nd, 2022 on the charge of second-degree manslaughter, and was also charged with tampering with physical evidence. She plead not guilty during her arraignment on January 24th, 2022. The Court found Oden to be eligible for supervised probation for a period of 5 years on April 26th, 2024.
Connie Oden was arrested on January 4th, 2022, following an investigation by Hancock County Sheriff's Deputy B.J. Burton, and was alleged to have assisted in administering methamphetamine by intravenous injection into the body of Wayne 'Scotty' James, sometime on or between September 23rd-24th. James was 56-years-old and originally from Tell City.
Oden has remained jailed since her arrest, on a $50,000 cash bond at Breckinridge County Detention Center. She has been sentenced to 5 years in the custody of the State Department of Corrections on the charge of Tampering with Physical Evidence, effective April 26th.
It was further ordered and adjudged that Oden's bond monies will be released in accordance with General Order 2023-4, that she will execute a Waiver of Search and Seizure, forfeit all seized personal property and, unless indigent, is liable for and will reimburse Hancock County for her costs of incarceration, which includes all medical costs expended on her behalf by the County.
Oden's 5-year supervised probation with an alternative sentence is granted pursuant to the terms and conditions of the probation order filed, and on the condition that she will not commit another offense during the period for which the sentence remains subject to revocation.
Additional conditions ordered by the Court are that Oden will be subject to graduated sanctions imposed by Probation and Parole in accordance with 501 KAR 6:250, avoid injurious or vicious habits, avoid persons or places of disreputable or harmful character, work faithfully at suitable employment as far as possible, support dependents and meet other family responsibilities, pay the costs as set by the Court, report to the probation officer, permit the probation officer to visit at home or elsewhere, answer all reasonable inquiries by the probation officer, promptly notify the probation officer of any change in address or employment, and obey all rules and regulations imposed by Probation and Parole.
The Court has ordered Oden to serve the following alternative sentences: home incarceration with or without work release for no more than 12 months, and home incarceration for a period of 6 months with ankle monitoring.

title: Michael Bickett Sentenced and Denied Probation
description: It was ordered by Judge Timothy R. Coleman of the Hancock County Circuit Court on Thursday, May 2nd, that Michael Bickettx
content:
It was ordered by Judge Timothy R. Coleman of the Hancock County Circuit Court on Thursday, May 2nd, that Michael Bickett's probation is denied, and that imprisonment is necessary for the protection of the public because it would unduly depreciate the seriousness of his crime.
Bickett (28), of Hawesville, was indicted on the charge of Wanton Endangerment, First Degree, which led to the death of Jacoby Gray (22), of Hancock County, in late December 2022.
The Grand Jury charges were, Count One: That on or about December 23, 2022 in Hancock County, Bickett committed the offense of Wanton Endangerment in the First Degree when he wantonly engaged in conduct which created a substantial danger of death or serious physical injury to Jacoby Gray; and Count Two: That on the same date, Bickett committed the offense of Operating a Motor Vehicle Under the Influence of a controlled substance (agg. circum.), Second Offense, when he was operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol/and or controlled substance.
Bickett is a convicted felon and had been released from prison in early 2022. This was an ongoing investigation, as the wreck and Jacoby's death both occurred in Indiana.
Sentence On May 2nd, Bickett was sentenced to one year in the custody of the State Department of Corrections on the charge of Wanton Endangerment, 1st Degree; thirty days in the custody of the Breckinridge County Jail on the charge of Operating a Motor Vehicle Under the Influence of Alcohol/Substance, 2nd Offense; and shall pay a fine of $200, court costs of $175, service fee of $425, and substance abuse treatment program provider fees.
These will run concurrently for a total sentence of one year in the custody of the State Dept. of Corrections. It is further ordered and adjudged that Bickett's license is revoked for 60 days, that he forfeit all seized personal property, will reimburse Hancock County for his costs of incarceration which includes all medical costs expended on his behalf by the County, his bond monies will be released in accordance with General Order 2023-4, and his probation is denied.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hawesville council hears complaints from Windward Heights group
description: Several residents of Windward Heights Subdivision attended the Hawesville City Council Meeting Tuesday evening, May 14th to voice their disagreement with the new water and sewer rates, saying that the…
content:
Several residents of Windward Heights Subdivision attended the Hawesville City Council Meeting Tuesday evening, May 14th to voice their disagreement with the new water and sewer rates, saying that the fee that has been levied on subdivision residents is too expensive. They said they don't think they are paying a fair rate compared to residents that live in the City of Hawesville.
Hawesville Mayor Robbie McCormick opened the floor for comments at the meeting and provided the group of subdivision residents with ample time to communicate their grievances.
For context, at the April meeting, McCormick announced that Ordinance 1-24 would go into effect soon with an average increase on the sewer rate between $8 and possibly $12 monthly (for customers inside city limits), and set up on a 20-year note, as reported in The Clarion. He explained that there were rate increases put into ordinances every year that weren't enforced during the previous administration, and that now it's necessary to enforce the raised rates.
He also stated that it's not what they want to do, but have to in order to meet their debt payment of $15K per month, otherwise they will be out of compliance and will not be able to stay liquid as a city. The raised fees will also help with the payment of the sewer plant and cost to treat the water, he said. The ordinance covers everything that it costs for residents, small businesses, commercial and industrial, and further that it is not a surcharge line; it is an actual bill/fee.
One of the Windward Heights residents, Dewayne Robbins, voiced on behalf of the group of residents attending that the fee is 'unfair' and that the letter they received stated that in the 2nd ordinance reading (in April), Windward Heights was excluded but the reason stated was ‘unknown'.
McCormick answered, 'I went back to 1972 in the ordinance book, in the minutes, and found no reason to why you would have been exempt from that.'
Mr. Robbins angrily said, 'I have a reason why we would be exempt, right now I'm already paying a $31 fee for the right to have Hawesville City Water and services which you render, which is only water & sewer. No one else in Hawesville or outside city limits pays that amount.
We have no representation on the council. We can't vote for you. We can't vote for the mayor. So we don't have an advocate. That's a problem we need to look at. If we're going to be taxed, we need a representative on the council. And, if we're going to be fair, we're going to pay a fee for infrastructure that ought to be a fairly shared burden.
So I'm asking you to re-address this ordinance. If we can make it a more fair and equitable fee, I have no problem helping the city pay for sewage and a new sewer plant that we spend $3M for. That's not the issue. The issue is – it's not fair the way that it's laid out for us right now.'
After some discussion McCormick said, 'We cannot spot annex. There's no law that allows us to annex Windward Heights. You have to be connected to the city limits. I can appreciate your stance. I look at this a little differently, Sir.
In 2016, there was an ordinance passed that included any and all residents living outside the city limits that had water and sewer, would be responsible for their tax assessed value divided by twelve, paid per month. When this ordinance went to a 2nd reading, Windward Heights was excluded. There is no reason being that we found that you were excluded.
There are 7 people living outside this city limit that are on sewer and water and they've been paying this rate for 8 years. So that's where I fall into the inequality at, Sir. So, we go back 8 years – If we'd been collecting this from you the whole 8 years, this city wouldn't be in the shape it's in. But it is because it was unlawful to write this ordinance without including any and every body.'
McCormick said the KRS was available to read for further understanding of his answers to their questions, and City Attorney Jamie Stephens read that aloud explaining the law saying, 'There's a few legality issues with it. First, you're correct on the fact that it's not a tax. It's a fee that's levied on utility services, that under KRS 96.170, the legislative body of the city has the right and the responsibility to provide utility services and establish the rates that we are to use in calculating all of that.
When that was done, we're also required in any exemption or any kind of fee that's levied has to have a public purpose. There was no purpose that was ever laid out in any of the minutes or ordinances that gave any reasoning for why they were exempting Windward Heights. That is illegal under the Kentucky Constitution for us to exclude a group for absolutely no reason and make other individuals pay that same fee.
When that was brought to our attention, I discussed that with the mayor and explained that I felt it was unlawful to do it the way that it was done, and that's how we tried to rectify the situation.'
McCormick continued, 'So you brought up snow removal and things like this. The City of Hawesville has had no snow removal in 2 or 3 years. We just bought a used salt spreader, so now there's snow removal in Hawesville. You brought up the other services, as far as not having some of the other services – street lights. I drove around 4 of these addresses. They have no street lights. You say that everybody has these services – I've got 24 people that live in the city limits of Hawesville that have no sewer, but they pay their taxable rate every year.
You're not being picked on and excluded from any services. We've got people spread out all across the board that aren't receiving services that the city offers, and you all are. The people that aren't receiving the services are still paying their full rate. That is an invalid argument, in my opinion.'
Mr. Robbins responded, 'I disagree entirely with that. You say that there's no reason why we should be exempt. I gave you the reason. The reason is that we already pay $31 that nobody else is paying – $21 plus two $5 fees.'
'Yes,' McCormick said, 'You do have the $5 fees. Everybody else is paying those fees too, Sir, except for the $21.'
Mr. Robbins then demanded, 'Either exempt the $21 or exempt the $48. You're obviously not going to do the $48.'
McCormick stated, 'I'm not going to exempt either one. You all are required to pay the $21 on the Windward Heights line rehab that happened about 4 years ago. You're paying that $21. Okay? You've got 8 more years to pay that. But, if you want to know the truth about it, there was never a loan set up to cover it to pay that back because the city was out of compliance so far, we couldn't get a loan to do that. So what we're paying every month for your rehab is interest. The only way we can pay this off is in total because there's not a loan, because our past administration was unable to get a loan.
We are doing you a favor on this. It was going to be a 20-year, $21 charge. Now, it's going to be a 15 or 16-year charge and as soon as we pay it off I'll do just like I did the rural water customers, I'll take the $21 off there. The $48 fee will be on there from now on.'
Mr. Robbins doubled down at that point, saying that Windward Heights residents are paying for services they're not receiving, and McCormick responded, 'And, Sir, you will continue to pay for sewer because that's all this states in this ordinance, is sewer. It doesn't cover any other services. It plainly states right here. This is not a city tax.'
City Attorney Jamie Stephens added, 'That's how it's calculated. It's a basis for calculation. It's not a taxation. You're paying for a service and that is what they determined that the service was going to cost in 2016. They took out loans on that. That is the basis. We're required to continue charging that or else default on the loans.'
McCormick said to Mr. Robbins, 'I'll tell you what I can do. I'll be glad to call the state in and let them set your rates. So when I do that, you say, ‘You know, you're right.' Because I can tell you, you're going to be paying an $89 flat water bill, because Breck County is paying that. And, you're going to pay several other add-ons, because the state has already dictated – this is what you're going to do (in that hypothetical situation).
We are responsible to do the fiduciary thing for the City of Hawesville. You all should have never been excluded from this ordinance. I didn't write the ordinance. I can't change it, by law. This ordinance cannot be repealed unless we go into default.'
Councilman Junie Morris added, 'Do you want the state to come in, and it be like the subdivision out on 54? Their sewer bill is $110 a month, for 19 years, plus their other bills. That's not counting the water.'
McCormick concluded, 'This was a 2-month process I went through because I was informed that we were not in compliance. So I searched and tried to figure out pushing numbers. This ordinance came to light. This is the ordinance that we are able to go back to. You all did take the major hit. Our citizens took an increase also. Everybody got an increase. We had to, to get to the number we had to reach.
With that $3M, we're making a $90,000 bi-annual payment – that's $15,000 a month. You were seeing these accounts grow that we had, to where we could start doing some things – our needs for the city. And then all of the sudden, in December the bottom falls out of it. When I asked, ‘Why is this happening?' This is the way we were told to pool and do this.
My goal had to be to satisfy the state, that we would put together a plan to gain $15K a month to pay this debt. That debt is included in this. The citizens received an increase on this, and they received an increase on water. Where I'm at, the equality falls back on – we've had these 7 folks paying it for 8 years. Is it fair that they're paying it and another group is not? No. I don't think any of you would argue that. We have done what we said we would do as a council. I've done what I said I would do as a mayor, in a fiduciary manner.'
After the required readings that were achieved in April, Ordinance 1-24 was passed by the council at this meeting and will stand, raising sewer rates for residents, small businesses, commercial and industrial. McCormick will 'revisit' this at the July meeting.
*Continued coverage of this council meeting will be in next week's edition of The Clarion.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Antique Tractor Show & Tractor Pull at Lewisport Heritage Fest
description: The Antique Tractor Show & Drive at the Lewisport Heritage Festival is a popular event happening on Saturday, June 1st, as well as the Antique Tractor Pull. The Show & Drive/Parade Organizer Brent…
content:
The Antique Tractor Show & Drive at the Lewisport Heritage Festival is a popular event happening on Saturday, June 1st, as well as the Antique Tractor Pull.
The Show & Drive/Parade Organizer Brent Wigginton, former Lewisport City Administrator, said, 'We've been having the Antique Tractor Show for a good ten years. We've had the Antique Tractor Pull for over 20 years. There will be a lot of really nice antique tractors there.
We had around 32 tractors for the show last year. Our goal is to try to double that if we can. We're shooting for double, but my guess is that we'll be up in the 40-50 range. I hope everybody comes out and shows their support for it.
We've reached out to some other antique tractor clubs in the area. We've talked to one of the clubs out of Daviess County, as well as Breckinridge County and Irvington. The clubs we've talked to, we've gotten favorable responses from them. We think just by doing that, we'll probably get more tractors this year.
We tried to advertise more than we have before. We get on chat groups for tractor clubs on Facebook, and I've also put the word out on several of them. There are people on these chat groups from all over the country. If we have good weather, we'll probably have a good turnout this year.
It's growing every year, and I see it continuing to grow. We're going to get a lot of pictures so we can really hit social media with it next year on all of the antique tractor social groups. That is how you grow it.'
Prizes 'We have $400 in sponsorship money,' Brent said, 'so we have $100 per category prize money for the Antique Tractor Show. We also have plaques for each category.'
T-Shirts 'We have shirts made for the Antique Tractor Show and the Antique Tractor Pull,' he said. 'Anyone who enters tractors into the pulls or show, they get a complimentary festival tractor show & pull shirt as well.'
Antique Tractor Show & Drive The Antique Tractor Show & Drive is at 11:00 a.m. on Saturday, and is held at the Lewisport Community Center. Judging and awards will be at 3:00 p.m., and the Antique Tractor Parade is at 4:00 p.m. People can bring their tractors in starting on Thursday, May 30th, Brent said. The Parade will go on a route around downtown Lewisport.
Antique Tractor Pull The Tractor Pull begins at 10:00 a.m. at the Lewisport Community Center on Saturday as well. There wasn't supposed to be another tractor pull in the area on the same date as the tractor pull at the Heritage Festival this year. However, one local pull has recently been rescheduled for Saturday so there will be a little competition for entries.
'We're fairly confident that if we have good weather that we'll have a good turnout at the Antique Tractor Pull too,' Brent said. 'We have a different company coming in with the sled this year so we think that will help. We found out that there may be a couple coming in from as far as Kansas this year.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Carolina Jones wins 300 hurdles at regional meet
description: Carolina Jones shows off the three medals she won at the Region 2 meet. The sophomore won the 300 hurdles. The HCHS track teams competed in the Region 2 meet at Green County Saturday. The Hancock…
content:
Carolina Jones shows off the three medals she won at the Region 2 meet. The sophomore won the 300 hurdles.
The HCHS track teams competed in the Region 2 meet at Green County Saturday.
The Hancock County boys team placed fourth. The girls were seventh.
'We did better in some events than we expected and worse in others. That's the way it goes in the post-season,' HCHS coach Wes Meserve said.
Carolina Jones was the lone individual winner from Hancock County as she won the girls 300 meter hurdles in a time of 49.35 seconds.
'She ran a great race and won by a full second. She was also our fastest leg on the 4×400 relays and earned a medal in the 100 hurdles, as well,' the coach said.
Wyatt Emmick placed second in the boys 300 hurdles in 42.57. The winner was Lucas Christian of Glasgow in 41.13.
Alex Basham placed second in the shot put with a throw of 49, feet 11 inches. James Singleton was ninth at 38–01. Kasey Webb of Edmonson County won at 51–09.5.
The HCHS boys 4×800 relay team was third in 9:15. Runners were Noah Henson, Max DeJarnette, Hunter Stephens and Emmitt Meserve.
The boys 4×400 relay team was third in 3:46. Runners were Emmick, Matthew Carroll, Mehkel London and Ben Baker.
Izzy Ross was third in the girls triple jump with a total distance of 31–03. Cynthia Austin of Glasgow won at 31–09.5.
'Izzy did well. She was our second qualifier for the girl's team. She probably would have ran a little better in her other events, but she landed awkwardly on her last jump and jammed her knee,' the coach said.
Wyatt Emmick ran fourth in the 110 meter hurdles after hitting a hurdle. His time was 16.72. Jake Bishop of Green County won in 15.97.
'Wyatt was in first until he clipped the second to last hurdle and almost fell,' the coach said. 'His time was still fast enough to qualify him for state, but it was really disappointing for him. He's worked so hard and beat all the top guys from our region in head-to-head competition.'
Basham was fourth in the discus with a throw of 128–10, and Singleton ninth at 111–06. Kelson McKinney of Green County won at 163–10.
Emmitt Meserve was fourth in the boys 3200 meter run in 11:20. Isaac Riggs won in 10:14. The HCHS boys 4×200 meter relay team was fourth in 1:33. Runners were Emmick, Carroll, Cooper Jones and Baker.
'They qualified for state and broke their own school record again. The boys 4×4 and 4×8 relays also qualified with at-large bids,' Meserve said.
Christian Yanez was fifth in the boys 100 meter dash in 11.76 seconds, and Ben Baker was 11th in 11.95. Kirkland-Lundy of Metcalfe County won in 11.38.
Cooper Jones was fifth in the boys 400 meter dash in 53.92 seconds, and Julius Winters was 11th in 57.57. Gage Bale of Green County won in 50.86.
Yanez was fifth in the boys long jump with a leap of 18–11.5 feet. Isaiah Ballard of Bethlehem won at 20–8.
Noah Henson was sixth in the boys 800 meter run in 2:13, and Henry Proctor was ninth in 2:18. Riggs of Bethlehem won in two minutes flat.
The HCHS girls 4×800 relay team was sixth in a time of 12:02. Runners were Izzy Ross, Jayda Meserve, Alivia Bernardi and Lyla DeJarnette.
Baker was sixth in the boys 200 meter dash in 24.23. Bale won in 22.93. Carolina Jones was sixth in the girls 100 meter hurdles in 18.9 seconds. The winner was Mallary Bailey of Owensboro Catholic in 16.78.
Lyla DeJarnette was sixth in the girls 3200 meters in 15:43, and Juliana Nevitt ninth in 17:46.
Ross was seventh in the girls 400 meter dash in 1:08. Cate Coppola of Green County won in 1:01.
Nahomy Yanez was seventh in the girls long jump with a leap of 12–09.5. Jillian Hammes of Washington County won at 14–10.5.
The HCHS boys 4×100 meter relay team was eighth in 46.51. Runners were Carroll, Camden Toler, London and Yanez.
Emmitt Meserve placed ninth in the boys 1600 meter run in 5:23. Riggs won in 4:34.
Eli Embry was 12th in the boys triple jump with a leap of 30–10. Christian of Glasgow won at 42–07.25.
Bernardi was 12th in the girls 800 meters in 3:02. Scarl Isenbarger of Catholic won in 2:33. Nevitt was 13th in the girls 1600 meter run in a time of seven minutes. DeJarnette was 14th in 7:15. Andley Bloyd of Green County won in 5:34.
The girls 4×400 relay team was fifth in 4:42. Runners were Jones, Meserve, Yanez and Ross. Glasgow won the girls team title with 183 points. Hancock County was seventh with 21 points as 15 teams competed.
Green County won the boys team title with 145 points. Hancock County was fourth with 52 points.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Logan Boling Completes Flight Training, will train pilots
description: Boling Chapel native, Logan Boling, has completed flight training school and will be instructing flight lessons soon. He said the
content:
Boling Chapel native, Logan Boling, has completed flight training school and will be instructing flight lessons soon. He said the current pilot shortage is what has nudged him in this change in career, along with his love of flying. His goal is to be a commercial airline pilot.
'I've always had an interest in flying,' Logan said, 'I just always enjoyed the airport process and flying in the big jets. I have a few friends from the area who got into flight training, and I decided I wanted to give it a shot.
I had been thinking about it for awhile and researching, and decided it was time. The first flight I ever took, outside of flying on a commercial airline, was an introductory flight with my flight school. I enjoyed that and decided to pursue it.'
He began his training in April of last year at ATP Flight School – Airline & Commercial Pilot Training Programs, in Indiana. He completed 250 hours of flight training, along with extensive classwork and studying at home, on May 29th, 2024. The school is located near Louisville, and he lived there for about 7 months for the training and rented a house with his younger brother, Jordan, who graduated from U of L and is currently working in that area.
Logan completed 6 Training Programs at ATP: Private Pilot License Instrument Rating, Commercial Single Engine, Commercial Multi-Engine, Certified Flight Instructor, Multi-Engine Instructor, and Certified Flight Instructor Instrument Rating.
He is a 2014 Hancock County High School Graduate, and played baseball from Little League through attending HCHS. He graduated from Western Kentucky University with his Bachelor's in Business Administration in 2019, and went on to earn a Master's in Business Administration at WKU as well. He then worked as Loan Review Specialist at Independence Bank in Owensboro.
'I'm planning on starting at Madisonville Community College as a flight instructor,' Logan said. 'I will build hours until I can meet my 1,500-hour requirement to fly for the airlines.'
He and his fiancé, Whitney, were engaged in March of this year. They met via a mutual friend in 2020. She is from Owensboro, and is a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Nurse at Owensboro Regional Health Hospital. They have planned their wedding for April 26th, 2025.
He said Whitney is excited about going flying with him. 'We haven't been up together yet,' he said, 'but she looks forward to it. We definitely want to travel, but we have nothing specific in mind yet.'
He and Whitney live in Owensboro. They love spending time with their 2 dogs, a golden retriever named Scout and a golden doodle named Rosie. He said he is hoping to be flying commercial in as soon as a year and a half, and that at some point he'd like to purchase his own small plane but not anytime soon.
Logan is the son of Hancock County Circuit Court Clerk Michael T. Boling and Vickie Boling. Vickie works at MPD, Inc. in Owensboro. His older brother, Daniel Boling, is District Judge in Hancock County.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Acerola
description: You may already know that acerola cherries are one of the best sources of vitamin C, but did you know that they also serve as a natural antihistamine that helps relieve seasonal allergy symptoms?!…
content:
You may already know that acerola cherries are one of the best sources of vitamin C, but did you know that they also serve as a natural antihistamine that helps relieve seasonal allergy symptoms?!
Acerola cherries are high in quercetin, a potent flavonoid with antihistamine, ant-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Including them in your diet can help reduce histamine release, and boost immune system resilience to pollen, mold and pollutants.
Here are some of this 'super' fruit's other reported health benefits: improves digestion, balances your body's pH (acid/alkaline balance), effectively relieves heartburn, anti-septic, balances blood fat levels, supports heart health & lowers risk of heart disease, regulates blood sugar, combats oxidative stress, lowers blood pressure, relieves cold symptoms, improves circulation, improves metabolism, anti-aging/boosts collagen production, skin astringent (topical use), antifungal, antidepressant, improves athletic endurance, can assist in healing the liver, and protects against cancer.
Studies have shown that acerola cherry extract can inhibit the growth of abnormal cells associated with lung cancer. Dehydrated, organic acerola cherry powder can be taken in capsule form, or added to smoothies, slushies, juice or just filtered water. It has been proven to help stop the spread and growth of lung cancer, and can also be taken in an extract or chewable form.
Acerola cherries are referred to as West Indies cherries, and accordingly grow on a shrub-like plant that is native to tropical regions of the Western Hemisphere. They are shown to have more vitamin C, a powerful antioxidant, than every other fruit, apart from rosehips. One hundred grams of raw acerola cherries provides 1,680mg of vitamin C!
They also provide vitamins A, B-1, B-2 & B-3, phosphorus, iron, calcium, potassium, magnesium, copper, protein and fiber. Please always do your research and/or check with your doc before adding acerola into your diet.
For those of you who have children, or if you're just young at heart, try adding a teaspoon of organic blue spirulina powder to your smoothies or slushies, along with a teaspoon of organic acerola cherry powder for a pop of color! Blue spirulina powder is a great natural food coloring and also adds a ton of nutrition. (*See my column in the 10-13-2020 edition of The Clarion on Spirulina. Blue spirulina has almost the exact nutrition profile as the green spirulina powder.)
Slushy Recipe
Place several ice cubes into your blender, add a handful each of frozen organic strawberries and frozen organic blueberries, a tablespoon or more of organic lemon juice, a cup or more of organic 100 percent pineapple juice, a teaspoon of organic acerola cherry powder, a teaspoon of organic blue spirulina powder, and a tablespoon or less of pure organic maple syrup. Blend and enjoy! (*Other frozen berries can be substituted or added, as well as other fresh squeezed juices. If the slushy is too thick, just thin it out a little with a bit more juice or filtered water and blend again.)
~Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: A Tribute to my Friend Donn Wimmer
description: I only knew Donn because of Nancy's Notes. Each week, I would take my 'notes' to his office. Usually, we would talk for a little while, then he'd say, 'I've got to quit talking. I have a newspaper to…
content:
I only knew Donn because of Nancy's Notes. Each week, I would take my 'notes' to his office. Usually, we would talk for a little while, then he'd say, 'I've got to quit talking. I have a newspaper to get out.'
We discussed my Nancy's Notes and his Stories from the Past. One day, he said, 'You made me cry.' I had written about my mother's struggles with arthritis and how she never gave up. 'What a sweet person he is,' I thought. I loved the stories about his childhood, and the pictures of him and his mother were priceless.
On my 80th birthday, I wrote about growing old. I wrote: 'If I live to be 100, I'm going to go bungee jumping or sky diving.'. . .'Oh, you can go sky diving now,' he said. 'I'll fly the plane, you jump, and I'll take your picture.' What a fun person, I thought.
He was a thoughtful person. When I wrote about the 3 little boys who wouldn't have a Christmas because their mom had lost her job, he reached into his pocket and handed me some money. 'Buy these kids some gifts,' he said. I did just that and their mom said they had the best Christmas ever.
We were both in our eighties. We reminisced about our childhoods and talked about the perils of getting old. We compared our lives of yesterdays and talked about how blessed we had been through the years. We voiced our concerns about how things are going in the world today and our fears for future generations.
I found I was talking to a very brilliant man. He had a lot of dreams through the years and he made them come true. He had amazing family that helped him achieve those things he wanted to accomplish.
Donn was devoted to The Clarion, and to the people of Hancock County. He said, 'The people of Hancock County need to know what's going on in their county.' He was so devoted that he never retired. When most people retire at 62 or 65, he stayed with it until the end. When a lot of newspapers were dying, he and his family made The Clarion thrive.
I'm going to miss you, Donn, and all your stories. You had so many adventures. This Final one was the biggest. I am sure they were all cheering up there when you crossed the finish line.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Lions Club Celebrates 65 Years at Annual Scholarship Dinner
description: Lewisport Lions Club President Dakota Basham
content:
Lewisport Lions Club President Dakota Basham accepts a 65 year patch from Lions Club Region Chair Bill Brown during the club's Scholarship Dinner Saturday.
The Lewisport Lions Club held their Annual Scholarship Dinner on Saturday, July 13th. They celebrated 65 years of service at the Lewisport Community Center and displayed place mats with the menu agenda from their Charter Night in 1959, listing the original members, some of which are still active today.
Lions Club Regional Chair Bill Brown presented members with a 65-year patch that will be added to their banner. Mr. Brown and his wife, Edwina, both taught in the Hancock County School System in the 1960s-1980s, and traveled to attend the dinner from their home in Sacramento.
Scholarships
Two recent Hancock County High School graduates received scholarships. They are: Jordan Payne and Sophia Reed. Jordan is the grandson of long time member Pat Payne, and great-grandson of long time member, the late Edgar Payne. Sophia is the granddaughter of the late Bobby Fallin, who was a member for over 50 years. Her scholarship was accepted by her grandmother, Alice Faye Fallin.
Jordan Payne accepts a scholarship award from Lewisport Lion's Club president Dakota Basham during the club's annual Scholarship Dinner Saturday.
Service Awards
For 30 years of service, awards went to the late Gary Marsch and to Keith Westerfield. Shelby Basham and Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory both received an award for 15 years of service. And, awarded for 10 years of service were Michael Roberts and Mary Margaret Hawkins.
Another special award went to Larry Hedden. He received the Finis E. Davis Fellowship Award for dedicated humanitarian services to the Kentucky Lions Eye Foundation.
Past & Present
The Club's longest living member is Layman 'Sonny' Hawkins, Jr., who was Club President in 1968 and 1969. 'During that time,' he said, 'we used to have horse shows and we held them behind the Community Center, where the Tractor Pulls happen now. We didn't have any lights back then, hardly. During my presidency, I got Kenergy to come in and put the lights up for us around the horse arena.
We had a Western show on Friday nights and an English show on Saturday nights. We enjoyed the horse shows and we had them every year. We had food booths and things like that. Jerry Ayers and I ran the novelty shop that was in the Community Center and sold little trinkets.
The Lions Club did not build the Community Center. Lewisport Industrial Community Improvement Corporation built it originally but couldn't maintain it so the Lions Club took it over a few years later. The late Charles Hagan and I did a lot of work there. I put all of the ceiling tile in the bathrooms back then. We helped put the names on the front of the building. The Hawesville Lions Club had sponsored Lewisport to become a Lions Club.'
The current Lewisport Lions Club President, Dakota Basham, is serving his second year as president. Julie Newton is Vice President, and Tom Evans serves as Secretary/Treasurer.
Basham explained what the Lions Club does internationally and locally saying, 'Our focus is on helping with blind people and helping with eyesight; We help get glasses out and help give eye exams. Locally, what we really try to focus on is just getting things back to the community.
Through the years, we've done dinners and chicken cooks. We're always at the HC Fair and HC Heritage Festival, and those are to raise money. We try to find ways to give those funds directly back to families in need, locally, whether it's families with children that are battling illnesses or a family that has run into hard times. If we know about those, we do what we can to help pay a bill or help them get groceries, etc.
We'll have boxes around town where people can donate their old glasses. We take those and give them to the international clubs and they recycle old glasses to give to people who need them. We've also helped with eye exams. There have been times when the schools contacted us and said there was a child that needs help with a pair of glasses and we've done that.'
The Lions Club owned the Lewisport Community Center building for many years. Around 15 years ago, the City of Lewisport took over ownership but the Lions Club helps manage the building, and continues to have their dinners and monthly meetings there. They meet on the second Thursday of every month at 5:30 p.m., and have almost 60 members.
Basham said that membership has stayed pretty consistent. 'There have been times when there are up years and down years,' he said. 'The last few years we've been really lucky having a lot of new people getting involved. We find ways to try new things that members suggest; New members bring new talents and we try to put those into action to help the community.'
The Lewisport Lions Club, in past years, had a membership of all men for a long time. Women started getting more active about 10 years ago, Basham said. 'They're all welcome,' he said. 'We need all the help we can get.'
This Scholarship Dinner was one of two main dinners that the Club has every year. The next annual dinner will be their Christmas Dinner to thank members for all of their hard work during the year.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Thyroid Health
description: The thyroid gland is located at the base of the neck and covering the windpipe (trachea) on 3 sides. Although small, it is one of the largest endocrine glands and produces hormones which help us to…
content:
The thyroid gland is located at the base of the neck and covering the windpipe (trachea) on 3 sides. Although small, it is one of the largest endocrine glands and produces hormones which help us to break down proteins, and regulate body temperature, heart rate and metabolism.
Because it has a right and left lobe, the thyroid is sometimes described as butterfly or bow tie shaped. It produces 2 hormones, and one is called T3, or triiodothyronine, which is the more active one. The second is thyroxine, or T4, which is more abundant. Both are secreted into the bloodstream.
To get an idea about the workings of this gland, here is a brief rundown. The hypothalamus directs the pituitary, which directs the gland, along with the adrenal cortex and the gonads. The hypothalamus secretes TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone), which goes to the anterior pituitary. Then, the pituitary makes TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone), which communicates with the thyroid gland. The thyroid responds by producing T3 and T4.
Because T4 is more abundant, it is known as the thyroid hormone. If there is an overproduction of T4, it can inhibit the TRH and TSH – that is referred to as hyperthyroidism. If there is underproduction, it is referred to as hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism could be caused by a problem in the thyroid gland itself, or in the anterior pituitary, or hypothalamus. If the root of the problem is in the thyroid, it is referred to as simply 'hypothyroidism'. If the problem is in the pituitary however, it is referred to as 'secondary hypothyroidism', and if in the hypothalamus, it is referred to as 'tertiary hypothyroidism'.
Low levels of thyroid hormone can cause: an enlarged thyroid,
cool extremities/low body temp.,
infertility,
swelling of the limbs,
carpal tunnel syndrome,
slow heartbeat/pulse,
dry and coarse skin,
thinning hair and hair loss,
low energy levels,
depression,
weight gain,
poor cognitive function/memory loss,
obesity,
constipation,
vertigo,
menstrual irregularities,
and in some cases, an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's Thyroiditis.
Thyroid disorders are, reportedly, more common in women. Hashimoto's usually occurs after childbirth and in the postpartum stage, with estrogen being a trigger, according to studies.
Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism, alternatively, is caused by an excessive production of thyroid hormones, and can cause: hand tremors, sudden weight loss, irritability, hyperactivity, intolerance to heat, high blood sugar, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, abnormal heart rhythms, increased appetite, enlarged liver, enlarged thyroid, bulging eyes, fine brittle hair and hair loss, increased perspiration, and in some cases a condition called Graves' disease that also occurs more in women, specifically between the ages of 40 and 60. Graves', unlike Hashimoto's, is reported to usually occur a whole year after childbirth and also involves estrogen.
Nutrition
Some foods to AVOID to keep your gland functioning properly are: bacon, corn, peaches, kale, wheat, unfermented soy, peanuts, sodas, and garbanzo beans (chickpeas).
Some foods that can nourish the thyroid are: bone broth, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, plantains, asparagus, fermented foods like kefir and kimchee that promote gut health, and seaweed (high in iodine, which most people are low in). In addition, studies show that staying well hydrated is also key in maintaining a healthy thyroid.
Herbs
Some traditional medicinal herbs for maintaining optimal thyroid health are: ashwagandha, lemon balm, ginger, sage, chamomile, echinacea, and turmeric. *Always do your research and/or check with your doc before supplementing with herbal remedies, especially if you are taking pharmaceutical meds.
~Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: RVBH Back to School Bash – FREE Event on August 2nd
description: River Valley Behavioral Health in Lewisport is having their Back to School Bash on Friday, August 2nd, and you won't want to miss it! The event is from 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. at 1210 4th St., and…
content:
River Valley Behavioral Health in Lewisport is having their Back to School Bash on Friday, August 2nd, and you won't want to miss it!
The event is from 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. at 1210 4th St., and there will be FREE BBQ, Kona Shaved Ice, inflatables, a Petting Zoo, haircuts for students, backpacks with school supplies for the first 200 students, door prizes for the first 25 teachers who attend, and raffles for a laptop, iPad and more!
President & CEO of RVBH in Lewisport, Dr. Wanda Figueroa-Peralta, said, 'River Valley serves 7 counties, including Hancock County. We're looking at expanding access to mental health services, and are interested in starting as early as possible. We're focusing on expanding services among children.
There is no health without mental health. It is important to support our children at an early age. Fifty percent of all mental health conditions start by age 14. Therefore, we should not be waiting until they're adults to make services available to them, or to inform the community about the actions and how to deal with emotional crisis. We believe that education and prevention are very important, and we see schools as our partners and we want to support the efforts of educators, parents, and community leaders in supporting our children and youth.'
Wanda said that with the Back to School Bash, they focus on supporting the community in several areas, one of which is children's mental health and well being. 'One in 6 children, ages 6-17, experience a mental health disorder,' she said. 'Sometimes unless they cause trouble with their behaviors it can be easily overlooked so we want to make sure that we support teachers, schools, parents, and also provide information to kids about how to deal with stressors and anxiety.'
Through this event, one of the ways they are able to support wellness is by providing materials with inspirational messages that are encouraging. The goal is to equip children with healthy ways of relieving stress and anxiety. She said that is because anxiety is the number one symptom of compromised mental health.
'The second thing is to provide access to educational resources,' she said. 'We know that some families have some financial stressors and that can hinder the children's academic success because they don't have all of the school supplies, and that becomes another stressor in the family. This fair ensures that all children, regardless of their background, have access to essential school supplies and educational materials. We want to level the playing field by ensuring that children have the opportunity to be ready from the perspective of having the school supplies that they need.'
She said it is a guarantee that they will have 200 backpacks with school supplies for children to receive at this event. 'Those are nice backpacks. We have anti-stressors that look like games included, but it's a way of how to use that to manage your stress. We have pencils that have inspirational quotes with our name and number, in case they need them.
Parents are provided with resources as well, about some of the services we provide. Last year, we had the opportunity to invite another community provider that provides a health screening for new moms. We have a new moms program. Even though we're focusing on school age children we know they might have younger siblings, and getting them information about some of the resources that we have available I think is important.'
Wanda said it is also very important to them at RVBH to recognize and support educators. 'That's why we have for the 25 teachers to obtain a care package,' she said. 'We wanted to give something to the teachers to say, 'We value you. We are in this together. We support your efforts. We respect your work.' And, get them some materials they could use like pencils, pens, stickers, notepads, etc. It's our way of saying thank you and recognizing their hard work, and our way also of networking with them so we can address any student needs.
Ultimately, we want to support the Hancock community. River Valley is responsible for mental health services and providing a safety net, a harbor, for the community. We love doing that. We make sure our board of directors has representation from every county. I love working with board members that know well their community.
Michael Boling (HC Circuit Court Clerk) is one of the board members and so is Teresa Roberts (Lewisport Volunteer Fire Dept. Chaplain). Both of them are fantastic; They bring an expertise and a desire to make sure Hancock County gets resources and thrives as a community.
We are invested in supporting the Hancock community. We have the participation of our elected officials. Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts, every year he stops by and he's been a great supporter of joint efforts, and so have many other community leaders in Hancock County.'
She added that RVBH is embedded in the community, and that they want to be part of the solutions, and also to celebrate the community. 'Hancock is a great community. I love the spirit and dedication of the leaders,' she said. 'We have expanded the clinic and we look forward to expanding services, especially with schools and serving more children and youth.
Suicide is the second leading cause of death in youth ages 10-24. It's important that we work together with parents, community leaders and schools on how we can start addressing mental health and wellness at an early age, and we can develop protective factors for them. That's something that we're very concerned about.'
More than 30 percent of youth have anxiety disorders, Wanda said. 'That's why we call it a 'Bash' because it's like a celebration and a way of helping kids get on a positive note. For some of them who are starting school, it causes nervousness. Also, we talk about the importance of de-stressing and finding ways to de-stress,' she said.
'We always give stickers and art materials that are colorful so they can create art or do things that kind of ease their mind when they are stressed,' she added. 'We want to be a resource to the community. We want to work with parents and educators in embracing kids and helping them thrive and do well in school. I believe that children's mental health and education are not a luxury, they are a necessity. We improve their future by supporting them now, and by making sure they have the resources they need to succeed.'
The River Valley Behavioral Health website is rvbh.com. If you are in crisis and it is a non-medical emergency, please call the National Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at: 988, or the RVBH direct crisis line at: 1-800-433-7291 (1-800-769-4920 for TDD/Hearing Impaired). The Crisis Line program is a 24/7 crisis intervention, information, and referral telephonic service provided free to individuals needing help. Also offered is other support for individuals in crisis, including a Crisis Stabilization Unit and a Mobile Crisis Team.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Two Arrested in Reynolds Station; man fled on foot
description: On Friday morning, July 13th, the Hancock County Sheriff Office was contacted by the U.S. Marshal Service asking for a deputy to...
content:
On Friday morning, July 12th, the Hancock County Sheriff Office was contacted by the U.S. Marshal Service asking for a deputy to accompany them to 2195 Yeakel Road in Reynolds Station, in reference to George Whisehart, who had multiple felony warrants out of the state of Illinois.
Deputy Aaron Emmick and U.S. Marshals went to the campground where Whisehart was staying in the Reynolds Station area.
Emmick explained, 'He had a popup camper and a vehicle that they were occupying, that was identified as being at that location. As we secured the camper, a female that was residing in the camper, Brenda Persico (of Illinois), exited the camper and we made contact with her. She was subsequently arrested on other charges.
He (Whisehart) was not in the camper at the time. While on the grounds and properties, as the Marshals approached a restroom facility, he exited and fled on foot. We began searching for him, and that meant that we searched buildings, outbuildings, surrounding properties, and houses, and made contact with land owners that we could make contact with.
We eventually were able to apprehend him on Concord Church Road. I arrested him on his Illinois warrants and he should have been signing a waiver of extradition to go back to Illinois today (Tuesday, July 16) in court. She (Persico) actually had local charges so she was arrested here.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Craniosacral Therapy
description: One of many modal
content:
One of many modalities in massage therapy is craniosacral, which works with the rhythms of the various body systems to find where the roots of stressors are, with an aim at restoring balance to the flow of cranial sacral fluid. It is a light-touch technique focused mainly on the head, spinal column and sacrum, and developed by John E. Upledger in the 1970s.
There are many health benefits that craniosacral therapy can offer to infants, children, adults and the elderly. It is gentle enough for all ages to benefit from, and can restore the natural position of the bones. It can also calm the nervous system, decrease pain & tension, improve the natural rhythm of the central nervous system, and promote the body's natural capacity for self-repair.
This therapy has been reported to greatly help with the challenges of autism in adults and children, for example. Studies reveal that it can also help with learning disabilities such as dyslexia.
In addition, it is reported to be helpful with treating: attention deficit disorder (ADD), hyperactivity disorder (HD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), chronic fatigue, motor-coordination impairments, brain & spinal cord injuries, TMJ syndrome, orthopedic challenges, fibromyalgia, chronic head, neck & back pain, migraines, headaches, scoliosis, nervous system disorders, tinnitus, birth trauma, digestive disorders, colic, insomnia, sports related injuries, loss of taste and/or smell, stress, depression and anxiety.
One study I found showed that 72 percent of patients with fibromyalgia who received craniosacral therapy saw improvements in their pain symptoms. Another with 300 participants on the autism spectrum who received this therapy showed that over 250 had positive changes in their general behavior, over 150 saw positive biological changes, 250 had positive sensory reaction changes, and over 200 had positive changes in social skills, communication and cognitive function, with almost 200 seeing positive changes in emotional stability as well.
The cranial plates can be released as a result of receiving this therapy, which takes pressure off of the brain, nerves and other structures. It also relaxes connective tissue (facia) throughout the body, which promotes focus, calm, deep relaxation and overall wellness.
If you have recently sustained a head or spine injury, for example, your doc might recommend a waiting period before you try this therapy. Always do your research before trying something new to make sure it is what's best for you!
~Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: New Hospitality, Travel and Tourism Career Pathway at HCHS
description: HCHS Teacher Kelly White with her family (l to r): Kendall, Kelly, Cameron and Kevin White. Hancock County High Sch
content:
HCHS Teacher Kelly White with her family (l to r): Kendall, Kelly, Cameron and Kevin White.
Hancock County High School Accounting & Finance Teacher Kelly White said she is very excited about the new Hospitality, Travel and Tourism Career Pathway she's developing, which will be offered this school year at HCHS.
Kelly attended the 2024 Annual Career and Technical Education (CTE) Conference in Louisville this summer and learned more about this new career pathway that students will have the opportunity to pursue.
The Principles of Hospitality class, and the Travel and Tourism Marketing class she'll be teaching this new school year are offered to freshmen and sophomores, and will provide those students an opportunity to complete this new pathway that is increasingly becoming more popular. She will also be teaching 4 classes of digital literacy this year: Computer Application, Microsoft Office Suite, and Word and Excel.
Hospitality, Travel and Tourism is a 'hybrid pathway' that involves taking Business and Family Consumer Science program courses. The Advanced Foods and Nutrition class taught by Heather DeJarnette, along with Lori Roberts' Principles of Entrepreneurship class, will provide students with a solid background, Kelly said, in which to continue on with establishing internships, employment, or degrees in the hospitality, travel and tourism sectors.
She has been working on selecting the curricula and standards for the 2 new courses she'll be teaching this year toward this exciting new career pathway. The CTE Conference she attended is designed to help teachers meet the 24 hours of professional development required annually, and she said it was instrumental in assisting her with planning and preparing.
'As a teacher planning to teach Principles of Hospitality and Travel and Tourism courses for the first time,' she said, 'these classes are essential. Hospitality, travel, and tourism industries are thriving sectors, offering a wide range of career opportunities for students. By teaching these classes, I aim to equip students with the necessary skills and knowledge to succeed in this industry, such as communication, customer service, teamwork, and problem-solving.'
She added that the classes she's teaching this year will provide students with a unique opportunity to gain experience about unfamiliar cultures, customs, and traditions, promoting cross-cultural understanding and empathy, and that she hopes to raise awareness about the impact of tourism on the environment and local communities, encouraging responsible travel practices among students.
'I believe that travel and tourism can be a transformative experience,' she said, 'leading to personal growth and self-discovery. I aim to inspire students to explore the world and discover new perspectives.'
Kelly went on to say that her background in teaching accounting and finance classes, as well as her past restaurant management experience will benefit her in teaching classes for this pathway and her students. She also served as a Future Business Leaders of America Advisor at HCHS for 10 years.
'I have 10 years of past management experience in the full-service restaurant industry,' she said. 'I am confident that my ability will help both myself and my students as we embark on this new pathway. My understanding of financial concepts and business management will provide a solid foundation for students to understand the economic and financial aspects of the hospitality, travel, and tourism industry. My experience in restaurant management will enable me to share real-world examples and practical insights with my students, making the learning experience more engaging and relevant. I am excited to use my background and experience to guide students through this new pathway, equipping them with the skills and knowledge necessary to succeed in this dynamic industry.'
When a student gets 4 classes successfully completed in one specific career pathway at HCHS, that makes them a 'Completer', which is truly significant in preparing them for a career in that field. If a student decides to take 2 classes toward one specific career pathway, that's referred to as 'Career Exploring', which is also valuable in helping them decide if they want to continue on that pathway or pursue another. This gives them a chance to explore if they're not yet sure, and find what they really want to do. They can take a couple of classes to test out the waters in their freshman and sophomore years and decide to complete that pathway or choose a different one.
'If they take my 2 classes, and take Advanced Food and Nutrition with Mrs. DeJarnette, and Principles of Entrepreneurship from Mrs. Roberts, for example, that is 4 classes on that pathway, that makes them a Completer,' Kelly explained. 'That lays the groundwork. If they are a Completer then there is a higher likelihood they will do very well.'
Kelly said there will be abundant opportunities for students to build fulfilling careers in the hospitality, travel and tourism field according to the data. For example, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has projected that employment in the leisure and hospitality industry, which includes the hospitality, travel, and tourism sectors, will grow at an annual rate of 5.8 percent between 2022 and 2032.
'The industry's projected growth rate is higher than the average for all occupations,' she said, 'indicating strong demand for skilled workers. By offering this pathway, schools can help prepare students for careers in a growing and dynamic industry, providing them with valuable skills and knowledge that will be in demand by employers.'
In addition, she said this industry offers a wide range of career opportunities, from entry-level positions to management and executive roles, and that by exposing students to this industry at the high school level, schools can help broaden their students' career horizons and encourage them to explore a variety of career paths. And, that these industries are important contributors to the global economy, supporting millions of jobs and generating billions of dollars in revenue each year.
By offering this pathway, she believes strongly that schools can help support the industry's continued growth and development, while also providing their students with valuable skills and knowledge that will be in demand in the years to come, as well as bringing those skills into their hometowns and contributing to the growth and thriving of Hancock County.
Kelly said she and HCHS Principal Ginger Estes began talks last year about changing the Accounting pathway into this one.
'I've taught Computer Applications every year but 2,' she said. 'I interviewed the 3 classes that we thought would have the most interest in that pathway as an assignment to my students. Principals of Hospitality was one, another was Travel & Tourism, and a third was Sports & Event Planning. I've taught Sports & Entertainment Marketing a number of times in my career but this is a little different because it's 'sports & event', and you can bring in wedding planning and any kind of event you're planning for.'
She asked her freshmen students last year to do a presentation and choose one of those, and then try to 'pitch it' to other students, so that she could gage student interest. She discovered that interest was very high, and some of those students have already signed up for her classes before the end of last school year when they did their scheduling.
At the CTE Conference Kelly met some fantastic people, she said, advisors and consultants who will be helping her develop the standards and curriculums for this new pathway at HCHS.
'The right people were in my groups and I was able to approach people who had good information,' she said. 'I ran into a lady who is doing the most awesome tour – Louisville Food Tours. She was doing walking food tours through some of the most beautiful neighborhoods of Louisville. Then, you go into different restaurants and sample. There is even a historical tour.'
A youth tour is offered, and she said she's planning on taking her students. She is also planning valuable hands-on learning experiences locally and maybe even in other states, she said.
'There are so many opportunities,' Kelly said. 'The Executive Director of the HC Chamber of Commerce, Tina Snyder, and I met and talked about how we can align students with the Chamber of Commerce locally over their high school career to get them more involved, and to shadow and see what community involvement and entrepreneurship looks like.'
HCHS is ranked in the top 25 of 165 districts in Kentucky. It is amazing teachers like Kelly that help foster that success, and great leadership that provides the resources for these stellar teachers at HCHS to be able to offer the very best to students, as well as wonderful parents, caregivers and other family members who encourage students to work hard and dream big, and a very supportive community.
Kelly and her husband, Kevin, live in Lewisport. They are both HCHS graduates, and are high school sweethearts. Kevin is a U.S. Air Force Veteran and has worked at Domtar for 26 years. Their 2 children, Cameron and Kendall, are both HCHS graduates as well. Cameron earned his Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from University of Louisville. Kendall is double majoring in Integrative Communications and Marketing at University of Kentucky.
By Jennifer Wimmer
