title: High-Speed Pursuit Ends in Downtown Hawesville
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Carl Newhard, 60, was driving in Lewisport on Tuesday afternoon, January 14th, in an old, red Chevy pickup truck with a camper on it, and Kentucky license plate. A Lewisport Police…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer Carl Newhard, 60, was driving in Lewisport on Tuesday afternoon, January 14th, in an old, red Chevy pickup truck with a camper on it, and Kentucky license plate. A Lewisport Police Officer was in pursuit of him, and Newhard speeded out of Lewisport toward Hawesville. Hancock County Sheriff's Deputy Jeff Hendrick observed the truck passing him at the intersection of Big River Road and River Road, and initiated his emergency equipment in an attempt to stop him.
Newhard continued speeding eastbound on River Road, making no attempt to stop. Deputy Aaron Emmick setup at the intersection of Main Street and Adams Street with spike strips. Those were successful in rendering 3 of Newhard's tires flat. Nonetheless, Newhard continued through the City of Hawesville on Main Street at 70 MPH, and ran through the stop sign at the intersection of Harrison Street and Main Street, as well as the traffic light at the intersection of Madison Street and Main Street. Deputy Hendrick advised that the truck made an attempt to cross the bridge into Indiana, before coming off the roadway and returning to the roadway on Bridge Street. Once on Bridge Street, the truck came off the roadway again, nearly striking the bridge pillar. After passing the pillar, Newhard crashed into the red caboose attached to the Hancock County Museum. Deputy Hendrick utilized the front of his vehicle to pin Newhard's driver door shut, to prevent further fleeing action. Newhard brandished what appeared to be a firearm out of the driver's side window, and pointed it at Deputy Hendrick, who then retreated to the rear of his vehicle before opening fire on the truck and striking Newhard with two rounds. Newhard dropped the weapon and placed his hands out of the window. Deputy Emmick arrived on scene and helped remove Newhard from the truck. After removing the man, the deputies found another firearm in the floorboard between his feet. The deputies provided medical treatment to Newhard before EMS arrival. He was then taken in an ambulance to Owensboro Health Regional Hospital. It is not clear at this time how severe his injuries are. Both deputies, thankfully, were unharmed. When the incident happened, a Hancock County School bus was in the vicinity. Bus Driver Mary Lou Brake, Bus Monitor Katie Hanks, and 13 students from various grades were onboard. A witness living close by told Channel 14 News that she was outside and saw the entire incident. She also said that her daughter had just been dropped off from the school bus while she witnessed the police chase. Hancock County Schools Superintendent Robbie Asberry said, 'Thank God that the students and staff were safe. No one was injured. The bus monitor and the bus driver did an awesome job. You never know how someone will react in the moment, but they did what their training tells them to do. Their first thought was to protect the kids and flee the area.' Mary Lou and Katie removed themselves and the students from the area, and they deserve the ultimate praise for their actions. The children also deserve praise for being very compliant, and following the instructions of their bus driver and bus monitor. Hancock County Schools Assistant Superintendent Nick Boling said Mr. Asberry contacted every parent of the students on the bus, and made home visits to the ones that were not contactable by phone. Early Wednesday morning, Mr. Boling and Mr. Asberry traveled to every one of the Hancock County schools to talk to the guidance counselors, and ensured that they have the mental health resources available for the students.
Kentucky State Police were called to investigate. Deputies canvassed the area in an attempt to locate security camera footage. Possession of footage was captured from 105 River Street. Deputy Emmick was assigned to the case for further investigation. The Post-Arrest Complaints for Newhard are as follows, Charge 1: Fleeing or Evading Police, 1st Degree; Charge 2: Disregarding Stop Sign; Charge 3: Wanton Endangerment – 1st Degree; Charge 5: Attempted Murder of First Responder (Peace Officer); and Charge 6: Operating a Motor Vehicle Under the Influence of Substance (189A.010(1C) – 1st (AGG CIR).

title: Hancock County Native Rebecca Stoen Named OMFA Education Director
description: Rebecca Stoen, Hancock County native, began in her new position as the Director of Education at the Owensboro Museum of Fine Art (OMFA) on January 13th, 2025. 'I'm really excited about this…
content: Rebecca Stoen, Hancock County native, began in her new position as the Director of Education at the Owensboro Museum of Fine Art (OMFA) on January 13th, 2025. 'I'm really excited about this opportunity,' Rebecca said. 'I think there is outreach that needs to be done within our community, and surrounding communities. That's something that Jason Hayden, the Executive Director at OMFA, and I have talked about quite frequently. Our intent is to work with elementary schools to welcome students to the museum, and let them know that they've got a place to visit, and that they belong in the museum and, hopefully, open up some doors for some future artists and art lovers…We're looking at doing some type of adult education as well.' Since 2014, Rebecca has worked part-time for OMFA. She started out with volunteering for the OMFA Summer Art Camps, in June and July, and later served as a gallery guard as well. 'I'm very thankful that the executive director and the museum board did welcome me into this position, and provided me with this opportunity,' she said. At a very young age, Rebecca made her very first visits to the art museum with her mom. She is an art lover, and an artist herself. When she has the time, she enjoys painting, drawing, photography, and collage work. 'When I was in college I had to take studio classes, but mostly art history classes. If I could have lived in the studio,' she said, 'I would have. I wish that there were more opportunities for students of any age to have a workshop like that. That's kind of what we're looking to do at OMFA, to branch out.' Rebecca graduated from Hancock County High School in 2009. While attending HCHS, she was on the Hornet Cross Country and Track & Field Team all four years. After graduation, she went on to earn her Bachelor's in Art History in 2013, at University of Kentucky. She moved back home, and began working full-time at HCHS for the next 8 years. She started at HCHS as a Reading Specialist Assistant and Media Center Specialist Assistant. She then moved to the positions of IT Instructor and Graphic Design Instructor, as well as being the Year Book Advisor. She also coached the HCHS Cross Country and Track Teams. Her next position was at Owensboro Community Technical College as an Academic Advisor for one and a half years, until she moved into her current position as the new Education Director at OMFA. 'Peggy Lynn was one of my very first art instructors at Hancock County Middle School,' Rebecca said. 'She wasn't scared of anything, and I think she really opened my eyes to working with ceramics. Students at that age don't always get to do that. I always enjoyed her class. She was very encouraging, and I think, sometimes, that's what it takes for kids to grow as artists, or art-loving people; They need to be encouraged. Sarah Sparks was my art teacher at HCHS. I was one of her students and later became one of her co-workers. She developed a wonderful rapport with her students, and she allowed them to know that art is for everyone. Sometimes students get into art classes and they don't feel like they're the most artistic student, but then at the end of the year or the semester they find that they actually are. Sarah really fostered that within her students, and within me. When I got to work with her, I got to see it from a different perspective. I saw all of the effort that she put into making sure that students learned about different mediums and techniques. Greg Tate, the current HCHS Art Teacher, I can say the same for him. He's a very talented individual as well. He really makes sure that the students' work is exhibited, and not just tucked away in the art room.' She added, 'In my opinion, people don't always value art the way that they should. When I sometimes tell someone that I have an art history degree, they laugh. I always explain to them that it's not a degree that you see every day, however it has served me well in the positions that I've been in. I've been able to relate to people because I have that art background. I've been able to relate to the kids who don't always feel like they fit in anywhere. With STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Mathematics), I think there are so many techniques and skills that artists or art lovers develop, or can develop, that are very useful within that area. I see everything as a work of art – from what a computer mother board looks like to how the highway systems are developed. It's design, and it's everywhere. That's why I think art has a place in STEM, because it is, literally, everywhere…People don't always see the connection between life and art. I think it's a crucial piece to being human – to growing up and seeing that everything is connected, and that everything has a meaning. Unfortunately, I don't think people take a lot of time to do that anymore. I think when you understand the history behind a piece, whether that be a painting, photograph, etc., it becomes something a little different than just a piece of artwork.' Rebecca is the daughter of Tina & Nathan Powers, who were awarded in '23 as Hancock County Historical Society Historians of the Year, and are very involved in keeping the Hancock County Museum thriving. Rebecca's grandparents are the late Franklin Meserve and Elizabeth Meserve, and the late Nellie Gray Powers and William Powers. Mr. & Mrs. Meserve worked for many years to help keep the Hancock County Museum thriving as well. 'Franklin built steamboat pieces that are currently in the Hancock County Museum,' Rebecca said. 'He was a wonderful man.' She said both of her parents showed unwavering support for her love of the arts. 'They encouraged me to take art classes when I was young,' she said, 'and made sure visual art classes and concert band would be on my class schedule. Where many parents would have told their children that an art degree was a waste of time, mine told me to do what I love to do. They understood the impact that art had on my life, and trusted that I would use it no matter where I landed.' Rebecca and her husband, Dennis, currently live in Owensboro. Dennis is a Network Engineer at PC Quest in Evansville. They married in October of 2020. Owensboro Museum of Fine Art is located at 901 Frederica Street, in Owensboro. The phone number is (270) 685-3181. To learn more about the art museum, please visit the website at: https://omfa.us/. Like and follow the OMFA Facebook, Instagram and X pages to stay updated.

title: Robert J. Douglas, Sr
description: Robert J. Douglas, Sr., 72, of Hawesville, passed away on February 15, 2025 at his home under the care of Hospice of Western Kentucky. He was born on March 23, 1952 in Tell City, IN to the late Lorrie…
content:
Robert J. Douglas, Sr., 72, of Hawesville, passed away on February 15, 2025 at his home under the care of Hospice of Western Kentucky. He was born on March 23, 1952 in Tell City, IN to the late Lorrie and Geneva Honeycutt Douglas. Robert was retired from Century Aluminum. He a great storyteller, loved telling jokes and enjoyed his homemade wine. Robert was preceded in death by his wife, Georgia Bourdage; son, Robert Douglas, Jr and a sister, Angela Bartley. Robert is survived by his siblings, Sue Clark, Rebecca Greulich, Lucinda Douglas, Philip Douglas, Jerome Douglas and Stephen Douglas; several grandchildren and many nieces, nephews and cousins.
No services will be held at this time. Gibson & Son Funeral Home has been entrusted with care. Share your memories and condolences with his family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Myrtle Virginia Brandle
description: Myrtle Virginia Brandle,95, of Hawesville, KY passed on to her Heavenly Home on February 17, 2025 at The Heartford House with a daughter Lottie Kennedy and a grandson Ricky by her side. Virginia was…
content:
Myrtle Virginia Brandle,95, of Hawesville, KY passed on to her Heavenly Home on February 17, 2025 at The Heartford House with a daughter Lottie Kennedy and a grandson Ricky by her side. Virginia was born on June 10, 1929 in Hawesville to the late Victor and Virgie Butler Carter. She was a member of Safe Harbor Christian Fellowship Church and Undenominational Church, lived her whole life in Hawesville, raised six children, she was a homemaker, enjoyed doing crafts and going to Karaoke. She was preceded in death by her husband of 36 years Leonard G Brandle, a daughter Marlyn Sue McFall and her husband Charles, son Sherman Brandle and his wife Linda, a granddaughter Mary 'Cat' Kennedy, two grandsons Tony and Scott Brandle, one great greatgrandson, brother and his wife Victor and Ann Carter, a sister Stella Carter Elliot and husband Frank a brother Darrell Carter, a son in law Bevin Kennedy and brother in law James McDaniel. Survivors include three daughters Lottie Kennedy, Konneta (Allan) Baize and Denise (Scott) Morphew; son Pressley Brandle; 27 grandchildren, 9 great grandchildren. 1 Great greatgrandchild and nieces, nephews and cousins.
Services are at 2:00 pm Saturday March 1, 2025 at Gibson & Son Funeral Home, Hawesville Chapel with burial following in Serenity Hills. Virginia's family will greet friends from 10 am until service time Saturday. Online condolences may be left for Virginia family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Swimming at Vastwood this summer? Can the fiscal court find enough lifeguards?
description: The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday morning, March 11th, and HC 911/EMS Director Damian Rice reported that the infrastructure is up and running on the county's Digital Radio Communications…
content: The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday morning, March 11th, and HC 911/EMS Director Damian Rice reported that the infrastructure is up and running on the county's Digital Radio Communications project. The court partnered with the schools and cities on this $3.2M project with the help of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding, which will allow the county to upgrade from analog to digital for clearer communication. Rice said they have begun testing and that the system is even better than expected as far as coverage. Installation at the schools will begin soon, as well as at dispatch and in the county's emergency vehicles. Lifeguards Needed Swimming at Vastwood Lake this year relies, again, on workforce availability, Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts said. Last summer the lake was closed to swimmers not just because of a shortage of lifeguards, but also because of water testing that revealed questionable safety. The water has been tested again recently showing that it is cleaner and safer, but the court is still asking that people interested would get trained and apply for lifeguarding jobs so that they're guaranteed enough staff to open the lake for swimming this year. Senior Services Report Every May is Older Americans Month (OAM) and the fiscal court always sponsors a picnic for seniors. This year's Senior Picnic is set for Friday, May 17th, HC Senior Services Program Director Lona Morton announced. Also, the date for Senior Games has been set for Thursday, September 12th at Vastwood Park. 'That is a day where all the other counties bring participants,' Lona said, 'and we do games and give out medals. We'll have food and entertainment throughout the day. I'm going to start working on getting some sponsorships for some of the food, etc. It will involve a lot of setting up and tearing down. It's going to be a fun day.' HC Clerk's Report Hancock County Clerk Trina Ogle reported the 2023 final settlement saying, '2023 was a pretty good year. We collected $350K in license fees, that's your vehicle registration. The average was about $30K higher than 2022. We collected $475K in usage tax, the percentage of tax you pay when you buy your vehicle. That was up about $75K. We collected $1M in ad valorem taxes (property taxes). That stayed the same because the vehicle values didn't increase so you didn't pay more property tax from 2022 to 2023. All in all, it was a good year. We took in right around $2,500,000 and we spent $2,062,000. I'm going to give you about $89K back.' Road Dept. Report The fiscal court recently ordered a single axle small truck at $194,887.55 for the HC Road Department. The decision was made by the court and Road Dept. Supervisor Dave Tindle to lease it on a 36-month term. They'll pay for half of the total amount during that term and payments will be around $2,706 monthly. At the end of the final term, they will have the option to purchase it outright or sell it and replace it if they need to upgrade again at that time. Occupational Tax Report 'It looks like, as of this date, $3,555,141.79,' Roberts said. 'That's down from $3,765,988.01 this time last year. We've caught up a little bit and the numbers look a little better.' The Occupational Tax Report was approved by the court. Treasurer's Report County Treasurer Melissa Johnson's report was approved by the court. 'As of this date, $9,704,765,' Roberts said. 'That's down a little bit from a year ago.' Economic Report 'The unemployment is at 4 percent, which is the same as we saw on the Career Center report,' Roberts said. 'Daviess had 4 percent, Breck – 4.6, Ohio – 5.7, and the average is 4.4. Our big three industries – the outlook is steady and positive. There is continued interest and expansion potential at Lewisport Industrial Park; Some property was sold there last Friday. The overall outlook remains positive and cautiously optimistic.' By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hornets win tennis match at Vastwood
description: The HCHS tennis teams began their season Monday with a match against Cloverport at Vastwood Park. The boys won while the girls lost
content: Lukas Anderson prepares for a backhand during a #1 singles win Monday. The HCHS tennis teams began their season Monday with a match against Cloverport at Vastwood Park. The Hancock County boys won 5-0 while the girls lost 2-1. Hornet #1 seed Lukas Anderson defeated Hunter Bradley 6-0, 6-0 in singles play. Tyce Boling won 8-5 over Waydon Poole and Alex Madden won 6-0, 6-1 over Philip Taul. Preston Blanton won 6-1 over Bradley. Kyle Anderson and TreMar London won by forfeit in doubles play. The Cloverport girls won both singles matches. Johnnie Taul won 6-4, 7-6 over Ella Chappell, and Madison Payne won 6-3, 6-3 over Audree Morris. Hancock's Ruchi Patel and Chiara Landes won by forfeit in doubles play. New HCHS head coach Dan Hopkins seemed pleased with his team's performance. 'All the guys that played did well. They hit the ball solidly and with confidence. 'Lukas is learning to be a singles net player and he was aggressive. 'The girls that played fought hard, but both are just learning to play. Ella's opponent was experienced and she (Chappell) almost won. We have several days of practice to get ready for our next match.' By Steve Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Iodine
description: The essential trace mineral iodine supports a healthy immune system, helps detox mercury, fluorid
content: The essential trace mineral iodine supports a healthy immune system, helps detox mercury, fluoride & chlorine from your body, increases energy levels, supports healthy thyroid function, promotes hormone balance, supports optimal blood pressure, protects from radiation, promotes healthy teeth, skin & hair, helps regulate metabolism, and studies show that it can help treat fibrocystic breast disease. Whole Food Sources Some of the whole foods you can add into your diet that are rich in iodine include: kidney beans, oats, potatoes, figs, quinoa, almonds, spinach, chard, sea veggies and pumpkin seeds. Always choose foods that are organically grown, non-GMO and purchase locally when you can! Salt There are iodized and non-iodized table salts, and most sea salt brands only have a small amount of iodine. Quality sea salts such as Celtic sea salt and pink Himalayan salt are less processed and thus contain more iodine. (*See my columns on Celtic Sea Salt and Himalayan Pink Salt in the 5-24-2023 & 8-1-2023 editions of the Clarion.) With a reported 90 percent of the U.S. population having access to iodized salt, why is there so much iodine deficiency? Consider this in answering that question: iodized salt does not have the 'balancing effect' of trace minerals, is over processed (BLEACHED!) and provides too much sodium. I don't recommend iodized or non-iodized salt. I recommend that you spend a little more and purchase a high quality Celtic sea salt such as Selina Naturally Brand. You'll use less of it because it is more potent, and you'll be getting the trace minerals that your body is asking for when you crave salt. Deficiency Symptoms of iodine deficiency include, but are not limited to: fatigue, memory challenges/brain fog, impaired vision, thinning hair, constipation, cold sensitivity (especially in hands & feet), muscle aches, dry skin, difficulty swallowing, problems with breathing, depression, speech disorders, infertility, thyroid problems & goiters, irregular menstrual cycles, challenges during pregnancy, and breast & prostate problems. The recommended daily intake of iodine for adults is 1,100 mcg. Always do your research first and/or check with your doctor, especially if you are on a certain diet recommended by your physician. Blood tests can help you determine the amount you need to supplement with. Be Well and God Bless You. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: HCHS tennis boys knock off Apollo
description: Lukas Anderson won 8-5 over Ben Austin in #1 singles. Preston Blanton fell 4-8 to Jamison Franey and Tyce Boling won 8-1 over Ben Halbig.
content: Tyce Boling makes a return during a tennis match at Vastwood. The team defeated Apollo 3-2 in Owensboro Tuesday. The HCHS boys tennis team took a big 3-2 match win over Apollo at Owensboro Tuesday. Lukas Anderson won 8-5 over Ben Austin in #1 singles. Preston Blanton fell 4-8 to Jamison Franey and Tyce Boling won 8-1 over Ben Halbig. Alex Madden and Caleb Ewing fell 6-8 to Evan Wilson and Connor O'Bryan in doubles. Tre London and Kyle Anderson won 8-1 over Nolin and Franey. 'It's amazing the boys pulled out this victory,' HCHS coach Dan Hopkins said. 'They (Apollo) play all their best players, but they did play two of their better singles players and their top doubles team. 'Tyce, Kyle and Tre won huge matches for us, but the MVP was Lukas who pulled out a tough match at #1.' Van Reska lost 4-8 in a JV match. Apollo won 5-0 over the Lady Hornets. Ella Chappell lost 3-8 to Morgan Shock, Audree Morris fell 0-8 to Jessica Pate, and Ruchi Patel fell 1-8 to Sami Ebelhar. Kylee Bowlds and Chiara Landes lost 4-8 to Anna Dilback and Adelyn Dilback. 'The girls lost but are getting better every day. Ella, Chiara and Kylee were very competitive,' the coach said. By Steve Wimmer

title: Hornet baseball team wins 11-1 in opener, falls 2-0 at Hartford
description: Dylan Mucker tags out a base runner trying to steal second base during the Hornets 11-1 win over Whitesville here Thursday. The HCHS Hornet varsity baseball team defeated Whitesville Trinity 11-1 in…
content:
Dylan Mucker tags out a base runner trying to steal second base during the Hornets 11-1 win over Whitesville here Thursday. The HCHS Hornet varsity baseball team defeated Whitesville Trinity 11-1 in five innings during the season opening game at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown Field Thursday. 'Our pitching did well for a first outing and really lived in the zone,' HCHS coach Brad Keown said. 'Our defense was solid with a very inexperienced varsity staff. We were able to make good plays with only having one error. 'Our hitting started slow but finally came alive. I felt like we executed in the small game and did well manufacturing runs.' The Hornets took the lead in the second inning when Lane Dixon crossed home plate on a ground ball hit by Kolby Keown. Dixon was pinch running for Brock Tindle. Trinity tied the game at 1-1 in the top of the fourth, but that didn't last long. Hancock County plated six runs in the home half of the frame. Jordan Payne got it going with a triple, Dylan Mucker and Carson Clark both had base hits and Dec Lewko smacked a double. Mucker doubled in the fifth to score Tindle. Mucker later scored on a passed ball. The final run came on a bases loaded walk, allowing Dixon to come home from third. Tindle started and tossed two innings. He allowed no hits, with two Ks and one walk. Payne allowed one run on one hit, with one K and five walks over two frames. Keown allowed no hits, with one K and two walks in one inning of work. Mucker was 2 for 3 at the plate with a double and two RBI. Louden Fluharty was 2 for 3 with a double and one RBI, Clark was 2 for 3 with one RBI, Lewko was 1 for 3 with a double and one RBI, Payne was 1 for 3 with a triple and one RBI, Keown and Jack Roberts had one RBI each. Dixon stole four bases, Mucker stole two and Tindle and Fluharty stole one each. Ohio County Ohio County scored two runs in the sixth inning then held on for a 2-0 win over the Hornets on Tuesday in Hartford. It was a scoreless game through five and a half innings when the Eagles' leadoff batter walked to begin the sixth. Landon Hiner then reached base on a bunt attempt and Graydon Barnard advanced to
third base. The next batter was intentionally walked to load the bases before Trent Shocklee doubled to center field. Two runs crossed home plate and the score was 2-0. Dec Lewko led off the seventh for Hancock County and the junior hit a line drive base hit. Jack Roberts followed with a line drive to left field and the Hornets had runners at first and second with no outs. Davey Hiner was on the mound for the Eagles and the senior struck out the next three Hornet batters to end the game. 'Ohio County's pitching and defense was really good,' coach Keown said. 'We only allowed three hits. We just ran into a buzz saw on the mound. 'We will get better and by the end we will be ready.' Jordan Payne started on the mound for HCHS and the senior pitched five strong innings. He allowed no runs on one hit, with three Ks and four walks. Lewko pitched the sixth inning. He allowed two runs on two hits, with two Ks and three walks. Lewko and Roberts both went 1 for 3 at the plate. By Steve Wimmer

title: Fireworks planned for Heritage Festival; food truck festival update
description: At the Lewisport City Council on Thursday, March 21st, City Administrator Jason Roberts said the planning for this year's Heritage Festival is going 'smoothly' and is scheduled for: Thursday, Friday &…
content: At the Lewisport City Council on Thursday, March 21st, City Administrator Jason Roberts said the planning for this year's Heritage Festival is going 'smoothly' and is scheduled for: Thursday, Friday & Saturday, May 30th, 31st and June 1st. 'Conexon Connect (fiber internet provider) and Independence Bank both sponsored $4K for fireworks,' Roberts announced. 'Yager Materials is sponsoring a tugboat and 2 barges for us to be able to shoot them off the river. That's gonna mix it up a little bit. We have all the bands picked so far. Thursday night, Randy Lanham is playing. Friday night, Blackford Creek, and then Saturday we'll have 2 bands since we're starting things a little early, which is Josh Merritt and Lohden Boys.' Food Truck Festival Update As reported in previous editions of the Hancock Clarion, the Hancock County Tourism Board announced their proposal to work with the City of Lewisport on having a Food Truck Festival in downtown this year. 'They still want to do the food truck thing but they decided they want to give the City of Lewisport $10K for a band and for us to come up with a time to have the event,' Roberts explained. Mayor Chad Gregory said, 'We were going to plan to have it in the fall. When we got more detail, we were going to bring it to the meeting. I'll go ahead and tell you, I was just throwing them ideas. The sidewalks down here in the square (downtown), we're kind of wanting to do something similar to the Louisville Pumpkin Trail, and possibly have the band there then, along with the food trucks.' Saturday, October 19th will land on the weekend after Fall Break for HC Schools, and is the date tentatively set for the festival. In planning the date, it was vocalized that they didn't want to have it during Fall Break in case people would be out of town and miss the festival. Audit Report The City's audit report was provide by CPA Jennifer Estes, Supervisor at Alexander & Company. She said the City has a strong net position, and that it has remained steady. 'I looked at a few cities around your same population,' Estes said. 'I picked 4 in a close range in population. None of them had a higher net position than you all did. Your debt balances went up, but it's kind of not reflected because that's your retirement balance they require us to put on there for how much your retirement plan is as a whole. It went up by $350K on your report. It's not reflective of where you're at on the day-to-day.' Gregory explained to council members, 'And, our cash is down. In a nutshell, that covid money that we had, we're spending it over time. That's what's happened.' Estes added, 'The covid money came in last year and you were still spending it out this year; It's not a concern. If you look at those federal and state grants from when that covid money came in last year, that number was over $500K in income. Some of those expenses are still coming out in this year. It's not really reflective; it's just crossed over.' Planning & Zoning It was approved by the council for Lewisport citizen Julie Vogt to serve on the City's Planning & Zoning Board. Budget Workshops The council discussed the scheduling of upcoming Budget Workshops. Gregory told council members, 'We can have one or a couple, whichever you prefer. I would prefer it be somewhere in the middle of April and the beginning of May.' Public Works Update Superintendent R.J. Simpson reported, 'Everything is going good. We've been doing some spring cleaning. We got a little mowing done. We went around and reclaimed some of the lawns that we had to dig up for services; we sowed grass, etc. The lift station has been completely bypassed now. It's all up and running good for now the way it is. We got all that installed and going good. We did a little bit of curb and sidewalk work on the concrete where we had some areas that were damaged. We got the new service truck in too; That is really nice. We've been putting it to work.' Police Dept. Update Chief of Police Greg Linn reported, 'We've been pretty busy since the last meeting. To date, we've had 57 calls since last month. Nick Jarboe (newest Lewisport City Police Officer who was injured during his training last year) is getting stronger every day. Timewise, we really don't know just yet, but as he's progressing we're starting to see light at the end of the tunnel so hopefully we'll have him back much sooner than later. Everything else is going pretty well. I went last week to the KLC Risk and Safety Conference in Bowling Green, a lot of good information. They had about 50 or 60 more attendees than last year, which is good.' Military Banners Councilman Kelly Vanover announced, 'I talked to the banner company (The Military Banner Program, owned and operated by U.S. Army Veteran Michael Martin). They're going to make us a (sample) banner. I talked to Jason about putting them on the poles around the park, etc. They are 18×36, and around $79-89 a piece with a 6-month warranty. They'll replace them if they get damaged; they're made of good vinyl. Sometimes communities ask for sponsorship from businesses.' Once the council makes a decision on how many to order, the banners will arrive in 3 to 4 weeks. There are 9 poles around the park downtown where they can be placed. Councilwoman Mary Margaret Hawkins also mentioned that she thinks the U.S. Flags in downtown Lewisport are 'way too small compared to other cities' while they were on the topic. Budget Amendment Ordinance City Attorney Charles Kamuf read aloud the Budget Amendment Ordinance (#23-5) for Fiscal Year 2023/2024, and it was approved by the council. This is an ordinance amending the City's budget for the fiscal year beginning on 7-01-2023 and ending on 6-30-2024. By estimating revenues, resources and appropriation of funds, the council has reviewed the budget and has made necessary modifications, and an annual budget proposal and message has been prepared and delivered to the city council, and approved. The Annual Budget is amended, for example, with General Fund Revenues now at $650,316, and the Road Fund at $32K. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Friends & Family Farmers Flea Market – April 6th, 10 a.m.-2 p.m.
description: The Friends & Family Farmers Flea Market is happening on Saturday, April 6th at the Hancock County Fairgrounds, located at 1430 KY-1389 in Hawesville, from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Show up and help…
content: The Friends & Family Farmers Flea Market is happening on Saturday, April 6th at the Hancock County Fairgrounds, located at 1430 KY-1389 in Hawesville, from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Show up and help make it a success! The Flea Market will have chickens, ducks, goats, shirts, tumblers, macramé, handmade lotions, soaps, wax melts, jams, jellies, baked goods and much more available at this eclectic community flea market. Local businesses, crafters, homesteads and farms are welcome! Per the U.S. Department of Agriculture, all goats and sheep must have scrapie tags and health certificates. Flea Market 2024 Dates The Friends & Family Farmers Flea Markets for 2024 are all held at the HC Fairgrounds and scheduled for: Saturday, April 6th and Saturday, May 11th, from 10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m.; Saturday, June 8th, from 5:00 p.m.-8:00 p.m.; Saturday, September 14th and Saturday, October 19th, (times to be announced). Contact Information If you have any questions on pricing for booths, etc., please call or text Lori Miller at 270-922-8524. Or, you can send a direct message via Messenger on Facebook. The FB Page is Friends & Family Farmers Flea Market. Flea Market History Friends & Family Farmers Flea Market began when Kevin Geer, Danny McFarland and their wives and children had this wonderful idea to hold a monthly flea market at the fairgrounds. It is a huge asset to the community of Hancock County as well as surrounding communities. They encourage new vendors to participate in the markets. Their vision with these flea markets is to build a stronger community. The markets also allow them to encourage what they are passionate about. They are hobbyists and homesteaders. They raise birds, goats and cows on their land, and their children help choose the breeds of birds and have learned how to build their coops and build fences. The coops they sell at the markets go back into medicine and food for the animals and also rewarding the children for their hard work. The idea is to help them build their hopes and dreams and nurture their plans to go forward and become farmers, entrepreneurs and small business owners. They started it for their children and everyone in the county and surrounding communities, Greer said. The flea market creates a way for people to sell their chickens, goats, quail, ducks, turkeys, guineas, emus, sheep, doves and more. Local businesses and start-ups have had great success selling such wares as: local honey, fudge, bread, ice cream, cast iron, farm equipment and yard sale items. 'This is an avenue for anyone who wants to benefit from it,' Greer added, 'a grassroots way to bring the community back together again.' They said they are really hopeful that this idea will catch on, and they are very passionate about encouraging people to shop local. Their dream is of a 'Thriving, Hometown, Small-Town America'. Their hope is to preserve a way of life and open up our communities, Greer said. Amish neighbors are invited to come out to these flea markets as well as local artists and anyone who wants to join and sell goods and services, advertise your business, hand out cards, etc. They also like organizing fund raisers through the flea markets, such as for benefiting an individual in the community with medical bills. Get in touch with these folks through the aforementioned contact information and get involved! This is a great way to keep small town communities thriving. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Lady Hornets find their groove with consecutive wins
description: Jordyn Waltrip smiles while getting a high-5 from coach Dwayne Wroe after she hit a 2-run triple for the Lady Hornet varsity here last Thursday. Lady Hornet's Lily Roberts struck out 17 batters and…
content: Jordyn Waltrip smiles while getting a high-5 from coach Dwayne Wroe after she hit a 2-run triple for the Lady Hornet varsity here last Thursday. Lady Hornet's Lily Roberts struck out 17 batters and Audrey Carnes hit a home run during Hancock County's 4-1 win over Ohio County during a softball game played at Vastwood Park last Thursday. 'This is the first time we've went the distance with Lily. She had good command so we let her stretch it to seven innings for the first time and she was impressive. She's still not a hundred percent but she's getting there,' HCHS coach Dwayne Wroe said. 'Audrey Carnes got her first varsity start and she hit one out of the park!' There was no score through three innings when Roberts struck out the side in the top of the third. Carnes came to the plate with one out in the home half of the third frame. The freshman jumped on an 0-2 pitch and belted the ball over the fence in center field. The Lady Hornets maintained a 1-0 lead until the fourth inning. Lily and Layni Roberts both walked and Emmalynn Higdon laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance the runners. Up comes Jordyn Waltrip and the 8th grader smacked a 2-run triple that put HCHS ahead 3-0. 'Jordyn's triple helped us separate from them and we were able to cruise on in,' Wroe said. 'We played well defensively.' Baylee Estes singled and later stole home to make the score 4-0. The Lady Eagles added a lone run in the sixth before Lily got the third out via strikes. Ohio County batters went down swinging 1-2-3 in the seventh. Roberts got the win by allowing one run on four hits, with 17 Ks and one walk over seven innings. Estes was 3 for 3 with a double at the plate. Kylie Westerfield was 2 for 3, Carnes was 1 for 2 with the solo home run, Lily Roberts was 1 for 2 and Waltrip was 1 for 3 with the triple and two RBI. Layni Roberts scored a run. Marshall County The Lady Hornets got a 6-1 win over Marshall County during their first game of the spring break trip to Ft. Walton Beach, Florida Sunday. Estes scored from third on a wild pitch and Hancock County led 1-0 in the third inning. The Lady Hornets returned the favor in the fourth when a Marshall County player scored on a wild pitch. The score was tied at 1-1 in the sixth but not for long. Layni Roberts doubled and Ava Riggs followed with a line drive triple. Riggs came home on an error and Hancock County led 3-1. Emmalynn Higdon later ripped a 2-run double and eventually scored on a grounder by Westerfield. The five run lead was plenty for the Lady Hornets as their defense did the job in the sixth. Lily Roberts finished things off with three Ks in the seventh inning. Lily got the win while allowing one run on two hits, with 16 Ks and three walks over seven innings. Riggs was 2 for 3 with the triple, a double and one RBI, Westerfield was 2 for 3, Ella House and Layni Roberts (double) were both 2 for 4, Higdon was 1 for 3 with the double and two RBI, Estes and Carnes both went 1 for 2, Bella Bryant was 1 for 1 and Lily Roberts 1 for 4. Taylor County The Lady Hornets continued to roll when they won 10-6 over Taylor County on Monday. A 4-run first inning for HCHS was highlighted by hits from Estes, Riggs and Aubree Mosby and a sacrifice fly by Lily Roberts. Waltrip was on the mound and pitching well until Taylor County got rolling in the fourth. Ryleigh French came in to finish the frame but not before the Lady Cardinals scored six runs. House tied the game at 6-6 with a 2-run double in the bottom of the fourth and the HCHS defense got six consecutive outs behind French. Lily Roberts knocked in two runs and Madyson Higdon followed with a 2-run double to make the score 10-6. French closed out the game on the mound and earned the win. She allowed two runs (none earned) on three hits, with one K and no walks over 3.2 innings. Waltrip allowed four runs (two earned) on six hits, with three walks over 3.1. House was 2 for 3 with two RBI, Carnes was 2 for 3, Westerfield was 2 for 4, Higdon was 1 for 2 with a double and two RBI, Riggs was 1 for 2 with one RBI, Lily Roberts was 1 for 3 with two RBI, Estes was 1 for 3, and Mosby was 1 for 4 with two RBI. Carolina Jones scored two runs. By Steve Wimmer

title: Simulator shows HCHS students what it's like driving drunk

content:
On Monday, April 15th, Hancock County High School hosted a Drive Safe Kentucky Presentation to help students understand impaired driving. title: Healthy Habits: Methylene Blue
description: This compound is not something I would normall
content:
This compound is not something I would normally point to in my columns because it is a synthetic medicine and I mainly stick to natural remedies. Methylene blue (C16H18CIN3S) is safe in very small doses and is an over the counter medicine that is worth taking a closer look at.
It is called a 'miracle medicine' because it has successfully treated a wide variety of illnesses, including but not limited to: gout, depression, covid & other viruses (antiviral), AIDS, autism, cancer, heart disease, brain fog, chronic Lyme disease, UTIs, septic shock, anaphylaxis, fatigue, memory loss, candida, inflammation, nerve degeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction and management & treatment of methemoglobinemia.
It is also called a 'metabolic medicine' because it works by hormesis – taken in low doses it is beneficial, and taken in high doses it could be toxic. In low doses, it acts as an antioxidant, improves memory consolidation and protects the brain, thus acting as a potential therapeutic for neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington's Disease (HD) and early Alzheimer's Disease.
Methylene blue, today, is kept on-hand in emergency rooms to treat cyanide poisoning or carbon monoxide poisoning. It has been around for a long time and there is plenty of peer-reviewed research available for you to read further about it. It was discovered in the late 1800s, the first fully synthetic drug in medicine, and utilized as one of the first antibiotics. It was also one of the first anti-psychotic drugs, and was used to treat malaria.
Methylene Blue Dosage The dosage recommendation is .5 milligrams to 4 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, of USP (pharmaceutical) Grade, 1 percent solution (0.5mg/drop). For example, if you weigh 130 pounds (roughly 59 kilograms), then you would need approximately 30 drops per day. In one drop is 0.5 milligrams. So you would take around 7 or 8 drops in filtered water, 4 times per day.
Consult with your doctor, of course, and do your research to see if this is an option for you. If you decide it is something that would benefit you, then make sure to do the math and calculate the correct dosage according to body weight and any other factors that you might want to consider.
Function How does methylene blue work? It acts as an artificial electron recycler. The electrons in our bodies are stored and produce energy, and they are in our mitochondria (our center of metabolism) as well. The food we eat is converted into electrons that are stored in the ATP molecule for energy.
Methylene blue can remove or add electrons (redox cycling), depending on what part of our bodies need them and what parts don't need them, within these important electron exchanges that go on in our bodies every day. It also assists mitochondria in transporting and absorbing oxygen (an oxidation-reduction agent), which improves the way our bodies use oxygen.
Contraindications Pregnant and lactating women should not take methylene blue. Also, those who are taking SSRIs, such as for depression, would not benefit from this medicine. There is a risk of serotonin syndrome, a life-threatening condition, when methylene blue is used with medications that raise serotonin levels, which includes opioids. Those taking SNRIs and MAOIs should not consider it either.
Also, methylene blue is processed in the liver and those with liver conditions may not benefit from it. The list of possible adversities to this medicine is too long to include here so please always do extensive research and talk with your health care practitioner first before considering this option.
Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Faye Davis
description: Faye Elizabeth Davis, 83, of Hawesville, KY passed away on April 28, 2024 at Hospice of Western Kentucky Hartford House in Owensboro Kentucky.
content:
Faye Elizabeth Davis, 83, of Hawesville, KY passed away on April 28, 2024 at Hospice of Western Kentucky Hartford House in Owensboro Kentucky. She was born July 4, 1940 in Jewett, Cumberland, Illinois the youngest child of Otis M. and Mildred Francis (Spann) Burlington. She was preceded in death by her husband Raymond Wayne Davis, two brothers and one sister, Melba Emery, Joe Don and Robert Faye is survived by her sisters, Mary Lou Ward and Julia (Chapman) Gunn. She was the cherished wife of Wayne Davis wed on November 8, 1958 and the wonderful mother of Carla Ann (Jerry) Van Cleve, David Wayne (Marsha) Davis, and Cynthia Renee (Tony) Byxbee. Nanny to five grandchildren, Jennifer Van Cleve, Jerry (Cherise) Van Cleve, Jessica (Daniel) Bianco, Peter Van Cleve Jr., and Tiffany (Charlas) McElhinny. She also had four great grandchildren, Nicholas, Aiden, Christopher, and Addyson. Faye enjoyed traveling, gardening, canning, and loved genealogy. She was a member of several genealogical societies and founding member of the National Society Descendants of Early First Responders and held the position of registrar. She was a member of The Order of the Eastern Star which she loved spending time with her sisters and brothers, harassing a few of them on occasion and being spoiled by others. She visited all 50 states and about 20 countries, loved cruises as well as road trips and was always ready to go. Her last days were spent thanking her granddaughter, Tiffany and praising her Charlie for always being there for her when she needed them. Following Faye's wishes, no services are being held. Gibson & Son Funeral Home has been entrusted with care.

title: Records fall in Great Gator track meet at Bowling Green
description: Olivia Coomes, at right, runs to victory in the girls' 100 meter hurdles during a middle school track meet at the high school last week. At left is Tell City's Lily Schneider, who lost by a fraction…
content:
Olivia Coomes, at right, runs to victory in the girls' 100 meter hurdles during a middle school track meet at the high school last week. At left is Tell City's Lily Schneider, who lost by a fraction of a second.
The HCHS track teams competed in the Great Gator Invitational at Bowling Green Friday. The Hornet boys team placed third. The girls were 13th.
Boys results The Hancock County boys 4×200 meter relay team placed second in 1:34. In the process they broke the HCHS school record by more than 1.5 seconds. Hornet runners were Wyatt Emmick, Matthew Carroll, Cooper Jones and Ben Baker.
'That was a huge race for us. Every boy ran in the 23s for their splits,' HCHS coach Wes Meserve said.
Alex Basham placed second in the shot put with a throw of 46–9 feet. James Singleton was eighth at 38–1, and Lawson Ward 13th at 34–6.5. Kasey Webb of Edmonson County won at 51–1.5. Singleton placed third in the discus with a distance of 120 feet. Basham was sixth at 113–11, and Ward 17th at 94–3. Josh Collins of Warren East won at 127–1.
'Both James and Alex were great in the throws. They are two guys I can always count on to score points for us regardless of who we compete against,' the coach said.
Baker placed third in the 100 meter dash in 11.56 seconds, and Christian Yanez was sixth in 11.81. Colin Anderson of Franklin-Simpson won in 11.33.
Emmitt Meserve placed third in the 1600 meters in 4:53. It was a personal best time and a new HCMS record for the 8th grader. Ethan Heavrin was 13th in 5:36. Andrew Champion of Greenwood won in 4:45.
'Emmitt went out with the lead boys, fell off slightly at the half then ran a really fast last 500 meters. That's a pretty rare time for a middle school kid,' the coach said.
The record Emmitt broke belonged to his father and coach.
Jones was third in the long jump with a leap of 19–5.5 feet, and Yanez ninth at 18–5.
Baker was fourth in the 200 meter dash in 23.85, and Camden Toler 21st in 26.19. Fisher Borders of Todd County won in 23.08.
Wyatt Emmick placed fourth in the 110 meter hurdles in 16.17. Jaylen Curry of Larue County won in 15.48.
'Wyatt beat the number one boy from our region. He's making huge gains and still has room for improvement,' coach Meserve said.
Jones was fourth in the 400 meter dash in 51.64, and 10th in 56.07. Jacob Dockery of Warren East won in 51.18.
'Cooper is looking great. He now has the fastest fully automatic time and second fastest time in the 400 for Hancock County.'
Emmick was fourth in the 300 meter hurdles in 43.86, and Ashton Vogt 11th in 49.28. LucasChristian of Glasgow won in 40.81.
Meserve was fifth in the 3200 meter run in 11:11. Simon Basham of Bowling Green won in 10:44. Noah Henson was eighth in the 800 meter run in 2:17, and Henry Proctor 13th in 2:31. Ian Cottingham of South Warren won in 2:06.
Yanez placed 10th in the triple jump with a distance of 35–4.25 feet. Lucas Christian of Glasgow won at 42–8.75.
Vogt was 15th in the high jump with a clearance of five feet. Hunter Holloway of Logan County won at 6–2.
The 4×400 relay team was fourth in 3:48. The 4×800 meter relay team was fifth in 9:42. The 4×100 relay team was 12th in 50.73.
Warren East won the boys team competition with 110.5 points. Hancock County was third with 81 points as 14 teams competed.
Girls results Carolina Jones placed fourth in the 300 meter hurdles in 50.02 seconds. Mia Dennis of Larue County won in 47.49.
'Carolina ran a personal best and is really improving,' Meserve said. Izzy Ross was fifth in the triple jump with a distance of 32–2.5. Scout Patrick of Larue County won at 36–3.
'Izzy jumped a PB and has the #1 jump in our region.'
Jayda Meserve placed seventh in the 400 meter dash in 1:10. Bailey James of S.W. won in 1:02. 'Jayda ran a PB and is responding well since we moved her from 100/200 to the 400/800.' Jones placed ninth in the 100 meter hurdles in 19.58. Tayannah Woods of Warren East won in 16.39.
Ross was 10th in the 800 meter run in 2:51, and Alivia Bernardi 18th in 3:13. Ryleigh Johnson of South Warren won in 2:23.
The HCHS 4×400 meter relay team was fourth in 4:46. The 2×200 relay team was 10th in 1:59. Addy Harrison was 12th in the high jump with a clearance of 4–2. Hannah Wiles of Greenwood won at 5–4.
Meserve was 19th in the long jump at 10–7.5. Nahomy Yanez 20th at 10–4.5. Greenwood won the girls team title with 107 points. Hancock County was 13th with 16 points.
'Our girls team is small in numbers but big in talent,' Meserve said.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Hornet tennis team pushes record to 9-4
description: Alex Madden reaches for a forehand shot during a tennis match at Vastwood Park. The Hornets took 4 of 5 matches during a 4-1 win over Ohio County for the HCHS tennis team Tuesday at Vastwood Park.…
content:
Alex Madden reaches for a forehand shot during a tennis match at Vastwood Park.
The Hornets took 4 of 5 matches during a 4-1 win over Ohio County for the HCHS tennis team Tuesday at Vastwood Park.
Coach Dan Hopkins changed up the lineup for this one as Alex Madden won 8-4 over Ben Moore in #1 singles play. Kyle Anderson won 8-2 over Noah Brigance, and Tre London won 8-2 over Omar Mujica.
Tyce Boling and Lukas Anderson fell 6-8 to Christian Byrd and Elijah Decker in doubles, while Preston Blanton and Caleb Ewing won 8-3 over Michael Truschke. and Taylor Stearsman. 'For the most part we played solid tennis. Preston and Caleb continue to play well together and Alex looked good at #1.
The HCHS girls team lost 0-5 to Ohio County.
Chaira Landes and Kylie Bowlds lost 1-8 and Ruchi Patel lost 2-8 in singles.
Grayson County The HCHS boys tennis team earned an impressive win with a 5-4, come from behind victory over Grayson County at Leitchfield Friday.
'This was our biggest win of the year,' HCHS coach Dan Hopkins said. 'Oddly, we got down quickly 0-4 and it seemed no one was playing well.'
Lukas Anderson lost 0-8 to Maddox Elmore in #1 singles play, and Tyce Boling fell 1-8 to Miles Mudd.
Preston Blanton lost 3-8 to Jordan Smith, and Caleb Ewing lost 2-8 to Ethan Kingley. The Hornets got on the scoreboard when Kyle Anderson defeated Brayden Kingley 8-4 and Tre London won 8-4 over Roger Pierce.
'When Kyle and Tre pulled out tough singles wins it made it 2-4. Then we came alive in doubles,' the coach said.
Lukas Anderson and Boling teamed up to win 8-5 over Jordan Smith and Brayden Kingley, and Blanton and Ewing finished off an 8-3 win over Lush and Winkelman.
'Lukas and Tyce played great together. Then Preston and Caleb, who've had a couple of big wins together, dominated. The match was tied and it came down to Kyle and Tre, who were 10-1 on the season, so I felt good about our chances.
Kyle Anderson and London won 8-4 over Burns and Glascock to secure the comeback victory! This doubles team is 11-1 on the season.
The Hornet boys team improved to 8-4 on the season with the win.
The HCHS girls team fell 0-9 to Grayson County.
'The girls lost to a much more experienced team. But they worked hard and continue to improve. Chiara Landes, Kylie Bowlds, Audree Morris and Ruchi Patel all lost by set scores of 0-8. Bowlds and Morris fell 0-8 to Emma Walker and Sami Woosely. Landes and Patel lost 2-8 to Neely Hornbeck and Collyns Elmore.
Butler County The Hancock County boys team won 5-0 over Butler County at Morgantown Thursday. 'I thought we played a little tight, but solid. Their team is rebuilding,' coach Hopkins said. Lukas Anderson won 8-1 over Jacky Qui in #1 singles action. Blanton won 8-2 over Jeffrey Parrish and Mikey Whitefeather defeated Preston Clark 8-4.
Kyle Anderson and London won 8-3 over Clark and Parrish in doubles play. Alex Madden and Boling made it a clean sweep with an 8-2 victory over Carson Joiner and Mason Kessler.
'I'm still looking for a second singles and doubles team that I can feel confident with at regional,' the coach said.
The HCHS girls played well during a 2-3 loss to Butler County.
Landes won 8-4 over Lily Glass in #1 singles. Patel fell 1-8 to Jenelle Kimmel.
Bowlds and Morris won 8-3 over Paisley Johnson and Kennedy Tucker in doubles play.
'We had to forfeit two matches so it ended up being a narrow loss. Audree and Kylie continue to play well together,' the coach said.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Charles Logsdon
description: Charles Thomas Logsdon, 83, of Lewisport, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, May 21, 2024, under the care of Hospice of Western Kentucky.
content:
Charles Thomas Logsdon, 83, of Lewisport, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, May 21, 2024, under the care of Hospice of Western Kentucky at the Heartford House. He was born in Maceo, Ky on February 27, 1941 to the late John Thomas and Katherine Sipes Logsdon. Charlie owned and operated Logsdon's Garage for many years in Lewisport and was a member of the Army Reserve. Charlie enjoyed spending time with his grandchildren, animals of all sorts, working in his garage and was a master tinkerer. He was preceded in death by his parents and a brother, David Logsdon. Charlie is survived by his wife of 53 years, Claudette Winkler Logsdon; daughter, Charla (T Tommy) Littlepage; son, Chad Logsdon; grandchildren, Lane and Leah Littlepage; sister, Karen (Mickey) Keenan; brother, Jim (Betty) Logsdon along with several nieces and nephews. Funeral Services will be held at 1 pm on Friday, May 24, 2024 at Lewisport Baptist Church with burial following in Lewisport Cemetery.
