title: Wes Meserve named Assistant Principal at HCHS
description: New HCHS Assistant Principal Wes Meserve. Wes Meserve will be the new Hancock County High School As
content:
New HCHS Assistant Principal Wes Meserve.
Wes Meserve will be the new Hancock County High School Assistant Principal beginning in fall for the ‘24/'25 School Year. Former HCHS Asst. Principal Dr. Jacob Bryant will be the new North Hancock Elementary School Principal, as Ginger Estes has retired.
'I just want to thank Principal Ginger Estes, Mr. Asberry and the Board for giving me this opportunity,' Wes said. 'I've taught in this district for 15 years and lived here pretty much my entire life. This is where I want to be. This is the community I care about and I care about these kids. I'm really looking forward to the opportunity to be able to step up into that leadership role.'
Wes is a 2002 HCHS Honors Graduate. He earned his Bachelors in Sociology at Kentucky Wesleyan College in 2006, and a Masters in Learning & Behavior Disorders in 2009 at Western Kentucky University. He is currently enrolled at Murray State University to complete his Rank 1 certification.
While attending KWC, he participated as an intern at the Green River Area Development District (GRADD), and after graduating was hired as a Community Development Planner. He was then promoted to Public Administration Specialist.
After 2 years at GRADD, Wes enrolled in WKU's Masters program for learning and behavior disorders and began working at HCHS in the Special Education Department. In 2010, he was hired as a Special Ed Teacher at HCHS and has worked with the English Department as a Co-Teacher for Grades 9-12 English courses. He was hired as the Head Cross Country Coach in 2009, and Head Track & Field Coach in 2013.
Wes and his wife, Hadley, live in Hancock County. They are blessed with 3 children: Emmitt, Ella and Elias.
For more on Hancock County Public Schools visit https://www.hancock.k12.ky.us/
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: First Responders Day lots of activities planned — bring the family
description: Satu
content:
Saturday, June 15th is Hancock County First Responders Day at Vastwood Park from noon to 4 p.m. Bring the whole family out and meet your local first responders!
All Hancock County Volunteer Fire Departments, Emergency Services, Law Enforcement, and Dispatchers will be at the beach house parking lot at Vastwood. Weather permitting, so will Air Evac and Amy Tipton with her highly-trained Search & Rescue Dog, Rocco.
Hancock County Emergency Management Agency Director Kyle Veach said First Responders Day will be a very big event, and that one of the goals is for parents to meet all emergency crews before an actual emergency may happen.
Touch A Truck
Touch A Truck The event theme is 'Touch a Truck' and there will be various emergency services equipment at Vastwood for children and adults to get familiarized with. This will also be a valuable opportunity to talk with emergency personnel in the county and ask questions about their procedures and the equipment they use.
Lewisport Volunteer Fire Department Chaplain and HC Emergency Services Assoc. Volunteer Teresa Roberts said, 'First Responders Day is for all ages, not just kids. The need to call for help from first responders is often a traumatic event and is very stressful.
Our hope in having all people come meet the first responders and touch a truck is to create good memories so that when that stressful time comes they have a good memory to help them connect to the first responders and ease trauma and stress. Not to mention the first responders creating good memories of those they serve as each event they respond to is a traumatic event that affects them too.'
Food Vendors & Booths
Food Vendors & Booths Food Vendors such as Sunny Daze, Kluckies and Hello Pop will be on site. Other booths will include: Audubon Area Community Services, RiverValley & Affiliates with their Mobile Crisis Team, Autism Advocates of Hancock County, Owensboro Health, Hancock County A.S.A.P, and more.
Children's Activities
Children's Activities There will be activities for children, including a children's cornhole tournament.
Sensory Free Hours
Sensory Free Hours Quieter activities are scheduled for autistic and special needs children. Those Sensory Free Hours will be from 10:00 a.m. to noon.
Cornhole Tourney
Cornhole Tourney The Cornhole Tournament will begin at 3:00 p.m. For more information please contact: HVFDAUXILIARY2023@gmail.com.
Sponsors
Sponsors Organizations helping to promote this important day by sponsoring are: Independence Bank and KY Farm Bureau.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: HCPL Reports at Fiscal Court Meeting
description: The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday morning, June 10th, and Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts
content:
The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday morning, June 10th, and Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts reminded everyone to mark their calendars and plan to attend the First Responders Day event at Vastwood Park on Saturday, June 15th, at the Beach House parking lot beginning at 10:00 a.m.
Libraries Report
Libraries Report Cindy Thorp was appointed as a new Hancock County Library Board Member, and HC Public Libraries (HCPL) Director Tina Snyder reported, 'We have a busy summer coming up at both of our libr ary locations and our book mobile. We invite you to our 70th Birthday Celebration for the library coming into existence in Hancock County.
ary locations and our book mobile. We invite you to our 70th Birthday Celebration for the library coming into existence in Hancock County. Hawesville Library will celebrate theirs on June 18th; That's when we officially became a library back in 1954. We're going to have a Birthday Party on June 29th at the Hawesville Library, from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.
Todd Biever is doing the music, we're having refreshments, and we have past staff coming for a group photo at 11:30 a.m., and past board members coming for a photo at 11 a.m. Leroy Lamar is our only surviving board member from our original library board.
We're really just celebrating that the library is still here and still moving forward. The first library was in the building that sat where this one is (225 Main Cross St.). There were 2 rooms to the side of the old jail and that's where the first library started.
I'm doing Facebook posts about our history; The first one was last week. I've gotten so many pictures, such as of Story Time from way back, and I'm sharing them just to bring back some fun memories from how long we've been here.
The Lewisport Branch Library will celebrate their 55th Anniversary in February. We'll be having a shindig for them too in February (2025).
We're a partner in the Summer Meals Program with the HC Schools System. Our parking lot is full from 10 a.m. until around 11:30 a.m., almost every day, with people coming in to receive their meals. This year they're doing a kind of grab-n-go opportunity. Both locations, Hawesville & Lewisport, are participating in that. Any child 18 and under (in Hancock County) can come in and get meals.
Our online resources – there's even a Chilton's Auto Manual online for those of you who are car repair buffs. If you can't find exactly what you're looking for (on the HC Libraries website: https://hcplky.org), you can come here and we'll help you find it and print it for you.'
Road Dept. Report
Road Dept. Report HC Road Dept. Crewman John Marvel reported, 'We've been mowing, and we're finishing up the last FEMA job that we have to do on Quisenberry this week. We'll get that, and then get ready for that box culvert in 2 weeks. Other than that, everything is going alright.'
Resolution 2024-10
Resolution 2024-10 The Court approved another truck lease with this Resolution for a single-axle Mack Truck.
Bid Opening
Bid Opening The Court held bid openings for blacktop, gravel and stone, etc. Those bids were taken into consideration but no decisions were made yet.
Occupational Tax Report
Occupational Tax Report The Occupational Tax report for the year to date is at $5,059,783.05 and was approved by the Court. Roberts said that is down from $5,950,139.11.
Economic Report
Economic Report HC Industrial Foundation Director of Economic Development Mike Baker reported, 'The unemployment rate is at 4.6 percent. That's down from 5.4 percent in March. Daviess County is at 4.3, Breck is at 4.8, Henderson is at 4.2, and Ohio County is at 6.1 percent unemployment. So they're still feeling the effects of closing that EV (electric vehicle) battery plant.
These EV battery plants, a lot of that talk has really slowed down. They've even suspended construction on one of the big sites in Kentucky. I think some people may be rethinking that a little bit, compared to what it was 6 months ago.
We still have good activity going on at the Lewisport Industrial Park. Two of those tenants are looking at purchasing additional acreage. We're getting closer to bringing that to you guys for you to take a look at it and to get your (Fiscal Court's) approval on it, and to see some expansion there.
Clearview Glass has a gravel pad started and they've got their trusses for their building down there so I hope to see that start sooner rather than later. He had a couple of revisions he had to make to his site plan with planning & zoning. I think all of that is taken care of now. If the rain will stop, maybe we'll start to see a building going up.
Lewisport Industrial Park continues to be the primary focus – on the small to mid-size businesses. That seems to be the best value for a return on our time now, for Hancock County.
The Big Three – Domtar, Southwire and Commonwealth, are all steady and going well. It continues to be a good barometer of the health of our local industry. Our ‘Big Three' continue to keep injecting new capital into these plants. That's the best barometer you've got is that these corporations are still putting money into Hancock County.
There are multiple locations with all 3 of these companies, and they could put that money into a lot of places but they're putting it into Hancock County. I can't tell you how important that is, especially in plants that are 50-years-old and 50 years plus.
There is no change with the Century status. I talked with one of their key people last week and they still contend that under certain conditions they will re-open but that remains to be seen.
There has been really no new information on the green smelter – the $500M grant that they're getting from the Dept. of Energy. We haven't heard anything new on that right now.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: McCormick named Citizen of the Year at chamber dinner
description: Rob McCormick is joined by his family after Rob was named ‘Citizen of the Year' by the Hancock County Chamber of Commerce duri
content:
Rob McCormick is joined by his family after Rob was named ‘Citizen of the Year' by the Hancock County Chamber of Commerce during their annual dinner Tuesday. The event was held at the Lewisport Community Center.
The honor of Person of the Year was bestowed to Hawesville Mayor Rob McCormick at the Annual Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Dinner Tuesday night.
The Dinner was held at the Lewisport Community Center, and this year's speaker was KY Secretary of State Michael G. Adams. Delicious food was catered by JJ's Pizza and local singer and musician Todd Biever provided the entertainment.
McCormick was presented with his well deserved 2024 Person of the Year Award by Chamber President Chelsea Boling. 'I'm so proud to be honored by this community and this Chamber,' he said, 'it's absolutely awesome. I appreciate it so much.'
He was chosen because of his huge heart for bringing everyone together and his talent for encouraging the kind of teamwork and camaraderie that is essential in making a City great. He listens to people and truly wants to help make their dreams for Hawesville a reality.
Hawesville City Manager Jake Powers said, 'Rob sees more talent and ability within a person than they may see in themselves, then helps bring it out. He always leads by example and understands the importance of a positive attitude and encouragement.
He's brought an immeasurable amount of knowledge and experience to Hawesville but isn't afraid to continue to learn. The strides Hawesville has made with Rob as Mayor have truly been remarkable and I'm honored and proud to be a part of it.'
Beginning his first term as Mayor just last year, McCormick hit the ground running. He and his administration have worked hard to build community involvement, and have renewed pride in the City by beautifying Hawesville and organizing 2 very successful Clean-Up Days.
They have made tremendous progress in a short amount of time. He and his dedicated team have worked diligently to take care of past audits and pay off all past debt. They've applied for grants to grow city resources, and have set up Town Hall Meetings allowing citizens to voice opinions and get involved in revitalizing downtown with help from the state's Brownfield Program.
They established a Code Enforcement Board, identified wants versus needs and budgeted accordingly, all with a fervor for running the City in a fiduciary and transparent manner. They also reach out to support the first responders in the City and are always looking for ways to help make sure they have everything they need.
Under Mayor McCormick's leadership, over $4K a quarter in electric cost has been saved due to proper management of the sluice gate, and a revenue stream on the water system was established that has yielded between $8K and $10K a month, a much needed budget increase for the City.
He and his team, along with volunteers, organized a Christmas celebration in downtown that citizens were asking for, and worked hard to find donations for decorations to make the event spectacular. They welcome citizens to attend city council meetings, and have been fulfilling McCormick's stated goal of working closely with the City of Lewisport and the Hancock County Fiscal Court.
Mayor Rob McCormick and his lovely and supportive wife, Lisa, are blessed with 4 sons, Jordan, Justin, Jarrad and Jon, and 18 grandchildren. They are local business owners of 4Js Supply in Lewisport.
He coached baseball for Hancock County High School and helped them win their only 3rd Region Baseball Championship title. He also volunteer coached for Babe Ruth, and in 2011 his All-Star team won the State Championship. He volunteer taught life skills classes at HCHS through Junior Achievement as well.
McCormick studied environmental chemistry at Western Kentucky University and worked for the Environmental Protection Agency for 7 years, as well as in outside sales for McElroy Metals for several years. He also served as a Hawesville City Councilman in past years.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Clearview Glass moving forward at Lewisport Industrial Park
description: Construction of the Clearview Glass Company building at Lewisport Industrial Park is now underway. As reported in The Clarion in early 2021, the company plans to move their entire outfit from…
content:
Construction of the Clearview Glass Company building at Lewisport Industrial Park is now underway. As reported in The Clarion in early 2021, the company plans to move their entire outfit from Owensboro to Lewisport.
Clearview Glass President and Co-Owner Dan Kinney reached an agreement in 2021 with the Hancock County Fiscal Court to purchase 2 acres of land in the Industrial Park, located on the west end of Lewisport. Hancock County owns property in the Park and have been selling tracts in an effort to encourage small to mid-size businesses to locate here.
HC Industrial Foundation Director of Economic Development Mike Baker said, 'We've been working with them and hoping that they would go ahead and start some kind of construction, and now they have. They've gotten everything squared away on their site plan, and now the construction appears to be going up rather quickly.
We're excited about that addition to the Lewisport Industrial Park. The building is on its way up and they're making great progress. This is all part of our economic development, what I call ‘shadow strategy', where we are really focusing on small to mid-size companies that provide a service or a product that, in many cases, supply our larger industries that are here and getting them to seriously look at relocating in Hancock County, and servicing these big plants from across the road instead of across the state or across the river.
The other tenants there are doing well so we're working with them and hope to see further expansion and growth in that Park. Underlying that philosophy is, we want to grow jobs 10, 15, 20 at a time, instead of 1,000 at a time, which is a very difficult proposition to undertake. Finding 1,000 people to work in an EV battery plant, for example, is a tall order.
Right now in the Lewisport Industrial Park, there is Precision Roll Grinder, Crescent Paper Tube, Contour Fabrication & Mechanical, Inc. (CFM) and Clearview Glass. Jason Young (Hancock County native) and his partner at CFM are seriously looking at expanding their presence in the Park as well.'
At the April, 2021 Hancock County Fiscal Court Meeting, Kinney announced that Clearview Glass would be purchasing 2 acres at the Park (at the corner of Bittel Road and McGill Lane) at $12K per acre, with an option to buy a third.
The company mainly focuses on commercial glass work such as aluminum storefronts, doors and glass entrances. They also do custom shower closures for homes and mirrors. They plan to build a fabrication shop and office space, and will be bringing their 11 employees to the new site once construction is completed. Their current site is located in Owensboro off Hwy 54.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: GRADD announces over $200K in funding for local Communities
description: The Green River Area Development District (GRADD), serving the Kentucky counties of Daviess, Hancock, Henderson, McLean, Ohio, Union, and Webster, has announced the acquisition of more than $200K in…
content:
The Green River Area Development District (GRADD), serving the Kentucky counties of Daviess, Hancock, Henderson, McLean, Ohio, Union, and Webster, has announced the acquisition of more than $200K in grant funding to support local communities.
GRADD, one of Kentucky's 15 Area Development Districts, provides public administration services to communities within its region. Acting as an extension of the staff for local city and county governments, GRADD offers a wide range of technical assistance. The recent grant funding secured by GRADD includes support for projects such as replacing aging playground equipment and constructing pavilions at the Centertown city park.
'This investment is a great step forward for our communities,' GRADD Executive Director Joanna Shake said. 'The projects will improve the quality of outdoor recreation opportunities for our residents. We are committed to continuing our efforts to secure resources that drive local development and prosperity.'
Grant Awards
Grant Awards are: $75,000 from the Tire-Derived Product Grant to Webster County for a 1,700-foot ADA-compliant poured-in-place walking trail inside Canaan Ridge Park. The project will use an estimated 25.5 tons of crumb rubber made from KY waste tires; and $14,800 from the Tire-Derived Product Grant to the City of Livermore to purchase and install 10 picnic tables and 10 benches at Riverfront Park and four benches and one table at the Depot Park. Benches and tables will be made from KY waste tires. The project will use an estimated 1.75 tons of crumb rubber.
The Crumb Rubber/Tire-Derived Products grant provides financial assistance to projects that further the purposes of the Kentucky Waste Tire Program by developing beneficial end-use markets for waste tires generated in KY. The grant is a 75/25 match grant, meaning applicants must provide a funding watch equal to at least 25 percent of the total cost of the project.
Additional grants awarded are: $25,000 to the City of Centertown from the Land and Water Conservation Fund to replace aging playground equipment with new swings, construct two new pavilions and add a 2,033-foot asphalt walking trail to the city park; and $87,680 to the City of Hartford from the Land and Water Conservation Fund to install playground equipment, resurface a basketball court, and renovate two baseball fields at Ellis Park. Baseball field renovations include resurfacing infields and installing new lighting, netting, scoreboard, and fencing.
The Land and Water Conservation Fund is a federal grant to protect important natural areas, acquire land for outdoor recreation and to develop or renovate public outdoor recreation facilities.
For more information, please contact GRADD Public Information Officer Jessie Saalwaechter at jessiesaalwaechter@gradd.com or Kentucky Council of Area Development Districts Public Information Officer Molly Haines at mhaines@kcadd.org.

title: Lewisport awarded $8M Grant toward Water Plant
description: The City of the Lewisport has been working on a Regionalized Water Plant for Hancock County, as reported in The Clarion, and were awarded $8M toward that $15M project. At the monthly meeting last…
content:
The City of the Lewisport has been working on a Regionalized Water Plant for Hancock County, as reported in The Clarion, and were awarded $8M toward that $15M project. At the monthly meeting last Thursday, June 20th, the Council approved for Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory to execute any documents to proceed on for that funding.
'We're on our way,' Gregory said. 'The $8M will be used for the construction phase. All of the plans with our goal to achieve have been submitted, but we do not have a set date for a construction phase yet. In the grant process, we are going to have the ability to be forgiven about $6M of that grant.'
There is discussion about the water plant being a stand alone plant for both Lewisport and Hawesville. With this regionalization discussion of a Hawesville interconnect, the project went from 101st to 2nd on the list for grant funding.
These 'generational projects' are being funded with millions of dollars in order to get small communities into compliance with PFAS regulations (plastic chemicals in the water from Teflon, for example), per Environmental Protection Agency requirements.
Ordinances & Budget Passed
City of Lewisport Attorney Charles Kamuf gave the second readings necessary for passage of the Sewer, Water and Gas Tap Ordinances. All Council members voted unanimously in favor of all 3 ordinances, as well as for the approval of the second reading of the City's upcoming Fiscal Year '24/'25 Budget.
Public Works
Superintendent R.J. Simpson discussed with the Council a proposed expansion of the Public Works maintenance building. Due to the City's growth and increase of equipment, there is a need to expand that building for storage. They are going to get some quotes for that and then come back to the Council for approval.
Police Report
Lewisport Chief of Police Greg Linn reported that they've been busy with calls. Officer Nick Jarboe came back to work in May after taking required time off to heal from an injury he sustained during his police academy training last year.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Remembering Stories From the Past
description: Prisoners were housed in the lower part of this building, and the jailer and his family resided in the upper part. The jail was torn down in 1977. Folks say if they do the crime they must do the time,…
content:
Prisoners were housed in the lower part of this building, and the jailer and his family resided in the upper part. The jail was torn down in 1977.
Folks say if they do the crime they must do the time, but jails like this were not fit for any human.
We've all seen TV programs on prisons in the U.S. and although they are certainly not a place to be, they are still fairly modern. Not so in Hancock County years ago. In the 1970s we at the Clarion had heard so many horror stories about Hancock County's 'dungeon' that we decided to investigate. My mother, Bernice Wimmer, and I went to the jail and asked jailer Jim Morris if he would give us a tour. Mrs. Morris started crying thinking we were going to make them look bad. We said no way is the condition of the jail your fault— we know you and Jim have a very old facility and you are doing your best to keep it as decent as you can.
Jim Morris unlocks the main entrance for my mother and me to see for ourselves the horible conditions prisoners had to live in.
Jailer Jim and his wife were well respected in Hancock County. We wanted to take photos and write an editorial pointing out the horrible condition prisoners had to live in. Our hope was officials would wake up and do something to improve, or get a new jail.
When the courthouse was modernized and the annex built in the 70s, the old jail was torn down and a new jail was located in the annex. Hancock County no longer has a jail, and prisoners are transported to the Breckinridge County facility by present Hancock County Jailer Roger Estes.
Man pleads guilty to killing his stepson
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (AP) A
Louisville man has pleaded guilty to fatally beating his teenage stepson to death. Media reported Joshua Gouker entered the plea on Friday to murder and other charges in Jefferson Circuit Court in the 2011 death of 14-year-old Trey Zwicker. Gouker initially told police his son, 17-year-old Joshua Young, was responsible for the killing but then changed his story about a year ago.
The Courier-Journal reports Gouker told the judge during his plea hearing that he is ready to 'accept responsibility' for using a lead pipe to beat the boy to death in a fit of rage.
He did not make a deal with prosecutors for leniency. Young is still set for trial in July on charges of complicity to murder.
Ky man arrested after toddler 2-month-old dies
WESTWOOD, Ky. (AP)
An eastern Kentucky man has been charged with murder after a 2-month-old girl died.
The Independent reported that 18-year-old Brett R. Thompson of Stanton was taken to the Boyd County Detention Center on Sunday. Kentucky State Police says an autopsy showed the child died from blunt-force trauma to the head.
Troopers and Boyd County Sheriff's deputies went to a house in Westwood on Saturday after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. The baby was taken to King's Daughters Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead. Troopers say an autopsy showed the child had died of multiple head and brain injuries.
Troopers say Thompson was the boyfriend of the child's mother and struck the infant in the head. The name of the infant and the mother were not released.
Hancock Clarion June 8, 1934
Prisoner Sets fire to bed in the Lewisport Jail Wednesday. Damages Jail property during rampage
Tuesday night about nine o'clock a young man giving his name as C. Weigel, Jr., and his address as 1480 Dixie Highway, Louisville, was arrested in Lewisport by TownMarshal John Y. Lott on the charge of speeding.
It is alleged that the man in a 1929 Model Chevrolet, delivery truck, bearing Jefferson County license T 43-858 was driving up Highway 60 through Lewisport at a rapid rate of speed; that he was unable to make the turn left the highway and in his attempt to get back on the highway, barely missed running into several cars and residences. He was arrested on the charge of speeding and placed in the Lewisport jail.
Early Wednesday morning he set fire to the bed clothing burning them up before the fire was discovered. It is also alleged he broke out the window pane and destroyed other jail property while he was on his rampage and before he could be subdued. The car is one which allegedly had been stolen from a party in Louisville and driven to Owensboro. The Louisville party had brought Weigel to Owensboro with them to drive the stolen car back to Louisville.
By the late Donn Wimmer

title: Court approves resurfacing of roads, county now 'Storm Ready'
description: Director of Hancock County Emergency Management Kyle Veach and Warning Coordination Meteorologist Mike Kochasic with the National Weather Service, who presented the Storm Ready sign that will be…
content:
Director of Hancock County Emergency Management Kyle Veach and Warning Coordination Meteorologist Mike Kochasic with the National Weather Service, who presented the Storm Ready sign that will be displayed in the county. Now that all requirements have been met, Hancock County is officially Storm Ready.
Professional Engineer Scott Phelps spoke at the Hancock County Fiscal Court meeting Monday, July 8th, and talked about some of the funding that the County will be receiving for resurfacing roads through the Kentucky Rural Secondary Program.
The 2 recommendations made by the state were voted on and approved by the Court. The first was paving KY 1700 from KY 144 to about Eagle Road, which is 2.573 miles, and an estimated cost of $250K. The second was paving KY 652 from the Daviess County line to KY 657, which is .871 miles. That cost is estimated to be $114K.
There will also be some flex funds that the Court receives annually, and those will total $135K this year. The Court will submit an actual county road for approval in order to get those funds released.
This has been an ongoing project of resurfacing roads in the county. The KY State Road Department and KY Transportation Cabinet funds are made available through this KY Rural Secondary Program, and Hancock County has many rural secondary roads, which are defined as 'farm-to-market' routes, through the large amount of agriculture and transporting of crops to market.
Rural secondary funding can be used for resurfacing, ditching, culvert replacement, soil stabilization, bridge repairs and guardrail replacement. The Fiscal Court can choose to use flex funds on the County road system, or give them back to use on the state system.
Storm Ready
The Fiscal Court was presented with a road sign from the National Weather Service in Louisville. It can be placed out in the county, and informs that the county is 'Storm Ready'. All requirements were met based on weather warnings, etc., to be considered storm ready. The sign will be placed on Hwy 60, possibly, but the exact location hasn't yet been decided by the Court.
With the installation of new sirens and a digital radio system, as well as the First Alert System that sends out calls and texts for certain weather warnings, along with other requirements that have been met, Hancock County is now officially storm ready.
Road Dept. Report
HC Road Dept. Supervisor Dave Tindle reported that the crew is still mowing on the routes. Some of their equipment needed repairing, and those have now been completed. They have also completed the installation of the box culvert on Eastwind Court in Windward Heights Subdivision.
