description: Hancock County's new Assistant County Attorney Robert Sexton was sworn-in on Monday, July 1st, by Judge Daniel Boling. Daniel served in the position before being elected as District Court Judge (38th…
content:
Hancock County's new Assistant County Attorney Robert Sexton was sworn-in on Monday, July 1st, by Judge Daniel Boling. Daniel served in the position before being elected as District Court Judge (38th District, Division 2) in the 2022 General Election.
Robert will be working alongside County Attorney Paul Madden, Jr., at Madden & Madden Attorneys at Law in Hawesville.
Paul said, 'Mr. Sexton is a seasoned attorney. I spoke to him and asked him if he would be interested in working with me as an assistant and he decided to do that. He brings with him over 30 years of experience, 20 of which was with the public defender's office.
When I learned he was retiring, I thought it would be good if he would be interested, and he thought it was a good way to spend his time. Rather than get entirely out of practice, he could do this part-time for awhile. It will benefit him, it will benefit me, and our community as well.'
Robert and Paul have already begun working together, and were in court the following morning of his swearing-in. 'We both went to court and that's what we're going to do for awhile,' Paul said. 'I want to make sure we're, kind of, thinking the same.'
Robert has been practicing for 34 years. He served as Regional Manager for the Department of Public Advocacy, and worked as an Assistant Public Advocate in Hancock County for many years. He is in the process of closing his office in Owensboro, Sexton & Vallandingham, PLLC.
'I had an office in Hancock County for several years,' Robert said, 'and I really love the community. It's a wonderful place, and I'm really happy to serve that community as the last stage in my career.'
The position is funded by the Office of the Prosecutors Advisory Council, which is part of the Kentucky Attorney General's Office. Year's ago, the decision was made that all county attorney's required at least a part-time or quarter-time assistant. District Judge Daniel Boling filled that role for 4 years, and since moving into the Judge's position in 2023, Paul has covered all tasks without an assistant.
Paul and Robert will work very well together. They both have many years of experience and are dedicated to serving the Hancock County community with integrity.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Police & Fire Chiefs Reports at Hawesville Council Meeting
description: At the Hawesville City Council Meeting on Tuesday evening, July 9th, Hawesville Chief of Police B.J. Burton and Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards delivered detailed reports. The remainder of the…
content:
At the Hawesville City Council Meeting on Tuesday evening, July 9th, Hawesville Chief of Police B.J. Burton and Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards delivered detailed reports. The remainder of the minutes will be covered in next week's edition of The Clarion.
Fire Dept. Report
Chief Richards reported, 'The total number of runs for the fire department this month was 32 fire runs and 3 rescue calls. That's keeping on track with what we're seeing month to month. There were 16 medical runs, 5 MVAs (Motor Vehicle Accidents), and a couple of cancelled calls and a couple of vehicle fires.'
Monday night, they had the in-house driver's training with KY Fire & Rescue, he said. They'll be doing the cone course on Saturday (7-13) at the HC Fairgrounds, required for driver operators to have annually, and they'll all be participating in that.
They have presented and should, Monday night (7-15), he said, approve their standard operating guidelines for boat operations that they've received from the County, and will have the Hawesville boat come back into service shortly. They are completing some rewiring work on it.
Brush Truck 205 is fully in service now. Richards extended a special Thank You to the Council, Domtar and HC citizens who made monetary donations to replace the HVFD brush truck that was destroyed in 2021.
'We headed out [in brush truck 205] to Vastwood for the fireworks display for the first time officially out in public,' he said, 'and reviews have been very good on that, hopefully that will last us a long time.'
Since last month, the department has gained one new member. Thomas McAleer has joined the department. He is transferring in from Meade County, and served several years there.
'I have 2 that are pending right now,' he said. 'One is Dylan Ashworth, one of our Juniors that has aged out [of the Junior Firefighter Program]. He turned 18 and has submitted his application for the department. The other one is Richard Gabbert. He moved back to the area from Alabama. Unfortunately, State Fire & Rescue transferring hours – they usually don't allow us to do that from different states so he'll go through his probationary periods and get all his training hours before he can start making runs.'
Richards added that by September they'll have 2 other Juniors that should age out and join the ranks of firefighter as well, and that the program is starting to bring some benefits to the department.
HVFD Blood Drive
On Wednesday, July 31st, from noon to 5 p.m. at the Hawesville Fire Station, a Community Blood Drive will be held. All donors must be at least 17, or 16 with a parental consent, weigh at least 115 pounds, check meds with center staff, eat a good meal prior, and must allow 56 days between donations. Donors must present a valid photo ID.
'This Blood Drive falls in line with Commonwealth's blood drive,' Richards said, 'to where you can give there, you can give here, and you can give back there again. They're not overlapping each other and we planned it out where they can give on all 3 if they want to.'
HVFD has submitted a list of items to House Insurance Service for the station and 2 different spread sheets went to them; One for administration and the other for operations. The administration came to just shy of $20K. That covers the office area for operating the business of the fire department. The operation side was totaled at $380K. All of the trucks are covered under the fleet insurance policies, and the boat through the marine policy with the County.
'Our total given to House Insurance for estimates on all that was $400K for our department assets,' he said. 'I was talking to Brandon and he had the recommendation of increasing that coverage to about $500K to make sure we cover everything that we have.'
Richards continued, 'The air packs, we've been working with the County to figure out how to replace all of those. The County [HC Fiscal Court] has offered to purchase 20 air packs for the County. What we looked at was going to be 38 total for the County. Dukes Fire Department has gotten some that have been donated. They have an AFG Grant in as well and are waiting to hear back from that for 10 additional.
The County said they would purchase those if the cities (Hawesville and Lewisport) could purchase, I think it is 5 or 6, that fill out the rest of the trucks. Essentially, the County has agreed to purchase, by the end of December, covering all of our first out engines. The first out that we have is a 5-man cab that covers all of our mutual aids. What they're asking for is the cities cover the city truck.
Our city truck is a 2-man cab but is required to carry 4 units (air packs). We were looking at getting that together and presenting it to the Council as well, once we get the numbers. The brush truck does not need them, only on the Class A engines. It'll be 203, 204, and 201, (201 is our city truck).'
Hawesville Mayor Rob McCormick said that the Assistance to Firefighters Grants (AFG) will be looked into for help with that. The 4 packs the City of Hawesville will need to purchase is estimated to be between $30K-$35K.
HVFD Pancake Breakfast
Mark your calendars for Saturday, September 23rd and plan to attend the HFVD Auxiliary Pancake Breakfast, 7:30 a.m. to 10 a.m. at 385 Main Street in Hawesville. Milk, orange juice, coffee, apple juice, sausage links, and, of course, pancakes are on the menu! The breakfast is Free of Charge with donations encouraged to help support the fire department.
Police Report
Chief Burton reported, 'This month, we served 2 warrants, and we had 14 total citations. The main thing, we're just trying to stop people from trying to pass during the grid lock downtown. People have been getting t-boned there for years. A lot of people try to pass there and it's a no passing zone; that's an intersection.
Calls for service – We took 2 domestic calls, at 15 River Street and one at the Dollar Store, that's been a couple of weeks ago. We pulled 30 vehicles and tried to give them some warnings.
Next month, we're going to have a Town Hall Meeting. We're going to talk at the meeting and talk to some people. We're going to try to have a Citizen's Police Night as well, and give them some information about what's going on, and where we plan to go from here.
I know a lot of people have questions about the houses coming down and what we're trying to do [with revitalizing the City/The Brownfield project], so we're going to address that. I'm going to try to get the Sheriff Office to be up here to talk to them a little about patrolling and things coming up. We're going to be getting into the holiday season coming around so I just want to keep you all informed on it.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: The Vultures
description: They have a place in the animal world. They get rid of dead and decaying animals they have found, keeping humans from having to deal with them. But, we now have a new kind of vulture. This one is much…
content:
They have a place in the animal world. They get rid of dead and decaying animals they have found, keeping humans from having to deal with them. But, we now have a new kind of vulture. This one is much more aggressive than those we have known in the past. They will find a cow about to give birth. As soon as the calf is born, they will peck the calf's eyes out, leaving it unable to see and helpless. If it gets up, it cannot find the way to the mother for food and it dies. Then, the vultures have a fine meal.
I have seen this in Hancock County. The vultures were surrounding a cow who appeared to be ready to give birth to her calf. I don't know how they knew this, but there were about a dozen, either on the ground by the cow or flying above it. I notified the farmer and he took care of the problem.
There are also vultures in the adult human world. They prey on our children. There are drug dealers who make their living finding vulnerable young people to get addicted. Then, the chain is started. The first victim is addicted so he finds another so he can sell him drugs, and so it goes on and on until the vulture has blinded so many young people to the dangers that the young people think it's alright to participate until something bad happens. Either someone gets caught or someone dies. Some victims were not even involved, like little Baby Miya. In 2022, an average of 22 children from 14 to 18 years died each week from drug overdoses. These deaths were caused by illicit drugs and counterfeit pills. 321,000 children lost a parent to drugs over a 10 year period.
Missing and exploited children are victims of the Vultures. In the United States, 460,000 children are reported missing each year. Of these, 19,706 are never found. Many become victims of human trafficking. Some become victims of the prostitution and drug world. Some are tiny, innocent victims.
A reporter was asked on TV what was the worst story she had to cover. Her story: A woman went to a bar one night and got drunk. She took a man home with her. The next morning, she got up to find the man and her 5-year-old daughter gone. They found her blood in his commode but they never found her. That Vulture was convicted of murder.
We must warn our young people of the Vultures. 'Never talk to strangers.' If a stranger gets too close, Scream: 'This is not my mommy (daddy)!' Never let a child go to the restroom by herself (himself). Tell them to report strange people to parents or teachers. Vultures have gone into schools and killed children.
Teach children self defense. Tell older children Vultures will try to blind them to the truth by saying, 'Your parents don't love you. I can take care of you better. Take this pill, it will make you feel better. Everybody is doing it.'
Teach your child to run and hide if there is trouble, and practice the buddy system. Never be alone. Always pray that God will watch over your children and keep them safe. Let us pray for each other.
– Job 28:7 There is a path which the vulture's eye has not seen.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Fiscal Court approves Medical Cannabis Vote option for Election Ballot
description: The Hancock County Fiscal Court discussed medical cannabis in Hancock County at their monthly night meeting on
content:
The Hancock County Fiscal Court discussed medical cannabis in Hancock County at their monthly night meeting on Monday, July 22nd. This is being looked at for all of the counties in Kentucky now, per the new legislation speeding up the timetable, which has been reported on in The Clarion in recent editions, per the news releases from Governor Beshear's office.
As you may know, the 2023 KY General Assembly passed Senate Bill 47, legalizing the use of medical cannabis and establishing a framework for state licensure of cannabis businesses in the Commonwealth, effective January 1st, 2025.
Local governments in KY are making decisions on how they will address this new industry that will become legal, and prospective cannabis businesses have already begun looking at state regulations and planning to become licensed by the KY Cabinet for Health and Family Services, as legislature has passed House Bill 829, amending the law to expedite the process of licensing and allows the Cabinet to begin issuing licenses this year rather than waiting until January 1st. Those licenses can be for: cultivator, processor, producer, safety compliance facility, or dispensary.
Cities and counties have the option to take action, or to not take action on whether these businesses would be allowed to operate in their counties/cities. Local governments can pass an ordinance by December 31st, 2024 to prohibit cannabis operations in their jurisdiction. They also have an option to pass a resolution to put the matter to a public vote, and an option of placing restrictions and/or collecting fees related to the businesses operating within the county or city.
The HC Fiscal Court voted on Monday and approved a resolution to allow the voters to decide if they are in favor of allowing cannabis businesses to operate in the boundaries of the county, as the resolution must be received by the County Clerk on or before August 13th, 2024.
The question will be on the regular election ballot in November, and the question on the ballot will look the same throughout the Commonwealth. The Court has made this decision in order to give the people of Hancock County a voice in this.
HC Animal Shelter Report
Ronnie York, Director of the Hancock County Animal Shelter and County Dog Warden, reported on the fees that have now been approved by the Court to be raised at the shelter, which reflect increasing costs for care.
The Adoption Fee has increased from $95 to $100. The Reclaim Fee has increased from $38 to $50. The Surrender Fee has raised from $30 to $50. Also, for those surrendering litters of puppies, the fee is $50 for the first 5 puppies, after that the fee has been raised from $5 for each additional puppy to $10 for each additional puppy.
Resolution to Resurface Crowe Rd.
The Court passed a Resolution to enter a memorandum of agreement with the Kentucky State Transportation Cabinet. The Court is receiving $171,000 to resurface Crowe Road, as reported in The Clarion in April. House Joint Resolution 92 includes $193K for Hancock County – $22K in Fiscal Year 2025 to resurface Old Mill Rd., and $171K for resurfacing Crowe Rd.
Sheriff's Office Report
The Hancock County Sheriff's Office tax settlements for 2023 were approved by the Court, as is done annually.
New Electrical Inspector
The County also has a new Electrical Inspector, Troy Mills. He's already been working with the current Electrical Inspector, Greg Carwile, who has resigned. Carwile works in other counties as well. He has become very busy and is resigning from a couple of the counties he serves.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Frederick Eugene Hubbard
description: II Timothy 4:7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race. I have kept the faith, now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord the righteous Judge will award to…
content:
II Timothy 4:7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race. I have kept the faith, now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord the righteous Judge will award to me on that day, an not only to me but also to all who have longed for His appearing.
Frederick Eugene Hubbard, 77, of Owensboro, passed on to his Heavenly Home to be with his Lord. He was born on April 3, 1947 in Hawesville to the late Joe and Wilma Irene Hubbard. He lived most of his years in Hancock County and graduated From Hancock County High School in 1965. After High School he joined the Navy. He grew up helping his Dad on the Hubbard farm. He worked 42 years at the Tile Plant in Lewisport. A member of Hawesville United Methodist Church and later attended Walnut Memorial Baptist Church in Owensboro for the last 20 years.
People who knew him called him Freddie, known as a man of integrity. He was a faithful and loving, husband, dad and grand-daddy. (A wonderful Man). He loved hunting and fishing especially with his grandchildren. Many weekends were spent riding the side by side, golf cart and the ATV on the Farm.
Freddie leaves behind his beloved wife, Malinda Butler Hubbard; two daughters, Teresa Hubbard of Louisville and Debra Brown of Owensboro; three stepsons, John, Tim and Stephen Dalton of Owensboro; three grandchildren, Alexandra Fallin, Lindsey Patrick and Parker Brown; two step grandchildren, Matisse Dalton and LaDonna Patrick; 4 great grandchildren, Keylee, Jacob, Allie and Harper Hylton; a sister, Wilma Jo (Ed) Oliver; sister-in-law, Betty Butler Sturgeon; brother-in-law, Billy Bulter along with several nieces and nephews. He will be missed by all.
Services will be at 2:00 pm on Tuesday August 13, 2024 at Hawesville United Methodist Church with burial following in Serenity Hills in Hawesville. Freddie's family will greet friends from 10:00 am until service time at the church. Memorial contributions may be made to the Heartford House in Owensboro, KY. Share your memories and condolences may be left for Freddie's family at www.gibsonandsonfh.net.

title: HCHS Marching Band are KMEA 2A West Regional Champions!
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hancock County High School Marching Band are the Kentucky Music Education Association (KMEA) 2A West Regional Champions! Congratulations Hornets!
HCHS Band Director Zach Buskill said, 'This is actually the first time we've ever won 2A, because the only time that we've ever won the regional competition was in 2019, and that was Class 1A; We were Class 1A at that time. This is only the second time ever that we've won a regional competition. It was awesome; The kids were super excited.'
The KMEA West Regionals Quarterfinals were held last weekend on Saturday, October 19th, at the Warren Central High School Stadium, in Bowling Green. The students celebrated their win with a crowd of parents and members of the Hancock County community who attended and cheered them on.
'We have so many props and so much equipment that it takes 20-30 parents just to get everything on the field,' Zach said. 'So, we had a lot of parents helping us. We had a lot of the community and families there that were cheering us on.'
The judging was divided into 6 captions, or categories. There were 2 music judges, 2 visual judges, and 2 effect judges.
'Essentially, all of those captions are totaled and that gives you your overall score,' he explained. 'Each caption has a different 'weight' to it, because some things are more important than others. We were First Place in every caption, in every category. And, for Overall, our score was First Place.'
The students were able to complete their entire performance on the field at last Saturday's competition for the first time. Their theme this year is 'High Noon,' with attire, movements, and music that excellently portray the Old West vibe. They continue to add movements over time and build up to performing it in its entirety, which includes a stand-off/fast draw that is exciting for the students to perform, as well as for the crowd to watch.
'We finished the show last Tuesday (at practice),' Zach said. 'We were able to perform the whole thing. We put it together. We had just finished learning, and the kids did a good job of getting that prepared quickly.'
He added, 'We talk a lot about becoming your best at the right time. I feel like the kids, over the course of the last week in their rehearsals, they've really started to peak and things really started clicking. That was evident based on how they performed; That was their best performance so far, on Saturday. The kids knew it, and they were talking afterwards, and were really excited about it because they feel like it was their best one yet. It's cool to see them realize that all of their hard work is starting to pay off, and that everything is starting to come together, and starting to peak. They are really excited, and it's something we're going to try to continue to build on this week as we finish preparing.'
This week they will practice, as usual, on Monday through Friday after school until 5:15 p.m. On Friday afternoon before the end of the school day, they will be performing for the HCMS and HCHS students and staff on the GN Excavating Stadium field.
'That will be cool because the kids and teachers will get to see it,' he said. 'It's kind of like a send-off for us, because it is the last time we're going to perform at home before we go to the championships on Saturday.'
Zach's parents, Jamie & Ann Buskill, of Owensboro, cook a meal for the students after their performances at every competition of the season, except for at regionals. They've been attending the competitions every year, and enjoy cooking, so they love to provide a hearty meal for the students after their hard work.
'The reason they don't cook during regionals is because when they go, they get there really early and it takes awhile to get everything prepared,' Zach said. 'Because 3A was going on beforehand, they weren't going to be able to get there early. So, just for the regional one, they don't cook. For all of the others, they do.'
The HCHS Marching Band students are leaving the school parking lot at around 4:00 a.m. on Saturday morning, October 26th, and heading out to Louisville for the championships. There may be a little bit less of a 'send-off' this year, due to the extra early departure time. And, they may not return home until around 1:00 a.m. or later, after competing.
In past years, the county fire departments, city police departments, and sheriff's department have organized a big send-off escort for them on their way out of town to the last competition of the year, with citizens standing along Main Street in Hawesville cheering them on with signs of support.
'If people want to support,' Zach said, 'they are welcome to come to Louisville and support the kids. We love seeing the community there. If you can't make it, hopefully, you can show your support on social media, or in some way to encourage the kids.'
HCHS will be one of the top 6 bands of the West region competing at the State Semifinals this weekend. The top 6 bands of the East and West regions combine to compete in the morning on Saturday, October 26th. Of those 12 bands, the top 6 will move on to the final competition that evening.
'We hope to be in the top 6 so that we can proceed to finals in the evening,' Zach said.
HCHS Marching Band performs at the Semifinals at 9:00 a.m. (CDT), held at L&N Federal Credit Union Stadium on the University of Louisville campus. The Class 2A Finals will begin at 5:00 p.m. (CDT) that evening.

title: HC BOE Meeting Spotlights Infrastructure Improvements
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hancock County Board of Education met on Thursday evening, October 24th, and approved the purchase of a special needs school bus, as well as approving the final 10 percent payment for the Track and Turf Field Project.
Board members approved verification of the punch list and payments on the Track and Turf Field Project, and the final payment for the project will be paid to GN Excavating and RBS Design Group. The beautiful new rubberized track at the HCMS/HCHS campus was completed last year.
Calendar Committee
Hancock County Board of Education member serving District 3, Brooke Payne, was approved to be on the Hancock County Schools Calendar Committee again this school year ('24/'25), as a Board Member Representative.
SBDM Allocations
The Board approved final School-Based Decision Making (SBDM) allocations. All of HC Schools will retain their tentative allocation, with HCHS approved to receive an extra $4,600, due to an increase in attendance.
KETS
The Board also approved the Kentucky Education Technology System (KETS) offer of assistance with funding technology from the state to school districts. This offer must be matched by the school district to receive the funding.
Treasurer's Report
Director of Finance Trey Anderson reported that the balance on-hand at the beginning of the month was $4,578,403.29. The total received for the month was $777,142.30. Total expenditures were $1,204,234.68, with a balance at the close of the month of $4,184,922.61.
Assistant Superintendent Statement
Hancock County Schools Assistant Superintendent Robin Poynter emphasized, 'Hancock County continues to make growth over the past 3 years taking the Kentucky Summative Assessment given to all public schools in KY for accountability measures. In 2021, Hancock County began analyzing the instructional needs of the students and training for teachers and administrators. Having come through a pandemic, the district found students needed a more individualized approach to learning due to the different levels of instruction received through a virtually focused instructional approach for several months. Mr. Asberry, Superintendent of Schools, made it the district mission to provide students what they need to be successful within the district. This meant training teachers with the best training possible to support all students in the classroom. In addition, much of the curriculum was updated to insure students were prepared with measures that closely mirrored the KY Academic Standards and supported our teachers with high-yield instructional strategies to help increase engagement and the enjoyment of learning. In the third year of support, training and curriculum improvements, the academic gains remain steady.'
The average 3-year growth for all HC Schools combined for Proficient/Distinguished scores are: Reading +4.2 Average Percent Growth (APG), Math +25.1 (APG), Science +2 (APG), Social Studies +7.5 (APG), Post Secondary Readiness +51.6 Percent Growth, and Graduation Rate +8.5 Percent Growth.
Poynter added, 'The one area 2 of the 4 schools declined in is writing. Both schools have a School Consolidated Improvement Plan for continued improvement steps and support for teachers to ensure students are receiving improved practice, feedback and coaching to develop in this area. Hancock County has also built a new holistic view of what makes a student successful for post secondary readiness outside of a one-time score of accountability given by the KY Department of Education. These descriptors are referred to as the 'Four Hancock County Success Pillars.' The first Success Pillar shows how HC Schools successfully developed our graduating seniors. This past school year, Hancock County earned a 99% graduation rate. Other graduation measures are the 18.4 average ACT Score and the dedicated 1,623 college/vocational hours earned by students over the past school year. The second Success Pillar shows how HC Schools developed grade level proficiency with their students according to the NWEA MAP Universal Assessment. This assessment is taken by students 3 times a year (fall, winter and spring).'
The spring 2023 to spring 2024 scores indicate the following grade level proficiency for Reading/Math: High School 69%/65%, Middle School 61%/61%, Elementary Schools 69%/68%. The third Success Pillar shows how HC Schools has developed work ready skills with students. Hancock County has a 94% attendance rate, 58% internship/service learning, and a 97% post secondary readiness score.
Poynter further added, 'There are a multitude of supports to help make this pillar possible with the support of local industries such as Domtar and Carmeuse. The fourth Success Pillar shows how HC Schools provide support for student wellness. With this Success Pillar, Hancock County has ensured that 100% of the students have access to a mental health provider, a health care provider, and a school resource officer at each of the schools. Hancock County also has a 100% achievement rate with the Safe School audits, and has 52 involvement activities offered at the high school to keep students involved in activities outside of the classroom. Overall, HC Schools offer a high level of instruction and opportunities for students to achieve, teachers continuing to learn and administrators learning how to support and build sustainable systems. Out of 168 district high schools in KY, Hancock County ranks in the top 20 for Quality Climate and Safety, the top 25 for Post Secondary Readiness and Science/Social Studies/Writing Content, the top 30 for Reading and Math, and the top 35 for District Overall Combined Accountability Scores.'

title: Hurnaween and Beyond: Hannah McCoy Brings Art and Joy to Makeup
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Hannah G. Wheatley McCoy (29) really enjoys her makeup artistry hobby, especially in October. She has been recreating herself into different characters each year, and posts the…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Hannah G. Wheatley McCoy (29) really enjoys her makeup artistry hobby, especially in October. She has been recreating herself into different characters each year, and posts the photos on her social media pages for people to enjoy. She has been using her creative talents to help others look their best for prom and other events as well, and that has evolved into beautiful bridal makeup artistry.
'From 2014-2018,' she said, 'I used to do marathon prom makeup days. If it was a Hancock County prom, or Tell City, or somewhere close and people knew about me, they would get in touch and I would just do prom makeup all day long. As we've gotten older, that has moved into bridal event makeup as well. It's been really cool to have these full circle moments with everybody. Cosmetics has always been an interest of mine. It is just something I've always enjoyed.'
She said makeup art is her biggest media art form, but she also likes to paint and draw on occasion.
'I don't paint or draw often anymore, but I do enjoy it when I do,' she said. 'My grandmother, Gayle Daniels, is the same way. She likes to draw, and is pretty talented at it. She's from here. She moved to Oregon in the '80s, and I love it when she visits.'
Hannah's middle name is also Gayle, after her mom, Holly Gayle. While in high school, her friends changed her first name into 'Hurna' just for fun, she said.
'I've loved makeup for a long time, and started doing special effects makeup close to a decade ago now, and so it became 'Hurnaween' when I did makeup art during the month of October,' she explained.
She began the Halloween character face painting, with her own face as the canvas, in 2014. She said one of her favorite Halloween looks that she's created is 'Venom' from Spider-Man.
'That one is time consuming, and it is a challenge for me to do it,' she said, 'but I love doing that one. In 2020, I spent a whole week doing Lady Gaga looks. That was probably one of my favorite things I've ever done.'
She said that she has set a goal to get two more Halloween looks posted for this year before October 31st. She has been very busy, and has not created as many as she usually does.
'I have only gotten the opportunity to do one look this year so far,' she said. 'It is from a TV show called 'Shoresy.' They are hockey players, so I found a cheap hockey jersey, and painted my face like a man. Years ago, I would do most days of October, and I would have an elaborate Halloween costume. It's more time consuming than people would think, but it is definitely fun.'
Her all-time favorite look she's created so far, she said, is when she turned herself into 'Joe Exotic' from the documentary Tiger King, on Netflix.
'Second to that,' she said, 'I recreated the cover to Lady Gaga's 'Artpop' album, and that was pretty spot-on. I was proud of that one.'
She didn't go to school for makeup art, and says that it is, 'truly a labor of love.'
'It's a hobby that I like,' she said, 'and I've gotten into it over time. I don't think I've ever done Halloween makeup on anyone else. Ever since I was in high school, I loved DC Comics and comic books. I feel like I've painted my face or had a costume of almost every iteration of Harley Quinn. I think it looks so cool.'
Hannah graduated from Hancock County High School in 2013. She played clarinet, alto sax and tenor sax in marching band, concert band and jazz band. She earned her Elementary Education Degree at Brescia University, and taught kindergarten at Owensboro Public Schools for 2 years.
'I'm on a hiatus from teaching, at the moment,' she said, 'because you can't pour from an empty cup. I'll go back to it one day; I'm just not quite there yet.'
She worked at Riverview Restaurant for 13 years, and is currently working full-time at Sunny Daze Sunshine Café in downtown Hawesville.
'I am a server,' she said. 'I love my job. I love my community. I love my people. We've definitely built something special over the years, all of us together.'
She said the camaraderie and close bonds they built at Riverview has followed them into the business at Sunny Daze. She enjoys working on the Sunny Daze food truck during local events as well. And, she is enjoying doing bridal makeup.
'I've gotten several weddings booked, coming up, which I was not expecting,' she said. 'I'm incredibly thankful that people even think about me being part of their big day. The more I do bridal makeup, I've realized how special it is that someone trusts you to make them feel their best self on one of the most important days of their life.'
She added, 'For me, it was always like a form of therapy, something I did to unwind, and let my creativity flow. But things have really taken off, where I get to make other people feel special; I can't wait to continue doing that. I never saw it going that direction, because I never wanted to see something that I do as a hobby, or for fun, as work. But it's not work, because you get to make someone else feel so much more important, and the spotlight is on them for the day. It's so special to be a part of that and watch their eyes light up; It's just so cool.'
Hannah is very professional, and the makeup kit she uses is exclusively for her clients, with a special set of brushes. She keeps all of her makeup artistry tools sanitized and fresh.
'I keep a small collection of complexion products,' she said. 'I will advise my clients to go to an Ulta or a Sephora to get shade matched to a complexion product, like a foundation or a concealer, so they have something that is their shade, that they know they are comfortable in for their wedding.'
A week or two before the wedding, she also includes a very valuable trial session.
'That's when we'll do our troubleshooting,' she said. 'Some people truly just don't wear a lot of makeup every day. The last thing you want on your wedding day when you're having all of the pictures taken, is to look back on a picture of yourself and you don't feel like you look like you. So, by going and having a trial run, they can see how the makeup is going to wear on them, and see how their face feels. If we need to change anything or make any adjustments, they can tell me what they liked or didn't like. Then, we can go from there and adjust it on the day of the wedding, and make it better and a little bit more streamlined for them.'
Hannah is the daughter of Craig and Holly Wheatley. She and her husband, Austin, married 3 years ago at Carie's Creek Wedding venue, in Hawesville. They currently live in Lewisport, and both grew up in Hawesville. Austin works at Alcoa, in Newburgh.
Hannah's Instagram Page, where she posts only photos of her makeup art creations, is: hurnaween@instagram. Her Facebook Page is: Hannah Wheatley McCoy. She said when she posts one of her Halloween looks on Facebook, she adds the hashtag 'Hurnaween,' so it is easier for people to find. If you'd like to schedule Hannah as your makeup artist for a special event, such as for your wedding, send her a message on Facebook Messenger.

title: Hawesville Park Construction could begin in March, Rec Center planned for future
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday, November 12th, and City Manager Jake Powers provided an update on the Park Project in downtown. The construction of the new park next to the Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department station could begin as soon as March of 2025.
As reported in The Clarion within the minutes of the October meeting, the Government Resources Accelerating Needed Transformation Program Grant that was applied for was awarded, and will cover matching funds on the previously awarded Land & Water Conservation Fund Grant.
The yellow house located on the lot will be demoed, along with the building behind it, and the site leveled out. The new park will be constructed in that entire lot, and include a basketball court, playground, picnic tables and benches.
The project is estimated at approximately $326K. The LWCF Grant award totaled $161,438. The GRANT Program awarded $156,736, leaving a little over $4K to secure through donations.
'We're still waiting on approval from the Kentucky Heritage Council,' Powers said. 'They tell us 'No work,' until that gets approved.'
There are also future plans for the old Presbyterian Church in downtown Hawesville on Main Street to be the likely site for a Community Recreation Center, if that arrangement can be made. Clean up could be done through the Kentucky Brownfield Program, and that could open up other opportunities, such as Community Block Grant funding to further finance the rec center project from that point forward.
'We received a very in-depth, detailed economic plan and community assessment,' Powers said. 'The assessment is about 24-pages. We're looking at the 150-page document to start submitting with any grants moving forward, and that will totally enhance and increase our chances of that funding being awarded. We're waiting for an ABCA (Analysis of Brownfield Cleanup Alternatives). That's who did the hazardous materials inspection, the second phase 2 on it. That, basically, gives a cost estimate for what we decide to do next. Then, we'll be able to plug those numbers into our grant application moving forward.'
Powers attended another Kentucky Brownfield Program last month, and the council approved a resolution to apply for funding through Brownfields Program Grants at the October meeting. The ongoing project with the help of Downtown Revitalization Coordinator Shane Barton, with Community & Economic Development Initiative of KY (CEDIK), has yielded valuable community assessments, thanks to community involvement. A grant application has been built for Revitalization and Reuse, and will be submitted in 2025.
The 100-paged economic plan was reviewed by CEDIK Economic Development Extension Specialist Beka Burton, who added the portion of the executive summary, and the council will then review it once more before submitting it next year, with the grant application. The plan can be used on any grant application moving forward, Brownfield related or not.
'This is proof of the investments we've made,' Powers said, 'and communication with the community to show that the community voice dictates. All of this past year and a half that the whole community has put into working on this, it is starting to come time to move on that.'
A resolution was approved at last month's meeting, authorizing the application process for and, upon approval, to enter into an agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency for the Fiscal Year 2025 Brownfield Grant Program. GRADD can only administer one grant per cycle, and the deadline to apply this year has expired. The plan is to build a much stronger application that will be submitted next year.
Powers added, 'With the Brownfield Project, the property the church has, we did the lead and asbestos phase one on it. That really fits and meets a lot of the criteria for this cleanup (ABCA) grant [lead and asbestos presence confirmed]. It really has the potential for the $5M to $1M clean-up money. Once I get the plans sent to me, the council can sit down and go through how they look for community involvement. Justice 40 is an initiative that pays you 40 percent more for community involvement. The church property fits a lot of the criteria they're looking for. I encourage anyone to speak to the church and their board, because that's a property that they can relieve liability on by going this route.'

title: Circuit Clerk Michael Boling outlines his main Goals for Second Term
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
On Tuesday afternoon, December 17th, District Judge Daniel Boling swore-in his father, Michael Boling, to serve in his second term as Hancock County
Circuit Court Clerk.
'It is neat to have your son swear you in,' Michael said. 'It's something unique, and a very special moment for me. It's really important to me that we have a judge that resides here in Hancock County. I think that's very important for all of our citizens. We had Judge John McCarty for so long, and he did a great job. For our small size, it's really important to have as many people as possible in positions that can benefit the county, or protect the county. That's something that is really special for me too.'
Michael began in his role in 2019, when previous Hancock County
Circuit Court Clerk Noel Quinn retired. He was appointed in May of 2022 to serve as the Second Congressional District Representative on the
Circuit Clerk's Executive Committee. Each supreme court district has a representative, and all of the officers from the Clerk's Association serve on the Kentucky
Circuit Court Clerk Association (KCCCA). There are 15 members, and it is each member's job to direct policy, and steer goals and objectives for all clerks, when it comes to working with the Administrative Office of the Courts (AOC), and with the legislature and the supreme court.
Circuit clerks keep up with all of the court records, record the hearings, and make sure that all of the documents are sent to the places they need to go. Their primary job is to be the custodian of court records for district,
circuit , and family court. They also issued driver's licenses until the summer of 2021, when the regional offices of the Department of Transportation voted to take the issuing of driver's licenses out of the clerk's offices.
Michael has served on the Legislative Committee for the
Circuit Clerk's Association since he started as clerk, and monitors the state legislature, when in session, and tries to identify and follow the progress of any legislation that pertains to the courts, or any kind of action the court does.
'Our biggest achievement, in my opinion, is that we were able to bring all deputy clerk salaries in close proximity to what deputy clerks make in the county clerk's office,' Michael said. 'Now, our deputies are much closer than what they used to be. They are not at the same level, but there used to be a huge discrepancy of 4 to 5 thousand dollars a year.'
With the raises that they've been able to secure in the legislature in the last two years, they have brought the salary discrepancy down to less than a thousand dollars difference, per year. This also helps in being able to retain and recruit good quality deputies for the operation of the court system.
'My number one focus since I started in January of 2019,' he said, 'has been the maintenance and upkeep of the Hancock County Judicial Center. I think the building was opened in the fall of 2011. The AOC has a 20-year mortgage on the building itself. I think it was $13.5M, roughly. Under this agreement, Hancock County technically owns the building, but the AOC has been paying the mortgage. At this moment, there are about 6 years left before the building is completely paid off. Until then, AOC is almost completely responsible for any maintenance, repairs, anything physically to do with the building. At the end of the 20 years, the county will receive total possession of the building. At that time, AOC will become a renter of space in the building. When that happens, AOC's responsibility financially for the upkeep of the building will be determined percentage-wise based on the amount of space that AOC occupies in the building.'
The main concern is that the roof has had leaking issues since it was first opened, going all the way back to 2011. And, these leaks are in widespread parts of the building.
'There are several different opinions and ideas about what has caused it,' he said. 'From the moment I started, getting this roof repaired to where the leaking has stopped has been my number one priority. As of today, I don't know that I'm any further along than I was in January of 2019, but we've been working on it. I've been working very closely with Judge-Executive Roberts, and County Attorney Paul Madden. We've met the AOC Director who just recently left, Katie Comstock. She came down to Hawesville in July of this year with some of her deputies, and we did a walk-through inspection of the building. They came to Hancock County, and looked at the building. It's hard to get the top dogs to actually come out from Frankfort to see something. I give them all the credit in the world for recognizing this problem. I feel confident that AOC is doing the best to work with us.'
The original contractor that completed the roofing work on the building had a 20-year guarantee on the work that was done. However, they have run into some road blocks with their efforts to get the long overdue, much needed roof repairs done.
'We're still in the process of doing that,' he said. 'We have been successful in getting approval from AOC to do biddings for the repair work. That is in progress but it is slow going. My intention is before this warranty runs out, we will have gotten the roof fully fixed with no leaks. In 6 years, when the note is paid, then the full upkeep of this building is going to fall back to Hancock County taxpayers. We want them to know that we're doing everything possible to get this issue fixed. Our previous County Attorney Harold Wayne Newton had taken some legal action in the very beginning of the construction, and it looks like it's possible we may need to do more.'
The other challenge with the building is the water. Since the building's first opening day for use, the water system has been very disappointing, and has a bluish-green color.
'The water system that was installed may have been designed for a building that has much more public traffic than what they actually have,' Michael explained. 'There is still an issue with the water having a bluish-green tinted color. The system relied on several hundred, I guess, of the public to be in this building every day drinking from the water fountains and flushing the toilets, etc., and we just don't have that volume. I think the system was built on the premise that there would be that much use of the water facilities in order to cycle all of the water through, and to make sure that it was clean and worked the way that it was supposed to. We've had it tested multiple times. From everything I can gather, it's not a danger health wise. However, I don't think anyone wants to wash their hands with or take a drink of water that has a bluish green tint to it, especially not in a public building that is still pretty new. We are also working with AOC to try to get that part of the building issue taken care of as well. Those two issues are the number one goals that I have for this coming term.'
He said he hopes that they will make enough progress to address both of those issues with the building, and get it in the best shape possible.
'The roof has leaked since day one, which was 13 years ago now. Who knows what the cumulative effect is,' he added. 'Hopefully, it's nothing huge, and something that will be able to be fixed and taken care of. We're just trying to figure out if we need to pursue legal action to enforce this warranty. It's very frustrating. We have a reasonable expectation that a brand-new building like that should not be leaking from day one. It angers me to think that at some point we could have to use more taxpayer money to fix this, which should have been fixed under the warranties. We were advised by the AOC that Taylor County had a similar issue with their building, in around 2012, and they were successful in their case and were able to get all of the repairs done without any extra expense. So, we kind of have a game plan on what that would look if we have to go that route, and that has made us feel better.'
Michael said a great project that was started around a decade ago by previous Chief Justice John Minton, was the implementation of the electronic filing system, with the Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts. This has been a step-by-step process, and he said the switchover is saving the state money, because with electronically sharing these documents through email, and scanning, it has cut down on the amount of postage needed.
In civil or juvenile cases, for example, there can be anywhere from 5 to 15 different parties, and with sending documents in every case and to all parties involved, it can be expensive. The electronic filing allows them to send court orders or documents, and share with everyone involved in the case, with just the push of a button.
'It is a good project,' he said. 'It's making good progress, and I think it certainly speeds up the whole process. Minton's goal, and the shared goal of everyone involved, was to push as much as possible to electronic filing. Instead of bringing over the written or typed documents, like was common practice up until the last few years, now much of the court documents are filed in the electronic system, and that automatically creates a record from the moment that they file it.'
Attorneys and agencies that work with the state and in the court system have slowly been switching completely over to the electronic system. If there is ever any question about whether or not a document or case was filed, this system automatically time stamps every document that is filed. The old paper files are still kept and maintained, but the electronic system makes the process run much smoother.
It has taken a while to build the new system, and different groups of people have been brought in at different times along the way, for this incremental transition to e-filing. The mandatory e-filing for attorneys involved in civil cases all started at one time, and then criminal, then probate, and so on.
'I think that doing this step by step, it has allowed everybody that's using it to get familiar with the system,' Michael said, 'and basically get comfortable with it. Some of the state agencies, like the Department of Community Based Services, are working their way through it now. There's still some work left to be done, but it's well on the way, and I think it's been a good thing.'
Anything that you have questions about, Michael says to reach out to him, and he will be happy to answer them. He is dedicated in helping the public become better educated on the court system, and anything related to his office. His phone number is (270) 929-9748. You can also stop by his office in downtown Hawesville, or send him an email to: michaelboling@kycourts.net
'I'm open to phone calls, text and emails. No time is too late or too early,' he said. 'If someone in Hancock County has a question that they think I might be able to answer, I'm always available.'
You can also go to the Kentucky Court of Justice website homepage, and there is a tab for all 120 counties. Tap on the Hancock County tab, and it will send you to the site containing available information for our county.
Michael also serves as a representative for Hancock County on the River Valley Behavioral Health Board, and the Audubon Area Community Services Board. He is the Chairman of the South Hancock Family Resource Services Center Board, and a member of the Lewisport Lions Club.
Michael's fiancé, Aleta Sisk, is the Director of Special Education for Hancock County Schools. Together they are blessed with five children: Daniel, Logan, Jordan, Elijah, and Jonah. Daniel and his wife, Chelsea, have blessed them with two grandchildren: Easton (5) and Dani (3).

title: Lewisport's Gage Gray Serves U.S. Navy Ceremonial Guard During President Carter's Funeral
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
United States Navy Fireman Gage Gray, of Lewisport, was selected to serve Ceremonial Guard detail in Washington, D.C., after completing boot camp last year at Great Lakes Training Center Navy Base, in Chicago, Illinois.
One percent of the U.S. population serves in the military, and only one percent of those who choose to serve are selected for the Ceremonial Guard.
Gage is a U.S. Navy Ceremonial Guard Casket Bearer, and had the honor of serving during Jimmy Carter's funeral services last week. Carter was the 39th President of the United States, and the longest living president, at 100-years-old.
He will also have the honor of being a part of the U.S. Navy Marching Platoon at President Donald J. Trump's Inauguration Day Parade on Monday, January 20th.
'A couple of months ago,' Gage said, 'they started prepping everybody. We started practicing every Wednesday and Thursday for the Inauguration. It's a cool experience because the contract here is only two years, so not everybody that's in the Guard gets to do it because they might be in that period when there's no inauguration. Just getting to be a part of a presidential inauguration, and then also burying a president, we're in a really rare time. Not many Guardsmen get to have that, or many military personnel in general.'
This is the 60th U.S. Presidential Inauguration, and will begin at the U.S. Capitol with the swearing-in ceremony. After the inaugural ceremonies and luncheon are concluded, the newly sworn-in president and vice president will be at the East Front steps of the Capitol reviewing military troops. Next, is the procession of ceremonial military regiments, citizens' groups, marching bands, and floats down Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House.
President Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance, along with their spouses and special guests, will be watching the parade as it passes in front of the Presidential Reviewing Stand.
'In the Inauguration Parade,' Gage explained, 'I will be a part of the marching platoon element. We call it a 'nine by nine.' It's nine ranks of nine people, and everybody in our command, which is about 200 of us. The majority of us will be in the marching platoon, marching during the parade, and then giving a presentation in arms to our new president…People say he has a mouth, but he produces results. I use it as a same analogy when it comes to sports, if you're one of the best players in the country, you can talk all the crap you want because you back it up; You prove what you're saying is right.'
Gage enlisted at the beginning of February, 2024, and arrived at boot camp near the end of that same month. He completed his training on May 4th of 2024, and will continue to serve in the Ceremonial Guard until May, 2026.
'I'm really grateful to get the opportunity to get to be here and do that,' he said. 'Just getting to be a part of that small group of people that can say they were part of the Ceremonial Guard is extremely humbling. In my graduation group, there were about 500 people, and only three of us were selected.'
His current rank is E-3, and he will be serving as a Navy Engineman (EN) when he goes out to fleet.
'I picked engineman, really, because I've always worked factory jobs and it was more hands-on stuff, and I wanted to keep something similar to that,' he said. 'My recruiter was an EN, and he kind of told me the ins and outs of what his job was and it interested me…My uncle, Dean McCann, was in the Navy for 9-10 years, along with my aunt, Kate McCann. They live in Omaha, Nebraska. When I was a kid, he'd tell me all the stories about him being in the Navy. I always thought it was cool. If there was any military branch that I was going to join, it was going to be the Navy.'
Gage arrived in DC for duty on May 6th, 2024, just two days after graduating from boot camp. He is at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling (JBAB).
'My day-to-day life – normally we wake up at around 4:30 or 5:00 a.m.,' he said. 'I get dressed in my ceremonial uniform. We all go to the Ceremonial Guard Building. The barracks is only like a 5-minute walk distance away. We all get ready there, and then we all get on a bus and get driven to Arlington National Cemetery. On a daily basis, it can range from one funeral to five, depending on how busy the day is. If it's a normal day, we get back here at around 3 or 4 o'clock. We'll come back and make sure we have all of our uniform items, and nothing is missing. Then we go back to the barracks and press our uniforms for the next day.'
The Ceremonial Guard serves in those duties on Monday through Friday. On Saturdays and Sundays, they have the day off. Gage said that on most Sundays, they tend to go to the building and practice.
'Most of my day, I'm burying old sailors or veterans that've passed away,' he said. 'You don't fully realize the impact that it does to families seeing that. Even as a kid, I got lucky that not many close relatives have passed away, and I've never really had that feeling very often. You have to keep yourself from treating it like it's just a regular day at work; You've got to catch yourself sometimes. It's really humbling to see stuff like that. There have been kids that I've buried that were younger than me. There have been some guys that were 18-years-old that I was helping put into the ground. That really puts some perspective on life, of how quick you can go.'
It is an important reminder of all the sacrifices that are made, have been made, and will be made by the brave men and women who serve to keep us free and safe. And it is also an important reminder of the loved ones that sacrifice along with them.
Gage visits his family in Hancock County every now and then, while on leave. He said that every time he comes home and then has to leave again, that he misses it more.
'I'll always be grateful for all of the people I had around me growing up in Hancock County, and the life I had,' he said. 'I've always been the type of person to believe that you wouldn't be who you are if you didn't go through the stuff that you went through. I'd like to thank all of the coaches I've had in my life, and all of the mentors that I've had in my life that've helped me.'
Gage will be 25-years-old this year, and is a 2019 Hancock County High School Graduate. He played football all 4 years of high school, and was also on the HCHS Track & Field team. He is the son of Genny McCann and Josh Gray. His grandparents are Cindy & Tommy Gray, of Lewisport. His aunt and uncle in Hancock County are Robert & Melissa McCann.

title: Breaking Ground: Vastwood Park's Splash Pad Project Underway
description: During the week following Christmas 2024, Hancock native, Gary Nugent, and his crew at GN Excavating & Trucking, were breaking ground at Vastwood Park for the n
content: During the week following Christmas 2024, Hancock native, Gary Nugent, and his crew at GN Excavating & Trucking, were breaking ground at Vastwood Park for the new Splash Pad to be constructed. The date for completion of construction has not yet been announced. Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts explained, 'We don't have a completion date because the weather would change that date. With the timeframe, we'll just kind of take that as it comes and keep moving forward to finish that. We're excited about that project, and what it means for Vastwood and our community.' As reported in previous articles in The Clarion, $200K was secured in 2022 from the Land & Water Conservation Fund grant for the construction of the Splash Pad, through the partnership with Hancock County and GRADD. Domtar Paper Mill, in Hawesville, donated $25K toward the project. In addition, Southwire, in Hawesville, has agreed to donate $50K to the project, and Commonwealth Rolled Products, in Lewisport, has agreed to donate $25K. The design was mostly completed in April of 2024, and construction could not begin as potentially planned that spring or summer, for various reasons. The Splash Pad will be located between the parking lot in front of the beach house and the tennis courts, at Vastwood Park, and just south of Vastwood Lake. The small building with equipment room and new bathroom facilities will be located next to the Splash Pad, and a little closer to the tennis courts. It will hold a maximum of approximately 2,700 gallons of water, which will be continuously recirculated from a holding tank. City water will be used, and then re-treated before it recirculates to be utilized again. This project is made possible with a combination of county funds, along with the aforementioned grant funding and private donations from some of the county's largest companies. The aim is for there to be no unnecessary waste, regarding the water. It does cost a little more, up front, for a recirculation system but that extra is recouped later. Hancock County is the only county GRADD serves that doesn't have a Splash Pad yet, and the youth and families in the area will be very happy to see it completed, and will really enjoy this new addition to the park for many years to come. As reported in The Clarion, the Hancock County Fiscal Court has a Land & Water Conservation Fund grant request in for an inclusive, multi-sensory playground at Vastwood Park. Roberts said they should be hearing back about that funding in the next month or two. The main, large playground was updated in 2022, and a new playground was also installed between the little league and t-ball fields in 2023. Grant funding has also been applied for to install more benches along the new hiking trails, more picnic tables, metal bench swings, and a replacement of the fitness stations.

title: Dr. Nathan James Brings Expertise to Complete Wellness
description: Dr. Nathan James, DC, has been a practicing chiropractor for over ten years, and began at Complete Wellness Medical + Chiropractic on February 1st of this year. He is now practicing at the Hawesville…
content: Dr. Nathan James, DC, has been a practicing chiropractor for over ten years, and began at Complete Wellness Medical + Chiropractic on February 1st of this year. He is now practicing at the Hawesville and Tell City locations. Nathan, or 'Dr. Nate,' as his clients call him, was born and raised in Rockport, Indiana. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Athletic Training at Heidelberg University, in Tiffin, Ohio. He then attended Logan University, in Chesterfield, Missouri, and graduated in 2014, which is the same university that the owner of Complete Wellness, Dr. Adam Brockman, DC, ND, attended. Nathan has practiced in 5 states, Virginia, Florida, Indiana, Mississippi, and Kentucky. He is skilled in various treatment modalities, and offers a tailored approach to patient care. 'I'm excited to be here,' he said. 'Everyone has been very welcoming. I'm not a local from Hawesville, but I am local to the area, and it has been good getting to know everybody. As a chiropractor, my personal philosophy is to empower the people I see, encourage them to take charge of their health, and to make health more of a priority in their lives, whether it be through diet, through chiropractic, or through other therapies. To me, it's not necessarily just about getting them out of pain and feeling better, it's more about keeping them doing the things that they love to do, or getting them back to doing the things that they love to do, such as taking care of their grandkids, taking that trip they've always wanted to take, or whatever it may be; just keeping them doing life the way they want to do it.' He said it has been a very seamless adjustment with starting at Complete Wellness, especially since he has worked at similar practices in the past. 'They have an integrated office, and offer a lot of different services, medical services and chiropractic services, so it is all familiar territory, and has been great,' he said. 'Dr. Brockman and I both have a sports medicine background, and that has added to the smoothness of the transition as well, I think.' He and his wife, Kelley, live in Reo, Indiana. They are blessed with 5 boys: J.R., Dean, Tucker & Cooper (twins), and Benny. Kelley is a wedding coordinator. Her business is Kelley James Events, and the website is: https://www.kelleyjamesevents. com/. Nathan and his family are very active in their community, and in their spare time enjoy motorcycle racing at different racing tracks in the tri-state area. title: Betty Lambert-Hayes
description: Betty Lee Lambert-Hayes, 82, passed away suddenly on March 11, 2024 after a long fought battle with cancer.
content: Betty Lee Lambert-Hayes, 82, passed away suddenly on March 11, 2024 after a long fought battle with cancer. She was born in Hancock County in 1942 to the late Eva-Lee and Dawson Lambert. Betty grew up on a farm in Gatewood with her parents and two brothers. It was there she learned the value of family, hard work, and developed her love of gardening. She graduated from Daviess County High School, attended college, and began a career in manufacturing in northern Indiana. After becoming a mother of two, she returned to Gatewood and began working at Swedish Match and ended her career by retiring from Commonwealth Aluminum. Betty was a devoted daughter, mother, sister, and Ma'maw. She tended to her mother and father until their passing. She enjoyed traveling and sightseeing along the back country roads with her children and grandchildren. Her main hobby was tending to her elaborate flower garden. It was there she would nurture each plant, watch the hummingbirds, and listen to the melodies of many other birds as they begged for a piece of cheese. She was survived by her brothers Glenn (Kaye) and Jurleow (Marlene) Lambert. Children Anita and Rick (Michele) Boyles. Grandchildren April Nichole Flake, Daniel Eversole, Zachary (Kasey) Eversole, Dakota Browning, Dalton (Kiersten) Moore, and Max and Jack Boyles. Great grand children Brennan Flake, Elijah, Ian, Oliver, Able, Romie Avalee Eversole, Ayden Browning, Maylynn, and Joslynn Moore. Great-great grandchildren Atticus and Ezra Flake. Private graveside services will be held on Monday, March 18, 2024. Visitation will be held at Gibson & Son Funeral Home, Lewisport Chapel on Sunday, March 17, 2024 from 2 pm until 4 pm. Expressions of sympathy may take the form of donations to Owensboro Botanical Gardens 2731 West 2nd Street Owensboro, KY 42301 or online at www.wkbg.org/donate.html. Share your memories and condolences with her family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Castle wins at Vastwood Park
description: Ava Riggs rips a double for the Lady Hornets during the team's loss to Castle High School here Tuesday. The Lady Hornet softball team took their first loss of the season when they fell 16-0 in three…
content: Ava Riggs rips a double for the Lady Hornets during the team's loss to Castle High School here Tuesday. The Lady Hornet softball team took their first loss of the season when they fell 16-0 in three innings to Castle High School (Indiana) here Tuesday. Hancock County is now 3-1. The powerhouse Knights led off the first inning with a double and a line drive single before Lily Roberts struck out the next two batters. Roberts got two quick strikes on the next batter and it appeared that Hancock County might get out of the inning unharmed. But, Sadie Winslett connected for a fly ball off the end of her bat. The ball fell in play and two runs scored for the Knights. It was all Castle after that as the visitors plated seven runs in the first inning and eight in the second. The game was called after three due to the 15-run rule. HCHS coach Dwayne Wroe talked about the game. 'I knew how good they were and we're not totally healthy yet. We had some bad luck in the first inning. With two outs the girl hit a flare that lands about a foot fair or we could have gotten out of the inning. Instead they got seven runs with two outs and it snowballed from there. 'I put in some young kids to get them some experience on the mound. We're trying to ease Lily back in with some innings to get geared up for All 'A'. Roberts was tagged with the loss on the hill while allowing eight runs (three earned) on six hits, with two Ks and three walks in one inning of work. Rayleigh French allowed seven runs (one earned) on five hits, with no walks in 0.2 frames, and Jordyn Waltrip allowed one run on three hits, with no walks over one inning. Gigi Lynch was the winning pitcher for Castle. She allowed one hit, with six Ks and one walk. Ava Riggs smacked a double for Hancock County's only hit. 'After the game I asked the girls what we did in the fourth game last year and nobody knew. I don't remember either so we'll just move on,' Wroe said. The Lady Hornets face a tough Apollo team Thursday then Meade and Ohio County next week before heading to Florida for their annual Spring Break trip. By Steve Wimmer

title: HC Democrat Party Selects Candidate for Lewisport Magistrate Seat
description: The HC Democrat Party selected Darrell Wall as their candidate at their executive meeting Monday. Wall will hold office...
content: In lieu of John Garner resigning from the Lewisport District (Dist. 1) Magistrate seat to serve as an SRO for NHES, the HC Democrat Party selected Darrell Wall as their candidate at their executive meeting Monday. Wall will hold office, as the Governor appointed candidate, until a candidate is elected at the General Election on November 5th, 2024. The newly elected individual in Nov. will take office immediately and fill the unexpired term. HC Republican Party The HC Republican Party met on Monday as well, but haven't yet selected their candidate to run against the Dem candidate in November. They will meet again on April 16th, as the executive committee needs more time to interview the candidates. Their chairperson resigned and they did elect Brad Gregory as the new chair. Independent Independent Candidates may pick up the nomination forms at the Clerk's office. The nomination form must be submitted by the June 4th, 2024 filing deadline to be voted on in November. Write-Ins Any qualified individual may run as a write-in candidate as long as they file a declaration on intent in the Clerk's office by October 25th. Their name will not appear on the ballot. It will be up to the voter to write the candidate's name on the ballot next to the coordinating office. Only votes for candidates who have filed the proper write-in filing paper will be counted.

title: Hwy 60 widening to resume April 3rd – Expect traffic delays & lane closures
description: Yager Materials in Owensboro was contracted by the KY Transportation Cabinet to widen Hwy 60 from just east of the entrance at Vastwood.
content: Yager Materials in Owensboro was contracted by the KY Transportation Cabinet to widen Hwy 60 from just east of the entrance at Vastwood Park to 1957, and work started in mid-April of last year. Traffic returned to a 4-lane and resumed normal patterns beginning Thursday, November 9th, 2023 due to weather and temperature variances, and starting on Wednesday night, April 3rd, Hwy 60 will go back to a 2-lane and work will resume. Work will occur daily from Wednesday, April 3rd through Monday, September 30th, between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m. The project will stretch from milepost 4.5 at John Pate Road to milepost 9.6 at KY 3101. Both westbound lanes will be closed until the work is completed. The passing lane on the eastbound side will be used for westbound traffic. Anticipate Delays/Adhere to Posted Signage KYTC Highway District 2 advises motorists to plan their routes accordingly, anticipate delays and adhere to all posted signage and instructions within the work zone. The work will involve removal and repairing of existing roadway, widening measures to accommodate increased traffic flow, and ensuring safer travel conditions. Traffic Advisories To receive traffic advisories and alerts for KYTC Highway District 2 counties via email, go to: https://public.govdelievery.com/accounts/KYTC/signup/13668. Click on the District 2 counties you regularly drive through or on any of the specialty corridors you travel. Confirm your subscription request when you receive the corresponding email message after signing up. The KYTC website is: https://transportation.ky.gov. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Carpet One Floor in Owensboro offers a promise; no cost for replacement
description: Carpet One in Owensboro is offering an incredible flooring promise, says owner Mark Hayden. 'The offer is called The Beautiful Guarantee, a limited on-time replacement warranty on Hardwood, Laminate,
content: Carpet One in Owensboro is offering an incredible flooring promise, says owner Mark Hayden. 'The offer is called The Beautiful Guarantee, a limited on-time replacement warranty on Hardwood, Laminate, and luxury vinyl flooring.' 'The promise is that you will love your Room-by-Room flooring, or we will replace it,' Hayden said. 'All Room by Room hardwood, laminate and luxury vinyl flooring products carry The Beautiful Guarantee, such that if at any time during your warranty period and after your floor is installed you wish to change your Room by Room floor to a different style or color, Carpet One Floor & Home will replace your existing Room-by-Room floor with another Room-by Room flooring product of your choice, subject to the Beautiful Guarantee terms.' To whom does The Beautiful Guarantee apply? 'The Beautiful Guarantee applies to the original purchaser of the Room by Room flooring product at the original installation site only, but does not apply to subsequent owners or renters of the Room by Room floor, or the residence in which such flooring product was installed.' The Beautiful Guarantee begins at the time your Room-by-Room flooring product has been fully installed. The length of your warranty depends on the level of warranty,' he added. 'It depends on which flooring product you purchased. For example; one diamond, two diamond or a three diamond flooring product.' 'If you wish to replace your Room-by-Room floor under The Beautiful Guarantee, then you need to call us within the applicable warranty period, and indicate you want to choose another Room by Room hardwood, laminate or luxury vinyl flooring product.' No Additional Cost for replacement Hayden states The Beautiful Guarantee allows you to replace your existing Room by Room floor with another Room by Room hardwood, laminate or luxury vinyl flooring product of equal or lesser value at no additional cost to you. If your new Room by Room floor happens to cost less than your originally selected floor however, you will not be entitled to a refund of the difference in cost. 'If you wish to replace your Room by Room laminate floor with a Room by Room hardwood floor, or a more expensive laminate Room by Room product, you will be required to pay the difference in cost for the upgraded flooring product,' he said. 'Additionally, you will have to pay the difference in cost in the event of a potential price increase of your originally chosen Room by Room flooring product during your warranty period. Replacement of your floor under The Beautiful Guarantee includes materials and labor (removal of old floor, disposal and re-installation of your new floor),' said Hayden. For all the coverage details on this guarantee, contact Carpet One in Owensboro at 270-685-5735.
