title: Conservation budgets increased; Hancock previously had lowest extension budget in Kentucky
description: It was reported at a recent Hancock County Fiscal Court Meeting that Hancock County has had the lowest extension budget in the w
content: It was reported at a recent Hancock County Fiscal Court Meeting that Hancock County has had the lowest extension budget in the whole state. The Division of Conservation provides assistance to 121 conservation districts for conservation programs across the state. Conservation budgets have now been increased, including a 2 percent raise mandated from University of Kentucky. The extension budget increased from $105K to $112K. UK pays for two agents, the 4-H and Ag Extensions. They pay all of the salary and the county provides the office spaces and phones. The others are paid for by Kentucky State University. 'The Soil Conservation budget is $78K,' Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts said, 'that's up $4,500 from last year. Both budgets went up.' Resolution A resolution was approved by the court that the governing bodies of Meade, Breckinridge and Hancock Counties, pursuant to KRS 65.210, have the power to enter into agreements in order to provide for the use of property on the basis of mutual advantage to provide services and facilities in a manner pursuant to governmental organizations that will accord the best geographic, economic, population and other factors that includes the needs and development of local communities. Crumb-Rubber Grant The Court approved a grant application process that, if awarded, will be applied for crumb-rubber product for curbs at Vastwood in Hawesville, for safety at the park. They'll be requesting that the KY Energy & Environment Cabinet Div. of Waste Management provide assistance under the Crumb Rubber/Tire-Derived Products Grant. Documents and agreements must be executed in association with grant funding and implementation of projects. Recycling Grant The court is applying for a grant to replace 6 of the recycling trailers that are in bad condition. They are replaced regularly. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Getting to know you; Aldridge & Aldridge Celebrates 48 Years
description: Joe Lee & Sandy Aldridge are celebrating 48 years in business this month, and Aldridge & Aldridge was awarded as Chamber Business of the Month. Joe Lee & Sandy Aldridge are celebrating 48 years in…
content: Joe Lee & Sandy Aldridge are celebrating 48 years in business this month, and Aldridge & Aldridge was awarded as Chamber Business of the Month. Joe Lee & Sandy Aldridge are celebrating 48 years in business this month, and were awarded Hancock County Chamber of Commerce March Business of the Month. They began Aldridge & Aldridge Accounting in 1976 in their home office in Hawesville. Joe Lee said their home office, to begin with, was essentially at their dining room table. They then moved their office to where it is located now, at 440 Main Street in downtown Hawesville, and rented half of the building. 'We bought the old Ogle's Grocery building and moved in there next,' he said. 'Then, we bought this building and moved back. The business just kept growing and, finally, the whole building came up for sale and we bought it and expanded.' Joe Lee & Sandy have been married 57 years. 'We were in high school together and I was a year ahead of her in school. We started dating, got married and we have worked hard,' Joe Lee said. 'I worked in an accounting firm in Indiana for 4 years. I started this one and I kind of just drug Sandy into it. She's been in it ever since. It's been good.' They both want to thank the community for 48 years of great clients. 'We haven't made too many people mad,' Joe Lee said jokingly. 'I always say, ‘I'm only as good as my last refund.' We've enjoyed it. We look forward to another year – one year at a time. We've met a lot of nice people. I've got good people working with me. We couldn't begin to do what we do without them. All of our office staff, all through these years has been really good. Good people, I'd hire them all back tomorrow.' They have raised 3 children in Hancock County, Tina, Beth and Darrin. Their son Darrin now lives in Boonville, IN. He said, 'Taxes and Tax Season are not something many people look forward to every year, but it is one of the two things that are ‘said to be certain in this world', per Benjamin Franklin. Service to the community Dad and Mom, and their many other employees over the years at A&A have provided a service to our community where families can feel at ease that their tax filing requirements are met. Starting your own business can have its ups and downs, but their partnership and patience has kept the business going strong! Their dedication to their customers and the community have set the bar high for great service.' Their daughter Beth (Aldridge) Schirmer now resides in Mississippi. She said, 'They love their community. I don't know any other couple that has poured blood, sweat and tears into their careers and Hancock County for as long as they have. You just cannot put a price on the amount of trust they have built with each individual client that has come across those office thresholds the past 50 years. A&A has shown us what a business built on knowledge, rapport and most importantly, integrity, looks like. My wish for them both is that they are able to retire and enjoy their hobbies during the remaining years that God graces them with.' Their eldest daughter, HC Chamber Executive Director and Director of HC Public Libraries Tina Snyder said, 'They have put their heart, soul and time into the business and serving the community for many years. They say that behind every great man is an even better woman. Mom is his rock, supporter, partner and encourager.Together, they have made their business successful in Hancock County. Outside of the office, Dad is engaged in his tractor hobby as a leader and as a participant. He's gained many friendships while on his tractor rides. It's a hobby that truly makes him happy. Mom enjoys reading, exploring nature while on vacations, embroidery and cross stitch. Once the busiest time of tax season is over, they will take a breath and get away for some much deserved rest and relaxation.' Joe Lee collects old tractors as a hobby and helps put on big 3-day tractor pulls in Mississippi and in Oak Grove, KY, usually for charities such as St. Jude's. He's been doing that for at least 10 years now, he said. Business Bureau Accredited Aldridge & Aldridge Accounting is Better Business Bureau Accredited and can be contacted via phone at (270) 927-6628 for pricing, hours, and to make an appointment. They are open Monday-Friday, and in summer months Monday-Thursday. A&A is closed on Saturdays and Sundays. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Waylon King
description: Waylon Knox King, 6, of Lewisport, KY left his earthly home on March 31, 2024, at Norton's Children Hospital in Louisville, KY.
content: Waylon Knox King, 6, of Lewisport, KY left his earthly home on March 31, 2024, at Norton's Children Hospital in Louisville, KY. Waylon may not have been on this earth for many years, but he made a big impact on the people that knew him. He was in many ways a typical boy; he loved riding his bike, visiting and playing with his friends, stuffed animals, and maybe not so typical he enjoyed axes and manchettes. He would help his dad chop wood and once missed the wood and hit his leg. He would ask his friends if they had ever been hit with an axe and he would state that he had. Typical of a young boy, he also liked BB guns, stuffed animals and playing Pokémon. Some of the people that he made an impact on are his parents; Bradley and Ashley King of Lewisport; sisters, Kayleigh, Rylee and Addison King, all of Lewisport; paternal grandfather, John 'Papa' King of Lewisport; maternal grandparents Charlotte Whorley and Mitchelle Board of Cloverport; several aunts, uncle, cousins and anyone else that had the pleasure of interacting with Waylon. Waiting for Waylon to join her is the his late grandmother Lola Dunn. A celebration of his life will be held 1:00 pm, Monday, April 9, 2024, with Bro. Jonathan White officiating at Cloverport Funeral Home. A burial will follow at Cloverport Cemetery. The family will receive friends and family from 10:00 am until service time. Cloverport Funeral Home is honored to assist the family of Waylon Knox King during this very difficult time.

title: Roberts blasts homer, Lewko throws strong in 9-4 win
description: Jack Roberts drives in a run during the win over Henderson then went 4 for 4 with a home run in a victory over McLean County Thursday. Jack Roberts hit a 3-run home run and Dec Lewko did not allow a…
content: Jack Roberts drives in a run during the win over Henderson then went 4 for 4 with a home run in a victory over McLean County Thursday. Jack Roberts hit a 3-run home run and Dec Lewko did not allow a base hit during the Hornets' 9-4 come-from-behind win over McLean County at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown Field Thursday. The Cougars came out swinging and scored three first inning runs. They added another in the second and the score was 4-0 in favor of the visitors. Brock Tindle walked and scored on a passed ball in the second and the boys closed to within two runs in the third when Roberts singled and scored on an RBI hit by Carson Clark. Dec Lewko was on the mound for the Hornets and the junior struck out two and got a ground out to end the fourth. Hancock County took the lead in the home half of the fourth on RBI hits by Roberts, Louden Fluharty and Clark. The Hornets led 6-4 when Roberts ripped the home run shot in the fifth. Jacob Shultz and Lewko were on base at the time and the three runs gave HCHS a comfortable 9-4 advantage. Lewko had the bases loaded in the sixth but got two ground ball outs to maintain the five run lead. McLean County went down 1-2-3 in the seventh. Lewko got the win in relief while allowing no runs on no hits, with eight Ks and three walks over 5.2 innings pitched. Kolby Keown allowed four runs (three earned) on three hits, with three Ks and three walks in 1.1 innings. Roberts was 4 for 4 at the plate with the home run and four RBI. Carter Lyday was 2 for 3, Clark was 2 for 4 with two RBI, Fluharty was 2 for 4 with one RBI, and Lewko was 1 for 3. Jordan Payne was 0 for 2 with one RBI, Shultz was 0 for 2 with two runs scored and Tindle and Keown each scored a run. Shultz, Clark and Keegan Wilson all stole one base each. Graves County Graves County plated 12 runs in the fourth inning during a 17-4 win over Hancock County at Ft. Walton Beach, Florida Sunday. Roberts doubled and scored on a base hit by Clark in the first inning and Tindle and Dylan Mucker followed with RBI base hits. The Hornets led 3-0 before Graves County battled back with a run in the second and four more in the third. Tindle pulled Hancock to withing one run when he knocked in Payne in the third. Graves County blew the game open in the fourth with 12 runs on eight hits. The game was called after five inning via run rule. Tindle was 2 for 2 at the plate with two RBI. Clark was 1 for 1 with one RBI, Kaleb Severs was 1 for 1, Payne was 1 for 2, Mucker was 1 for 3 with one RBI, Lewko and Roberts were both 1 for 3. Payne, Fluharty, Noah Keown and Wilson all pitched for Hancock County. Calisle (Ohio) banged out 12 hits during a 15-0 win in five innings at Ft. Walton Beach Monday. Severs was 1 for 1 at the plate for the Hornets. Lewko and Mucker both went 1 for 2. Tindle allowed six runs (one earned) on five hits, with four Ks and no walks over two innings pitched. Lane Dixon and Shultz pitched in relief. Hopkinsville The Hornets played another tough team when they fell 10-0 to Hopkinsville Tuesday. The Hancock County defense held the Tigers to three runs through five innings until Hopkinsville broke loose with seven runs in the sixth. The Hornets did not score in the home half of the inning and the game was called via run rule. Clark was 1 for 1 at the plate. Roberts and Payne both went 1 for 3. Keown allowed eight runs (six earned) on four hits, with four Ks and six walks over five innings pitched. Fluharty allowed two runs (none earned) on two hits, with two Ks and one walk in one inning of relief. By Steve Wimmer

title: Tommy Dean Hunt
description: Tommy Dean Hunt passed away Tuesday April 2, 2024, in Owensboro, KY surrounded by his loving family, including six of his grandchildren. He was born August 3, 1944, to the late Theodore and Elsie…
content: Tommy Dean Hunt passed away Tuesday April 2, 2024, in Owensboro, KY surrounded by his loving family, including six of his grandchildren. He was born August 3, 1944, to the late Theodore and Elsie Hunt. He grew up in Masonville, KY, lived in Maceo, KY and spent the last 20 years or so in Lewisport, KY. Never meeting a stranger, Tommy made many great friends along the way who he always enjoyed stopping to catch up with. Tommy served his country in the Marine Corp during Vietnam. He spent 6 years working for Carpenter Local 549 and then the rest of his working career working as a boilermaker out of Boilermakers Local 40 retiring in 2001. After retirement he continued to work in his shop, not only welding but repairing anything that would show up. Continuing this right up to his passing, he enjoyed a good challenge and helping others while doing it. He also served his community on the Hancock Planning and Zoning Board and Board of Adjustments. Tommy enjoyed fishing most of all not only with a host of great friends, but also with his wife. Some of his favorite spots were Guntersville Lake, Lake Barkley, and KY Lake. He also enjoyed riding his Harley, gardening, being outside or in the shop and helping anyone in the family on their latest home project or renovation. He was a lifelong blood donor and was always willing to help someone in need. Anyone that knew him would tell you there wasn't anything he couldn't do or fix. Tommy was preceded in death by a brother Joffrey Hunt, sister Violet Potts and niece Darlene Hendrick. He is survived by his companion of 40 years, Gayla Robertson Hunt of Lewisport; four sons, Adam (Holly) Hunt of Hawesville, Blake (Ami) Hunt of Lewisport, Wayne Hall of Owensboro and Brandon (Natali) Hall of Knottville; a host of grandchildren; and great-grandchildren who loved to visit 'Papaw' up on the hill; mother-in-law, Mary Woodward of Owensboro; and several nieces and nephews. He is also survived by his beloved dog 'Buddy', and cats, Mister, Tomboy and Lucy. The funeral service for Tommy will be 10 AM Saturday at Glenn Funeral Home and Crematory. Visitation will be Friday from 3 PM until 7 PM **(with Boiler Maker Rights at 6:30PM) and Saturday, 9 AM until time of service at the funeral home. Burial will follow at Owensboro Memorial Gardens. In lieu of flowers, the family requests donations be made to Hospice and Palliative Care of Western Kentucky, 3419 Wathens Crossing Owensboro, KY 42301 or The American Diabetes Association, P.O. Box 7023 Merrifield, VA 22116-7023. Memories and condolences for the family of Tommy Hunt may be left at www.glenncares.com

title: Mary Robbins Davis
description: Mary Robbins Davis, 84, passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by her family and returned to our Heavenly Father on April 6, 2024. Mary was born on April 11, 1939, in Hawesville, Kentucky to…
content:
Mary Robbins Davis, 84, passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by her family and returned to our Heavenly Father on April 6, 2024. Mary was born on April 11, 1939, in Hawesville, Kentucky to Catherine & John Robbins and had three siblings. At the age of 17, she met the love of her life and soulmate, Floyd Davis,
and wed on August 10, 1957. They were married for nearly 60 years until his passing on April 19, 2017. Upon marriage they moved to Arlington, Virginia, where Floyd was in the US Army. After the birth of their son, they moved to Jeffersontown, Kentucky, where they had two daughters.
and wed on August 10, 1957. They were married for nearly 60 years until his passing on April 19, 2017. Upon marriage they moved to Arlington, Virginia, where Floyd was in the US Army. After the birth of their son, they moved to Jeffersontown, Kentucky, where they had two daughters. While raising her children, she was a thrifty and creative homemaker, school crossing guard, and retail associate at Bacon's. Mary always loved hosting family holidays; cooking and feeding everyone. She enjoyed sewing, camping, square dancing, playing cards and Dominoes, her Card Clubs, and talking on the phone. She was a strong inquisitive woman who wasn't afraid to speak her mind. She loved to laugh, tell jokes, read the newspaper and books (her favorite was the Bible). She was a previous member of Southeast Christian Church for many years and currently a member of West Broadway Baptist Church.
Upon retirement, she and Floyd were fortunate to travel extensively, creating many great memories and wonderful friendships. She never met a stranger and was loved by all. Everyone was always welcome at her home. In more recent years, she came to love 'porch therapy' with her special neighbors.
Her greatest accomplishments were being a wife, mother, and being 'Two Mom' to her grandchildren.
She is survived by her three loving children Barry Davis, Lynn Nuxol (John), and Gina Lutes; son-in-law, Mike Lutes; sister, Patsy Young, brother, Logan Robbins (Linda) as well as nieces, nephews, and many wonderful friends. She was most proud of her grandchildren and loved them so very much, Ashley Robinson (Brent); Nicole Talley (Eric), Jason Nuxol (Sarah); Sean Lutes (Whitney), Sarah St. Clair (Eddie), Emily Lutes (fiancé, Philly Thompson); step grandchild, Amy McKiernan (Cary), and great grandchildren, Parker, Erin, Noah, & Raegan Robinson, Archibald Lutes, Eva & Peter St. Clair, and Jack & Lyla McKiernan.
A special thank you to Hosparus Health for their support in her final weeks. Visitation from 2-8pm on Friday April 12, 2024, Owen Funeral Home –Jeffersontown, 9318 Taylorsville Road. Funeral Service at 12:00pm on Saturday April 13, 2024, at Owen Funeral Home. A private family burial will be at a later date in Breckenridge County.
In lieu of flowers, memorial gifts may be made to Hosparus Health or The ALS Association.

title: Roberts throws no-hitter on spring break trip
description: Lily Roberts fires a pitch for the Lady Hornets during the All 'A' regional at Whitesville Tuesday. The senior struck out 17 batters during the 8-0 win. Roberts also threw a no-hitter during a 3-0 win…
content:
Lily Roberts fires a pitch for the Lady Hornets during the All 'A' regional at Whitesville Tuesday. The senior struck out 17 batters during the 8-0 win. Roberts also threw a no-hitter during a 3-0 win over Franklin Simpson while on the spring break trip to Florida.
Lily Roberts threw a complete game no-hitter during the Lady Hornets' 3-0 win over Franklin Simpson on Friday at Ft. Walton Beach, Florida.
Hancock County grabbed a 1-0 lead in the first inning on a sacrifice fly. Baylee Estes singled then stole second and third base before coming home.
Roberts was striking out batters left and right and the Lady Hornets plated two insurance runs in the fourth.
Ella House led off the frame with a triple and Roberts followed with an RBI hit. Carolina Jones entered the game as a courtesy runner. She later scored on a wild pitch and the girls led 3-0.
Roberts and the HCHS defense did the job from there and the Lady Hornets completed their spring break trip with a win.
Roberts allowed no runs on no hits, with 15 Ks and one walk over seven innings pitched. Roberts was 1 for 2 at the plate with one RBI, and Layni Roberts was 1 for 2. House was 1 for 3 with the triple, and Audrey Carnes was 1 for 3 with a double. Estes was 1 for 3.
Lafayette Hancock County fell 13-2 to Lafayette last Thursday. It was the only loss the Lady Hornets suffered during their trip to Florida.
Kylie Westerfield smacked an RBI triple in the second inning and later scored on a hit by House. Lafayette tied the score in the third then plated eight runs in the fourth. Three more in the fifth and the game was called via run rule.
Lily Roberts allowed one run (none earned) on three hits, with four Ks and no walks in two innings pitched. Jordyn Waltrip allowed nine runs (two earned) on seven hits, with one walk over 1.2 frames. Ryleigh French allowed three runs (none earned) on three hits during 1.1 innings on the mound.
North Laurel Kylie Westerfield had three hits and Lily Roberts allowed just one run during a 4-1 victory over North Laurel on April 2nd at Ft. Walton Beach.
A 2-run hit by Westerfield scored Estes and Emmalynn Higdon in the second inning. The Lady Hornets went ahead 3-0 in the fifth when Westerfield scored from third base on an error by the North
Laurel catcher.
Laurel catcher. North Laurel plated their lone run in the sixth and they had a runner at third when Roberts secured the third out via strikes.
Aubree Mosby gave HCHS an insurance run when she scored on a wild pitch in the seventh. Roberts got two more Ks and a pop up to House at second to end the game.
Roberts allowed one run on four hits, with 12 Ks and one walk over seven frames. Westerfield was 3 for 4 at the plate with two RBI. Carnes was 1 for 3.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Boys fall to Aces in All 'A' regional
description: Dylan Mucker makes a snow cone catch as a Catholic baserunner gets back safely at second base during the Aces' 6-1 win over the Hornets in the All 'A' regional played at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown…
content:
Dylan Mucker makes a snow cone catch as a Catholic baserunner gets back safely at second base during the Aces' 6-1 win over the Hornets in the All 'A' regional played at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown Field Monday.
Owensboro Catholic broke open a close game with three runs in the fifth inning then went on to win 6-1 over Hancock County during the All 'A' regional at Vastwood Park Monday.
The Hornets grabbed the lead in the first inning when Dylan Mucker was hit by a wild pitch with the bases loaded. Louden Fluharty, who was also hit by pitch, scored on the play.
Brock Tindle was on the mound for HCHS and the senior struck out Brady Atwell to end the first inning. The Aces tied the score when a run scored on a defensive error in the second.
The Hornets looked to go back in front when Jack Roberts and Fluharty led off the third with back-to-back hits. Catholic got out of trouble with a double-play before Roberts was tagged out at home trying to steal.
The Aces took the lead with a run in the third, and Mason Moser did real damage with a 2-run hit in the fifth.
Tindle allowed five runs (four earned) on four hits, with five Ks and three walks over five innings. Dec Lewko allowed one run on two hits, with two Ks and one walk in one inning of relief.
Fluharty and Kolby Keown were 1 for 2 at the plate for Hancock. Roberts was 1 for 3.
Logan County Logan County plated eight runs in the sixth inning during a 9-4 win over Hancock County at Ft. Walton Beach Thursday. The Hornets took a 2-0 lead on Kolby Keown's 2-run triple in the fourth inning.
Jordan Payne and Carson Clark scored on the play.
Logan County countered with a run in the home half of the same frame, but Lewko helped put HCHS back ahead by two runs with a leadoff triple in the fifth. Jack Roberts followed with an RBI single and the score was 3-1.
The game changed in the sixth. The Cougars utilized four hits and three walks to bring in eight runs. Clark knocked in a run for the Hornets in the seventh before the third out was recorded.
Lewko allowed nine runs (four earned) on six hits, with six Ks and three walks over 5.1 innings pitched. Noah Keown allowed no hits or runs, with one K in 0.2 innings of relief.
Keown was 1 for 2 with the triple and two RBI, Clark was 1 for 3 with one RBI, Payne was 1 for 3 with a triple, Roberts was 1 for 3 with one RBI, Lewko was 1 for 4 with a triple and Dylan Mucker was 1 for 4.
Anderson County The Hornets saw a 5-0 lead disappear during an 11-5 loss to Anderson County in the final game played on the spring break trip to Florida.
Roberts ripped an RBI hit to score Lewko in the first inning before the offense produced five straight hits in the third.
Roberts, Payne and Louden Fluharty all had singles then Clark banged a line drive triple. Mucker followed with a base hit and the score was 5-0 in favor of Hancock County. The Bearcats countered with five runs in the bottom of the third and suddenly the game was tied.
Anderson County added two more runs in the fourth and four in the fifth. The Hornets had base runners in the fifth through seventh frames but were unable to bring any home.
Fluharty allowed five runs (one earned) on five hits, with three Ks and one walk in three innings pitched. Keegan Wilson allowed four runs (two earned) on no hits, with one K and three walks through one inning. Noah Keown allowed two runs (none earned) on two hits, with one walk in two innings of work.
Fluharty was 2 for 3 at the plate with a triple. Mucker was 2 for 3 with a triple and one RBI, Roberts was 2 for 4 with one RBI, Clark was 1 for 4 with a triple and one RBI, and Lewko was 1 for 4.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Noah Abbott Organized Give-A-Dog-A-Ball Event at HC Animal Shelter Raising $275
description: Noah Abbott (13), of Hawesville, hosted the Give-A-Dog-A-Ball Event at the Hancock County Animal Shelter on Saturday, April 6th.
content:
Connor Stewart, Sadie Bloyd and Skylar Stewart playing with one of the dogs, 'Bubba', at the HC Animal Shelter Event Saturday. The event was organized by 13-year-old Noah Abbott, of Hawesville. 'Bubba' has been at the shelter for quite a while. He played well with everyone, even a two-year-old child!
Noah Abbott (13), of Hawesville, hosted the Give-A-Dog-A-Ball Event at the Hancock County Animal Shelter on Saturday, April 6th and raised donations totaling $275. All of the money collected went to Shelter Supporters of Hancock County, who go above and beyond to provide medical care for the dogs who are brought in that may have more costly issues.
The event was Noah's idea and held from 8 a.m. until noon. All who wanted to participate called and set up a time so that everyone would each have plenty of quality time in the play yards with the dogs. Some guests donated $5 to walk the dogs after play time.
Noah served creative refreshments to everyone attending. He served lemonade from a cute fire hydrant, 'Scooby Snacks' and 'Puppy Chow' from dog dishes, as well as paw print themed cupcakes.
He also made 'Rate-Your-Date' cards for each participant to fill out after they played with the dogs, to share with the community so they can get to know the dogs better and, hopefully, get some of them adopted into new homes. The HC Animal Shelter has been full to capacity for some time now and this was a great idea to help them get noticed and adopted.
Noah recently started volunteering at the shelter. How his idea first came about for this event is, one day as he and his mom, Tiffany, were driving home from the shelter he said to her, 'I just love all of them and I wanna help.'
'He said he wanted to right all of the wrongs in the world,' Tiffany explained. 'I told him he may not be able to right all of the wrongs, and he cut me off and said, ‘Yeah, but I can try.'' So Noah spoke to Hancock County Animal Shelter Director Ronnie York and asked him if he could have the event that he had this idea for at the shelter.
'Mr. York was as excited as Noah was,' Tiffany said. 'With the help of volunteers Cindy Atkinson and Coleen Garcia, and a little help from his dad, Josh, and I, Noah was able to host an amazing event. We had seventeen people attend the event, lots of treats and toys were brought in, as well the donations.
He is a great kid and loves to help his community any way he can. In the past, he has raised funds to help his former elementary school's FRYSC (Family Resource Youth Services Center).
He has collected stuffed animals for the HC Courthouse to give to children who may be a little nervous while being in the courtroom. He has donated part of his profits from a lemonade stand to an individual in a neighboring county who was battling cancer. He also recently started speaking at schools and parent support groups about what life on the (autism) spectrum is like.
Once he gets an idea in his head, he is pretty steadfast in seeing it through. That's how the event at the shelter came to be. He really is a great kid. When Noah was diagnosed with autism at age three, we were told he would never speak.'
Josh & Tiffany will be celebrating 15 years of marriage in September. Josh is the Infrastructure (IT) Manager for Commonwealth Rolled Products. They are blessed with 5 children; four are adults now. Noah is their youngest and is homeschooled.
The couple also work together on the home business they began last year in September – Tiffany's Timeless Treasures, located in their home at 1570 St. Rte. 1389. They are open Monday-Friday, noon-6:00 p.m., and appointments can also be scheduled on weekends. The phone number is: 270-702-6557. The website is https://tiffanystt.com/.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Refined Cane Sugar
description: Refined sugar (white granulated sugar/table sugar) is sugar cane, and sometimes sugar beet, that has been refined, stripped of molasses and most
content:
Refined sugar (white granulated sugar/table sugar) is sugar cane, and sometimes sugar beet, that has been refined, stripped of molasses and most all nutrients.
Many white and brown sugars that are made from cane are bleached using bone char. What is bone char? It is produced by charring animal bones, primarily cattle and pigs.
Refined sugar digests very quickly and therefore can cause insulin and blood sugar levels to spike up. Powdered sugar (confectioner's sugar) is actually 3 percent cornstarch (an anti-clumping agent).
Many brown sugars are white granulated sugar with molasses mixed back in. Most all brown sugars you find at the grocery store are highly refined and processed. Turbinado sugar is raw cane sugar with the surface molasses removed. There are some unrefined brown sugars, such as Sucanat (SUgar CAne NATural – SU-CA-NAT). Then there is natural, dark brown molasses unrefined cane sugar and dark muscovado brown sugar.
Before purchasing your brown sugar next time, if you insist on using it for certain recipes, do your research and choose one that is truly natural and unrefined. As for refined cane sugar, I recommend that you stop using it and stop eating foods and beverages that contain it. That goes for high-fructose corn syrup too!
Negative Side Effects Refined cane sugar has a long list of negative side effects, including but certainly not limited to: fluid retention, hyperactivity, tooth decay & gum disease, anxiety, depression, lowered immune system, raised cholesterol, weakened eyesight, fatty liver, headaches, migraines, emphysema, weight gain, obesity, kidney disease, yeast infection, gallstones, kidney stones, arthritis & joint pain (inflammatory), asthma, coronary heart disease, appendicitis, osteoporosis, decreased HGH (human growth hormone), destroys gut health/interferes with optimal digestion, worsens skin conditions, and an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease, hypoglycemia & diabetes.
Refined Sugar Alternatives Local, organic, sustainably harvested honey is a great substitute for sugar and you can manage to use it for just about anything in place of sugar, including baking. With baking, there are many recipes that use honey as well as ways to substitute honey for sugar and keep the correct dry/wet ratio. For instance, if the recipe calls for milk, you can substitute the honey in place of both the milk and the sugar. There is also a way with chocolatey sweet baked treats to compensate for the extra moisture honey adds to the batter – add some organic, raw cacao powder to balance the wet/dry ratio.
When substituting honey for sugar in your ice tea, for instance, first add a tablespoon or less of honey to warmed filtered water and stir, then add to your iced tea. This will help with the way that honey tends to glob up when it gets cold. You can also easily add honey to hot coffee to sweeten instead of cane sugar. The warmth of the coffee usually breaks the honey down easily and incorporates it into your morning beverage. It's great in hot tea as well.
Local honey is best because it also provides you with some armor before allergy season; it gets you accustomed to those pollens around you before they begin to stir up in allergy seasons. Also, honey is so much sweeter than sugar. Go easy! You will probably not use as much honey as you did sugar to get your desired sweetness.
I've written in previous columns about the dangers of sucralose and I recommend that you avoid completely all of those artificial sweeteners such as Splenda and Sweet'n Low. If you don't believe me, just stop using it completely as well as eliminating all beverages like diet sodas and foods that contain it, and then see how much better you feel! I bet your digestive challenges will cease, for one. (*See my column on the dangers of artificial sugars in the 12-1-2022 edition of The Clarion.)
Organic coconut palm sugar is another healthy alternative to refined cane sugar, and it can be purchased in a syrup as well. Also, organic stevia leaf/powder, organic sorghum molasses, organic blackstrap molasses and organic maple syrup, if purchased from a company with integrity, can be good choices. As far as monk fruit sweetener and others, I will be covering those in future columns. Agave nectar is questionably healthy, and so I recommend organic maple syrup instead.
Be Well and God Bless You!
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hancock County set to receive $10,242,000 for local improvements
description: On Thursday, April 17th, Representative Scott Lewis announced more than $10M in state funding returning to Hancock County to invest in roadways and essential infrastructure. 'I am proud to announce…
content:
On Thursday, April 17th, Representative Scott Lewis announced more than $10M in state funding returning to Hancock County to invest in roadways and essential infrastructure.
'I am proud to announce that after a long process, more than $10 million in state funding is coming back home to Hancock County,' said Lewis. 'Throughout this process, the legislature was able to develop an impactful yet fiscally responsible budget that will serve both our community and our commonwealth over the next two years.
State Road Plan The community will also see improvements in local roads, as the state road plan provides: $2.1M in FY25 to improve the connection between US-60 and Cannelton Bridge approach at Hawesville, $24K in FY25 to install guardrails on KY-261, $525K in FY24 and $5.25M in FY25 to pavement conditions on US-60, and $900K in FY25 and $1.25M in FY26 to widen US-60 from Lewisport to KY-1957.
'These investments into our roadways are also investments into our communities,' Lewis said. 'This funding will not only give more peace of mind to our drivers, but also provide a path to future opportunities for our district.'
Local Road Projects Lawmakers continued their efforts to ensure taxpayer dollars are invested in the best manner possible, changing the way the state provides funding for local road projects to ensure projects are awarded based on priority, rather than politics. House Joint Resolution 92 includes $193,000 for Hancock County – $22K in FY25 to resurface Old Mill Rd., and $171K in FY25 to resurface Crowe Rd.
'Representative Scott Lewis is an incredible advocate for his constituents,' said House Speaker David Osborne. 'Scott has worked tirelessly throughout the budget process to ensure that his district receives the funding it needs, all the while supporting our commonwealth's need for fiscal responsibility.'
Lawmakers adjourned the 2024 Regular Session on Monday, April 15, after passing more than 200 pieces of legislation that includes bills and resolutions aimed at strengthening educational opportunity, providing law enforcement with more tools, and investing in local communities to increase access to jobs. While the legislature will not reconvene to act on legislation until January of 2025, lawmakers will hold interim committee meetings throughout the year. These meetings will focus on monitoring how legislation is being implemented and researching issues for the next session.
For further information on the 2024 Regular Session or to learn more about the Kentucky General Assembly, visit legislature.ky.gov.

title: HC Rescue Squad Changing to Fire & Rescue
description: Hancock Clarion 1975: EMERGENCY SQUAD TAKING SHAPE—Fromleft, Rev. L.C. Garett, his son, Kendall Garrett, and Marvin Payne are principals in th
content:
Hancock Clarion 1975: EMERGENCY SQUAD TAKING SHAPE—From
left, Rev. L.C. Garett, his son, Kendall Garrett, and Marvin Payne are principals in the formation of the new Hancock County Rescue Squad. The squad will offer its services in case of tragedies or disaster. Already numbering about twenty-five members, the squad will hold an organizational meeting on Tuesday night, January 13, in the Circuit Courtroom of the Hancock County Courthouse.
left, Rev. L.C. Garett, his son, Kendall Garrett, and Marvin Payne are principals in the formation of the new Hancock County Rescue Squad. The squad will offer its services in case of tragedies or disaster. Already numbering about twenty-five members, the squad will hold an organizational meeting on Tuesday night, January 13, in the Circuit Courtroom of the Hancock County Courthouse. The Hancock County Rescue Squad, established in January of 1976, will now be changing over to HC Fire & Rescue. Their responsibilities will be assumed under the Volunteer Fire Department umbrella now, Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts said.
'Fire and Rescue will provide the same emergency services that they have always provided to our county,' Roberts added. 'Anyone that meets the volunteer fire department statutory requirements is welcome to apply. This streamlining update of departments will boost efficiency in regards to training and preparedness.
We are so blessed in our community to have the volunteers that we have in all departments. Our Fire and Rescue Department is filled with selfless individuals that put others ahead of themselves. We are thankful to have them.'
There are 17 members, and HC Rescue Squad Chief Kenny Stuart (52) has been with the squad since he was 18. His wife, Melinda (Wheatley) Stuart, has served on the squad for many years as well.
All of the HC Rescue Squad equipment that was housed at their one station in Hawesville will now be housed at the county's fire stations, including two sets of Jaws Of Life (JOL) with corresponding pumps, equipment for cutting & spreading, large & small hydraulic tool sets, various sizes of airbags for lifting, 2 trucks with battery set-up & power inverters, back boards, spine boards, 2 boats, sub-water flares, etc.
After the tragedy in Hancock County of two local 18-year-olds, Michael Couty and Leslie Baker, losing their lives when their vehicle went over a bridge on Middle Knottsville Road is when the County's squad first formed. The two teens were on their way to go bowling with friends.
Vice-Regent of Yellow Banks Chapter DAR Debra Owens is the late Michael Couty's sister. 'The Rescue Squad was created as a result of my brother's death,' she said. 'For years, we wondered why he passed away at such a young age, but then we realized his death was the sacrifice to save so many other lives because it caused the rescue squad to be created.'
Former HC Rescue Squad Chief Dennis Wheatley recalled how the squad was first organized saying, 'Jim Fallen was judge and he was quite ambitious about it. We had some help from Daviess County and different places to organize.
Cletus Garrett (Rev. L.C. Garrett) was probably the first chief. God allowed us to be a part of some of His miracles. We actually started to pray about what we were doing.'
The Hancock County Civil Defense Squad, as it was officially titled in the beginning, was established as an all-volunteer emergency organization serving the entire county. The very first emergency that the 33 original members responded to was a missing 14-year-old boy named David Sullivan on Sunday, February 15th, 1976.
Members enlisted the help of Kentuckiana Radio Emergency Action Citizens Team, Daviess County Rescue & Emergency Division and others, totaling over 300 rescue service members and individual volunteers, and successfully returned the boy to his family at 12:30 a.m., after he'd been lost in the woods for over 6 hours.
Unfortunately, there aren't as many rescue squads as there used to be across the Commonwealth of Kentucky because most of them have been absorbed into the fire departments.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Council decides to return City of Lewisport's first fire truck to HC Farm Museum
description: City Administrator Jason Roberts said everything is 'going as planned' for the 2024 Heritage Festival, at the Lewisport City Council meeting on Thursday, April 18th. The festival is scheduled for…
content:
City Administrator Jason Roberts said everything is 'going as planned' for the 2024 Heritage Festival, at the Lewisport City Council meeting on Thursday, April 18th. The festival is scheduled for Thursday, Friday & Saturday, May 30th, 31st and June 1st.
Roberts said the Heritage Festival Committee has made some changes on this year's t-shirts and on a couple of other details, in an effort to save a little extra money. All of the bands are booked: Randy Lanham on Thursday night, Blackford Creek on Friday night, and Josh Merritt & Lohden Boys – 2 bands on Saturday night.
Conexon Connect and Independence Bank are sponsoring fireworks for this year's festival and Yager Materials is sponsoring a tugboat and 2 barges to shoot them off the river. (*Full details will be in an upcoming edition of The Clarion.)
Lewisport's First Fire Truck Council members approved the decision to move Lewisport's very first fire truck back to the Hancock County Farm Museum. The truck was at the museum for several years until the museum committee asked for it to be moved to the Lewisport Volunteer Fire Department. The committee wanted to make room for an antique farm truck at that time.
The fire truck has been stored at the Lewisport fire station since, but they no longer have room for it. The Hancock County Rescue Squad has now been disbanded and the Lewisport Fire Dept. will be housing some of the equipment, including a boat, and they will need the extra room. (*See full article on the HC Rescue Squad in this edition of The Clarion.)
In the discussion to return the City's first fire truck to the HC Farm Museum, Councilwoman Josephine Hagan recalled the day when citizens first saw the truck. 'I can remember it was 1951 when they drove the fire truck into Lewisport,' Hagan said, 'and everybody stood out on the street like we had won the lottery.'
Police Dept. Report Lewisport Chief of Police Greg Linn reported the good news that Nick Jarboe, new Lewisport Police Officer who was injured during his police academy training last year, will be returning back to work without restrictions made on May 6th.
'He's been released from the doctor on that,' Linn said. 'We had firearms training earlier today. This past month we've had 38 calls for service. It's slowing down a little bit. Everything else is doing well.'
Public Works Update The Public Works crew has finished up the spring hydrant flushing and getting some of the hydrants fixed that weren't working well. Two new crew members took the pesticide test and passed, and the new truck recently purchased is doing very well.
Military Banners Councilman Kelly Vanover provided an update on the military banners that will be placed in downtown Lewisport. The City has around 12 now and they plan to purchase more in order to have approximately 30 total. They are durable and double sided, with a thank you to all of our veterans in active duty military as well as the City's logo.
Council members will be deciding on a uniform size and ordering them so they can be placed by Veterans Day this year. As soon as they get all of the details, Vanover said citizens will be able to submit information on local veterans they'd like featured on the banners. Each of the new banners they may order are estimated at around $80 each, and the company they will likely be ordering from is veteran owned.
Second Reading of Ordinance #24-1 City Attorney Charles Kamuf read aloud the second reading of Ordinance #24-1, an ordinance amending the City of Lewisport's Annual Budget for the Fiscal Year 7-1-2023 through 6-20-24.
Kamuf outlined what was previously reviewed and approved by council members, which included: the City's Gas Fund amended from $1,424,300 to $1,554,500; the Water Fund amended from $1,128,825 to $1,954,299; the Sewer Fund amended from $486K to $646,025; the Fire Dept. Fund remaining at $34K; the Parks Fund remaining at $5K, the Heritage Fund amended from $34,300 to $37,800; the Municipal Fund remaining at $6K, and the American Relief Fund remaining at $66,075; with Total Assets of $5,779,162, and estimated fund balances at the end of the year at $46,641.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Lady Hornets are Class 'A' state runners-up
description: The HCHS Lady Hornets softball team poses with the All 'A' state runner-up plaque after going 5-1 during two days of action last weekend. Pictured front row from left: Lily Roberts, Layni Roberts,…
content:
The HCHS Lady Hornets softball team poses with the All 'A' state runner-up plaque after going 5-1 during two days of action last weekend. Pictured front row from left: Lily Roberts, Layni Roberts, Kylie Westerfield, Emmalynn Higdon and Ella House. Back row: coaches Todd Keown and Lindsey Clark, Madyson Higdon, Baylee Estes, Ansley House, Audrey Carnes, Bella Bryant, Carolina Jones, Ava Riggs, Jordyn
Waltrip, Aubree Mosby, Ryleigh French, coach Taylor Morris and head coach Dwayne Wroe.
Waltrip, Aubree Mosby, Ryleigh French, coach Taylor Morris and head coach Dwayne Wroe. Livingston Central scored three runs in the fourth inning then held on to win 3-0 over Hancock County in the championship game of the All 'A' State Softball Tournament at Jack C. Fisher Park in Owensboro Sunday. The Lady Hornets claimed the state runner-up trophy for the sixth time. The girls won five consecutive games over the weekend before falling in the title game.
'I'm super proud of all the girls,' HCHS coach Dwayne Wroe said. 'It's the sixth time we've been runner-up since I've coached. It's disappointing, but Livingston is a great team.'
The Lady Hornets had a chance in the third inning when Emmalynn Higdon, Jordyn Waltrip and Baylee Estes connected for three consecutive hits. The bases were loaded, but the next two HCHS batters struck out and popped up.
The Lady Cardinals got an RBI double from Hadley Hargrove after a runner reached base on an error in the fourth. Another Lady Hornet error resulted in a run before Higdon made a diving catch in right field for out #2. She threw to the cutoff and Ella House fired the ball home. Layni Roberts made the catch, but the runner was safe and the score was 3-0.
Hancock County went three up and three down over the next three innings.
Lily Roberts led off the seventh with a hit and Layni Roberts followed with a line drive. The girls might have rallied if not for a great catch made by the Livingston short stop. The Lady Cardinals' defense recorded the next two outs to claim the title.
'We've got some good veteran leaders and some good younger kids who had a great experience. You hate to finish second place, but runner-up in the state is not too shabby,' Wroe said.
Addison Tramble was the winning pitcher. She allowed no runs on five hits, with seven Ks and one walk over seven innings. Lily Roberts took the loss while allowing three runs (none earned) on four hits, with eight Ks and no walks.
'I can't say enough about Lily. I tried to get her some rest when I could and I'm really proud of what she's done after coming back from an ACL injury,' the coach said. 'I wouldn't know where we would be without her.'
Estes was 2 for 3 at the plate for HCHS. Higdon and Waltrip both went 1 for 2.
Semifinals Hancock County out hit Russellville 12-2 during a 10-0 win for the Lady Hornets in a state semifinal game Sunday.
Estes and Audrey Carnes led off the game with back-to-back hits before House delivered the first RBI. Ava Riggs later knocked in a run and the score was 2-0.
Carnes, House and Layni Roberts all had RBIs in the second and Hancock County led 6-0. Estes and Carnes knocked in a run each in the third before the Lady Hornets secured the final run in the sixth when Ryleigh French stole home on a wild pitch.
Bella Bryant got the win on the mound while allowing no runs on one hit, with two walks over four innings. Lily Roberts pitched two shutout innings.
Estes was 3 for 3 at the plate with one RBI and three runs scored. Carnes was 3 for 4 with two RBI, Riggs (RBI), Bryant and Waltrip all went 1 for 2, House was 1 for 4 with a double and two RBI, and Lily Roberts was 1 for 4. Layni Roberts was 0 for 1 with one RBI.
Quarterfinal The Lady Hornets earned a tough, 2-1 win over Bracken County in Sunday's early morning quarterfinal contest.
Estes singled and stole second base in the third then scored on a hit by Carnes to give HCHS a 1-0 advantage.
The Lady Bears quickly tied the score when Kyndall Johnson led off the fourth with a home run to left field.
Hancock County answered back in the home half of the same inning. Bryant singled with two outs and Kylie Westerfield, who was in as a courtesy runner, advanced to third. The senior then scored on an error and the girls were back in front, leading 2-1.
Lily allowed a double in the sixth, but ended the threat with a ground out and a strike out. Roberts set down two batters via strikes in the seventh and Estes ended the game with a catch in center field.
Roberts got the win while allowing one run on three hits, with 13 Ks and one walk over seven innings. Ella Johnson took the loss.
Carnes was 2 for 3 at the plate with one RBI. Bryant was 1 for 2 and Estes 1 for 3.
Raceland Lily Roberts won a 1-0 pitchers duel and Madyson Higdon knocked in the winning run during a Lady Hornet victory over Raceland in Saturday's final game of pool play. Roberts and Raceland pitcher Davanna Grubb held both teams scoreless through six innings.
Raceland threatened to score in the sixth when a base runner tried to steal home after a pitch got away from Hornet catcher Layni Roberts. Roberts recovered the ball and threw back to home plate and Aubree Mosby was there. The third baseman, who was charging on a bunt attempt, made the tag for the out.
Layni Roberts was hit by a wild pitch in the seventh and Riggs moved courtesy runner Westerfield to second with a sacrifice bunt. Madyson 'Boom' Higdon then singled to center field to bring home Westerfield.
Lily Roberts and the Lady Hornets defense set down the Lady Rams batters 1-2-3 in the seventh for the win.
Lily got the win while allowing no runs on four hits, with 14 Ks and two walks over seven frames. Grubbs allowed the one run on four hits.
Higdon was 1 for 2 with one RBI. House and Waltrip both went 1 for 3.
Somerset Lily Roberts and Ava Riggs had four RBI each during a 15-4 win over Somerset in tournament action Saturday.
Hancock County plated three runs in the first inning and five more in the third to take control. House doubled in a run in the third and Lily Roberts followed with a hit. Layni Roberts was hit again by a wild pitch, which left the bases loaded for Riggs.
The sophomore walked to the plate and smacked a line drive triple that scored three runs. Riggs scored on a ground out and the rout was on. The girls added two runs in the fifth and five more in the sixth. Waltrip, Ansley House and Ella House all had RBI doubles to highlight the sixth.
Lily got the win while allowing no runs on two hits, with six Ks and no walks over three innings. Waltrip allowed three runs on one hit, with one K and two walks. Bryant allowed one run on two hits, with one walk in two innings.
Lily Roberts was 4 for 5 at the plate with four RBI. Ella House was 3 for 5 with two doubles and two RBI. Ansley House was 2 for 2 with a double and two RBI, Carnes was 2 for 2, Riggs was 2 for 3 with the triple and four RBI, Estes was 2 for 4 with one RBI, and Waltrip was 1 for 2 with a double and one RBI. Emmalynn Higdon and Layni Roberts both scored a run. Bryant had one RBI.
Covington Holy Cross Emmalynn Higdon belted a grand slam home run in the second inning and the Lady Hornets blew out Covington Holy Cross 14-2 in Hancock County's opening game of the state tourney Saturday. Baylee Estes and Audrey Carnes hit home runs in the same inning!
Higdon came up with the bases loaded in the second and sent a 2-2 offering over the fence in center field for the slam. Two batters later Estes hit an inside the park homer, and Carnes followed with a home run to center field. HCHS led 6-0.
The Lady Hornet offense produced eight more runs in the third inning and the Covington coach threw in the towel.
Lily got the win. She allowed no runs or hits, with five Ks and no walks in two innings pitched. Bryant struck out the side in her only inning on the mound, and French allowed two runs (none earned) on two hits in one frame pitched.
Higdon was 2 for 2 with the homer and four RBI. Carnes was 2 or 2 with the homer and two RBI, Bryant was 2 for 3 with two RBI, Estes was 1 for 3 with the homer and two RBI, Ella House and Layni Roberts both went 1 for 2, Riggs was 1 for 3 with a double, and Lily Roberts had one RBI.
Perry Central Bella Bryant hit a home run and the Lady Hornets defeated Perry Central 3-1 in Leopold last Thursday.
Audrey Carnes put HCHS in front 1-0 on an RBI hit in the fifth inning. A hit by Ella House left the bases loaded and the score jumped to 2-0 when Lily Roberts was hit by a wild pitch.
Roberts was on the mound and in control. She got help from the defense when Aubree Mosby turned a double play and Baylee Estes caught a line drive in center field.
Bryant, an 8th grader, led off the sixth with a home run to center field and the score was 3-0. The Lady Commodores plated a run in the home half of the sixth before going down 1-2-3 in the seventh.
Roberts got the win while allowing one run on four hits, with 10 Ks and two walks over seven frames. A. Gogel took the loss for PCHS.
Emmalynn Higdon was 2 for 3 at the plate, and Bryant was 1 for 1 with the homer and one RBI. Carnes was 2 for 4 with one RBI, and Estes was 2 for 4. Mosby was 1 for 3, and House and Ava Riggs both went 1 for 4.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Rick Kreisle
description: Charles Richard 'Rick' Kreisle, 70, a cherished father, DaDa/grandddad, great granddad, and the loving husband of Brenda Faye Kreisle, went home to be with the Lord, Tuesday, April 23, 2024, at…
content:
Charles Richard 'Rick' Kreisle, 70, a cherished father, DaDa/grandddad, great granddad, and the loving husband of Brenda Faye Kreisle, went home to be with the Lord, Tuesday, April 23, 2024, at Tidelands Georgetown Memorial Hospital.
Mr. Kreisle was born the son of Charles Harrison Kreisle and Patsy Vaughn Morris Tableman on May 6, 1953, in Fort Worth, TX. He was the oldest of four children, Wally, Paul, and Joe. He was an United States Army Veteran and was an employee with International Paper for over 30 years. Rick enjoyed the simple pleasures of life including working, fishing, hunting, and riding his golf cart to the Circle K. He was a humble man with a servant's heart. Above all, he loved the Lord and never missed an opportunity to give his testimony of how God healed him. On any given Sunday, you would find him going to church and worshiping his Lord. He was a devoted husband who loved and took care his wife (Nanny Girl) for many years. As a proud father, he raised his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren in a home filled with love, laughter, and singing.
Rick is survived by his mother, Patsy Tableman; his wife, Brenda Kreisle; his children, Micaela Kreisle (Joe Collins), Amanda Kreisle-McCants, Jeff McCants, Tiffany Dawn Kreisle, and Charles 'Bubba' Kreisle (Kyleigh); seven grandchildren, Patrick Ross Kreisle, Rachel 'Rach' Kreisle, Matthew 'Matlock' Kreisle, Becca 'Becca Boo' McCants (Brandon Altman), Jacob Rhett McCants, Joshua Elijah Elder, and soon to arrive, Charles James Kreisle; and two great-grandchildren, Charles Reid Kreisle and Blakelee Mae Altman. He is also survived by two brothers, Paul Kreisle (Lisa) and Joe Kreisle (Renee); aunts, uncles, cousins, and many nieces and nephews.
He was predeceased by his father, Charles Harrison Kreisle, his step-father, Jim 'Pappy' Tableman; a brother, Wally Kreisle; and his mother-in-law, Pauline Browning.
A Celebration of Life Service was held at 4PM, Friday, April 26, 2024, at the Family Worship Center, 249 Wedgefield Road, Georgetown. Officiating will be Pastor Justin Flowers.
The Kreisle family will greet family and friends immediately after the service.

title: John McCarty hikes the ancient pilgrim path in Spain
description: John McCarty, former Hancock County District Court Judge, is currently hiking The Camino Frances pilgrimage. He and his siblings...
content:
John McCarty (far right) in the Pyrenees, near Saint Jean Pied-de-Port, France, with his sister, Mary Raley, his brother, Ralph McCarty, and Anne Black, their friend from Vermont. They are currently hiking The Camino Frances pilgrimage, a total journey of around 485 miles, and will complete their trek in early June.
John McCarty, former Hancock County District Court Judge, is currently hiking The Camino Frances pilgrimage. He and his siblings, Ralph McCarty and Mary Raley, along with a friend from Vermont, Anne Black, will be covering around 478 miles total, or 770 km, in 30-35 days.
They began on Thursday, April 25th at Saint Jean Pied-de-Port, France, the traditional start of The Camino Frances, and will be finishing their journey at Santiago de Compostela, in northwestern Spain.
The group completed day 7 of their hike on Friday, May 3rd, which was about 20 percent of their nearly 500-mile trek. They don't have a guide and it's just the 4 of them, but they are meeting people from all over the world along the way, John said. This is a first for all of them to be making this popular and ancient pilgrimage.
'We've walked about 165 kilometers,' he said. 'We're averaging around 21-22 kilometers a day. Some days are longer and some are shorter. Everything is going well. We've had some dicey conditions. Our second day going over the Pyrenees (Mountain range), between France and Spain, we had 70-mile-an-hour gale winds and driving winds. It was very dangerous because there are no guard rails, nothing to protect you if the winds push you off of the mountain.
We are carrying packs; My brother and myself are carrying our packs. Anne and Mary are sending their packs ahead to the next places that we plan to stop, but carrying day packs.'
They are booking hostels, or public albergues on the Camino de Santiago only for pilgrims, along the way. They flew into Madrid, Spain and then took a plane over to Pamplona (where the famous Running of the Bulls takes place every year in July), and took a bus from there over to Saint Jean Pied-de-port where they began the hike.
'One place we stayed had multiple beds, maybe 20 bunk beds in a room,' John said. 'We are booking them a day or 2 ahead of time mostly, because you don't know how far you can go each day, so you don't want to book something that you can't make it to. We have a plane scheduled for June 5th; Our plan is to finish before then.'
He said that all of their stops along the way have been amazing. 'There are lots of fabulous, old churches,' he said. 'We've passed through Basque Country in Spain and we're at the end of it. We're going to start getting into a different little area soon.
There are a lot of olive & walnut groves, and vineyards. There are lots of good wines; They serve wine at most meals. Burgos will be the largest city we go to. We're just kind of going at our own pace. There's no schedule. People have done this for centuries. We've got a book and we're kind of going by what this person recommended we do. We're not required to go any distance, we just kind of go as we need to or want to.
Two of the 8 days we've had rain; that's not bad. The rest of the days have been sunny. It's been in the 50s and 60s, and today we're up in the 70s. We've got pack covers and rain parkas. Your feet don't stay dry, so at night we usually try to hand wash some clothes in the sink and hang them up in the room to dry so maybe we can have them dry by the next day. Two changes of clothes is all we have.
It's tremendous. Carolyn (John's wife) really wanted to come but her mother is 97 and needs her help right now. She couldn't come, but we're going to have to come back and do it again, or do another part of it again with her.'
On this trip so far, John said they've met people from Australia, New Zealand, Denmark, Finland, Korea and Ireland, to name some, as well as from the states. 'We've met people from California, Utah, Idaho, Texas, Virginia, Connecticut, Vermont, New Hampshire, just everywhere,' he said. 'We've kind of been having conversation along the way.
We might walk with somebody for a few kilometers. This morning, I walked with a guy from England. We talked about retirement and different things, things we do back home. It's interesting; it really is. It's an awesome thing. You have to be a little bit adventurous to do this. We're in a strange country and we don't speak Spanish very well at all. But, a lot of people speak English proficient enough where we can get across what we want to say.'
People from all over the world do this pilgrimage at various times of year, and year round. 'They can join in anywhere, stop in anywhere. This is something you do on your own,' he explained. 'Some people do groups, they'll sometimes do the last 100-kilometers in a group or something. We're doing the whole thing. We don't have a guide. All we have is our phones, our apps and our book.
Before, we did some research, but mostly we tried to get ourselves in shape before we left; That was the big thing. Since January, I've been out training. I found that hiking in Vastwood Park and Jeffreys Cliffs prepared me quite well for some of the hills. There are more hills and bigger hills and bigger mountains here, but still they prepared us quite a bit.
I've walked the newer trails in Vastwood up in the woods. I've walked them multiple times during the day; I walked them twice or three times just to get the length. They got me in relatively good shape with me doing them a number of times.'
The book they are using as a guide for the journey was written by one of the premier authors on the subject, the late John Brierley. It is titled: 'A Pilgrim's Guide to The Camino de Santiago, St. Jean – Roncesvalles – Santiago, The Way of St. James, The ancient pilgrim path also known as Camino Frances, A Practical & Mystical Manual for the Modern Day Pilgrim.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: Taking Care of God's World
description: A picture of the Northern Lights sent to us by reader Janette Haynes Hays Twice within just a little over a month, I beheld the wonders in the sky. Saturday night a call came, 'Go down to the river…
content:
A picture of the Northern Lights sent to us by reader Janette Haynes Hays
Twice within just a little over a month, I beheld the wonders in the sky. Saturday night a call came, 'Go down to the river and look at the sky.' When we got there, the city lights made it hard to see anything so we went to the overlook outside of town. There, dancing across the sky, was the pinks and greens and purples. It was an amazing sight but I realized it was nothing compared to what those up north were seeing.
We went to Evansville to see the solar eclipse. It became dark with an eerie, yellow glow and it got cool and the wind began to blow. Some street lights came on. Everyone cheered and watched the sun come back.
A few years ago, we hosted an exchange student from Norway. He stayed for a school year. We learned a lot about him and his country. Northern Lights are something he takes for granted. He sees them often and very plainly. They light up the whole sky. He was a snow boarder and he brought pictures of himself snow boarding down a glacier. He was wearing shorts and a t-shirt. The sun made the air warm. Only the melting glacier was cold. They have strict pollution laws and their skies are a beautiful unpolluted blue.
Justin (as we called him) loved to fish. He said their waters are so clear you can see the fish you are trying to catch. He could not understand our polluted waters. He asked: 'Why would anyone just throw their trash on the highways? Why would we allow factories to put out their pollution in the air? Why would we allow GMOs and pesticides to pollute our food supplies?
Why would teenagers want to get drunk and make fools of themselves? Why would girls allow themselves to get pregnant before they graduated from high school? Why do girls have to wear tops to beaches? . . .Guys don't have to.' He had a lot of questions that made me stop and think about what we are doing to ourselves and our environment.
I see so many people with COPD. They carry their oxygen supply with them. They did not get that way from breathing fresh air. So many people have allergies. Growing up, I never knew anyone with allergies. We have no idea what we eat. There are no warnings on many food labels. I just found a warning on a bag of potato chips that stated they could cause cancer. 'Hazardous to health' warnings are on many things we use or consume and we ignore them. We can't complain about the world we live in; we created it.
About that eclipse: Remember how it was when the sun was hidden? That's how it will be when we create enough pollution to hide the sun.
The Lord gave us this great big, beautiful world. And we don't appreciate it enough to take care of it. Once it is gone, it will not come back.
by Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Tennis players fall in regional tourney

content:
Chiara Landes eyes the ball before striking a forehand during a recent tennis match at Vastwood. The HCHS tennis teams' seasons came to an end following losses in the regional tournament played at the Owensboro Tennis Center Saturday. title: New Business in Hancock County – EmpowerFit HC
description: Carli Mosby Smith taught her first fitness c
content:
Carli Mosby Smith taught her first fitness class Saturday at Vastwood. Her new business is EmpowerFit HC, and she is offering classes 3 days a week for all levels.
Carli Mosby Smith, of Hawesville, has recently started offering fitness classes for all levels in Hancock County through her new business, EmpowerFit HC. This is a way for her to provide a service in her hometown that she has become very passionate about – health and wellness.
Carli received her certification as a group exercise instructor through the International Sports Sciences Association in April. Currently, she's teaching classes 3 days a week at Vastwood Park. She also posts healthy recipes, motivation tips, and other fitness and wellness information on her Facebook Page – EmpowerFit HC.
'I started my health and wellness journey maybe 4 years ago right after I had my daughter,' Carli said. 'Before that, I was an athlete but I didn't give much thought to what I was doing and what I was putting into my body. I got really serious about it and I absolutely fell in love with exercise and working out. During that time, I found that I am encouraged and more accountable when I'm exercising with other people.'
Carli is the daughter of Chuck Mosby and Terry Conder. She and her husband, Kyle, and their daughter, Ellie, live in Hawesville. They moved back to Carli's hometown in Hawesville last August. Kyle is originally from Louisville. He is an IT Tech at Hancock County Schools. Ellie is 3 and will start preschool in August at Rise and Shine.
'Louisville has a ton of opportunities for group fitness classes and gyms,' Carli said, 'and I knew Hancock County didn't have anything local like that. We have gyms but not the classes that you have to drive 30 minutes for. When I started thinking about what I could do here in terms of fitness classes for myself, I realized that there weren't a whole lot of options and decided I'd do it myself. I've gotten a really great response from folks so far.'
She held her very first fitness class at Vastwood on Saturday, May 18th and had around 10 people signed up. 'So far, we've been having them at the tennis court at Vastwood Park. It is a pretty good space and not super busy. Mostly, we'll be doing them outside at Vastwood. For days when weather is an issue, I'm currently working with the school board and they're going to let me into one of the gyms. Once we get that contract going, I'll be able to offer classes in the winter and when it's raining.'
When Carli attended Hancock County Schools she played volleyball, basketball and softball. She attended University of Louisville after graduating HCHS in 2011, and has earned her Master's in Social Work. She works full-time from home as a Quality Improvement Professional for Humana.
While playing sports during high school, she tore her ACL three times. She had to have 3 different knee surgeries, and still has 9 screws in her knee. That experience, she said, has made her dedicated to exercising in a safe way. She teaches her classes with plenty of warm-up time, stretching and cool downs, and always offers low impact alternatives to all of the movements.
'I think that's why I've continued exercising and working out,' she said. 'For me, those experiences were disappointing and a let down. I've found some ways to work out so that I can either do modifications for my knee pain or just do strength training, which makes me feel empowered.'
She named her business EmpowerFit because she wants people to know that her classes are focused on being empowered. 'People can be a little hesitant or concerned about working out depending on their fitness level,' Carli said. 'My classes are for everyone regardless of their age, gender, fitness level, exercise knowledge, etc. I wanted to make sure that in the name of the business that folks realize that this is a space to be empowered and work toward your wellness goals.
All of the moves that we do, I make sure that every move has a modification. That could mean using less or no weights, or even just doing a lower impact or no impact move. Each member of the class really is in charge of their own workout, meaning that they can go as hard or as easy as they want to, or need to, depending on how they're feeling that day.
Most of my classes are a combination of strength conditioning with some elements of cardio built in. So things like high intensity interval training, or Tabata. That's mostly what I do and so that's what I'm most comfortable with, but I'm also trying my hand at a few different styles of exercise as well that I've never taught before.
For example, I'll be teaching my first kick boxing class on Saturday, May 25th. I've been doing kick boxing off and on for about 2 or 3 years now. I've just loved it and so I want to try to share that with others as well. I'm super excited. I have quite a few people already signed up so I think that will be a popular one.
All of my classes at EmpowerFit start with a warm up. We do at least 6 minutes of getting our bodies warm and doing some dynamic stretching, and sometimes longer than that depending on what we're doing. Then we do the bulk of our class. I try to do some different styles to keep people engaged. We always end with a cool down and some really good stretching to prevent injury. I really try to make sure people know how to do all of that correctly as well, because that's just as important as doing the moves correctly for the heart of the workout.'
EmpowerFit HC Facebook Page is Carli's public business page. You can will find out how to sign up for her classes on the page. At the end of each month, she posts the next month's schedule for the classes she's offering. Her website, she said, will be up and running soon, so keep an eye out for when she posts the link on the FB Page.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Literacy Award and Teacher of the Year Award Recipients
description: Re
content:
Recognized at the HC Board of Education meeting last week were the 3 Teacher of the Year Award recipients, as well the Educator Award for Literacy recipient.
Campbellsville Teacher of the Year Award recipients are: HCHS Social Studies Teacher Trevor Garrison, HCMS 7th Grade Math Teacher Mitzi Mattingly and retiring NHES K-1 Teacher Shelly Gray.
The Western Kentucky University Distinguished Educator Award for Literacy recipient is District Literacy Coach & Interventionist Briana Pulliam.
Trevor Garrison
Trevor Garrison HCHS Principal Ginger Estes said, 'Trevor has been with us just a short time. This is his third year. The kids and teachers adore him. He has already presented at huge conferences. He just brings a wonderful breath of fresh air for us and it's exactly what our kids need. This morning he was giving a pep talk to our juniors before they took their social studies test and it was like a big pep rally. That's what he's about. I'm super proud of him.'
Shelly Gray
Shelly Gray The new NHES Principal for the ‘24/'25 school year Dr. Jacob Bryant spoke about retiring teacher Shelly Gray and her Teacher of the Year Award saying, 'Miss Shelly is a complete asset to our school. She goes above and beyond for any student or staff member – anybody that needs any support, she's our go to. If we have any question with anything in those lower grades, she's had some type of experience with it and she's the one that we always go to as our person there.
If we just get an ounce of Shelly Gray's talent, that would make a great teacher, so you can imagine the phenomenal things she has done for our school and for our students. I can't thank her enough. We will miss you.'
Asberry added, 'All across the state, we've had people come in and observe our classrooms and, without a doubt, they always say something positive about Ms. Gray and her classroom, every time. You will be truly missed.'
Mitzi Mattingly
Mitzi Mattingly HCMS Principal Traci Sanders said, 'Mitzi is an asset to HCMS. When the kids come out of there, you can see the growth each and every year.'
Briana Pulliam
Briana Pulliam Superintendent Robby Asberry announced, 'This was an award all across the state of KY. There were 100 nominations across the state. We are honored to be able to have the Western Kentucky University Distinguished Educator Award for Literacy. I know no one more deserving than Ms. Briana Pulliam.'
SHES Principal Jennifer Howe said, 'Ms. Pulliam has helped to make me a better principal. She was one of the very first staff members that came into my office when I was hired on 5 years ago. She wanted to know my purpose and my ‘why' – why I chose Hancock County and why I chose South Hancock.
That's her passion. Her passion is Every staff member that she works with, every student in our building and not just our building but across the district. When we were looking at this award, Briana Pulliam's name was the first one to come up for nomination. It was a no brainer in the write up for the award because she lives it every day.
She has helped spearhead and lead this work in literacy that we've done in Hancock County. I've told every visitor that has come into our buildings that when you want movement in something and want it to work and want people behind it and someone that's passionate and believes in it, it's Briana Pulliam.
She has done that and she has done an amazing job. It's not only affected our staff and students, but she's affected staff and students across the district. We couldn't be more proud to have her at our school and in the district.'
Pulliam said, 'I'm really teary eyed right now because some of the people that I love that I started teaching with are getting honored tonight. This award is wonderful. I feel very privileged and honored to have it. It's only because of the people that I work with. They're phenomenal and they want what's best for kids all the time, like I do. Thank you.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Basham, Emmick and Jones place top 10 at state track meet
description: Hancock County athletes competed in the KHSAA Class 1A Track & Field State Championship 2024 at the University of Kentucky track complex Thursday. Three Hornets had top 10 performances. 'We had a good…
content:
Hancock County athletes competed in the KHSAA Class 1A Track & Field State Championship 2024 at the University of Kentucky track complex Thursday. Three Hornets had top 10 performances.
'We had a good showing at the state meet with three top ten finishes and season best performances in four events,' HCHS coach Wes Meserve said. 'I was very proud of how they all did. Most of our athletes matched or passed their previous season bests.'
Alex Basham earned a medal after placing seventh in the shot put event. His best throw was 47–7.5 feet. Kasey Webb of Edmonson County won at 53 feet, one inch.
Wyatt Emmick placed eighth and earned a medal in the boys 110 meter hurdles. Emmick ran a personal best time of 15.96 seconds. Oliver Veliquette of Louisville Collegiate won in 15.18.
Carolina Jones had a season best time of 48.89 seconds to place 10th in the girls 300 meter hurdles. Sophie Maynard of Raceland won in 45.69. The HCHS 4×800 meter relay team placed 11th in a season best time of nine minutes flat. They ran 19 seconds faster than ever before. Runners were Noah Henson, Hunter Stephens, Max DeJarnette and Emmitt Meserve. Bishop Brossart won in 8:07.
'Our relay splits in the 4×800 were much better than we've seen all season. We averaged about a five second improvement per kid. That's a huge amount of progress,' the coach said.
The HCHS 4×200 meter relay team was 12th in 1:34. Runners were Emmick, Matthew Carroll, Christian Yanez and Ben Baker. Fort Campbell won in 1:29. Emmick placed 14th in the boys 300 meter hurdles in 42.62. Veliquette won in 39.32 seconds.
Basham was 16th in the discus competition with a throw of 121–6 feet. Kelson McKinney of Green County won at 169–08.
The HCHS 4×400 meter relay team was 19th in a season best time of 3:46.33. Runners were Emmick, Carroll, Mehkel London and Baker. Fort Campbell won in 3:25.
Izzy Ross placed 22nd in the girls triple jump with a distance of 29–9 feet. Natalie Svidal of Walden won at 36–6.
Beechwood won the boys state title with 81 points.
Beechwood won the girls state title with 91 points.
Coach Meserve shared his thoughts on the season and for next year.
'Our goal this season was to give all of our athletes specialized coaching for their events. Nick Locke was a state champion in shot put, Casey Baize jumped in college, Mariah Earhart ran distance in college, Tanner DeWitt worked closely with Bob O'Brien (retired Owensboro sprint coach of multiple national champions), and Tyler Walz ran in college.
'Our athletes had coaches who were knowledgeable in all of the events and that really helped us to break records and send kids to state.
'In addition to our staff, both state qualifying hurdlers have been doing extra workouts with coach Mason Aschenbrenner (a former college hurdler) and their form and times have improved noticeably.
'It was a very successful rebuilding year and I'm excited to see what this young team does in the next few years.'
By Steve Wimmer
