title: Nancy's Notes: My Dad
description: My dad was a prankster. He especially liked to play pranks on our relatives who came from up North, near Chicago. When they cam
content:
My dad was a prankster. He especially liked to play pranks on our relatives who came from up North, near Chicago.
When they came to visit, the first thing Daddy would do was take the kids to the tobacco patch to help him de-worm the tobacco. Those kids were city kids and had no idea what tobacco was. They were excited to do something different.
Dad would have them pick that wiggly worm off, then he would tell them they had to bite their heads off. They'd gag and run to the house –'Uncle Clarence tried to get us to bite that worm's head off. It had big eyes and was green and it got all over me. No way am I going to bite its head off!'
Then, he'd take them to the persimmon tree. He'd pick off a couple green ones and give them to the kids. He'd say, 'Chew them good. The longer you chew, the sweeter they get.' By the time they chewed a whole one, their mouths were so puckered they couldn't complain.
Then, there was the time Uncle Carl came over. He had a lot of hair around the bottom of his head but had none on top. Daddy told him he had a recipe for a cure for baldness. Uncle Carl wrote down the recipe for baldness: Take a cup of green persimmon juice, mix it with 2 tablespoons of alum. Rub this mixture all over your head. Place a shower cap over your head and sleep with it overnight.
'Will this really make me grow hair?' Uncle Carl asked.
'No,' said my dad, 'but it will make your head shrink to where what you've got will fit.'
Then, there was the outhouse. We had remodeled our house and had added a bathroom. Daddy told our men visitors the bathroom was for the women but the men still had to use the outhouse. He would say, 'Now, if you're afraid it's a two-holer, I can come and sit with you.'
'Oh no,' they would say. 'We live in a big city. Something is always happening there. We're not afraid.'
So, Daddy would light up a lantern and send them down the path.
'Watch out for snakes,' he'd say. 'They don't usually come out at night but you never know.'
Dark was really dark back then. You could not see your hand in front of you. Sometimes the wind would blow out the fire in the lantern and we'd hear a frantic 'Help!' coming from the outhouse.
When things had settled down for the day, the girls would go to the bedroom and lay on mats on the floor. The guys would head to the front porch. The folks would be up talking and laughing ‘til the wee hours of the morning.
The relatives would go back up North and tell everyone about their vacation in Kentucky with their hillbilly family. In years to come, I would see some of them and they'd say, 'Remember the summer Uncle Clarence tried to make us bite the head off that tobacco worm?' or 'How about that outhouse?' and we'd all laugh.
When I ask my older kids what they miss most about their childhood, they all say the laughter.
Recently, I overheard a teenage boy say, 'We spent a week at Grandma's house this summer. It was so boring. I spent my whole time playing video games.'
I wonder what the favorite part of his childhood will be.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Fiscal Court Approves Proclamation on Shipyard Safety
description: The Proclamation on Shipyard Safety is new for this year, and was approved by the Hancock County Fiscal Court at the mont
content:
The Proclamation on Shipyard Safety is new for this year, and was approved by the Hancock County Fiscal Court at the monthly night meeting on Monday, June 24th.
Shipyard Safety Recognition Day is set for Friday, July 14th, 2024, to promote safety awareness. A strong safety culture and environmental protection are top priorities of Evansville Marine Service, which received the AEU 2023 Safety Award.
Evansville Marine Service employs residents of Hancock County and transports goods to communities along the Ohio River and Green River. The safety of those employees is of utmost importance, and ensures that they are better able to support their families, contribute to the community and make an impact in society.
Air Med Care Presentation
The Court was provided with a presentation from Air Med Care (emergency air evacuation medical transportation services). The presenter talked about their Fly You Home Program that offers the option of, if you're out of town and need to go to the hospital, they can actually put you on a plane and care for you while they fly you back to your hometown hospital.
The prices on that program are likely going to significantly increase in July of this year, they announced, and so they are trying to get the word out to people so that if anyone is interested they can go ahead and sign up for it now.
All full-time County employees are covered with Air Med Care services. The presentation provided brief updates and new opportunities such as the above-mentioned program. These services are available for all citizens in the County; anyone in the general public can sign up.
Budget Approved
The Fiscal Year 2024/2025 second reading and adoption of the new budget was approved by the Court.
Salt Bid
The Court awarded a salt bid, a reverse bid through the Kentucky Association of Counties (KACo). That price set through KACo is $117 per ton of salt. Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts said, 'That basically gives a salt bid price if we need salt at a certain price. We're o.k. right now regarding the salt that we have; we had a mild winter. If we need some, they do a reverse auction, and we already have the price set through KACo.'
Representatives with the Kentucky Rural Secondary Program were scheduled to speak at this meeting and talk about some of the funding that the County will be receiving but had to cancel due to illness. They have tentatively rescheduled for the July 8th HC Fiscal Court day meeting.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Don't Allow Stress to Build
description: Cortisol and adrenaline, both produced by our adrenal glands, are the 2 main components in regulating stress. When we stay stressed...
content:
Cortisol and adrenaline, both produced by our adrenal glands, are the 2 main components in regulating stress. When we stay stressed, they can become overactive and cause health problems.
According to my research, cortisol is a 'stress hormone' that works through the bloodstream, and adrenaline is a neurotransmitter that is similar to a hormone but works through the nervous system.
Both of these help to adapt our bodies to stressors. The more stress we have, the more our adrenal glands are activated to help us adjust. Stressors can be physical or emotional and, in my opinion, the root is usually spiritual. We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against our enemy in the spirit realm. So, above all else, put on the full armor of God (Ephesians 6:10-18), and leave it on.
The 2 adrenal glands are positioned above the kidneys. The interior of those glands consists of neurological tissue, and that is where adrenaline is produced and released. The exterior is made up of glandular tissue, and that is where cortisol is located.
They are designed to activate during short periods of time, and it's our sympathetic nervous system, referred to as 'fight or flight', that activates them. Our parasympathetic nervous system deactivates them.
When we are stressed for periods of time and have difficulty returning to a state of well-being, it could be that these adrenal glands have not yet 'deactivated', and we get stuck in that fight or flight mode.
This over-activity can cause many health problems, including: increased heart rate, high blood pressure, digestive system challenges, reproductive challenges, brain fog, disruption in sleep patterns/reversed circadian rhythms, lack of focus, memory loss, diminished bone health, hair loss, dismantled collagen from joints & skin, chronic inflammation, and the loss of important vitamins and minerals such as potassium and thiamine (B1).
To find out whether or not your body is stuck in stress mode and producing excessive cortisol, ask your doctor for a sensitive test that measures adrenal production, such as the Heart Rate Variability Test .
Sleeping well throughout the night is key in healing overactive adrenal glands. Secondly, collect several go-to coping mechanisms that will help calm you down during high stress times, such as deep breathing. Don't allow yourself to stay stressed, to where it can then build-up and cause unhealthy cortisol levels.
Eat more foods that are high in magnesium, vitamin D, and potassium when they have been depleted from stress. You can increase your vitamin B1 levels as well by supplementing with nutritional yeast flakes or tablets, for example.
Don't drink caffeine after 2 p.m., and get to sleep by 10 p.m. each night. Our Human Growth Hormone (HGH) is released and other hormone levels balance out when our sleep patterns are regular, and especially when we are in a state of deep sleep between the hours of 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.
Adaptogens such as ashwaghanda paired with a nervine like valerian root are excellent for helping relieve anxiety, and to help with getting a full night's rest naturally, and they are not habit-forming. *Always do your research and/or chat with your doctor before trying any herbal remedies, especially if you're taking pharmaceutical meds.
Massage, acupressure, acupuncture, exercise and positive affirmations are also helpful in managing stress and anxiety, to name a few more possible remedies.
~Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

Obenchain Farms, in Hawesville, has been accepted into the 2024 Kentucky Farm Bureau (KFB) Certified Farm Market Program.
Owners Justin & Chrystal Obenchain are Hancock County natives. Justin purchased his family's farm from his grandfather, the late Jim Obenchain, in 2015, and they produced their first crop of corn in 2016.
As a member of this prestigious program, the market has committed to providing top-quality products and services to its customers. This certification ensures that Obenchain Farms meets the highest standards of quality, freshness and marketing appeal.
Justin is President of the Board of Directors for the Hancock County Farm Bureau, and Chairman of the Agriculture Development Board and the Extension Council for Hancock County. Chrystal & Justin are celebrating 14 years of marriage this year, and are blessed with 2 children, Connor (8) and Harlan (5).
KFB President Eddie Melton is excited about the continued growth of the program. He remarked on the increasing demand for locally grown foods, which is a positive development over the last few years, and added, 'We look forward to another successful season of providing farm-fresh goods to customers by some of the best producers across this state.'
This is the 29th year of offering the program, and interested parties can visit: kyfb.com/certified, e-mail: kfbcertified@kyfb.com, or 'Like' the Certified Farm Market Facebook page @ facebook.com/KYCertifiedFarmMarket, to learn more.

title: Outlaw Metalworks Owner Clint Hylton Speaks at Chamber Breakfast
description: A Hancock County Hornets 2-layer piece created by Clint Hylton, Owner of Outlaw Metalworks. Clint Hylton, of Hawesville, was the speaker at the Hancock Cou
content:
A Hancock County Hornets 2-layer piece created by Clint Hylton, Owner of Outlaw Metalworks.
Clint Hylton, of Hawesville, was the speaker at the Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Breakfast Tuesday. He is a Chamber Board member, and Owner of Outlaw Metalworks LLC, established in 2023. The Breakfast was held at the HC Career Center, sponsored by Kenergy and catered by JJ's Pizza.
Clint explained that his journey in blacksmithing began in 2015. He purchased a portable forge, took some classes, and started practicing in the shop he built next to his house. He said he is more interested in the ornamental side of blacksmithing, and started with making beautiful metal flowers.
'A rose for example,' he said, 'I would get some rose blanks and hammer texture all of the petals out and form a stand. Then, I would put it on there and form it with a torch – the whole rose itself. I started selling quite a bit of those, especially around Valentine's Day and for wedding anniversaries.'
He decided to get a table instead of ordering the blanks and is now cutting his own. Once he had the table, his friends began asking him to make signs for them. He downloaded a few programs and said he basically taught himself by watching YouTube videos to get the hang of using the programs for the designs. When word got out that he was making signs, others began reaching out to him for sign making, monograms, yard art, etc.
'After I get my sign orders completed that I have right now,' he said, 'I'm starting to do a little bit more yard art.'
He built his shop, he said, with the goal to create an old blacksmith, barn look. The 24×24 shop has a coal forge and a gas forge. He made the Lewisport City Hall sign, and Matt Gray's Hawesville Gym sign, and is currently waiting on signs to come back from being powder coated for A&B Florist and EMazing Cupcakes & Treats.
He has his own powder coating oven and will eventually start doing that on his own as well. He currently takes everything to Shane Ball at County Line Powder Coating. 'Shane does an excellent job,' he said.
Upcoming Events
Clint often displays his decorative metalwork pieces at vendor shows. An Outlaw Metalworks booth will be set-up on Saturday, July 27th in Hardinsburg at the Summer at the Grounds event, held at the Breckinridge County Fairgrounds. He will also have a booth at the HC Chamber Picnic at Vastwood Beach House planned for Tuesday, September 10th, which begins at 6:00 p.m.
He sets-up a booth in Indiana on occasion, he said, and will be at Schwartz Amish Style Family Restaurant in Eckerty, IN again this fall. He creates awards for local car shows and fishing as well, and said he can create just about anything. 'With the table,' he said, 'the possibilities are endless, really.'
Clint was born and raised in Hawesville. He worked at Century for 13 years, and went to work at Southwire in 2015. He is a Team Leader in the rod mill. His parents are Kenny & Dee Dee Hylton. Clint and his wife, Jamie, are blessed with two daughters, Kendra and Mikayla.
To Place an Order
To place an order with Outlaw Metalworks, you can direct message Clint on Facebook Messenger. His FB Page is: Outlaw Metalworks. You can also call or text him at (270) 314-2537, or email him at: Chylton76@gmail.com. His website is new and he will be adding to it moving forward. You can visit the website by typing in: https://outlawmetalworksllc.com. Once your order is ready, he will deliver to you or meet you somewhere for pickup. He also ships out orders and is already shipping out to 13 different states.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Dave Taylor's Book is Published!
description: The late Dave Taylor's book has been published by his wife, Jamie D. Taylor, and was released on Wednesday, July 17th. The beautiful...
content:
The late Dave Taylor's book 'What I Learned From Dying' is now published and available in soft cover on Amazon.com.
The late Dave Taylor's book has been published by his wife, Jamie D. Taylor, and was released on Wednesday, July 17th. The beautiful book is titled 'What I Learned from Dying' and features the complete collection of his columns published in The Clarion during his battle with cancer.
'I believe what Dave achieved with his columns every week was amazing,' Jamie said. 'I saw how hard it was for him, physically and emotionally, to write those columns. He was very dedicated to his morals and ethics as a journalist and not inserting his own opinion or belief.
For him to go from being so professional and very black and white to putting his heart in these columns and being completely vulnerable, and opening up his heart about his fears, his dreams, and his state, I was just so proud of him.
He always wanted to publish a book, and I just feel like this was my way of making sure that his dream came true. I couldn't make all of his dreams come true, but I could make this one come true.'
Jamie self-published the book via Kindle Direct Press with Amazon, and decided against releasing a Kindle version (digital copy) because she said she really wants Dave's book to exist in the world in a physical copy.
'If people have to buy a copy,' she explained, 'it is existing. And, if they read it and they never read it again, maybe it will end up at a Goodwill and someone else will pick it up. Or, maybe they'll have it sitting on their coffee table and someone will say, 'What is this?' Then, they have to pick it up and it's a way of Dave physically still being around.'
The cover of the book is the portrait that was made with Dave's ashes, and the digital version just isn't the same for that important reason as well. It may be released in hard cover also.
Dave had texted Aaron Kizer, the artist who created his portrait, just 10 hours before he passed away, asking him about painting it for him. That text is included in the book. Aaron also kindly accepted a commission to complete Jamie's portrait, which was also completed with Dave's ashes.
'Even though he was very sick,' Jamie said, 'Dave died unexpectedly. He wasn't on hospice. He wasn't at the hospital. We went to church that day and to the home improvement store. We were doing regular things. The final chapter is just about our last weekend together, and some of the very deep conversations that he and I had.
I'm very proud of it. I'm so proud that it's another way for me to share Dave with people. I just hope that people who have cancer or love someone with cancer can pick it up and relate to it, and just understand that you can live a good life while you're going through these things.'
One of her goals is to help people understand what someone with a terminal illness is going through, what it's like to love someone with a terminal illness, and how you can support them.
'You figure out what's important and what's not important really quickly,' she said. 'He really did carry all of that very well. We just always prayed for God's will to be done. Dave always said, 'God, I pray that you take the cancer away, but if that's not Your will then just help me to handle it the way you want me to.''
The process of writing the book was tough for her, and reading through all of his columns again was difficult. Dave had journaled their relationship in them. He told about how they got engaged and about when they married.
'It was great to share it with the community,' she said, 'and I'm ready to share the book with everyone too. It printed beautifully; It's a beautiful book.'
Jamie also included a Foreword with words from my father, the late Donn K. Wimmer, former Editor and Publisher of The Clarion. Dave worked at The Clarion for many years, is from Hancock County, and became one of Dad's good friends over the years.
'I chose the release date (7-17) because it's my son's birthday,' Jamie said. 'He's turning 18, and it's a special date for me. Also, it's about 6 weeks before Dave passed (in 2022). I had thought I could have it done at the one-year anniversary [of Dave's passing] but that really wasn't allowing myself any time to heal or grieve, or just get my feet back underneath me. I definitely didn't want the second year to pass without it being published.
If there are any book clubs or churches who would like me to come and talk about the book, our prayers and our experience with cancer, I'm willing to do that. I want to share how faith can get you through these really hard times.
I'm so proud of Dave, and I'm so grateful that I'm able to fulfill this lifelong dream that he had. I feel like it's a wonderful way for me to honor Dave, his legacy and his work.'
'What I Learned from Dying' is currently available for purchase in soft cover on Amazon.com. You can contact Jamie with any questions, or to schedule a speaking engagement at: davetaylorproject@gmail.co m .
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Former President Trump Shot in Assassination Attempt
description: The 45th President of the United States Donald J. Trump survived an assassination attempt Saturday, July 13th at his campaign rally in...
content:
Former U.S. President Donald J. Trump signals to the crowd while being rushed off the stage after being shot during an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, PA Saturday.
The 45th President of the United States Donald J. Trump survived an assassination attempt Saturday, July 13th at his campaign rally in Butler, PA. Suspected rooftop shooter Thomas Matthew Crooks (20) was killed by authorities. Trump's upper right ear was hit by a bullet. He is reportedly doing well and attending the RNC Convention in Wisconsin as scheduled. PA Firefighter Corey Comperatore (50) was hit and killed by one of the bullets while shielding his wife and daughter. David Dutch (57) and James Copenhaver (74) were wounded by stray bullets and are in stable condition. Others sustained minor injuries. House Speaker Mike Johnson announced that a full investigation will be conducted, with Secret Service Director Kimberly Cheatle to be questioned at the hearing.

title: Hancock County Fair- July 31st-August 3rd
description: The 2024 Hancock County Fair is Wednesday, July 31st-Saturday, August 3rd at the Hancock County Fairgrounds in Hawesville. This award winning fair offers rides, delicious foods, competitive events,…
content:
The 2024 Hancock County Fair is Wednesday, July 31st-Saturday, August 3rd at the Hancock County Fairgrounds in Hawesville. This award winning fair offers rides, delicious foods, competitive events, exhibits, pageants, motor sports, livestock & animal shows, and more. Don't miss this most fun and looked forward to event of the summer!
Rides
All of Casey's Rides are Free with the $10 Gate Admission each day (Thurs., Fri. & Sat.). Children 2-years-old and younger have Free admission. Rides open on Thursday & Friday at 5:00 p.m., and on Saturday at 2:00 p.m. *On Saturday, August 3rd, Rides will be open from 1:00 p.m.-2:00 p.m. for Special Needs Riders ONLY, organized by Autism Advocates of Hancock County.
Food
Hancock County Future Farmers of America Students will be offering COLD Coca-Cola products again this year! They also help with clean-up each year, and putting produce and crops out on display. They do a great job and their help is greatly appreciated by the HC Fair Board.
The Hornet Band will have hamburgers & hotdogs, and the HCHS Girls' Softball Team will have potato twisters & pizza rolls. The Lewisport Lions Club will have their ribeye & pork chop sandwiches, Knights of Columbus will have delicious hand-dipped quality ice cream, and the Hawesville Lions Club will have all sorts of deep-fried goodness, including corndogs, French fries, jalapeno poppers, chicken nuggets and cheese sticks!
The Amish will have fried pies & iced coffee, and the award-winning Sunny Daze Food Truck will have Philly cheese steak sandwiches and other tasty offerings. You can cool off with Hello Pop's Shake-Ups & Ice Pops as well, and there will be a Fruit Cabob Booth again this year.
There will also be meatloaf sandwiches, chicken quesadillas, baked potatoes, pulled pork nachos, Boston butt sandwiches, and mutton sandwiches! And, the Sunshine Circle Homemakers will have their Saturday Morning Pancake Breakfast from 8:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. in the Amish Booth (across from the Lewisport Lions Club booth). The cost is $7 for adults, and $4 for children, and includes: pancakes, sausage, juice, milk and coffee.
Wednesday
There is Free Admission on Wednesday at the Fair. The exhibits entries start at 2:00 p.m., and there is a Raffle for a chance to win money to pay for your admission into the Fair! The Fair Board encourages everyone to bring their produce, canned & baked goods, crops, and all other entries!
Fair Board President Tim Cecil said, 'We give a $100 check to the adult 18 and over, and to the child 17 and under. For EACH entry you put in, you get a free raffle ticket and a chance to win $100. There is an adult box and youth box to place your raffle tickets in. We draw names from those boxes during the Fair and call out the winners.'
County Wide Church Service Night on Wednesday begins at 6:15 p.m. Come out and join in prayers for this year's Fair to be a safe and enjoyable one for all who attend and for all those who volunteer and work very hard to put it on!
Thursday
Thursday at the Fair is a full day of fun, with baked goods entries due at 8 a.m., Laser Tag at 4 p.m., and an OPEN Livestock Show this year at 5:30 p.m., open to Hancock County and ANYONE in surrounding areas. Evan Tate with the HC 4-H Extension Office is the Organizer.
The fun Pony Cart Racing Event is back this year, and begins at 5:00 p.m. The Annual Talent Show starts at 6 p.m. At 7:00 p.m., there will be an ATV/UTV/Side by Side Timed, Obstacle Course Event (practice laps, 5-6 p.m.), a Pony Pull, and Zach Jennings Band will be performing! The Miss Teen & Hancock County Fair Queen Pageants will kickoff at 7:30 p.m., at the Pavilion Stage.
Friday
Friday is another fun-filled day with the Haflingers & Mule Pull at the Horse Arena starting at 4 p.m. Laser Tag is from 4 p.m.-9 p.m. And, performing at 5 p.m. is Cory Axton! At 6:30 p.m., the Tiny Tots and Little Miss & Mister Hancock County Pageants will be starting. Go Kart Racing begins at 7:00 p.m., as well as a performance from Dan Hall.
Saturday
Saturday begins with the Annual Pancake Breakfast at 8 a.m. The Baby Contest and Youth Sports begin at 9 a.m. The 4-H Rabbit Show is at 10 a.m. ATV Drag Racing, Doll Show, Hobo Contest and Bubble Gum Contest all start at 11 a.m. The Cake Walk is at 11:45 a.m., and Homecoming is at 1 p.m. The Pedal Tractor Pull for children and the Pet Show both begin at 2 p.m. The Ice Cream Eating Contest and Demo Derby begin at 4:00 p.m. More Laser Tag starts at 4 p.m., and the Ranch Sorting Event starts at 5 p.m. Hancock County Junior Prince & Princess Pageant begins at 6 p.m. And, the Fun Mule Show starts at 6:30 p.m.
Talent Show
The Talent Show will be held at the Produce Stage on Thursday, August 1st at 6:00 p.m. Categories are: Child Sing/Instrumental, Child Dance/Variety, Teen Sing/Instrumental, Teen Dance/Variety, Adult Sing/Instrumental, and Adult Dance/Variety. Each category will have cash prizes: $30 for 1st Place, $20 for 2nd Place, and $10 for 3rd Place. The $100 Grand Prize is sponsored by Kyle Culbreth with KY Farm Bureau. Contact Leah Marsch with any questions at: leah.marsch@gmail.com.
Demo Derby
The Demolition Derby presented by A&C Demos is on Saturday, August 3rd with Inspection at 4:00 p.m., and Show Time at 7:00 p.m. The Total Purse is $8,400! Limited Weld, Wire Class, MWFA Street Stock, and Mini Cars Categories will each have 1st, 2nd & 3rd Place Prizes: $1,200 for 1st, $600 for 2nd, and $300 for 3rd. There is a Powerwheels children's event as well. For more info., please contact Eric Adkins at (270) 316-8171.
Ranch Sorting
The popular 2-Man Ranch Sorting Event will be held on Saturday at 5:00 p.m. There is a $10 Gate Fee. Proceeds benefit St. Jude's Children's Research Hospital. Categories are: Open $25/Man (50 percent payback), Youth $20/Man (40 percent payback), Draw $25/Man (50 percent payback), and Beginner $25/Man (50 percent payback). Negative coggins are required. Call Amy Lambert for more info. at (270) 993-4087.
A lot of hard work goes into this event; It takes 40-50 head of cattle to make it happen! Don't miss this family fun event, with money raised for a worthy cause. The barn is packed each year for the Ranch Sorting, and it sometimes lasts until past midnight!
Parking & Shuttles
Fair Board President Tim Cecil and VP Kyle Hoskins said there will be more parking space for this year, as well as another EXIT OUT on Friday & Saturday nights. Traffic can exit the Fair from the 'Back Gate' on those 2 nights, out onto 2181, and then take a left from 2181 back onto Hwy 60. *There will be 2 tractors and 2 shuttle wagons available for those who park a distance from the fair to pick you up and take you directly into the fair!
Thank You
The HC Fair Board extends a Huge Thank You to the businesses and individuals who donate, as well as the many volunteers who make the Fair a success each year. Tim said, 'It would be hard to put this Fair on without them. A lot of our people donate their time helping us. Businesses and individuals donate money. It's really appreciated. It couldn't be done without our area businesses and volunteers.'
Kyle added, 'Everybody just comes together and helps put it on. It's like one big family when it's all said and done.'
Fair Board Member for 14 years, and Board President for 25 years, Franklin Powers, is happy to continue helping with the Fair, and is an invaluable consultant, as well as leading the Board in Prayer at the start of each meeting, as he always has done in past years. He and his grandson are placing the picnic tables out at the fairgrounds for people with grandchildren, for example, who need a place to sit while the children ride rides, etc. He had requested overseeing that this year as well, and the Board greatly appreciates him!
New Bathrooms for 2025
The new bathrooms have not yet been completed but will be for next year! The Board was waiting on a bid for months, and it came in a couple of weeks ago and was a lot higher than anticipated. They said they didn't want to be in the middle of construction during this year's fair but it will be completed for the 2025 HC Fair. The new bathrooms will be housed in a building with a covered porch on the front, and with concrete around it to park strollers, wheel chairs, etc.
The Hancock County Fair is held at the HC Fairgrounds, located at 1430 St. Rt. 1389, in Hawesville. Fair Catalogues are available at HC Farm Supply, Weber Store, Woosley's Farm & Feed Supply, Independence Banks, First Financial Banks, Bill's IGA, JJ's Pizza, Thompson Tire and Papa T's Auto Parts. The website is: https://www.hancockcountykyfair.com and the FB Page is: Hancock County KY Fairground.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Kim Harper is new President at Independence Bank
description: Kim Harper, Independence Bank's New Market President for Hancock County. Kim Harper is now serving as Market President fo
content:
Kim Harper, Independence Bank's New Market President for Hancock County.
Kim Harper is now serving as Market President for Hancock County at Independence Bank. Previous President Wade Gaynor has accepted a President elect position with Independence Bank in Henderson County.
Retired President Rick Embry played a monumental role in bringing Independence Bank to Hancock County, and chose Kim to be a part of that venture over 20 years ago. She has been with the bank from the very beginning.
'I started in April of 2001, initially, to be Rick's assistant,' Kim said. 'It migrated into Lending and then Location Manager. That's what I've been for the past 23 years, is the Location Manager and a Consumer & Commercial Lender. Location Manager means that I am leading the team of Tellers and CSRs (Corporate Social Responsibilities), and taking care of the facilities. It's a good location and there are GREAT people who work here so there's little guidance needed because they're so seasoned.'
Kim was working with Rick's wife at Commonwealth Aluminum in 1985, and when Rick was looking for an assistant, his wife thought of Kim and recommended her. 'That's how it all started,' she said. 'We didn't even have a building here at that time. We were in a mobile unit, a little trailer over here. We watched it being built. I'm very proud of the location and all of the people here. You can't do this job without a great group of people.'
Friday, July 19th was Wade's last day working in Hancock County. On Monday, July 22nd, he began his work in Henderson County. He accepted the position with Independence Bank as President elect, due to retirements happening, and starts in that specific role on January 1st, 2025.
'I've had a wonderful 6 years serving Hancock County,' Wade said. 'It's been great to be back home, and I'm looking forward to the next chapter.'
Kim's position as Market President for Hancock County is over both Independence Bank branches, Hawesville and Lewisport. The Lewisport branch Location Manager is now Kelly Tyler. Previous Location Manager, Larry Heddin, retired in June and Kelly filled that role bringing 22 years of experience with the bank.
'Larry had retired after 17 years with us,' Wade said. 'We already had a plan in the works. Larry let us know that he was going to retire well in advance and it was a natural fit for Kelly to step into that role. She's been here 22 years. She came in one year after Kim came along. She knows much of this community, and she's done a good job in her first month down there, and now Kim Harper will lead the whole County. She'll be leading all of the marketing efforts, community outreach, maintaining her Lending role with the Bank, of commercial and consumer, growing customer relations, and overseeing both the daily operations and future strategy.'
Wade said the transition will be seamless, and explained why saying, 'Kim already took care of the daily operations. She is taking on a bigger role, which is well deserved. She is more experienced than I am in most areas, and she has the help of Missy Noble, who's been with us for 7 years now. Our staff in Hawesville and Lewisport have been here for years. We haven't experienced a lot of turnover because we have such a great culture.'
Kim is starting in the new position with confidence and excitement. 'I've done everything in this Bank, literally everything,' she said. 'I'm not worried about it. I'm a little anxious, but in an exciting way.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: When God shows us His wings
description: A reporter was walking with a firefighter down a road in a burned out forest when they came across a bird in the road. It's head was down and it's wings were formed like a bubble around it's body. The…
content:
A reporter was walking with a firefighter down a road in a burned out forest when they came across a bird in the road. It's head was down and it's wings were formed like a bubble around it's body. The firefighter picked the bird up to see if there was any life in it and quickly realized there wasn't. But cuddled under those lifeless wings were three baby birds.
Sometimes it takes a really dangerous situation for me to realize. God, like that mother bird, has saved me or my family. When I was young, I got into so many dangers. I thought, 'He's going to quit following me around to protect me.' But He never did.
I was traveling down a busy highway one day when I topped a hill to find a car headed toward me at a high rate of speed and he was in my lane. There was no time to think or plan what I could do. Suddenly, I heard a voice say, 'Watch his hands.' As I got closer I did just that. They didn't move. At the last minute I swerved and passed him on his lane. I watched my rearview mirrors and saw him pull to the side of the road. I went back to check on him.
There, I found an elderly gentleman, his hands grasping the steering wheel, his knuckles white. His face was white and frantic looking. I realized he had seen me and frozen with fright on my side of the road. I wondered if God had whispered to him, 'Stay in this lane.'
I was glad God had told me, 'Watch his hands'. Because I never would have thought of that. I still thank God for His protection that day for my family and me. With me in the van were 5 of my kids and beside me in front was a foreign exchange student from Denmark. I shudder to think what a head-on collision would have done.
We get busy with our everyday lives and sometimes forget there is God watching over us, protecting us and guiding us in the way we should go.
He will cover you with His feathers, and under His wings you will find refuge. -Psalms 91:4.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Junior Firefighter Program offered to HCHS students
description: The Junior Firefighter Program, offered at Hancock County's volunteer fire departments, is open to youth in the county age 15 to 17...
content:
The Junior Firefighter Program, offered at Hancock County's volunteer fire departments, is open to youth in the county age 15 to 17. Hancock County High School Students who participate in the program gain valuable, hands-on skills toward a possible career as a first responder. Their training also fulfills some or all of their community service hour requirements at the high school.
Lead Junior Firefighter Advisor at Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department Hunter Stanley said the Junior Firefighters are allowed to participate in all of the trainings that they do, and once they get a certain amount of training hours they can even respond to calls. He encourages youth in the county to join the program.
'I think anybody that wants to pursue a career path in any sort of first responder area – police, fire, EMS, of course, they should try it out,' he said. 'It's also good just to build up community service hours. Everything that they do at the fire department counts for their community service hours for school.'
2024 HCHS Graduate Dylan Ashworth has finished his Junior Firefighter Program training at Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department, and was recognized with a plaque at graduation in May for completing over 1,000 community service hours.
Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards said Dylan has submitted his application at HVFD, as he has aged out of the Junior Firefighter Program, and is now interested in joining the ranks of HVFD Firefighter.
Recruitment at HCHS
'We're going to try to get over to the high school several times this year and reach out to students,' Hunter said. 'It will probably be during their lunch break, and we'll set up in the HCHS Commons Area. We plan on doing that 3 or 4 times this school year ('24/'25).'
If you're interested in joining the Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department Junior Firefighter Program, please email: hawesvillefire@gmail.com. You can also reach out through the HVFD Facebook Page.
The Lewisport Volunteer Fire Department, Dukes Volunteer Fire Department, and South Hancock Volunteer Fire Department may offer Junior Firefighter Programs as well. Youth in the county who reside closer to those departments and would like to participate at those stations are encouraged to inquire and apply through their corresponding Facebook Pages, or in person at those stations.
By Jennfer Wimmer

title: HC Museum President Speaks at Chamber Breakfast
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer The Speaker at this month's Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Breakfast was HCPL Librarian and Hancock County Museum President Kelley Richardson. The Breakfast was held at the…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Speaker at this month's Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Breakfast was HCPL Librarian and Hancock County Museum President Kelley Richardson. The Breakfast was held at the Lewisport Branch Library, on Tuesday, October 8th.
Congratulations to 4 J's Supply, in Lewisport, recognized as the October Business of the Month. The Hancock County Industrial Foundation sponsored the Breakfast.
Kelley talked about how she and the board members are in the process of consolidating the Hancock County Historical Society and the Hancock County Museum into: The Hancock County Historical Society and Museum.
'We feel that we can better serve the community by joining the two groups and sharing resources,' she said. 'We have about 10 active members, but we would like to build that number, and have more people to volunteer at the museum.'
Mark Your Calendar
She also announced some upcoming programs at the HC Museum. Mary Jane Owens will be at the museum on Sunday, October 20th, from 2:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., telling some spooky stories. And, on Saturday, November 30th they will be hosting the 3rd Annual Christmas Open House.
'I encourage everyone to come and visit the museum, and join us in trying to preserve the History of Hancock County,' Kelley said.
The HC Museum, located at 110 River St. in Hawesville, is open every Sunday from April-October from 2-4 p.m., except on holidays. Monthly meetings are every 3rd Tuesday of the month. The HC Historical Society meets at 5:30 p.m., and the HC Museum meets immediately after. Anyone is invited to attend and join. Building maintenance, museum displays, activity planning and brainstorming on how to get new members to join are discussed at meetings.
Private Tours
Private tours can be scheduled during the week for groups and individuals. Anyone interested in scheduling may call Kelley Richardson at (270) 922-7114, or Nathan & Tina Powers at (270) 927-6524. The email is: hancockcountykymuseum@gmail.com.
