title: Incumbent Gregory Faces Challenger Miller in Lewisport's Mayoral Race
description: Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory began his first term in 2005, and is running for re-election. His challenger, Eddie Miller, is running to serve as Lewisport Mayor because he said he thinks it is time for…
content:
Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory began his first term in 2005, and is running for re-election. His challenger, Eddie Miller, is running to serve as Lewisport Mayor because he said he thinks it is time for a change.
Gregory said his mission is to continue to keep the City of Lewisport in sound financial shape, and to try to keep rates sustainable for its citizens. Miller said his main goal is to take care of the people of Lewisport, and help the people of Lewisport.
Chad Gregory
'My mission is also to keep the City of Lewisport safe,' Gregory said, 'and to let the citizens live their everyday lives, and not have to worry about a shaky government. I want to keep rates as low as we can, and still run a profitable business. I don't want people to have to worry about what their rates are going to be, because I'm going to try to keep them as sustainable as it can be for them.'
He expressed how seamlessly he and the Lewisport City Council members and all of the City's employees are able to work together. He also said that everyone on the City of Lewisport team is of the highest caliber; Everyone involved is dedicated to running the city with the utmost integrity, and they truly care about the citizens in the community.
He added, 'We have a great city council; They are excellent to work with. They trust me, and I trust them. They trust me to run the City of Lewisport, day to day. The employees are top-notch. They know what is expected of me, and they know what their everyday function is.'
Eddie Miller
Eddie Miller has lived in Lewisport for 15 years, and has taught martial arts in the county for almost 20 years. His wife, Sona, is a Guidance Counselor at North Hancock Elementary School. They are blessed with one son, Nic Miller.
'We've been here for a long time, and in the county for almost 40 years,' Eddie said. 'I taught Kasho Martial Arts at Lewisport Elementary School and South Hancock Elementary School. I've helped out at Hancock County High School with senior projects, when they've had martial arts students. I've been a Cook at the HOP Shops Truck Stop in Lewisport for the last 3 years.'
He expressed that he plans on putting the people of Lewisport before the 'bank account,' and wants funding to be spent in helping the people of Lewisport.
'I'm running for mayor, as a frustrated citizen who has had enough,' he added. 'I believe the people of Lewisport deserve to be treated better by their mayor. I would appreciate your vote, because it's time for a change. I have experience with people. I'm not a politician, I'm just a frustrated citizen. I'm giving the people a choice. It's time they have a choice, for a change. I plan on taking care of the city like it should be taken care of. We have three bars in this town, and not one thing for anybody under 21 to do. That has to be changed. We're going to have to find something for people under 21 to do in this town. As soon as they get their license, they're gone from Lewisport because there is nothing here for them. I want them to want to stay, and raise their own families here. This is a nice town. We need lots of things for the people to do; there's no place to go anymore. I also plan on taking better care of the roads during the wintertime.'

title: HCHS Marching Band Places Third at Class 2A Finals in Louisville – Congratulations Students!
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hancock County High School Marching Band was one of the top 6 bands of the We
st region competing at the State Semifinals last weekend. They earned the Kentucky Music Education Association 2A West Regional Champion Award on October 19th, for their stellar performance in Bowling Green, which sent them to the Semifinals competition on Saturday, October 26th, held at L&N Credit Union Stadium on the University of Louisville campus.
The students competed on Saturday morning at 9:00 a.m., and put on an excellent performance, once again, earning them a spot in the Finals competition that night. They were competing against 11 other high school bands in the morning; the top 6 bands of the East and the top 6 bands from the West regions were competing. They won Third Place, which sent them to compete in the Finals that evening. Saturday night, they competed against the other 5 top bands of the region, and brought home the Third Place Award.
'They did great,' HCHS Band Director Zach Buskill said. 'For us, the big thing is always making it to State Finals; That's always the goal. And, that's such a special accomplishment. The other goal is to get a Distinguished rating, a marching band score that is 80 or higher. We had both of those things happen. The kids were just really excited. This is the fifth year in a row that we've made State Finals; That's really special too. Our seniors, they've been in State Finals every single year.'
The HCHS Marching Band students put on a special performance last Friday for HCMS and HCHS students during the school day, in the afternoon. Afterward, they had to get rested up, and be back at the school very early the next morning. They left the parking lot for Louisville at 4:30 a.m., with a great send-off from parents and others. The local police and fire departments took the time out of their busy schedules to give them an escort on their way out of town as well. Despite it being in the wee hours of the early morning, there were even Hancock County citizens waving and honking their horns for them along Main Street in Hawesville, as they traveled through on their way to the competition.
The students arrived in Louisville, set-up, and performed at 9:00 a.m.
for Semifinals, and the weather was quite chilly, which was a challenge. When they performed again that evening, thankfully, the weather had warmed up significantly.
'That day is like 3 days in one,' Zach said. 'Truthfully, it was super hard this year, because we had to leave so early, and when we got there it was COLD – low 50s, and windy. That makes everything tougher. We could not do it without all of the parents that help us. We probably have about 20-30 parents that help us set-up props and move everything. Without them, there is no way we could have done it. We're really fortunate that we have such a great group of parent helpers. Also, that morning performance was cold, and that's especially tough for our brass players. When you have cold metal on your face and you're trying to play, it is a real challenge. The kids handled it really well. In the afternoon/evening, it warmed-up into the 60s, so it wasn't nearly as much of an issue for the Finals performance.'
When they returned to Hancock County at around 1:00 a.m., the students were welcomed back with a much deserved, celebratory escort from our wonderful local police and firefighters again, all the way back to the high school parking lot.
'It made the kids feel really special,' Zach said. 'I am super proud of our students. They worked really hard, and just did such a great job this season. I'm really happy that they got to experience all of their success. It was such a big achievement on Saturday. We're really thankful to all of the parents, and to all of the community that has supported us and helped us. We look forward to next year, and continuing to do our best.'
Next, HCHS Band students are preparing for their annual Veterans Day assembly performance. Some of the students have All District Band auditions, and All State Round 1 auditions, coming up in the next 2 weeks. They'll also be preparing for the annual Holiday Concert performance in December, and the Christmas Parades in Hawesville and Lewisport.

title: Meet the Candidates: Hancock County Board of Education Elections
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The General Election is next week, on Tuesday, November 5th, and voters will have the opportunity to choose which candidates will serve District 2 and District 5 on the Hancock County Board of Education (BOE).
Veronica Taylor is challenging incumbent Donna Quattrocchi for the District 2 Hancock County BOE seat. Mary Beth Emmick Morris and Charles Todd Duncan are both running for the 5th District BOE seat. Incumbent Shane Ball is running, uncontested, for the 4th District BOE seat.
Current Board Members
The current Hancock County BOE Members are: Vanessa Cox – District 1 (2023-2027); Brooke Payne – District 3 (2023-2027); Donna Quattrocchi – District 2 (2001-2024); Shane Ball – District 4 (2020-present); and David Emmick – District 5 (2001-2024).
Veronica Taylor
Veronica Taylor, of Lewisport, is a 1971 Hancock County High School graduate, and the daughter of the late Joe & Catherine Taylor. She said she is very passionate about education in all forms, and cares about providing students with many opportunities.
She fulfilled her dream to become a scientist, earning 4 science degrees. Throughout her career, she has worked for the agriculture industry, in laboratories, and on field studies. She was a microbiologist, a plant breeder, a statistician, and retired from her role at the Department for Scientific Support at the Center for Veterinary Medicine in the Federal Drug Administration.
Since moving back to the county in 2020, she has served on the Hancock County Schools Foundation Board for two years, a nonprofit organization established in 2013 to support opportunities for students, and has spoken in classrooms, and volunteered with projects at HC Schools. She helped establish Hancock County Community Kitties, and is a Friend of the Hancock County Public Library.
'I would like people to know that I'm not an outsider,' she said. 'Even when I was away from here, I did support the school. I wanted to be at a place where I could give back something to a community that helped raise me. It's a place that has lots of opportunities, it's a good place to live and work and has a good sense of community. I am a product of Hancock County Schools; I grew up here. I have been away, but I'm glad to be back, and I am very interested in the development of my community.'
She explained her philosophy on learning saying, 'I think the purpose of the school system is to prepare students to be productive, contributing members of the community. And, to that end, I think the school should provide access to the tools that make students successful adults, no matter how success is defined for them. I think schools provide a community service. I am particularly interested in STEM because I became a scientist. I don't think science, technology, engineering and mathematics are the end all and be all of what schools are. I think in many of the technical trades, those things are evident, even though people tend to think of them in terms of college.'
She added, 'I think that we need to pay attention to the average student, as well as the gifted and talented student. And, critical thinking is a very important part of being a successful human, and being able to solve problems.'
Donna Quattrocchi
Donna Quattrocchi is running for a 6th term on the Board of Education, serving District 2. She is a 1976 HCHS Graduate, and the daughter of the late Bill & Jean Shutt. She worked at Owensboro Health Regional Hospital for 43 years. She was Director for a number of years, and Manager of Nursing Service for 26 years. In 2014, she transferred to the Critical Nurse Specialist position.
Donna has been extremely dedicated in serving on the board. Even through battling a serious illness in the last 2 years, she has only missed one board meeting. She said she thinks it's important that the board is committed to setting a high vision of expectation for the students, and that the quality of instruction is clearly defined by the goals that the members set for the superintendent.
'You have to have a strong belief in what is possible for the students and their ability to learn,' she said, 'and to teach all students at the highest level possible. I think we have to be accountable-driven. Listening is both internal as well as external, which includes the teachers and all staff, as well as the parents and people in the community. We need to be united as a board, as a team, even if we don't agree on everything.'
As a senior board member, Donna said it is one of her main responsibilities is to bring the board together as a team.
'Each member brings a different expertise and skillset that makes us better as a board,' she said. 'It's important to hear all of the different sides. It's twice as important to listen as it is to speak, that way everybody gets the opportunity to share and then we can come up with the best decision.'
She supports continual professional development for the teachers, and said she is very happy with the IMSE trainings that have been provided to all of the teachers in the district, with LETRS and Orton-Gillingham, as well as the expanded career pathways they've established at HCHS.
Donna is blessed with two children, Matthew and Jeannie. Matthew, is a Pharmacist at Deaconess in Evansville. Jeannie is Public Administration Specialist with GRADD, serving Hancock County.
Charles Todd Duncan
Charles is currently Assistant Superintendent for the City of Hawesville, and has served in the position for almost one year. He has worked for the City of Hawesville for 9 and a half years total. He was previously on the Public Works crew for the City of Lewisport for just one month shy of 10 years. He also worked for Chappell's Key Stop, in Lewisport, for 14 years, where he was a gas station attendant and mechanic.
Charles graduated from Hancock County High School in 1994, and since has earned his Class 4 Water License, Class 3 Distribution License, Class 2 Waste Water Treatment License, and a Class 2 Waste Water Collection License.
'My goal is to get everyone an equal opportunity to have a good education,' he said. 'I'm for smaller classroom sizes, and I'm for all of the kids learning. I'm kind of old-school in my ways of thinking. If something isn't broken; don't fix it. But, if something needs to be addressed, and the money is there to address it, then it needs to be addressed. I think every kid should have an opportunity to have a good number of books to learn from in the classroom. I think we need to put education first, and I've never seen a kid, yet, learn from a brick. Big buildings are not number one, in my eyes. The number one thing is to get a good faculty and staff, and instruments for the kids to learn.'
He added, 'I urge everyone to get out and vote in November. I want to see everybody get out and vote. That is one reason why I'm running for this seat; I want to give people a say.'
Charles and his wife, Amy K. Duncan, are blessed with one son, Charles Jacob Duncan (16). Amy is an Office Manager at S&V Fabrication.
Mary Beth Morris
Dr. Mary Beth Emmick Morris, OD, Lewisport native, was recognized in 2022 at the Capitol in Frankfort by the General Assembly for being the Kentucky Optometric Association's President. She is a 2009 graduate of Western Kentucky University, and a 2013 graduate of the University of Houston, College of Optometry.
Upon returning to Hancock County, she acquired Meade Family Eye, and practices at all 3 locations- Meade Family Eye, Hardinsburg Eye Care, and Emmick Eye Care.
Mary Beth is the daughter of Rosemary and David Emmick. David is retiring from his many years of serving District 5 on the Hancock County BOE. He was Vice Chairman for several years, and since 2022 has served as Chairman. Mary Beth is hoping to begin filling the role in his place in 2025.
She serves as President of the Hancock County Public Library Board, and is past President of the Hancock County Chamber of Commerce. She serves on multiple committees, volunteers with her church, and is a member of the American Optometric Association.
Mary Beth and her husband, Jordan Morris, are blessed with 4 children, Bradyn, Turner, Georgia Fay, and Pearl.

title: Hardinsburg Turkey Trot 5K is happening November 28th – Sign-up NOW!
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The 3rd Annual Hardinsburg Turkey Trot 5K Run and 2K Run/Walk will be held on Thanksgiving morning, Thursday, November 28th, in downtown Hardinsburg at the Breckinridge County Courthouse Square, and begins at 8:00 a.m. Central Time. This event is FREE for children 17-years-old and younger.
All proceeds will benefit Shop with a Cop, in memory of the late Jerry Critchelow, who served 30 years as a Kentucky State Police Officer, and 10+ years as a School Resource Officer (SRO) at Ohio County High School.
The organizer, Wade Weatherholt, is Jerry Critchelow's nephew.
'He developed Shop with a Cop for impoverished kids in Ohio County,' Wade said. 'Last year, they served over 100 kids. Each kid gets anywhere between $50-$100 to shop for Christmas. They go in with the police officers, and are able to get things they need such as blankets, clothes, jackets, etc. They also help them purchase one toy, or one item, that they want, as well as the things they need. I wanted to do this in memory of my uncle. Shop with a Cop was near and dear to his heart, and he fundraised for it throughout the entire year. Since he passed away in April of '22, his daughter, Amanda Fitzgerald, is continuing to organize it. My goal is to fully fund it every year with this race, and to help take a burden off of her of doing fundraising throughout the year, and to continue to honor my fallen uncle, and let his legacy live on through that organization, by doing it in a fun way that promotes physical activity, and just having people be thankful for their health on a day of giving thanks.'
Canned Food Donation
A canned food donation for the Good Samaritan Center is also encouraged for free participants.
'People can do that, if they want,' Wade said. 'We partner with the Good Samaritan Center. It's right here at the start line. Somebody from their organization will be there at a drop-off location. You're encouraged to bring can goods, because I wanted to do something in our community as well. Even if families aren't able to do that, I don't want that to deter them from being a free runner coming to participate in the event too. I just try to encourage parents or kids to do that, as an act of service to help more of those individuals here in the community.'
Canned good donations will go to a local food bank to help families in need. Especially around the holidays, they are running low in non-perishable goods, and this will help them be stocked for helping as many as possible.
This is Wade's third year of organizing the event. He said they had 300 total participants last year, and his goal for this year is 400.
'I just want to continue to make it a big event and a fun event,' he said. 'I have a race management group out of E-town that comes, and it'll be all-electric timing chips, so the times as the runners finish will get sent directly to your phone.'
Awards
Special awards will be presented to the top male and female race finishers!
5K and 2K Options
'I have a 5K option for people, if they want to run or walk the 5K,' Wade said. 'There is also a 2K option, which is a smaller 1.2 mile walk option for individuals that may just be getting started, and for people who don't want to do the full 3.1 miles, that's a smaller distance option.'
Registration
There is also a QR Code to scan on the flyer/advertisement. You can scan the code with your phone, and that will take you directly to the website for registration, and to track the results of the race on November 28th.
You can register up until the day of the event. Registering early, however, will provide you with a $5 discount. The price will be $20 for those who register before November 20th. After the 20th, the price will be $25. All runners registered before November 20th, will receive a special race t-shirt.
T-Shirts
Race day t-shirts are not included in the free registrations. They can be purchased for $10 during checkout.
Location
The race is held at Breckinridge County Courthouse Square, located at 208 Main Street, in Hardinsburg, Kentucky.

title: History Teacher William Fogle holds Second Annual Dreidel Competition at HCHS
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Hancock County High School History Teacher William Fogle held the Second Annual Dreidel Competitions this week at HCHS. The competitions began on Wednesday, December 18th, and continued on through Friday.
'It kind of happened as an accident,' William explained, 'because I started giving out dreidels and 'gelts,' or replica coins from ancient Israel, but inside it contains chocolate, as kind of a seasonal gift to my colleagues here. It became very popular, so I thought why not have a dreidel competition. 'Dreydl' is a Yiddish word that means 'top' (spinning top). It's basically a Jewish children's game; a game of luck and chance. In the Jewish community we use it to reinforce and to reteach our history, the history of Hannukah, which was the retaking of the Temple, and the taking of ancient Judea back from the Greeks.'
He orders the game pieces every year for the competitions, and sometimes also brings game pieces that have been in his family for a long time, to show the students and his co-workers. He said he started playing the game with his family when he was only around 4 or 5-years-old.
'The origin of the game itself goes back to when the Greeks that controlled Judea at the time had forbidden any sort of religious study, primarily among our youth,' William said. 'The game became a way for our children to study in the temples, because the Greeks allowed gambling. Basically, the dreidel game is just a game of luck. You spin it, and based on whichever Hebrew letter comes up, you have to do a certain thing. Either you win a pot, or you'll donate something, or nothing happens. It dictates four different outcomes, and it's strictly chance.'
Both this year and last year, William has organized dreidel games for both the students and the adult staff at HCHS. The staff games were held on Wednesday, after school. The student dreidel games were held during the school day on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, and he said he expected that upwards of 100 students would be participating this year, as they did last year.
'The thing that energizes me is how popular it became with the student body here last year,' he said. 'I had at least 100 kids in and out of my classroom during SWARM session, which is essentially like a study hall. That's when I have it for the kids. They come in specifically for the dreidel contest, and I ask them to sign in so I can keep track of who's here and who's not. It was just a constant flow of kids last year to try this. I have a male and a female champion, and I always provide some sort of prizes to make it interesting. They seem really excited and energetic over this, and I'm happy to do it again this year.'
The competitions are set up so that 4 students can play dreidel at one time. In the front of his classroom, he has the game set up on a large table.
'I just do this for entertainment and cultural value,' he said. 'Hannukah, this year, coincides with Christmas. The timing coincides with the end of this calendar year, academically.'
Hanukkah 2024 is celebrated on Wednesday, December 25th through Thursday, January 2nd, 2025. The dreidel game is played with a four-sided spinning top, or dreidel, and it has four Hebrew letters on it: nun, gimel, hey, and shin. Each one of those is also an instruction in the game.
The four letters are an acronym for the phrase 'nes gadol hayah sham,' which translates to 'a great miracle happened there,' commemorating when the Jewish people went to light the Temple's Menorah, the seven-branched candelabrum, and found that only a single cruse of olive oil had not been contaminated. A miracle happened when they lit the Menorah, and the one-day supply of oil lasted for eight whole days, until new oil could be prepared under the conditions of ritual purity.
'Everyone starts out with four pieces of 'gelt,' which are chocolate coins,' William said. 'If you get a 'nun,' for instance, you do nothing – you neither win anything nor lose anything, and you keep your four pieces of chocolate. If you roll a 'gimel,' you get everything in the pot. If you get a 'hey,' you get half of the pot, and if you get a 'shin,' you have to put a token in. The game goes around and around like this, until there is only one winner.'
Taking the time to organize these competitions each year, and getting the students engaged in playing the game, as opposed to just reading about it in a textbook for instance, really is the ultimate way of learning about this cultural tradition. It puts the participants right there with generations of people who've played the game for centuries. This is a great, hands-on way to teach students. They will remember the experience, and may even teach younger siblings to play, or teach their own children one day as well.
'I've been really surprised at how popular this has become,' he said. 'On the first day of school, I had kids coming up to me asking me when the dreidel contest was going to be. There is no national dreidel competition, so I thought, why not us? I just really want this to be something for our kids. It was a constant flow of activity last year, when I did this for the first time. I set up some flyers around the school, and then they let me know when they can come in and play dreidel. I accommodate anybody who comes through the door.'
This year, the first-place prize for the student winner and the adult winner is a $50 Amazon card. The second-place student prize is a gift certificate to Subway. Last year, William gave gift certificates to local restaurants in Hancock County, for the prizes.
'One of the places that I bought a gift certificate from last year no longer offers that, so I just came up with the Amazon idea this year,' he said. 'I certainly use it as an opportunity to explain some things about Jewish culture and history, and in such a fun atmosphere like that, the kids are more than willing to participate in that and learn about it.'
He said he plans to continue having the dreidel competitions every year. These games are not only fun, but foster inclusivity and promote awareness of Jewish culture and traditions.
'I would like to do it every year,' he said. 'I was pleasantly surprised about how well it took off.'
William is always thinking of new ideas and good programs the students can benefit from. Last year, he came up with the idea to start a Mock Trial Team at HCHS, and has started the team this year. They began practicing in October, every Monday after school, and will have their first regional competition in January. The Kentucky High School Mock Trial Association Regional Tournament will be held at the Owensboro Judicial Center on January 25th and 26th, 2025.
'This year it's a civil case,' he explained. 'We get a fictional civil case, and we will argue in a regional competition in Owensboro, in front of a panel of judges that will be actual judges and/or lawyers and other people in the legal community. We have 13 other teams in our grouping, that range from Louisville to Paducah. We have, what I consider, a really sharp bunch of kids that are throwing their all into this. It should be interesting. The team is mostly made up of freshmen and sophomores, with the thinking that they'll be with it for a couple of years. I think they are going to do really well. We meet after school, like a club. These kids put together their arguments, the same as you would as a lawyer. You have your opening, your closing, you prepare your evidence, and prepare for examination and cross-examination of witnesses. We even have kids who will be playing various witnesses in this case. I'm impressed with the effort and the quality these kids have brought to this. We're limited to a team of 15, plus an artist, and we have met that requirement.'
William is teaching U.S. Government this school year. He has five sections of government, which are mostly taken by freshmen, and is also teaching one section of dual-credit Political Science.
His main hobby, when he isn't teaching, is international traveling. He has been affiliated with the METAdrasi Organization in Greece for many years, and travels to Thessaloniki during the summers. Last year, he volunteered at a center there doing art therapy with refugee children. This year, he volunteered his time doing refugee work in Moldova for three weeks, to help support Ukrainian refugees at the Chabad Lubavitch Jewish Community Center in Kishinev.
William has also been invited to guest lecture twice during his trips to Europe, at Aristotle University in Greece. And, he usually sets up an online group every year, so his students at HCHS can follow his travels during their summer break.
William has been teaching for over 20 years in Europe and in the U.S. He began teaching at HCHS in 2022, and said he loves it. He also sponsors the HCHS Chess Club.
He earned his first degree at Lycee-College des Creusets in Sion, Switzerland, and his Bachelor's in Political Science and History at Indiana State University, with multiple minors. His Spanish Degree and teaching credentials, he earned at University of Southern Indiana, and his first Master's at Western Kentucky University. He's currently completing an Education Specialist Master's Degree with Principal Certification through University of the Cumberlands.
He has served on the Advisory Board for the U.S. Servas National Board for several years, and has been involved with them for 40 years. For a few years now, he has also volunteered as a mentor at the International Center of Owensboro.
William's bestselling book, 'A Stroke Survivor's Tale: A Survivor and Caregiver's Resource,' was published by AR Press in 2022, under his pen name, Liam Bernard, and he'll be working on a second edition soon. He's also currently working on his first novel. After that, he'll be writing 'Teacher Tales,' he said, which will be a reflection on his experiences in teaching on both sides of the Atlantic.
William and his wife, Dee, live in Owensboro. They celebrated 25 years of marriage this year by taking a trip to Ireland during the summer.

title: Lewisport Council begins the year with new Member
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer United States Air Force Veteran Roy A. White, of Lewisport, was elected by the people in November to serve on the Lewisport City Council. This will be Roy's third term serving as a…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer United States Air Force Veteran Roy A. White, of Lewisport, was elected by the people in November to serve on the Lewisport City Council. This will be Roy's third term serving as a member of the Lewisport City Council, as he has served two terms on the council in previous years. All other members are incumbents serving for another term, which is two years. The six incumbents who ran for re-election in November to serve on the council were: Marsha Johnson, Kelly Vanover, Josh Roberts, Tori Sipes Shively, Josephine 'Josie' Hagan, and Mary M. Hawkins. Roy received 409 votes, causing him to win Hagan's spot on the council. He began after being sworn-in at the first monthly meeting of the year, on Thursday, January 16th. 'I want to represent the people the best I can,' he said. 'My goal is to be faithful to them, and be true to the laws of the land…I want us to have good, clean water, and I want to make sure our sewer system stays good, and keeps working good like it is.' Roy said he's looking forward to the new water plant being built. The funding has been coming in for that new reverse osmosis water plant to be built behind the Lewisport Library, and it will have the capacity to provide for all of Hancock County. 'I would like to see that even if I have to hang around another 2 years (run for another term),' he said, 'and I'd like to make sure that we've got our water purified for drinking and everything else, for the health and well-being of the people…I don't know whether I'll run again or not. I'd like to, but if I think somebody is more qualified, I wouldn't want to knock them out of it either. I'm 78-year-old, and I'm kind of a firm believer that anybody ought to retire when they get around 80 or 82, at the most.' He said that he also thinks it is very important to keep the city safe, especially for the children and the elderly. 'If you can think of anything that would help make our city safer for our elderly people and our kids and grandkids,' he said, 'let me know.' Roy welcomes citizens to ask him any questions they have. He says sometimes he goes out to Los Amigos, in Lewisport, for lunch and that you can feel free to come up to him and voice your concerns. There is always time set aside at the council meetings for public comments, of course, but not everyone has the opportunity to attend because of their work schedules, or lack of childcare, etc. 'I'll try to give you a good answer,' he said. 'If I don't have one for you, I'll have some of the other council members or the mayor get back with you to give you an answer.' Roy is the son of the late Opal Elizabeth DeJarnette White and Earl LaMar White, U.S. Army Veteran, who served during WWII. He graduated from Hancock County High School in 1965, and served four years active duty in the U.S. Air Force, from 1966-1970, and two years of inactive duty until 1972. His father had moved the family back to Hancock County from Michigan when he was very young. They lived in Hawesville, and then moved to Lewisport when he was a teenager, in 1959. 'Me and Dad were watching Combat one night, a TV show. Vic Morrow was running down the street and getting shot at, and I asked Dad, 'Were you in a predicament like that?' He said, 'Yeah, and it's not a bit of fun…If I were you, I'd go join the Air Force.' Because they knew the draft was after me; I was about ready to get drafted, and that's what I did. In the Air Force, I was a C-130 Mechanic. We hauled paratroopers if they wanted to parachute out somewhere. When I was stationed overseas in Taiwan, our planes went to Vietnam to take supplies and troops over there, back and forth.' When Roy returned from overseas, he began at Southwire Rod & Cable, in Hawesville, and worked there for almost 40 years. He retired in 2010. In the 1980s, Roy's younger brother, Larry White, was in the U.S. Army Reserve and talked him into getting in the program, he said. 'They wanted me to lose an E grade, from E4 down to E3, and then I was going to have to have a dependency waiver to get in the Army Reserve, so I joined the National Guard for a year, and when my year was up, they didn't want me to transfer to the Army Reserve. So, I got out of the Guard, and joined the Army Reserve. They let me keep the rank then, since the Guard let me keep it,' he said. During that time in the U.S. Army Reserve, he transferred out to the U.S. Coast Guard Reserve for about 2 years and 3 months, and then went back to the U.S. Army Reserve. 'They let me back,' he said. 'I went to serve in Bowling Green in '95, I think it was, and I was over there about 3 years. Then I got in the 87th Division Exercise at Fort Knox. When I went to Bowling Green, I made E6. When I went to the 87th Division, I made E7. In 2001, I put in another promotion packet.' Between those times of service, Roy and local U.S. Army Veteran Jim Domerese, both in the Army Reserve at the time, were teaching the Total Army Intensive Training Course (TAITC). They taught those for several years together. 'We traveled to Paducah, Bowling Green and different locations,' he said. 'We taught a class how to give a class; TAITC is teaching other people how to do the training courses.' The 87th Division Exercise changed over to the 85th Division Exercise. They changed the name but kept all of the same people, and Roy was then stationed at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina, and trained there, as an Observer Controller. 'We watched these other people do these tasks out in the field, and we graded them on it,' he said. 'The next year, we went to California, to Fort Irwin, and we were doing the same thing out there. We came back, and I put another promotion packet in to the 100th Division Headquarters, in food service, in Louisville, not too far from the airport. We went around and inspected food service records of all the companies…I ended up retiring as a Master Sergeant, and served between 26 and 27 years, total.' Roy has served on the Hancock County Board of Adjustment for around 6 years, representing Lewisport, along with Wesley Pate. Now that he will be serving on the Lewisport City Council again, he can no longer also continue to be on the HC Board of Adjustment, per the guidelines. He also ran for the District 1 Magistrate seat in 2018, and again in 2022, but did not win in those elections. Roy is a believer, and a faithful Christian. 'Prayer is our strongest tool that we've got,' he said. 'If it falls under God's will, then it will be done. In Proverbs 3:5, 6, it says to trust in the Lord, with ALL your heart, and lean not to thy own understanding…I think He knows us better than we know ourselves.' He told the story of why his father chose the name Roy for him. 'I was born in Dearborn, Michigan, in 1946. My dad and mom got married in June of '42. Dad went into the military, I think in '43. Mom and Dad had been married 9 months to the day,' he said, 'and she had their firstborn son, my older brother, Lenthel White. Then Dad got drafted into WWII in the Army. He'd send pictures home to Mom and them. They only had a picture of Dad from the waist up. After my dad got through with his military service, overseas, he was telling me a story one time about him and a guy named Roy Crocker. They became good buddies, and both believed in the Lord (Christ Jesus). They were out on maneuvers one day, and were coming back to camp, and they came to a fork in the road, and he said both roads went back to camp. He said Roy wanted to take one road, and he wanted to take the other road. He said about 45 minutes coming back, he heard a bunch of gunfire. He said when he got back to camp the next day, he found out Roy didn't make it. After Dad got back home, my older brother said, 'Hey Mom, look! Dad has legs.' He never had seen any pictures of Dad, to make sure he still had his legs. That was probably in '45. Then in '46, Mom and Dad were blessed again and had a child, and it was me. He named me after his best buddy, Roy Crocker, who lost his life during WWII, in Germany. I have felt blessed my whole life because I was named after his best friend.'
Roy's wife, the late Paula Lynn Jett White, sadly, passed away with cancer in 2015, and at only 58-years-old. They had been married since 1975. He is blessed with 4 children, Erin Beth, John, Laura, and Daniel, as well as 11 grandchildren, and one great-granddaughter.

title: Heartbreaking Detail Emerge in Case of Baby Miya's Death
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer It is with a very heavy heart that we at The Clarion provide this new information released on the tragic death of eight-month-old Miya Rudd, of Ohio County, who was found deceased…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer It is with a very heavy heart that we at The Clarion provide this new information released on the tragic death of eight-month-old Miya Rudd, of Ohio County, who was found deceased and hidden in her family's home in Reynolds Station in June of last year. At the time when original details were released, Miya's cause of death was yet to be officially determined, and the investigation is still ongoing. The report from the state medical examiner revealed that the cause of Baby Miya's death is still undetermined, however the autopsy report showed that meth was in her system, according to the results returned from toxicology testing. A missing child investigation began on June 6th, 2024. When Kentucky State Police first questioned Miya's parents, Tesla N. Tucker (29) and Cage C. Rudd (30), at their residence in Reynolds Station, they stated that they had not seen her for a month. KSP had opened the missing child investigation after a search warrant and welfare check was conducted. Tucker and Rudd were arrested at that time. Both were charged with Possession of Controlled Substance 1st Degree (Fentanyl), Possession of Drug Paraphernalia, and Abandonment of a Minor. Rudd was also charged with Possession of Controlled Substance 1st Degree (Methamphetamine). They were detained at Daviess County Detention Center at that time. A search was conducted by KSP on Friday, June 14th, 2024, and that's when Miya's body was found in the residence, and hidden in a concealed manner. After processing the scene, Baby Miya's body, which was in a state of decomposition, was taken by the Ohio County Coroner's Office and transported to the KY Medical Examiner's Office in Louisville. Tucker and Rudd, as well as Miya's grandfather, Ricky J. Smith (56), and Brodie C. Payne (28), were each charged with: Abuse of a Corpse, Tampering with Physical Evidence, and Failure to Report the Death of a Person. Tucker and Rudd were additionally charged with: Trafficking in Controlled Substance, 1st Degree (Greater than 2 grams-Methamphetamine), Trafficking of Legend Drugs, Trafficking Marijuana, Child Abuse 1st Degree, and Engaging in Organized Crime. KSP Troopers later charged Payne for his role in the illegal drug operation held at the Rudd residence, where he had been residing for approximately 6 months. Payne was charged with Trafficking in Controlled Substance, 1st Degree (Greater than 2 grams-Methamphetamine), Trafficking of Legend Drugs, Trafficking Marijuana, Engaging in Organized Crime, Possession of Paraphernalia, and Wanton Endangerment – 1st Degree. The Daviess County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit had begun a drug trafficking investigation on Payne months prior. Tucker, Rudd, Smith, and Payne have been charged with murder and child criminal abuse in connection to Miya's death. These four have all been indicted, and the next court date is February 3rd. Tucker is currently detained at Ohio County Detention Center. Rudd, Payne and Smith are detained at Davies County Detention Center.
The investigation has been ongoing by KSP, Ohio County Coroner's Office, and the KY Medical Examiner's Office.

title: Historic Flooding Leads to State of Emergency in Kentucky
description: Rainfall began Friday evening, February 14th, and continued through Saturday in the Commonwealth. Over 300 roads were closed in Kentucky, as of Sunday morning. Governor Andy Beshear declared the state…
content:
Rainfall began Friday evening, February 14th, and continued through Saturday in the Commonwealth. Over 300 roads were closed in Kentucky, as of Sunday morning. Governor Andy Beshear declared the state of emergency for the Commonwealth on Sunday, February 16th, and President Donald J. Trump quickly approved an Emergency Declaration for Kentucky on the same day. Beshear thanked President Trump, and said it was the fastest that he had ever seen a president sign off on an emergency declaration. Federal disaster assistance for all 120 counties in the Commonwealth is available to supplement the response efforts necessary for emergency conditions in the areas affected by severe storms, straight-line winds flooding and landslides that began on Friday, and continued. FEMA already had boots on the ground in KY on Sunday, and is authorized to coordinate all disaster relief efforts and provide appropriate assistance to save lives, protect property, and public health & safety, and to lessen or avert the threat of catastrophe, which will be provided at 75 percent federal funding. Jeremy Slinker was named as the Federal Coordinating Officer for federal response operations. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet has called the flooding 'historic.' Over one thousand rescues were made as of noon on Sunday, and Beshear announced that KY was in the search and rescue phase. Hancock County drivers were advised not to attempt to drive on flooded roadways over the weekend. There was flash flooding and also some snow covering on the 900 block of Happy Hollow Road, Quisenberry Road at KY HWY 1700, Squirrel Tail Hollow Road, Tick Ridge Road, Lyonia Easton Road, Horse Fork Road, Middle Knottsville Road, and others. The following roads were still closed, as of Tuesday, in Hancock County due to high water: Muddy Gut Road, Knox Lane, Speaks Lane, Waitman Station Loop, Toler Bridge Road, State Route 661, Ray Road, Richardson Road, and Driskell Lane. The most affected areas in the Commonwealth were in Eastern Kentucky. It is unbelievable and extremely sad that many have lost their lives due to floodwaters and winter weather over the last several days. It is advised, due to incoming winter storm weather, for drivers in Hancock County and surrounding areas to stay off of the roads, if at all possible. Heavy snow is likely for Tuesday evening through Wednesday afternoon, February 19th. Roadways will be slick, and hazardous conditions will negatively impact the Wednesday morning commute for many in the area. Total snow accumulations are expected to be between 2-6 inches, according to the National Weather Service. Hancock County Schools were closed on Tuesday, and students completed non-traditional instruction (NTI) via packets kept at home. It was announced on Tuesday afternoon that HC Schools would also be closed on Wednesday, February 19th, with students completing NTI Day 9 assignments at home, and those will be due at a later date. Like and follow the Hancock County Public Schools Communication Facebook page to keep updated on further school closings. Like and follow the Hancock County Kentucky Emergency Management Facebook page to stay informed on road closings.
To check the Ohio River water level at the Cannelton Lock & Dam, which is measured every hour, go to: riverweather.com.
In the event of an emergency, please dial 911. Non-emergency calls can be made to (270) 927-1311. The Hancock County Sheriff's Office is open Monday-Friday, and can be contacted at: (270) 927-6247.

title: Jesse William Daniels
description: Jesse William Daniels, 83, of Lewisport, passed away from this earth to his heavenly home on Monday, February 17, 2025 at Hartland Villa. He was born in Hawesville on May 25, 1941 to the late Jesse…
content:
Jesse William Daniels, 83, of Lewisport, passed away from this earth to his heavenly home on Monday, February 17, 2025 at Hartland Villa. He was born in Hawesville on May 25, 1941 to the late Jesse and Ivo Hazel Morgan Daniels. Jesse was a member of Chestnut Grove Baptist Church and was a lifelong farmer. He also worked production at Schwab Safe Company and American Olean Tile. Jesse was a member of Hilltop Trail Riders, enjoyed working and breaking horses and loved all animals and children. He was preceded in death by a grandson, Austin Arnold; granddaughter-in-law, Rikki Arnold; sister, Becky Roberts; brother, Brown Daniels; nephews, Darrell Daniels and Brian Roberts He is survived by his wife of 63 years, Patsy Poole Daniels; daughters, Ladonna (Dewayne) Arnold, Cindy (Darrell) Moffitt, Jessica (Ricky) Brown, Miranda (Caston) Bailes and Beverly Bell; grandchildren, Amanda, Adam, Amy, Daniel, Brittany, Ashley, Kirk, Ben and Billy; 9 great grandchildren; special friends, Halli Dant, Mike Landers and Mike Dean along with several nieces and nephews.
Services will be held at 2 pm on Saturday, February 22, 2025 at Gibson & Son Funeral Home, Lewisport Chapel with burial following in Chestnut Grove Cemetery. Jesse's family will be greeting friends on Saturday at the funeral home from 9 am until 2 pm. Share our memories and condolences with his family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Sellout Crowd Gathers for Annual Hancock County Farm City Dinner & Ag Awards Maxwell Named Ag Person of the Year
description: The Annual Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Farm City Dinner & Ag Awards event was held on Monday evening, February 17th at the Hawesville Baptist Church Life Center. HCHS Ag Teacher Josh Smith, and…
content:
The Annual Hancock County Chamber of Commerce Farm City Dinner & Ag Awards event was held on Monday evening, February 17th at the Hawesville Baptist Church Life Center. HCHS Ag Teacher Josh Smith, and Hancock County Future Farmers of America students attended and served the guests, as they do each year. FFA students led the opening ceremony, and an invocation was given by HCHS FFA Chaplain, Izzy Ross.
Tickets were sold-out for this favorite yearly event, and Chamber President Jake Powers welcomed the crowd of 250 people. Chamber Director Tina Snyder recognized the agricultural members of the HC Chamber of Commerce. Many elected officials were in attendance this year, including Senator Boswell, Judge-Executive Roberts, Mayor McCormick, Mayor Gregory, Magistrate Baker, Magistrate Gray, and Judge Boling, as well as HC Industrial Foundation Chair Mike Baker. Scholarship awards were presented, and this year's Ag Scholarship went to Sadie Obenchain. The Chamber Scholarship was awarded to Rayley Higdon. The Hancock County Agriculture & Natural Resources and 4-H Youth Development Extension Agent, Evan Tate, announced the Person of the Year, Paul Maxwell, Co-owner of Maxwell Brothers Lumber. Paul, his son Nathan, and his son-in-law Brandon Tuell, operate the very successful sawmill business, and they generously donate toward projects in the community each year. Paul Maxwell is the last remaining founder. His brothers, Tom and Joe, retired a number of years ago. He has persevered over the years, and has continued to improve and upgrade the business, even when faced with recovering from a near fatal saw accident in 1987. Their family-owned sawmill operations began in Lewisport in 1986. The Grain Yield Contest award winners were announced, and S & J Emmick Farms won the award for corn, at 321.2 bushels, using DeKalb Brand seeds, developed by Bayer Crop Science. Boswell Farms was the winner for soybeans again this year, at 93 bushels, also using DeKalb seeds. It was proudly announced that the Hancock County Fair was, yet again, the recipient of one of the highest awards achievable. HC Fair 2024 was the runner-up for Most Progressive Fair, at the Kentucky Association of Fairs & Horse Shows (KAFHS) Convention at the Galt House in Louisville, for Zone 1, Division A. The guest speaker, Kentucky Commissioner of Agriculture Jonathan Shell, is a fifth-generation Kentucky farmer from Garrard County. He became the youngest member of the General Assembly when elected to the Kentucky House of Representatives in 2012. A year later, he was elected as Kentucky's first-ever Republican House Majority Floor Leader. 'I've got the best job in the state of Kentucky,' Shell said. 'Every day I get to wake up and work on your behalf and see the best of the best in every corner of the state, especially around our young people. And Jake Rudy, our State Treasurer for FFA, did a great job today talking about agriculture.' He reminded attendees that this week is National FFA Week, and encouraged everyone to post on their social media pages, and share something about their FFA experiences. 'It's the best leadership organization that we've got in America,' he said. 'And raising up young kids towards making sure that you've got new leadership for the future is extremely important.' Shell said U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins attended the 4-day National Farm Machinery Show this past week in Louisville, and that it was the very first place she visited after being confirmed and sworn-in on February 13th, where she received a large reception, and made time to talk to farmers. 'We brought her in front of 20,000 people at the Championship Tractor Pull,' he said. Shell said he watched as a young FFA student, Cyrus Williams, waited patiently to get a chance to speak with Rollins. When Cyrus got his chance, he wanted to make sure she knew about the KY program 'Raising Hope.' The mission of the program is to support and advocate for the mental health of KY farmers. 'I watched that 16-year-old young man get the courage in his head to turn around and talk to the top Ag person in America about a beautiful program that we've got here in the state,' Shell said. 'That's what these programs mean for the future of what we have to offer here in places like Hancock County, and in every community of the state. When you pour back into these young people in FFA and 4-H, and these leadership programs, you're going to pay dividends on the back end. I think that is truly an amazing story to be able to tell, for him to have the wherewithal and courage to be able to do that. And you've got young kids right back in the kitchen right now (HC FFA students) that have that same kind of courage that are building that up in themselves because of you in this community, and how you're showing them what it means to be an adult and to care about something in this state.' At Shell Farms and Greenhouses, they raise cattle. Jonathan and his wife, Brooke, and their four children also grow flowers, corn and pumpkins.
'Every day when I wake up,' he said, 'I go as a farmer, and I go on your behalf as commissioner…I love raising kids on the farm. There's no better way that I have found in my life, including in myself, to be able to instill the hard work, what a handshake means, what it means to be a part of your community, to have faith in your community, and to have faith in God, than to be able to raise kids on the farm. I feel sorry for people that don't get that opportunity because of what it meant for me when I was growing up. One of the things that we're doing at the Department of Ag right now is trying to bring that experience to kids that don't have it. When you think about Ag education in KY, for as long as I can remember we basically have done it in high school. If you get Ag education in high school, you get to be in FFA…But we've lost a generation. We know that if we don't get them earlier and start teaching these kids where their food comes from and what it means much earlier, we're going to lose another generation. Myself, the lieutenant governor, and the education commissioner have put together this program. We're calling it 'All In for Ag Week.' ' All In for Ag Week is March 17th-21st, and will be every year, and may even possibly be twice a year. They've created a curriculum with the education cabinet for teachers that can be found on the KY Ag website. 'On the website, we've got an education cachet now where the elementary school teachers can go to get all the stuff that they need so that they can teach Ag in the classroom,' he said. 'Our hope is that we've got farmers in the community that have signed up for a real Ag experience where we can also get these kids on a farm to see what they're doing.' Shell said they are dedicated in working on agriculture and economic development at the department every single day. 'We try to focus on 4 main areas: our row crops around research and infrastructure, around our livestock, around how to get further processing and more processing for our livestock industry, and then our vegetable production,' he said. 'How do we increase that to where we're creating demand in our schools and our hospitals and other places in order to get locally grown food into those locations and into retail ballots? Lastly, we focus on unformed retail, direct marketing, and tourism in the state. Around research and development, we look at how can we expand our opportunities around grain markets here in KY. This is an area of the state that used to have a really nice area to go send your grain to in Meade County. That's gone. How do we replace things where you can get your grain sold more locally, and increase those basis points so we can compete on a national and international level?…What we need to be able to do is consume more of that in the state, whether it be in biofuels, in feedlots or poultry operations, to be able to consume more of that here so we're using more of it, increasing those basis points and controlling our own destiny…So, how do we create that demand around that here in the state of KY?' He concluded his speech with talking about livestock operations, and asked the question: How do we increase that processing and production? He also strongly encouraged every farmer who works together with their family members to appreciate that time together, even when they don't see eye to eye on how to go about doing something. 'A lot of times we don't think about agriculture as economic development like it would be in manufacturing or a factory,' he said. 'You all are a big manufacturing county here. When you think about ag and the manufacturing side, the processing side of it, let me tell you a few of those success stories that we've got here in KY. Just down the road, in Henderson and Robards, you have the Tyson facility. They process 1.3M chickens a week in that facility. They employ 1,200 to 1,400 jobs on that location as well. Not to mention all the farmers that are producing those chickens to be able to supply it into their hundreds of farmers. And then hundreds more farmers that are supplying the corn that goes into those feed mills in order to feed those chickens. That's truck driving jobs and other jobs that are associated with a huge impact of a processing facility like that. Just north of here in Jefferson County, they process 10,500 hogs a day. That's another 1,200 to 1,400 jobs that are in that facility that are local. Not to mention the hog farmers out in western Kentucky, and the corn and soybean farmers that are supplying it. Agriculture and the processing that we do there, that end-user and consumption, is an economic driver and creates that economic viability that we have. So, you think about local consumption that we have moving into vegetable production. When you think about a school district, I'll give you one example – Marion County, Kentucky has 22,000 people in it. They have 3,000 kids in their school district. They feed 800,000 meals in that school district a year. And, usually, if you've got a hospital in your community, it's the largest food consumer in that community. How can we build out those demands so that folks like the Obenchains and others across the state can help build that local demand and do it in a way that really makes a difference on farm income, cash receipts, and profitability? We created a program that will work with the Hospital Association right now, how food is medicine. How do we focus on getting more locally grown food in their cafeterias, in their vending options? Most importantly, how do we work on post-patient care around medically tailored boxes? Think about how many times you've gone to the doctor and they just want to push pills to you or do procedures, etc. Well, instead of working on sick care, how do we work on well care, on that front-end option? How do we work with our local businesses and local communities to try to offer options on subscription food services or prescription food services? Those are the kind of things I'm working on to try and think outside the box in order to help build and create that demand…With tourism opportunities, we have the KY Bourbon Trail, so what about a KY Proud Trail? Building out a website for that you can create an ag-staycation in any county in the state of KY around your lodging, your entertainment, and your food options. We're working on all of these things and trying to figure out: How can we create as great a market share and opportunities as we can for local producers in every county and every community in this state? There's so much more that we want to accomplish. When you think about procurement issues in our schools on the local, state, or federal level, how do we get barriers out of the way and make it as easy and simple as possible for a farmer to be able to sell directly in? When you think about economic development and ag specifically, a lot of times we create the investment we have, the big investment, but we don't always create the jobs associated with it. It's one area that we're finding difficulty, especially around economic development and incentive opportunities. It's not just those jobs inside, it's those farming jobs, truck drivers, it's an impact beyond. We're working with the legislature this year to try and create an opportunity for ag economic development, to work in conjunction with our economic development cabinet to expand those opportunities for investment to come into this state, to really grab ahold of a lot of the processing that we need in this state – more freezer space, more cold storage space, cut, can, and freeze facilities that are packaging for food service directly here in the state of KY. We're so excited about the opportunities that we're trying to help foster, create and identify, so that we can really make a difference in every community that we represent. I love being your commissioner of agriculture. We've got some of the best employees in the entire world at the Department of Agriculture. These are hardworking people…They really care about their jobs, and they're doing a great job. We've tried to create an atmosphere around the department, of innovation, success, and gratitude…I just want to say how grateful I am to be here with you all today, and how grateful I am that you've entrusted me to be your commissioner of agriculture, to work on your behalf. I promise you, as a farmer, I'm going to be the hardest working employee that you all have to pay through your tax dollars. Every single day, I'm going to wake up and put my feet on the ground and have you in mind…How many of you in here in the morning, as a farmer, you and your son, or you and your dad, or your granddad, you all get together and talk about what you're going to do that day? There's several of you in here that do that. You get together in the morning, you try to think about what you're doing, and then you try to go do it. Me and my dad and my granddad used to do that every morning, and we'd fight every morning. We'd all say the same thing, but we'd all be saying it in a different way. Somebody ended up cussing at somebody, and somebody ended up falling away. I see some of y'all laughing; I know you've done it…Think about the people that you've got in your life and what they mean to you and what they're going to mean to you when they're not here anymore. I'd encourage you, whatever you're doing, just enjoy it, even the fights that you're having with your family, the good times, and the bad times. I would enjoy every moment that I possibly could with the people that have come before you and the people that are coming after you.'
Details of the development of the Hancock County Ag Business Recruitment Initiative were also provided at the dinner, as well as information on community gardens, the Young Ag Leaders Program, and Annie's Project, which enhances business skills, and currently has three local participants. In addition,10,000 investments have been made through the Youth County Agricultural Incentives Program (CAIP). The program has been going for 5 years now, as of March, 2025. Approximately $120K is invested in conservation programs in the county, each year. To learn more about ag and natural resources programs in the county that provide education, training and technical assistance to individuals, businesses, and youth, please visit the Hancock County Extension Office website at: hancock.ca.uky.edu/anr. Dinner sponsors were: Farm Credit Mid America, Superior Ag, Big H Ag Supply, Kyle Culbreth/Farm Bureau Insurance Agency, Hancock County Fiscal Court, Hancock County Farm Bureau, Inc., SNS Seed, Ohio Valley Insurance, Maxwell Brothers Lumber, Wright Implement, Storm Insurance, Hancock County Farm Supply, Katie Kolonich/Edward Jones, Cargill, H & R Block, First Financial Bank, Emmick Eye Care, Justin Nugent/ReMax Real Estate Executives, and Hancock County Conservation District.
A Special Thank You also goes out to: Hancock County Grain Committee, Hancock County Cattlemen's Association, Hancock County Future Farmers of America, Bill and Dave's Smokin' Pit, S & J Emmick Farms, and Hawesville Baptist Church. To learn more about the Kentucky Department of Agriculture, programs offered, and more about the exciting missions that Commissioner of Ag Jonathan Shell outlined in his speech, please visit the website at: www.kyagr.com.

title: Audit shows Hancock Schools 'strong and stable' – Graduation set for May 24th
description: The Hancock County Board of Education Meeting was held on Thursday evening, March 14th. County native Kris Kemp, CPA and partner at Alexander Thomp
content: The Hancock County Board of Education Meeting was held on Thursday evening, March 14th. County native Kris Kemp, CPA and partner at Alexander Thompson Arnold, provided a review of the district's financial audit saying that, overall, they are still 'strong and stable' in their financial footing as they have been in the previous years. Calendar Amendment Due to the days missed for weather, the Board approved a calendar adjustment. The last day of school will now be Friday, May 24th. Graduation Dates SHES Graduation is at 9 a.m. on Friday, May 24th, and NHES Graduation is at 1 p.m. on Friday, May 24th. HCMS 8th Grade Graduation is at 6 p.m. on Thursday, May 23rd in the HCHS Gym. HCHS Class of 2024 Graduation is at 6 p.m. on Friday, May 24th in the HCHS Gym (Baccalaureate and Senior Parade are on Sunday, April 28th). Annual District Audit Report Kemp reported that there were no problems with the information received of the district's financials saying, 'The net excess expenditures over revenues was $123K. You managed $27M of revenue and got your expenses within $100K. A pretty good year. There was an increase in assets of a couple million dollars and that's because there was a bond issued during the year. Most of the increase came from that. The long term activity of $2.8M was a part of the increase in assets. Most proprietary funds are coming from state and federal, and there's not as much control over that. You manage within those boundaries and HC has done a really good job of that. Part of our delay was getting some of the single audit work done. When we do the audit, we do the whole school board – all of the information within the state that you guys control, and then we do a separate audit for all federal revenue that flows through. We've had to do that the last 2 years with covid monies that came in. All the students activities used to be off the books. They accounted for it but it didn't have to be put into the financials (but do now). With the nickel tax, there's been a big jump in capital improvements over the last 5 years. In reviewing all of the student activity funds, there are no red flags. We look at every transaction. Hancock has clean financials and it's been clean the last few years that we've done it. The revenues have increased more substantially and at the same time you haven't exceeded beyond a reasonable level.' HCHS Presentation HCHS Principal Ginger Estes provided a year in review for the high school. 'Our scores we got in October, our ACT benchmarks went up considerably in English, down a little in math, stayed about the same in reading and went down in science. Those are some areas we've worked on. For our KSA (KY Summative Assessment), at the end of the year last year we went down in reading and math. We went up one in science. Our combined writing score went up considerably, and our social studies went up. When we did our CSIP (Comprehensive School Improvement Plan) for this year, all of our teachers got together and we looked at all of our data. We looked at all of our ACT and KSA scores, CERT (College Equipped Readiness Tool – to help students prepare for ACT), and we looked at stations and decided what the needs analysis is (what we need to improve on). Transition readiness – we almost had 100 percent students, with the bonuses we were able to get 113.8 percent. We're really proud of that. Our graduation rate went up 4.5 so we were at 94.9. Our current transition readiness is at 96.4 percent, that's without any of the bonuses – like if a student has all of our high demands like accounting or engineering and their CT benchmarks, that counts double for us. That's not factored in and we have a lot of that. Our juniors took the NOCTI (National Occupational Competency Testing Institute) yesterday, which is the nursing industry cert., and 26 students took it and 22 passed. Numbers for transition went up for ninth graders; we're up 27 percent. We have a couple of years to get those kids' ACT scores benchmarked and get that going.' Pathways 'Our current pathways are: engineering, agriculture, graphic design, culinary, allied health, welding, industrial maintenance, diesel and business,' she said, 'and, business is an archway for: accounting, financial services, entrepreneurship and administrative support. All of those are working in our Hornet Smart Store. Kids are designing different shirts, emblems, hats, and if you ask them for it they come up with a way to build it. It is cool to see this hands-on experience. Two of those are track pathways -Domtar and Yager. Those are going strong. Our college level classes, Dr. Bryant has worked very closely with OCTC recently, adding some dual credit classes with some teachers. Student self-service has been going great, that is online where kids can login and talk to a counselor or see Dr. Bryant, so that kind of alleviates some anxiety a kid might have. New this year, we transitioned from CERT, which was how we did our needs analysis data for ACT. Our MAP data will be stronger because now it also has an ACT predictor. We're MAP testing all of our 9th and 10th graders in math, reading and science and next year we'll add juniors so we'll see what that ACT predictor does for us.' Social Studies Training 'Social Studies training was provided for all of our teachers and we did some great stuff,' Estes added. Science Workshops HCHS Asst. Principal Dr. Jacob Bryant had science powered workshops with the science teachers weekly. 'We're really digging in to try to develop those scores,' she said. 'He does a really great job with that.' Orton-Gillingham (OG) 'We took our high school English teachers and reading specialists to SHES on Tuesday afternoon,' Estes said. 'It started with Briana Pulliam coming to us with a dyslexia lesson at the high school which was SUPER awesome. (Pulliam is District Literacy Coach/Interventionist, C-SLDI -Structured Literacy Dyslexia Interventionist, IMSE -Institute for Multi-Sensory Education, OG Certified Educator for HC Schools.) Every teacher in our building really learned different symptoms and what that looks like. Nobody had really ever told us those things at the high school level. We talked about LETRS (Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading & Spelling), the training the elementary schools have done fabulous work with. Ms. Howe invited us to come see and we took our English teachers. The second graders were doing Latin suffixes and prefixes with a race game. We learned so much. That developed a next step for us with OG at HCHS. We realized they're doing a lot of this really great work through third grade right now but that means there is a little bit of a gap between 3rd grade and coming to us. We're working closely with Ms. Poynter and with Ms. Pulliam and the elementary schools. We will continue to grow. Social studies and science are our big ones; we want to reduce our novice numbers.' PBIS 'We are growing PBIS (Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports) and we were just awarded the Silver,' she said. 'That's great work.' Student Life 'We have a lot of athletics at the high school level, a lot of dances. It's just as important to us as scores. Having those well-rounded, balanced individuals – we encourage all of our students to belong to something whether it be an athletic sport, etc.,' Estes said in closing. 'We have fantastic teachers. All of our teachers work super hard. I can't ask for a better staff and I can't ask for better kids. We're just in a really great spot. We give back by spending time at the elementary schools doing our reading. It's so cute to watch our kids come back after being over there because they feel like celebrities. It's really great for them to be able to do that.' New Job Descriptions HCHS Guidance Counselor Danny Gray is retiring at the end of this school year and the Board approved the new job description of Student Success Advisor, which will soon be posted and applications can then be submitted. 'This is a counselor type position,' Superintendent Robby Asberry said. 'We're just renaming it and we'll probably have some different duties for that position.' He said they will be looking at the position and 'tweaking it' for the needs of the students. Another job description was also approved – Temporary Program Assistants. 'This is temporary help for when our preschools come in early to the schools and are trying to get acclimated,' Asberry explained. 'We do that every year.' Treasurer's Report Financial Director Trey Anderson reported, 'The balance at the end of the month was $5,054,584. Receipts were $2,186,025. With Expenses of $1,161,800. For a balance at close of $6,135,967.' By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Family Dollar/Dollar Tree Closing Lewisport store as part of all 100 stores
description: The parking lot at the Family Dollar was full taking advantage of their closing sale. You may have read in numerous articles recently that nearly 1,000 Family Dollar Stores will be closing in the next…
content: The parking lot at the Family Dollar was full taking advantage of their closing sale. You may have read in numerous articles recently that nearly 1,000 Family Dollar Stores will be closing in the next year. Lewisport's Family Dollar/Dollar Tree Combo-Store, located at 8240 US Hwy 60, is one of those that will be closing its doors soon. The store has only been open for just a little over a year and is the first of its kind in Lewisport. The land was purchased on December 17th, 2021 and construction of the building started in 2022. A huge going out of business sale began on Monday, March 18th with everything in the store except tobacco products, alcohol, prepaid phone cards, gift cards and credit cards, marked 50 percent off. Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory said, 'It really wasn't surprising that they closed here. They were closing 1,000 stores, and their fourth quarter earnings were pretty dismal. I do hate it for the employees over there that are going to lose their jobs. I'll certainly be thinking of them. With that building there, it would be a good potential site for a new business to locate here in Lewisport.' In 2015, Dollar Tree purchased Family Dollar for over $8B. It is reported that there has been difficulty in the absorption of the chain, resulting in a $950M impairment against the Family Dollar trade name, a $1.07B goodwill charge, and Family Dollar will spend over $594M re-branding and closing stores. Dollar Tree's plans are, reportedly, to close around 600 Family Dollar stores in the first half of this year, and over the next several years 370 more, as well as 30 Dollar Tree stores. By Jennifer Wimmer
