title: Judith Boswell
description: Judith 'Judy' Nell Boswell, 77, tossed her wheelchair to the side and sprinted into the arms of Jesus on Tuesday July 16, 2024. Judy was born in Owensboro, Kentucky on March 7, 1947 to the late Ralph…
content:
Judith 'Judy' Nell Boswell, 77, tossed her wheelchair to the side and sprinted into the arms of Jesus on Tuesday July 16, 2024.
Judy was born in Owensboro, Kentucky on March 7, 1947 to the late Ralph and Edna Boswell. She was their first-born blessing which provided her with an incredible amount of strength and perseverance (some might call it stubbornness). Judy would grow to need this tenacity after contracting Polio at the age of 5. She was truly a miracle child and, after a long stent in the Iron Lung, survived even when her team of doctors told her mother there was no way. Although the disease stole her ability to freely move her arms and legs, it never could quite steal her joy or her will to live life to the fullest.
Judy went on to graduate from Daviess County High School in the class of 1965. In order to navigate the school in a pre-accessible era, Judy often caught a ride up and down the stairs with local NASCAR legend, Darrell Waltrip. This was a story she loved recounting! Soon after graduating, she completed her certification at the International Correspondence School. She utilized her newly acquired skills to help keep the accounting (and men) of Boswell Farms in line until November of 2022. Judy was also able to give her time and talents to Bethlehem Methodist by serving as their treasurer for over three decades.
In addition to her skills as a math whiz, Judy had several other gifts. She was a master crocheter and lovingly created blankets and shawls for the people around her. She was an award winning back tickler. She was a sous chef to her mother's famous home cookin'. And she was the very proudest of aunts. Her greatest accomplishment was helping with the raising of her nieces and nephews and several neighborhood children. She loved and cherished each of them for their own special talents.
She was preceded in death by her beloved parents, her trusted brother-in-law (Joey Fischer), a very special nephew (Noah Boswell), and the sweetest great niece (Emelia Claire Aud). We can only imagine, and grin through our tears, at the joyful reunion that must have taken place.
She is survived by her three siblings, Joel and wife Joyce Boswell, Gerald and wife Linda Boswell, and Sondra Fischer; nine nieces and nephews, Aaron Boswell (Nicole), Chad Boswell (Amy), Ryan Boswell (Tiffany), Tiffany Rust (Jerrod), Joy Kaye Abel (Cory), Ross Boswell (Kelly), Sara Aud (Kyle), Joseph Fischer, Adam Fischer (Kaitlyn); and a host of great nieces, nephews, cousins and lifelong friends.
Funeral services will be held at 10 am on Friday, July 19, 2024 at Bethlehem Methodist Church, with visitation beginning at 9 am at the church. Burial will follow in Owensboro Memorial Gardens. Additional visitation will be held on Thursday from 4 pm until 7 pm at Gibson and Son Funeral Home, Lewisport Chapel. Memorial contributions can be made to the Methodist Children's Home where Judy was a faithful supporter. Share your memories and condolences with her family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Matt Ramsey's Fundraiser for HC Football is This Saturday – Don't Miss it!
description: 'Cooker of Deliciousness' Matt Ramsey with his wife and 2 children in Panama City during Fall Break last year (l to r): Jake
content:
'Cooker of Deliciousness' Matt Ramsey with his wife and 2 children in Panama City during Fall Break last year (l to r): Jake, Rachel, Matt and Zoey.
Since featuring Hawesville native, Matt Ramsey, in The Clarion in 2022, the popularity with his cooking tutorial videos has grown tremendously. At that time, he was already at a million followers on TikTok, and now he has 1.4 million, as well as one million on Facebook, and 425K on Instagram.
He is a self-taught cook, and it all began about 15 years ago when he purchased a Weber Grill and started cooking for friends and family. He is an RN and worked at Owensboro Regional Health Hospital for 22 years, 7 years in the ER and 15 years in the cardiac cath lab, and decided to take his leave last August to be the 'Cooker of Deliciousness' full-time!
Along with the fun, detailed and humorous cooking videos he posts, he also writes excellent informative blogs and has begun doing cooking event fundraisers. On July 6th, he helped to raise over $1,000 at Bill's on the Hill in Hawesville, where he worked as a teenager. The dollars raised will be given locally in the Hancock County community. He has also organized an event to raise money for HC Football, happening this Saturday! (*details below)
Matt is thrilled to be able to take his new career to the next level, and also find ways to give back to his hometown community. He said his goal has always been to keep everything simple for his viewers and readers so that they can easily prepare any of his food creations that he presents to them.
'I try to keep most things simple to where people will want to attempt them,' he said. 'A lot of people, if you get too in-depth, they just don't even want to mess with it. They feel it's overwhelming and they don't want to do it. So I try to keep things simple to where people will want to try to make them. I aim to get 2 or 3 recipe blogs on there a week.'
Just before the fundraising event at Bill's IGA, he and his wife, Rachel, and his best friend and his wife flew out West for a 10-day vacation, which involved some cooking and videoing for his social media as well.
'One of the companies I work with is Browsey Acres,' he said, 'a wagyu beef company owned by Travis Browne and Ronda Rousey, the famous UFC Fighter. Travis was a famous UFC Fighter as well. We started out by going to their ranch and stayed there overnight. It's in Southeastern Oregon, out in the middle of nowhere.'
The family-owned farm produces high quality wagyu and poultry. While there, Matt said he had the pleasure of cooking twice before they had to take off for their next adventure. 'I grilled chicken the night we got there,' he said, 'and then made steaks the next morning for breakfast. We had 6 hours of driving the next day, so we had to leave right after breakfast.'
Matt and Rachel were celebrating their 21st Wedding Anniversary on the day they were traveling to the ranch. They loved getting to visit Browsey Acres, see their process first-hand, how much they care about what they're doing, how invested they are in raising their animals with integrity, and their dedication in producing the highest quality products, he said.
From there, they set out for some sightseeing at Crater Lake and played golf on the Oregon Coast in Bandon. 'We went to Mount Hood, and then to Seattle for 5 days. We did Olympic National Park and went to a Mariners game,' he said. 'I filmed with a friend of mine who's also a social media influencer that lives up there – Seattle Butcher's Wife (Misty Banchero).
We went to the famous Pike Place Fish Market and I bought a salmon and they let me go behind the counter and catch it. We cooked the salmon at her house as well as pork chops, steaks, and a bunch of vegetables. We had a good time. I just made one big video for the entire trip. We flew to Reno and then drove everywhere else and flew out of Seattle. We ended up driving 1,860 miles in 9 days. It was a lot of driving but it was fun; It was worth every mile.'
They flew home on Friday, July 5th and got back at about 7 p.m., he said. Then, he was expediently off to Bill's to get ready for the fundraiser the next day, that he coordinated with former local owners, Wayne Stephens and Billy Stephens, Jr.
He explained, 'Rita Stephens called me and said, 'We don't own the store anymore but it's our legacy. We care a lot about it and we just want to do something for the community and to bring people in.' They were always really good to me when I worked there so I agreed to come up and cook for free. They provided the meat, and the current owners (Wazeem 'Zeem' Raheem and Mafaz Ansar) plan to donate the profits locally.' (*They are in the process of deciding where, specifically, they will donate to.)
Kay & Larry Ramsey, Matt's mom and dad, helped him cook at Bill's. 'We got everything cooked, and started serving at 10 a.m.,' he said. 'We were smoking Boston butts and they just take awhile, and bologna as well. We were going to be there until 2 p.m., but we sold out of everything at noon. We did pulled pork sandwiches and fried bologna sandwiches; We just kept it simple. They were both a big hit. We also sold whole Boston butts and whole bologna chubs and they both sold out pretty quick.'
Matt works with a couple of grill companies now as well, Primo ceramic grills, and Recteq wood pellet grills & smokers. He also works with the owners of Bacon Up, a real bacon grease cooking product created by brothers and their sister, who are all originally from Owensboro.
Upcoming Fundraiser Event
On Friday, July 26th and Saturday, July 27th, Matt will be at The Pour Haus Pub & Eatery in Tell City, starting at 3:00 p.m. on both days. 'Typically they close at 9:00 p.m.,' he said, 'but if it is super busy both nights, they'll just keep going until it slows down. I came up with a popup menu for them and they're going to make those menu items.
It's going to be a fundraiser. On Friday, it's going to benefit a couple of programs at Apollo High School. On Saturday, I'm going to donate everything I make to Hancock County Football. I won't be cooking; I did the menu and I'll just be there to talk to people and hang out.
We have a band playing on Saturday night of Hancock County people, Brandon Wheat, Joe Madden, Jeremy Williamson and Eric Huff – The Midnight Ramblers. They will play from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.'
The menu will be the same on Friday and Saturday. Matt created the appetizers, main courses and desserts. The appetizers will be: Loaded Poutine Pots and Honey Buffalo Coffee Rubbed Wings. The desserts will be: S'mores Croissants and Sweet & Savory Crunch Wraps.
He said he made the S'mores Croissants just a few weeks ago and they turned out REALLY GOOD, but that the Sweet & Savory Crunch Wraps are most likely going to be even better! 'They're going to have peanut butter, chocolate, marshmallow cream, potato chips and bacon,' he said.
For the entrees, Matt has planned a Breakfast Burger – a 'smash burger' with fried bologna and egg, as well as: Brisket Grilled Cheese, Sloppy Joe Grilled Cheese, Crack Chicken Pasta, Marry Me Chicken Pasta, and Pulled Pork Loaded Baked Potatoes.
'I've grown to the point that I've gotten super busy,' Matt said, 'but I also want to still try to use that for good. That's why I wanted to do this fundraiser to help some programs that I care about. Hopefully, we can continue to do things like that in the future. . .I've done a couple of videos for Kentucky Pride, the farmers coalition that supports KY farmers and their families. I like doing things that represent Kentucky as well.'
Matt's chocolate lab, Squire Maximus, is still a very important part of his family. He played a major role in the growing following that Matt has now. He began posting videos in December of 2020, and when those had started gaining some traction, Rachel told him that if he hit 100K followers that she would agree to them adopting a puppy. That motivated him to keep going, he said, and he has met that first milestone and many others since then!
Matt & Rachel were married at Lewisport Baptist Church on June 26th, 2004. She is from Lewisport, and the daughter of Alan & the late Ginger Frakes. Her step-mom is Diana 'Dee' Frakes. She and Matt met in high school and are both HCHS graduates. Rachel is the Director of the Social Security Administration in Owensboro.
Their daughter, Zoey, is going to be a freshman at Apollo in the fall and is attending Cheer Camp at UK for cheerleading this school year. She's very talented, and her dance troupe won the state title last year. Their son, Jake, is an outstanding wrestler, and was Regional Champ last year. He's still wrestling and will be a junior in high school in the fall.
You can check out Matt's latest cooking videos and blogs on his website: Cookerofdeliciousness.com, or @cookerofdeliciousness on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook. If you taste something at one of Matt's events that you'd like to make at home, you can visit his website or one of his social media pages, and there are easy to follow, step-by-step instructions!
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Summer Food Service available until School begins on August 26th
description: As you may know, the Ha
content:
As you may know, the Hancock County Board of Education approved an alternative calendar for the 2024/2025 school year, as reported in The Clarion in the 5-23-2024 edition. The first day of school is Monday, August 26th, and the Summer Food Service Program Grab-n-Go deliveries ended on July 26th, but there is a plan in place for families to receive food assistance until school starts!
Hancock County Schools Superintendent Robby Asberry explained, 'We have reached out to our Family Resource Youth Center Coordinators at each school. They will ensure that those families in need receive food assistance.'
On the last week of the Summer Food Service Program deliveries in the county, recipients were provided with all of the information necessary to continue receiving food assistance until school begins, Asberry said.
The Hancock County District Calendar Committee meets annually, and is made up of community members, parents, teachers, and staff. They recommended the alternate calendar schedule to the HC Board of Education members, it was unanimously agreed upon, and then approved during the monthly BOE meeting in May.
Why was the decision made to push the start date back for students? One reason voiced by longtime BOE Member Donna Quattrocchi at the May meeting, was that some parents had been asking for a change in order to have more time with their children in the summer.
Some community members have voiced concerns of the later start date causing a later end date, and thus diminishing Summer Break 2025, but that is not the case. The last day of school is scheduled for May 23rd, 2025. Fall Break, Christmas Break and Spring Break were not affected with the change either.
Board of Education Member Brooke Payne said, 'It's based on the state requirement for the hours, but we always had some comp time that we would use for free make-up days. We did lose one day we normally have off that we had to give up for it.'
When asked what the main reasons to start school later were, Brooke said, 'For one, to give the kids a longer summer break; That was a huge deal. And, it also gives our teachers a little bit more time too, to prepare their classrooms and get their trainings done and everything. Then, a big factor is always that it's so hot in August. So we kind of felt like that was better for the kids that ride buses too. One thing that we were able to do because of the NTI (Non-Traditional Instruction) days that were allotted, is instead of doing traditional snow days, those will be NTI days.'
The KY Department of Education's NTI Program provides continuation of learning on days when the entire district is closed for health or safety reasons. On NTI days, the district can make a plan for continuing instruction for students and provide for student and teacher interaction. Up to 10 NTI days can be approved to count towards student attendance days in the school districts' calendars by the Commissioner of Education.
District Calendar Committee Leader and HC Schools Assistant Superintendent Nick Boling said the new calendar also allows more time for staff to engage in additional professional development over the summer. The change creates additional staff training opportunities as well, that would otherwise not be possible.
There are staff and teacher Work Days scheduled for August 15th, 19th, and 22nd. Opening Day for teachers and staff at HC Schools is Friday, August 23rd. They will all be well prepared and ready to welcome back the students when they begin their first day of school this year on August 26th!
Asberry stated, 'I've had many community members reach out to me expressing their appreciation for this calendar change.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: HCHS/OCTC Partnership promotes Student Success
description: For the pas
content:
For the past several decades Hancock County High School has partnered with Owensboro Community and Technical College (OCTC) to provide opportunities for qualifying HCHS students to take college-level courses. The partnership has gradually gained more traction, more popularity and more support from the state over the years, and has expanded to now offer 3 different ways for students to earn college credit while attending high school. Those are: concurrent enrollment, dual credit, and early college.
In past years, OCTC general education classes, such as Psychology 101, were offered as night classes at the high school for students to take while attending high school, with a college instructor from OCTC traveling to HCHS to instruct those. Now, and for the last several years, students have had the option to earn dual credit classes by riding to the OCTC Campus on HC School buses, and then back to the high school for the remainder of the day to complete their high school level courses and/or extracurriculars at HCHS.
The concurrent enrollment option for students provides college-level classes offered at the HCHS Campus and taught at the high school by HCHS staff who have dedicated their time to gain that extra training to teach those classes. And, the third option, which is referred to as 'early college', offers the opportunity for students to graduate simultaneously with their high school diploma and a degree from OCTC. Early college students are also offered the option to ride HC School buses to and from OCTC.
Concurrent Enrollment
Professor of Communication and Humanities and Fine Arts Department Head at OCTC Dr. Meredith Skaggs said, 'Concurrent enrollment is one of the most true things that KCTCS (KY Community and Technical College System) and OCTC does for our mission because it is the most accessible college credit. It's in an environment that is safe for the student, it is with the support of the high school and the college, and students who are, particularly, first generation who may not think they are capable of gaining some confidence in themselves academically, that they are capable to succeed through that pathway.'
For concurrent enrollment to be offered to students, a number of teachers at HCHS have to be certified through OCTC to have the same credentials as any college faculty member. They have to meet those same accreditation standards, are certified through the college, and they also must participate in annual professional development through the college, Dr. Skaggs explained.
HCHS Principal Ginger Estes has vocalized her appreciation for the teachers at HCHS who are willing to do that extra work in order for students to have this opportunity at the high school. There are currently 8 teachers at HCHS who meet the criteria for teaching college level courses. Those teachers also have the responsibility to enter grades for students into 2 different systems, turn in assessment materials to OCTC, and participate in professional development. They learn an entire different system in order to make concurrent enrollment function seamlessly at HCHS so the students can have this excellent advantage.
Dual Credit
Dual credit students at HCHS have the opportunity to take any class on the OCTC Campus, as long as it's not a pre-admission program, Dr. Skaggs explained. They would later have to gain admission into Tech or Nursing, for example, to take pre-admission courses, but students can take any of the prerequisites to those programs. Last school year, over 125 dual credit college classes were taken by HCHS juniors and seniors.
The college level courses from OCTC offered at the HCHS Campus change from year to year. The solidified list, so far, for this school year are: English 101 (Writing I), English 102 (Writing II), Biology 112 (Intro to Biology), Biology 113 (Lab), Education 201 (Intro to Education), Math 126 (Technical Math), Math 150 (College Algebra), and AHS 115 (Allied Health/Medical Terminology).
Last school year, there were 50 HCHS students attending classes at the OCTC Campus. Some students earn college credits for their first year of college, and some even earn part of their second year of college requirements as well. Students who pass their dual credit courses with a grade C or higher may count those classes for both state high school graduation requirements, and as college credit.
This ongoing, increasingly expanding, wonderful partnership between HCHS and OCTC offers students an extremely valuable edge in entering the workforce, and toward their chosen career paths. Not all of the career pathways at HCHS have credit available onsite at the high school. Some of those are only offered at OCTC through the Dual Credit Program.
Early College
In comparison, early college allows students to graduate from HCHS with an OCTC degree as well. Students enrolled in Early College for this school year will begin their classes at OCTC on August 19th. Bus transportation will be available Monday-Thursday, and pick up will be at 7:30 a.m. at the high school. A bus will pick up at OCTC at 2:00 p.m. to return students to HCHS.
HCHS also offers a variety of Career Pathways with corresponding preparatory courses toward those pathways, as well as Industry Certifications. The TRACK (Tech Ready Apprentices for Careers in Kentucky) Program is offered through the KY Department of Education (KDE), and provides learning for those studying diesel mechanics and engineering, and that education continues after high school graduation.
Career Pathways at HCHS
HCHS has had great success with Career Pathways, and has the highest ACT average in the region! The Career Pathways offered this school year are: Engineering, Culinary Arts, Accounting, Graphic Design, Diesel Mechanics, Welding, Industrial Maintenance, Agriculture, Early Childhood Education, Allied Health, and Business, which is an archway for Financial Services, Administrative Support, and Entrepreneurship, as well as 2 new pathways added for this school year, which are the Hospitality, Travel and Tourism Pathway, and Plumbing Pathway.
When HCHS students have completed 4 classes on a specific Career Pathway, that qualifies them as a 'Completer', and greatly increases the likelihood of success on that career path moving forward. There are almost 40 teachers at HCHS who are certified in teaching classes toward these Career Pathways.
For the new Plumbing Career Pathway offered this year, HC Schools Superintendent Robby Asberry said, 'We have not been able to find an instructor but it is still approved for this school year. We are still looking; We thought we had one and that fell through. If we don't find one, we'll keep it on the books and as soon as we find one, and are able to implement that, we will.'
Apprenticeships with a local plumber will be established, he said, once they've secured an instructor.
Allied Health Pathway students, for example, are also engaged in Work-Based Learning opportunities, through the Health Care Innovation Center and MedCert. This growing system offers students opportunities and experiences in the Hancock County community to work and learn.
Culinary Arts Pathway students at HCHS have the option to work at catered weddings, school banquets, HC Chamber of Commerce Breakfasts, and other events. These hands-on opportunities throughout the school year greatly enrich their learning experience, and helps them gain valuable skills. The students do all of the cooking, serving and developing in the Culinary Department at HCHS, which has a full-size, professional kitchen. (*See full feature on the HCHS Culinary Dept. in the 2-2-2024 edition of The Clarion.)
HCHS juniors and seniors who are interested in pursuing a career in Early Childhood Education have been working with younger students at North and South Hancock Elementary Schools and Hancock County Middle School in various ways throughout each school year to gain valuable hands-on learning experiences. And, HCHS Ag students participate in community service projects, such as building picnic tables at Vastwood Park, for example.
Industry Certifications
The developed and ongoing partnership with Southwire allows students to earn while they learn. All of the classes offered at HCHS through the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Department are phenomenal. Engineering students can also partner with Domtar for a TRACK Program where they actually get paid to go to school. They can earn college credit and a formal internship at Domtar in Hawesville.
This partnership relies on a joint partnership with OCTC for that very specified curriculum. Students get paid by the hour and earn college credit, with the additional agreement of 4 years of on-the-job training.
For Diesel Mechanics Pathway students, HCHS has partnered with Yager Materials in Owensboro. Students go to Yager every morning for their jobs, and then return to HCHS for their core classes. Those students are required to take college level classes as well, which is also made possible through the partnership with OCTC, and then they can choose between Domtar or Yager, through the TRACK Program.
Yager also pays students by the hour to learn while they're in the classroom at HCHS going over their program. It's a 4 year commitment, and students can work their way into full-time positions.
Industry certifications are also available to students through AutoCAD (a commercial 2D and 3D computer-aided design and drafting software application). Students enrolled in the 3D printing class at HCHS Campus can achieve even more advanced levels of learning with this technology.
With the 3D printers, students have been making sellable merchandise such as key rings. Last school year, students 3D printed a new 'heart' for one of the mannequins used in health sciences classes.
The HCHS Technology Student Association was awarded 12th in the State Competition in Louisville for one of the PVC kayaks they made in the spring, with the help of these technologies. They 3D printed electric guitars for the competition as well.
Students also create merchandise for the Hornet Smart store such as shirts, mugs, hats, emblems, stickers, and more, as well, and even process their own catalogue. They can create merchandise for local businesses when the opportunity arises as well, which provides hands-on learning for the students, and benefits the school and those businesses.
Additionally, students have the opportunity to work in-house at HCHS with a sublimation printer, vinyl cutter & printer, laser engraver, metal plasma cutter, and state of the art welding equipment.
HCHS offers many 'gateways to the future' for students, as HCHS Principal Ginger Estes has referred to them, which are the Early College, Dual Credit, and Concurrent Enrollment, explained above, as well as the classes offered for Career Pathway completions, Industry Certifications, Work-Based Learning, internships, apprenticeships, and earning a high school diploma. HCHS began Work-Based Learning with apprenticeships and on-the-job training in 2018.
Estes and other staff members have been working to develop more partnerships with teacher apprenticeships. They are also dedicated to working closely with the HC Industrial Foundation and the HC Chamber of Commerce to establish more partnerships with local businesses that will provide even more experiences for students to gain valuable employability skills in their chosen career pathways.
For a high school student to be considered 'transition-ready' in the Commonwealth of KY, they have to be either college-ready or career-ready. To be college-ready, they must meet an ACT benchmark of: 18 in English, 19 in Math, 20 in Reading, or have a C or higher in a college level class.
In order to take a college level class they have to have an ACT, except when they're juniors because most of them haven't had a full ACT at that point. In those cases, OCTC allows them to use their Grade Point Average and a teacher recommendation.
For a student to be career-ready they have to pass an end-of-course test, earn an industry certification in one of the programs of study, or be part of a TRACK apprenticeship through the KDE. Last school year began with 90 percent of HCHS seniors already transition-ready!
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Grant Awarded Forwards Plans for Park in Hawesville
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, October 8th, and City Manager Jake Powers announced that the GRANT (Government Resources Accelerating Needed Transformation)…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, October 8th, and City Manager Jake Powers announced that the GRANT (Government Resources Accelerating Needed Transformation) Program grant that was applied for was awarded.
This will cover matching funds on the previously awarded Land & Water Conservation Grant. A green light for moving forward soon with the plans for construction of a park next to the Hawesville Fire Station downtown.
The yellow house located on the lot would be demoed, along with the building behind it, and the site leveled out. The park would be constructed in that entire lot, and include a basketball court, playground, picnic tables and benches. The entire project is estimated at approximately $326K.
The LWC Grant award totaled $161,438. The GRANT Program awarded $156,736, leaving a little over $4K to secure through donations.
McCormick said, 'We did have an institution willing to give us a nice chunk of change for the rest of it, and other things we need to do. Jake did a great job on this federal grant to cover the matching portion of the park. The storm water plant is the same deal. We applied for a grant through the federal to cover the matching portion of the 12.5 percent we were going to have to pay, and the federal government has stepped up and are paying that, so this storm water plant will cost us zero money also. There will be no add-ons. Those are two great things that our city manager and city clerk (Amy Roberts) have worked on in finding these; It really helps us a lot.'
Jake reported to the council that the cyber security assessment has been received and reviewed. The next step is identifying new changes that need to be made with the City, that were recommended by the company.
'We were hacked,' he said. 'It wasn't major. Jason Bevill handled that very well, and efficiently wrapped it up. It was cleared up immediately.'
Resolution-Brownfield Grant Funds
Jake attended another KY Brownfield Program meeting last week, and the council approved a resolution to apply for funding through Brownfields Program Grants.
He presented the information to the council saying, 'This project with Shane (Barton, Downtown Revitalization Coordinator, Community & Economic Development Initiative of KY-CEDIK) being hands-on, has been a part of it, and we've gotten some of the phase one assessments done. This grant we're applying for is going to: Revitalization and Reuse. The minimum amount is $500K, and then it goes to increments of $1M-$4M. One of those amounts is what we'll be applying for. The deadline is November 14th. I'll be working with Amy Matheny (GRADD Community Development Planner). I'll be writing the grant myself, and GRADD is able to assist.'
He continued, 'We can get a really good application built. It will be around a 100-paged economic plan. Beka Burton (CEDIK Economic Development Extension Specialist) has just recently sent her portion of the executive summary on the plan to Shane. He'll be sending it to us for review. Amy said this plan can be used on any grant application moving forward, Brownfield related or not. This is proof of the investments we've made, and communication with the community to show that the community voice dictates. All of this past year and a half that the whole community has put into working on this, it is starting to come time to move on that.'
McCormick read the resolution aloud, which authorizes the application process for and, upon approval, to enter into an agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for the Fiscal Year 2025 Brownfield Grant Program.
Jake added, 'With the Brownfield Project, the property the church has (old Presbyterian Church building on Main St.), we did the lead and asbestos phase one on it. That really fits and meets a lot of the criteria for this clean-up grant [lead and asbestos presence confirmed]. It really has the potential for the $5M to $1M clean-up money. Once I get the plans sent to me, the council can sit down and go through how they look for community involvement. Justice 40 is a bill that pays you 40 percent more for community involvement. There is so much to it. It is a big grant. The church property fits a lot of the criteria they're looking for. I encourage anyone to speak to the church and their board because that's a property that they can relieve liability on by going this route.'
Senior Living Funding
Councilman Danny Doyle asked if grants were available toward senior living funding, and immediate emergency needs. One of his ideas was a fire blanket to keep close to your oven, or somewhere that a fire may potentially start.
'We're going to see if there is funding to purchase that type of equipment for seniors,' Jake said, 'and at-risk residents in the city. I have reached out to GRADD, asking about a grant for that specific funding.'
Cyber Security Grant
The Council approved a cybersecurity grant resolution that authorizes the mayor to enter an agreement with the Kentucky Office of Homeland Security (KOHS), and act as the correspondent for the project, as the City of Hawesville will be applying for KOHS Cyber Grants that would be focused on supporting cybersecurity improvements for critical infrastructure.
The Kentucky Intelligence Fusion Center (KIFC), created within the KOHS, improves intelligence sharing among public safety and public service agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. KOHS provides many funding opportunities for the Commonwealth's critical infrastructure, and a new FEMA grant supports many cybersecurity improvements for critical infrastructure entities within the Commonwealth and across the nations.
The State Homeland Security Grant Program (SHSGP), FEMA grant, provides reimbursement funding to support cybersecurity improvements to KY's critical infrastructure, such as vulnerability assessments and vulnerability assessment software, training for IT personnel, funding for the contracting of managed service providers, replacing consumer grade routers and switches with business or enterprise grade equipment, software or services that can help monitor incoming/outgoing network traffic, and software of services that can help manage devices on the network.
Police Report
In Chief of Police B.J. Burton's absence, he submitted a report, and McCormick read it aloud for the council: 'The month of September was safe and enjoyable. I wanted to share with everyone the total calls and responses taken this month, as I continue to move forward and make the city a more safe and enjoyable place.'
McCormick said, 'I think he is really doing that. He reported that he had one arrest; 8 citations – 5 stop signs, 3 speeds; one warrant served; no civil citations; 13 traffic stops without citations; 5 calls for service; and 1 accident. He contacted approximately 25 vehicles. He also, this month, brought back the Ford Explorer. It's definitely a major upgrade. We're still in discussion on what we want to do with our older police car. We're thinking about making it a utility car for Jake or Amy, which would save us from paying mileage for those trips.'
Fire Department Report
The Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department Chief, Shane Richards, and crew were busy with trainings, in company with the other 3 department's members, at the new Dukes Volunteer Fire Department station, and at the station at the Lewisport Volunteer Fire Dept. on Tuesday evening, and Chief Richards was not present to give a report. For Fire Prevention Week, October 6th-12th, the focus was on smoke alarms.
On the Hawesville Fire Department Facebook Page, the September report was posted as such: 37 calls for service, 21 EMS assist, 9 motor vehicle accidents, 3 fire alarms, 2 gas leaks, 1 aircraft incident, and 1 structure fire.
HVFD accepted 2 new applicants into membership in Sept. Congratulations Brandon Boone and Hunter Mattingly! They are ALWAYS looking for new members! For more info., send an email to: hawesvillefire@gmail.com.
The HVFD, LVFD, DVFD, and South Hancock Volunteer Fire Dept. members all participated in the Annual HC Fall Fire School. Firefighters trained on extrication, and man vs. machine, and reported that they learned a lot. A thank you is extended to HC Emergency Services for all the hard work and effort to make the fire school happen each year.
Junior Firefighters
The Junior Firefighters participated in Hancock County Fall Fire School, and Alarms & Sprinklers Training in September. The Junior Firefighter Program at HVFD is open to youth ages 15-17. For more info., please email the department at the above email address.
Burn Ban
The KY Fire Hazard Season Burn Ban is October 1st-December 15th, enforcing NO BURNING within 150' of woodland, 6 a.m.-6 p.m. If you burn, please wait until after 6 p.m., when winds die down. Reminder: Please, only call 911 if there is an emergency. Otherwise, call Dispatch non-emergency number at (270) 927-1311.
Open House
The FREE HVFD Annual Open House is October 31st, 5-8 p.m. There will be trick-or-treating, and fire prevention education with 'Sparky' the Friendly Firefighter. The HVFD station is located at 385 Main Street, in Downtown Hawesville.
Code Enforcement Board
Donnie Snyder was approved and sworn-in as a new volunteer Code Enforcement Board member. Volunteer board members: Chuck Jones (1-year term), Stephanie Clark (2-year term), and Robert McCann (3-year term) were approved at the 10-3-2023 council meeting, to enforce the city's new ordinances passed in July of last year – Water & Sewer Reclassification & Rate Increase, and Nuisance Ordinances.
Snyder will be serving for a one-year term, now that Jones has fulfilled his one-year commitment. Chief of Police B.J. Burton is the Code Enforcement Officer.
McCormick explained last year, 'This Code Enforcement is not set up for us to make revenue off of, it's set up to where [citizens] will clean their properties. We don't want to have to fine anybody…'
Superintendent Report
Superintendent Brian Patterson reported that the annual fee for testing equipment at the water/sewer plant has been costing over $9K. He reached out to another company who can do the testing for thousands less. He also reported a recent water leak that he and the crew located, and repaired.
'We were losing 176K gallons of water a day,' he said. 'Our plant was almost maxed out until I found it.'
He also found a better deal for the city's meter sets, he said. They were purchasing a $250 set, 6 in a box, and he found boxes of 10 for $120 cheaper.
Brian added, 'We found out with the survey, they were supposed to have been doing it all along – monthly maintenance report on our wells. It's never been done since I've been here. I'm putting that into effect, and also inspecting the trucks every Friday – all of the tires, oil, everything.'
McCormick said, 'We were maxed out. Our superintendent has done a very good job in cost savings this year. He's found another way to save money. There's some good preventative maintenance going on too. Superintendent, I appreciate you in everything you're doing. You've done a great job.'

title: 2024 General Election Ballot Measures
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Citizens in the Commonwealth of Kentucky will see 2 constitutional amendments on their ballots to decide how they will vote on, presented in a 'yes' or 'no' format. Hancock County voters will also see the option on this year's general election ballot to vote for or against allowing cannabis businesses to operate in the boundaries of the county.
Constitutional Amendment 2
Amendment 2, which is, essentially, a school funding initiative, is very controversial. Voting in favor of this amendment would give the KY General Assembly the option to provide financial support to students outside of the public education system, beginning with the 2025 legislative session, and start to create a way for charter school funding, and also possibly private school vouchers.
Those opposed say that public funding should only be used for the public school systems. Those in favor say it gives parents the option for their tax dollars to go toward educational opportunities outside of the public school system.
Constitutional Amendment 1
Constitutional Amendment 1, if passed, would ensure that only citizens of the United States can vote in elections in the Commonwealth of Kentucky. Those who are opposed have vocalized that the measure is useless, because they believe there is no problem to solve with this, no clarification needed in the wording.
Those in support express that it is necessary for clarification. By presenting the question on the ballot, they say that it will make sure that the citizens of KY, and not the courts of KY, decide on whether non-citizens (illegal immigrants) can vote in elections or not.
Other states, including Missouri, Idaho, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Wisconsin are all joining the Commonwealth in adding a similar question on their general election ballots this year as well, in order to change the wording, essentially, to clarify that only legal, naturalized citizens of the U.S. can vote in elections, in their states.
KY Medical Marijuana Program
In addition, the Hancock County Fiscal Court voted on Monday, July 22nd, at their regular night meeting this year, and approved a resolution to allow the voters in Hancock County to decide if they are in favor of allowing cannabis businesses to operate in the boundaries of the county.
All counties in Kentucky were given the option to decide if the question would be on the ballot, per the new legislation speeding up the timetable, which has been reported on in The Hancock Clarion in several editions this year, with the news releases from Governor Beshear's office, as well as with coverage of the HC Fiscal Court meetings.
As you may know, the 2023 KY General Assembly passed Senate Bill 47, legalizing the use of medical cannabis and establishing a framework for state licensure of cannabis businesses in the Commonwealth, effective January 1st, 2025.
Local governments in KY are making decisions on how they will address this new industry that will become legal. Prospective cannabis businesses have already begun looking at state regulations and are planning to become licensed by the KY Cabinet for Health and Family Services, as legislature has passed House Bill 829, amending the law to expedite the process of licensing and allows the Cabinet to begin issuing licenses this year rather than waiting until January 1st. Those licenses can be for: cultivator, processor, producer, safety compliance facility, or dispensary.
Cities and counties have the option to take action, or to not take action on whether these businesses would be allowed to operate in their counties/cities. Local governments can pass an ordinance by December 31st, 2024 to prohibit cannabis operations in their jurisdiction. They also have an option to pass a resolution to put the matter to a public vote, and an option of placing restrictions and/or collecting fees related to the businesses operating within the county or city.
The question on the ballot will look the same throughout the Commonwealth for those who live in counties where the option to vote has been approved. The HC Fiscal Court approved the resolution in order to give the people of Hancock County a voice in this.

title: Allen Ray Johnson
