content:
Allen Ray Johnson, age 75, passed away on October 16, 2024 with his family and the loving care of Hospice of Western KY in Owensboro, KY.
He retired from Logan Aluminum and spent his well-deserved retirement with his grandkids and cheering on the Kentucky Wildcats. He was a member of Newton Springs Baptist Church and relied heavily on his faith.
He was proceeded in death by his parents Earl B and Mildred Johnson, and son Scott Allen Johnson.
Allen is survived by his children Holly (Don) Smallwood, Nathan (Christine) Johnson, Ethan (Nikki) Johnson, and Courtney Johnson; grandchildren Trey Smallwood, Liberty Smallwood, Karlei Johnson, Carter Kimmel, Collins Johnson, Tommy Johnson, Konner Johnson, Ellington Johnson, Scarlett Johnson, and Karcen Johnson; stepdaughter Brittany Buster and step-grandchildren Brycen and Jamycen.
Allen was a devoted father, brother and Poopaw. He was the best encourager and will be deeply missed by his family and friends.
Funeral services will be held at 2pm Sunday, October 20, 2024 at Geary Funeral Home in Fordsville. Visitation will be Saturday, October 19th from 4pm to 8pm and Sunday from noon until service time at the funeral home. Condolences can be made at www.gearycares.com.

title: Three county natives bring Friendsgiving back Home
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
On Saturday, November 9th, three county natives and friends since childhood, Chrystel Roach Blair, Amanda Wethington Scott, and Sally Hargis Gregory will gather at The Party Barn in Pellville for their celebration of Friendsgiving.
Their yearly celebration has been growing each year, and what was once a gathering of 3 to 8 people, now welcomes almost 40 people. They've invited teachers, family members and other mentors who've impacted their lives, and helped them to become the successful Christian women they are today.
They'll be sharing food, praying together, fellowshipping in Christ Jesus to encourage one another, and giving back to the Hancock County community where they were born and raised.
As a way of giving back this year, these three wonderful ladies will be blessing families in the community with Giving Baskets that they've decorated, and are filling with donated items. They began Friendsgiving about 4 years ago, and always find a way to give back. In previous years, they've traveled together to celebrate, such as to California and Florida.
'This year, because my dad was at hospice,' Amanda said, 'we couldn't commit to traveling, so we decided to do Friendsgiving here in Hancock County.'
Her father, the late Bernard Wethington, passed away this year on October 11th, at the young age of 66. He and Amanda's mother, Margaret, shared almost 50 years happily married together, in Lewisport.
'Friendsgiving is a way to bless others,' Amanda said. 'We think that God has kept us together. The three of us have been able to lean on each other through our strong faith, and our belief in God, and it has enabled us to bless other people. Our religion, and our belief is very important to all of us, so that's why we want to do this, is to share, and encourage and empower other women. Continuing friendships and taking care of your friendships as you go through life is very important, and to have that sister to lean on. Because we have such a strong bond, one of the reasons we're opening up this year and inviting others is so that they can see what this bond has enabled us to do. That's something we want to encourage people to do, is just to make those connections. That's what we hope to create with this, so that it grows, and they can have that network of people to reach out to.'
They decided that every time they get together, they would always give back somehow. They said that God has been so good to them, and they just want to bless others.
'We may be at a restaurant and tip somebody really nicely, for example,' Chrystel said. 'We were in an airport coming back from a trip one year, and this lady was sitting next to us. She was telling us that she had a grandson and didn't have the money to buy him things he wanted. We keep Scriptures with us, and we gave her a Scripture. Before we got off the plane, all 3 of us emptied our wallets out, and we told the stewardess to give it to her, and we wrote her a note that said, 'Smile, God loves you.' '
At their Friendsgiving get-togethers each year, Chrystel said they set an intention to 'pour each other full.'
'So many times you get weary on your journey,' she said, 'and sometimes you just need somebody to pour into you, and let your cup overfill.'
One of her favorite Scriptures is Proverbs 27:17 – As iron sharpens iron, so a man sharpens the countenance of his friend.
'We always tell each other that,' Chrystel said, 'because, if one of us is down or needs encouragement, we'll pray together. We'll just say, 'Hey, I need you to fast about a situation.' So, that's really a big one – 'iron sharpens iron.''
Amanda, Chrystel and Sally all graduated from Hancock County High School in 1997.
'As I get older,' Sally said, 'I realize what a blessing it was to grow up in Hancock County. I have so many wonderful childhood memories and the best friends I could ever ask for that have been with me through all of life's ups and downs. We started planning trips once a year so we can get together and reconnect with each other. We three talk everyday but it's so nice to get away together for a few days and just relax and have a good time. Last year, we decided we would invite our mothers to go with us and we planned a little retreat. We played games, read devotionals, and had a big Thanksgiving meal together. It was wonderful and we really enjoyed reconnecting with each other's family. Our mothers have even become good friends. This year, we decided we would do it again, but in Hancock County this time, and invite more women because we know what a blessing it is to get together with friends. We want to give back to the wonderful little town we grew up in.'
For the Friendsgiving retreat in Florida, in addition to their mothers, they also invited Chrystel's aunts, who they call 'Bonus Moms,' Elizabeth Watkins and Mary Anne Young.
This year, they've invited 36 people, and will gather at Vickey Fulkerson's Party Barn. They're having a potluck with traditional Thanksgiving dishes, as well as games, and music.
'Food and music are our common connections,' Chrystel said. 'We'll have Scriptures up, and devotions, and we'll have two people speaking that will pour into the women. We want people not to sit with their friends because we want them to meet new people. We're really creative with the games we'll be playing. Basically, we want to just give back and pour into them, and thank them for being so instrumental in our lives. I always call them 'Ushers of Destiny,' because they've helped us get to where we're supposed to be.'
They are also asking those attending, and anyone in the community, if they know someone who is in need, and are accepting donations for the Giving Baskets they are preparing, for blessing locals with.
'This is just what we do,' Chrystel said. 'It has just happened to come back to Hancock County. We think that it is going to take off. I think there are going to be some people from churches that say, 'I would like to do this for the women at my church.' So, we're just going to say, 'Let God lead you.' We started it, you take the baton, you run the race, pass it to someone else. Kind of like the movie The Forge. You impart in one, and then that one goes and gets another, and another one gets another, and just pours into them and ministers to them, and that's how you build up the Body of Christ. I just always want to do what my Father has me to do to be an example and to be a leader. We really feel like God is going to open up a door through us ministering to other people.'
Chrystel wrote an encouraging letter, and sent it to her friends, which she hopes will benefit anyone reading this: 'When you know this mandate has been placed upon your life, you need an Aaron and a Hur to help lift up your arms. They don't try to take over or be in the lead, because they know you're packed with God. Because they know the importance of your purpose, they support and build you up. They don't let pride, shame, or fear keep you from finishing your assignment. When you falter, they alter your steps. When you bend, they straighten you up. When you almost give up, they help take the load and carry it for a while…Make sure you keep an Aaron and a Hur close by you, to cover you in prayer, so that when the battles of life arise, you'll still have enough faith in you to prevail and help you in battle.'
Chrystel recently attended a national church missions conference in Chicago, and serves as a delegate. There were attendees from Ghana, Africa, and she made sure they had everything they needed while visiting the U.S. She is a Special Education Teacher at Jefferson County Public Schools, and the daughter of Denice and James Roach. Denice recently retired from teaching for many years at Hancock County Schools, and James is retired from Aleris. Chrystel is blessed with one son, Taylor, who is 8-years-old.
Sally is an Occupational Therapy Assistant at University of Kentucky Chandler Hospital, in Lexington. She is the daughter of Terri & Sue Hargis, of Hawesville. Terri was a physical therapy assistant, and now works as a security guard at the Hancock County Courthouse.
Amanda is a Continuous Improvement Superintendent at Kaiser Aluminum, and is blessed with 4 sons: Trey Shaffer (23) works at Commonwealth; Colby Stagner (16) is a junior at HCHS, and is working on his associate's degree through the dual-credit program at OCTC; Donald Scott (8) is in 3rd grade this year; and Wyman Scott (7) is in first grade, both attend South Hancock Elementary School. She and her husband, Robert, live in Philpot, and attend Pellville Baptist Church.

title: Hancock County Honors Veterans with Annual Veterans Day Program
description: Hancock County VFW Post 5186 will host the Annual Hancock County Veterans Day Program at the Hawesville Baptist Church Fellowship Hall on Veterans Day, Monday, November 11th. Veterans Day is always…
content: Hancock County VFW Post 5186 will host the Annual Hancock County Veterans Day Program at the Hawesville Baptist Church Fellowship Hall on Veterans Day, Monday, November 11th. Veterans Day is always observed on the eleventh month and eleventh day, and the ceremony begins on the eleventh hour (11:00 a.m.), memorializing the effective end of the Great War (WWI) after millions of casualties, in 1918. What was once Armistice Day was renamed Veterans Day in 1954, when soldiers who'd fought in WWII and in the Korean War asked Congress to recognize American Veterans of all wars, in order to properly recognize and honor all of our brave heroes. The Hancock County Road Department will be delivering the tables to the fellowship hall, and Hancock County VFW Auxiliary members will be decorating and preparing in advance for the program. Post Commander Homer Newman will welcome everyone, and Post Service Officer and Chaplain Wayne Stephens will be leading the Opening Prayer. Posting and retrieving of the colors by Hancock County High School Junior ROTC members will be followed by the Pledge of Allegiance to the United States Flag, and Brother Brian Adkins, Pastor of Central Baptist Church, will sing the National Anthem. The Recognition of Prisoners of War (POWs) and Those Missing in Action (MIAs) table will be presented by Billy Stephens. Post Historian LT Newton will be reading aloud the list of fallen comrades from this past year. The tolling of the bell, as well as Taps will accompany the reading. The presentation and folding of the U.S. Flag Ceremony includes the meaning behind each fold, and will be led by Vietnam Veteran Jim Domerese, with other veterans assisting. The Chair of the Hancock County VFW Auxiliary Youth Activities and Scholarships, Barbara Spindell, will be presenting the Patriot's Pen Award to the Hancock County Middle School student winner, who submitted their written essay. Post Commander Homer Newman will be presenting the Voice of Democracy Award to the Hancock County High School student winner, who submitted their patriotic-themed recorded essay. The Hancock County High School Choir, led by HCMS/HCHS Choir Director Kenny Basham, will be singing patriotic songs, and the Hancock County Homemakers Quilting Club will be presenting patriotic quilts. There will be two Wreath Presentations. One will be led by members of the Hancock County Fiscal Court, and one by Debra Owens. Former Commander of VFW District 4 Department of Kentucky, Purple Heart, Bronze Star Vietnam Veteran Barry Smith will be the guest speaker. The food will be provided by Bill & Dave's Smokin' Pit, and desserts will be provided by local churches. The raffle winner will receive a beautiful Henry Golden Boy .22 Lever-Action Rifle this year, and there will also be a couple of other prizes awarded. The Closing Prayer will be led by Hawesville Baptist Church Pastor, Brother Kyle Page.

title: Plans for 'Lighting of the Square' announced at Hawesville Council Meeting
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, November 12th, and Mayor Rob McCormick announced the date and plans for this year's Christmas celebration.
Lighting of the Square will be held on Friday, December 13th, at the Town Square in downtown Hawesville, and begins at 6:30 p.m. McCormick said the community is encouraged to arrive early. There will be Christmas decorated inflatables for the children, sponsored by Southwire, and local food trucks. Local vendors are encouraged to set up as well.
'I've talked to from Madden's office up to the corner,' McCormick said, 'and asked them if they would please light and decorate their buildings, and light them especially, because last year it was a little dark walking down Main Street on the north side of the street. They've all agreed they would do that for us. We're hoping and praying for no rain and cold. If you want to, show up at 6:00 p.m., and just mill around and meet with people, because they'll show up early. Chief Burton's done a great job in speaking with the gentleman that does the lights, Aaron Walls (Owner of Purple Walrus Lawn Company, in Lewisport). He donated all the lights. He's going to donate them all, and do the Christmas tree. He is going to wrap everything. He did all of the ones out there today. Southwire will have a table set up. We've reached out to the other plants in town, they just haven't gotten back with us. We talked to the Chamber of Commerce about trying to get some vendors as well…We're trying to grow a small amount this year.'
They are discussing the possibility of having Main Street blocked off, so people can walk to the Nativity Scene, and to local businesses that will be open during the event, such as Blackford Creek Bakery. People could also stop at local vendor tables that are set up along the way.
Blue House located at 265 Main St.
McCormick said, 'We took possession of the blue house, at 265 Main Street (in downtown Hawesville). The deed has been signed over to us; we now own the house. We took bids this week. We advertised in The Clarion and accepted bids on tearing the house down. We received 3 bids, $12,000, $14,000 and $22,000. We put the bid in at the best and low, not just low. In this situation, I feel confident in the conversations Jake and I have had with the gentlemen, that we try to move forward with this at the $12K bid price, given by Greg Wettstain. We have the money available to tear the house down. One of the stipulations was that the lot had to be leveled. That's in the bid specs.'
He opened the floor for questions and discussion, and asked for the council's approval to move forward on this project, so it can be completed before the Christmas break. The council members all voted in favor, and the project was approved.
If some tentative arrangements cannot be made, he said it may be necessary to block the roadway and divert traffic for approximately two days during the demolition.
'This is a major milestone for the City of Hawesville to have that house down,' he added. 'I hope it continues to inspire others to keep their houses up.'
Fire Chief's Report
Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards said there were 35 calls for service in October, including 19 EMS assists, 7 fire alarms, 4 vehicle accidents, 3 gas leaks, 2 structures, and a couple of field fires and vehicle fires.
'It's been busy,' Richards said. 'October is always one of our busiest months. We had our open house, and 468 people went through the station for fire prevention, on Halloween night, definitely a success that evening.'
He said several attended fire school, and the week prior to that, they did a lot of training that's offered regionally.
'The main ones that went down to that,' he said, 'we've brought on two new firefighters in the last month – Brandon Boone, and Richard Gabbert. Both of those were participating at fall school. They have acquired their needed hours, and are now able to make runs, so they're coming on pretty quickly. Our Junior Program, we had another Junior, Chris Gillespie, that aged out and moved into the firefighter ranks. That puts us at 3 Juniors that have completed their program and have moved on to the fire department. Those guys come on the dept., and are ready to make runs as soon as they're voted on; When they turn 18, the next thing they are voted on. Over the last several months, that's added 6 people to us. So, big strides there. We are always looking for membership; That is ongoing. A couple of projects going on at the station, as of late, the boat is fully in-service, and ready to go, as is the brush truck.'
The 35 Self-Contained Breathing Apparatuses (SCBAs/air packs) that the Hancock County Fiscal Court ordered toward what each volunteer fire department in the county needs, have arrived and are in-house at the stations. The Court agreed to cover the cost for 25 of those. The City of Hawesville will pay for 4 of those ordered air packs, the City of Lewisport will pay for 4, and Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department (HVFD) will pay for two.
Richards said they are getting the training finished up on the new air packs, and getting them striped up with identifications, and they'll go into service shortly.
'We have a couple of projects in-house,' he said. 'We changed to LED light. It was done by members, out of their pockets. They did that because they wanted to. It will save on the energy bill with those 8-foot lights. All those are now LED. There are plans to move forward with the ones in the rest of the building. Probably in the course of the next year, we'll switch over to LED completely. There is a lot of good work going on.'
Pancake Breakfast
There will be a Pancake Breakfast on Sunday, December 1st, at the Hawesville Volunteer Fire Department, located at 385 Main Street, in downtown Hawesville, from 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Donations will be accepted. The HVFD Auxiliary and the Junior Firefighters are working together to make it a great breakfast this year, so come out and support your local volunteer firefighters!
'Your service is very important to us,' McCormick said.
Police Chief Report
Hawesville Chief of Police B.J. Burton reported, 'For October, 2 arrests, a total of 12 citations, and I served 4 warrants this month, 15 traffic stops, without citations, a call to service, and one accident. This month coming up, we're going to prepare for the Lighting of the Square. We're getting all of that set up, and getting Main Street lit up. We're fixing to have a second vehicle striped and in-service completely.'
Superintendent's Report
In Superintendent Brian Patterson's absence, Mayor McCormick said, 'Things that are going on with the water system, we're working on Wood Street. We had a sinkhole. It was getting ready to go in. We're running new tile through there. The cost of that project is going to be $7,000 or less. We paid $5,300 today. That's one of the projects we're working on right now.'
He added that, with the council's approval, the city will be moving forward soon with the new water meters. He said the testing of the new water meters that the city has installed in several locations has shown that the they are working very well, and are extremely accurate in catching water leaks early.
'We do eventually want to move forward with the whole system being replaced,' he said, 'but I want to wait until we get all of our audits caught up before we delve into that. Because, you're talking about several hundred thousand for the whole system. They are paying off, because it tracks water down to the 10th of a gallon. It has already been helping.'

title: Revving Up Futures: High School Racers Aim for Careers in Automotive Tech
description: Three Hancock County High School students, Camden Burden (15), Brayden Roberts (16), and Jayden Porter (17), all of Hawesville, enjoy racing cars at local dirt tracks in their spare time. They love…
content:
Three Hancock County High School students, Camden Burden (15), Brayden Roberts (16), and Jayden Porter (17), all of Hawesville, enjoy racing cars at local dirt tracks in their spare time. They love racing and repairing their cars so much, that the hobby may even lead to lifelong careers for all three of them. Camden is the son of Cody Burden and Courtney Nugent; Brayden is the son of Britney Stofer; and Bayden is the son of Kimberly and Ryan Porter. Currently, they've been racing at Windy Hollow Speedway in Owensboro, Cedar Ridge Speedway in Morgantown, and Western Kentucky Speedway in Madisonville, which will soon be Paducah International Speedway.
They are all enrolled in the Diesel Program at HCHS, and HC Schools Transportation Director Brice Duncan teaches the classes. Owner of GN Excavating and Trucking, Gary Nugent, donated toward the project to build a classroom in the shop onto the HCHS bus garage, and also donates $10,000 a year toward the valuable program. After high school graduation, they all plan to attend Lincoln Tech College, in Nashville, and study to become automotive or diesel techs. When they are not racing cars, in school, or doing homework, the boys spend most all of their spare time working on their race cars. Courtney and her husband, Joseph Nugent, bought the old GN shop from his brother, Gary, and that's where the boys work on their cars. They all say that the hobby is expensive and time consuming, but that it pays off and is a lot of fun. Jayden, a senior this year, has been racing since age 14. He and his younger sister, Brooklyn, and his older brother, Mason, have raced at Windy Hollow Speedway over the years, and that's where it all began for him.
'When my brother started racing at Windy Hollow Speedway, I decided that I wanted to give it a try,' Jayden said. 'I started building my own car in our backyard over the winter, and didn't really learn anything until I was already doing. I just built the car and went straight to the track and figured it out from there. I wasn't the best driver, but after a year, and friends I made at the track, I was taught a lot and have learned a lot. I would definitely encourage others to get into racing. It's an amazing environment of pushing your hardest to win against others, but you've got to be tough and have a strong mindset, because it's not just racing you get to do, you have to maintain and work on your cars too.' He added, 'When I first started, all I learned was the basics. My dad was the one who helped, but neither of us knew too much about cars, so we relied on YouTube. This season, thanks to finding Joseph Nugent and Cody Burden, they have taught me just about everything I know, from regular maintenance to taking an engine apart, and from rebuilding to rear ends. I'm always willing to find extra time to spend in the shop to learn more. Cody has always been there when I needed help with a car, or if I have some stupid idea, even if he knew it wouldn't work, he helped me try it out anyway so I could learn. He's done so much for me in my racing life. He's even been there for me when I wasn't feeling the best or having bad days. It's always a joy to be working on something in the shop with him. He can brighten your day with the stupidest jokes.' This summer, Camden and Brayden, both sophomores at HCHS, started racing. Camden ran up to Jayden at Windy Hollow Speedway one day and asked if he could ride in his car, and from then on out decided he wanted to race. Camden then encouraged Brayden to start racing as well. Cody, Camden's father, has raced since he was a toddler, from go-karts to big-body cars. Camden and Brayden have watched a lot of dirt track racing over the years before trying it themselves. Along with watching his father race, Camden also had the honor of watching his grandpa race, the late Dallas Burden. 'I wouldn't be the kind of racer I am if it wasn't for my dad,' Camden said. 'He's done it his whole life and our crew look up to him and Joseph for answers. Dad has spent so many late nights in the shop building our cars, or welding stronger cages; We would all be lost without him. We joke that dad builds them and Joe funds them. Sure, sponsors help, and having more would definitely help ease Joseph's mind, but we are running all these cars out of our own pockets. My Nana helps me when she can, and then our other sponsors are: DNJ of Drakesboro, Bozart Auto Sales, Service, and Towing in Cannelton, and Rob's Roadside. It's an expensive sport, but I have to tell you, it's worth it. It's a rush getting out there and being with all those cars. I'm still learning, but I don't ever want to stop.' Camden's step-father, Joseph, has raced from derby to dirt track racing as well. Joseph runs the wrecker at Windy Hollow Speedway, and Courtney, Camden's mom, takes racing photos at Windy Hollow and Cedar Ridge Speedway.
'I owe getting into this to Camden and Joseph,' Brayden said, 'and a bunch to Cody too. Joseph built my first car for me when I walked up to him after one night of going. Here I am a 16-year-old kid, and he hands me this car and says, 'Drive it.' It was a rear-wheel-drive car and I tried, but I prefer a front-wheel-drive. I loved doing it so much that I traded my dirt bike for my very own mini stock. Joseph and Cody are teaching me everything they can about it. The majority of my summer, I spent at Joseph and Courtney's house (to work in the shop there). I think I went home one weekend. My mom missed me, but I was always there or in the shop. I fell asleep in a car once while trying to strip it out.' Courtney said she normally stands in the middle to get good photos of the cars as they race. She said that with the cars whizzing by, and the dust flying, it keeps her on her toes. She has also raced in the past, and Joseph and Cody continue to race as well. Courtney, Joseph and Cody all work full-time, and spend most of their free time helping the boys with their racing hobby. Cody and Joseph help them with building and repairing their cars and teaching them how to do the work themselves. They also help them perfect their racing skills. Cody is a mechanic. Joseph works at GN Excavating, and Courtney is an office manager, and manages three different mental health offices in Rockport, Tell City and Dale. 'It does cause anxiety watching your kids go round and round in circles with a huge group of other cars,' Courtney said, 'but they love it.' The final race of the 2024 season was the 'Enduro' at Cedar Ridge Speedway on Saturday, November 9th. Because some parts for their cars didn't arrive in time, the boys decided not to race in it, and are focused on getting their cars ready for next year's season. The racing season for 2025 starts at the end of March, beginning of April. During the off-season, they stay busy planning for the upcoming races.
'They are going to tear down their cars, tear down some motors, rebuild some motors and rebuild some body panels, etc., on the current cars they have,' Courtney said. 'All the cars are parked here, so they all work out of here. All three race Chevy Cavaliers. Two or three of the cars currently have the push rod motor, and they are hoping, during this off-season, to switch it to an echo-tech motor.' They are already planning for a 4-day race at the end of August, beginning of September, 2025. Friday night's race will be at Paducah International Speedway. Saturday night's race will be at Cedar Ridge. Sunday night's race will be at Windy Hollow Speedway, and Monday night's race at Western Kentucky Speedway. They have to stay within all the regulations of each speedway, and staying within those parameters, cut down as much weight as possible to make the car go as fast as it can go. Most importantly, of course, is making them as safe as they can be.
They said if you want to try racing, and don't already know someone who races, then find someone who races and just ask. 'They do want to encourage other kids to race, because the generation nowadays, kids their age, need to get out there to keep racing alive,' Courtney said. 'Adopt a racer at a race track and ask them if you can learn from them, and then find sponsors. For the 2025 season, that's what the guys will be doing while they're building their cars, is finding small businesses to sponsor stuff for their car. That's what I would encourage other guys, and girls to do.' Local sponsors can help with, for example, racetrack fees, car parts, and whole vinyl wrap arounds for cars, as a promotional racing billboard. Courtney has a mini stock of her own, an '01 Chevy Cavalier, and has raced it at Cedar Ridge Speedway. 'I enjoyed it,' she said. 'It is a rush. I would totally recommend doing it if you have the chance, or if not, riding with someone, because it doesn't take any time for the guys to strap in an extra safety seat and harness, and you can have an amazing experience. As much as I loved it, I do prefer standing in the middle and taking pictures.' There aren't age categories, and so the boys race with others who are older and younger. The only categories the racetracks have are different classes for each division. For the 2025 season, the boys will race mini stocks (4-cylinders), and they've all chosen Chevy Cavaliers. Joseph and Cody have worked on these engines and know more about them, making them the best choice. Jayden just purchased an '01, Brayden's is an '05, and Camden's will be an '01 as well. They started out driving economy cars (entry-level). 'Economy is, basically, you can pull any fully-stocked car from the roadway, and all you have to do is put a roll cage in it, paint it, roll bar, and of course take the windshield and everything else out, but it has to be completely stock, and you can run it. That's how they started out,' Courtney said. 'I'm still learning. I normally will sit in the shop with them and edit pictures while they are all elbow deep in engines.' The boys are doing well in school, and if they happen to have a race on a Sunday night or a school night, their parents make sure they get as rested as possible and that they don't miss any school days. 'I'm proud of all 3 of them,' Courtney said. 'We have all made an agreement that if you don't go to school following a race day, you don't get to race the next weekend. They go to school and they keep up their grades. I'm super proud of them for it.' They spend so much time with racing during their free time that they don't have time to do things that would not be good for them. They don't get bored. It keeps them busy, and out of trouble.
'That's what my husband jokes about. He would rather spend a bunch of money on race car parts than have to worry about them out doing drugs or something stupid. Nowadays, I don't ever have to wonder where they're at. Normally, they get off the bus, they do their chores, do their homework, and then they're in the shop,' Courtney said. The boys encourage everyone to come out to Windy Hollow Speedway next season and watch the races, because it is an awesome and exciting show. After the races on Tuesdays, the announcer at the track, Blake Smith, posts on the Facebook Page, and 'Let's Talk Racing,' airs on 92.9 FM. He goes over the race results for Windy Hollow, and interviews some feature winners. They also sometimes record the races, and post the videos on YouTube. 'We put Go Pros in their cars at the beginning of the season,' Courtney said, 'so we could watch and help them learn. The cameras help Cody and Joe see if they're turning too soon, or turning too late. The cameras help them figure out how to help them, since they can't be on the track with them sometimes. We'll all sit down at suppertime the next day, hook it up to the laptop, and watch. They learn a lot.'
Jayden's first race he placed fourth position. He has consistently finished in the top 10 and top 5. This year, for his economy season, he was third in point at Windy Hollow Speedway. For Brayden and Camden's first year of racing, both had top 5 finishes. 'They didn't place too high in the points because they came in in the middle of the season,' Courtney said. 'We're hoping for a better 2025 season. 2024 was their learning, so we're happy with it. Cam does have a second-place finish, and he's very proud of that one.'
Safety gear is important, and they all wear helmets and flame-resistant racing suits. Courtney explained that the dirt track racing helmets are specifically designed to handle the unique impacts and conditions of this kind of racing, and have extra ventilation, a wider visor for better peripheral vision, and a more robust construction compared to standard motorcycle helmets. 'It can get pretty rough,' she said, 'depending on the track, and sometimes rollovers do happen. So far, none of my kids have rolled their cars. Brayden has taken out a light pole at Windy Hollow Speedway. In a battle down the back stretch, he got pushed down the backstretch and he and his opponent got into a light pole. It had taken out the lights for a few minutes, and then they all turned back on. The only cable that had snapped was the cable for the caution light, so they weren't worried about that. He still wanted to go after that.' At this year's Hancock County Fair, Brayden ran his dirt bike in the off-road vehicle drag racing event. Joseph helped with the go-kart racing, and Courtney took photos. 'When I'm at Windy Hollow I stand at turn four,' she said, 'so when the green flag drops, I get pictures of them hammering down or getting them sliding into three and out of four. When I'm at Cedar Ridge, I stand in between turn one and two. I love doing it. My goal is to be asked to take more pictures at other tracks, and travel more with the kids.' The fanfare at these racing events varies, but the drivers will usually get a chance to wave to fans in the crowd as they go down the front stretch. You will see their hands pop out of their window nets as they wave, and children attending enjoy lining the front fence to cheer them on. Once the green flag drops, they are gaining as much speed as they can to win the race. Get out to one of the local speedways, and cheer on Brayden, Camden and Jayden next season to show your support! Keep an eye out for the announcement of the 2025 Season Schedule at Windy Hollow Speedway by liking and following the Facebook Page.

title: Hawesville City Council
description: The Hawesville City Council met for their last time this year on Tuesday, December 10th, and Hawesville Mayor Rob McCormick led the recitation of oath and initial swearing-in before the new year of…
content: The Hawesville City Council met for their last time this year on Tuesday, December 10th, and Hawesville Mayor Rob McCormick led the recitation of oath and initial swearing-in before the new year of all council members. Running for re-election in the General Election in November were incumbent Hawesville City Council members Pat 'Junnie' Morris, Kevin Linn, Tracy O. Johnson, Justin Basham, Danny Doyle, and Wayne Herndon. Matt Patterson ran for a seat on the council as well, and with only 147 votes, will not fill one of those 6 seats in 2025. All current members will continue, and serve another term. To continue the details of the minutes for the December council meeting that were provided in last week's edition of The Clarion, City Manager Jake Powers initiated discussion on the possibility of another pilot water meter with the city 's original meter company, Ferguson. The city has been engaged in a pilot test of 10 meters through a company called Fortiline, that began in June of this year. So far, the Fortiline water meter pilot has revealed that these meters are much more accurate at reading, and will save money on manpower, fuel, and catching water leaks quicker. The manual readings the city 's crewmen have to do monthly on the more antiquated meters wouldn't be necessary, as the new system has software that sends out a cellular signal, reads the meter once an hour, stores the data, and 3 times a day sends a text message that is logged to a webpage assigned to the city 's administration. It generates the billing data and provides access to the meter readings directly to the water customer. Customers can log directly into the portal and see what their meter readings are. 'I want to present to the council that who we'd gotten our meters from previously, before this pilot with Fortiline, they have offered to do a pilot test through them with their meters,' Jake said. 'They sat down briefly with Superintendent Brian Patterson and I. They said they'd be happy to come in and speak with the council , if you all did want to hear from them.' After discussion, the council made a decision to invite the representatives of Ferguson to do a presentation on the water meter pilot that they are offering, at the January council meeting.

title: Jane B. Jordan
description: Jane B. Jordan, 88, of Lewisport, passed away on Friday, December 13, 2024 at Heartland Villa in Lewisport. She was born in Livermore, KY on May 30, 1936 to the late Alfred and Eula Mae Vance…
content:
Jane B. Jordan, 88, of Lewisport, passed away on Friday, December 13, 2024 at Heartland Villa in Lewisport. She was born in Livermore, KY on May 30, 1936 to the late Alfred and Eula Mae Vance Brashear. Jane was a registered nurse and a member of Lewisport Baptist Church and was retired from Commonwealth Aluminum and Heartland Villa Center. She enjoyed Kentucky Wesleyan basketball, University of Louisville basketball, golf and playing the piano for Union Baptist Church, Lewisport Baptist Church and multiple funerals and weddings. Jane was preceded in death by her husband, Arthur C. 'Art' Jordan; siblings, Chris Carver, Mildred Day and Jackie Boling, granddaughter Corissa Lindley and great granddaughter Magan. Jane is survived by her daughters, Gaye (Craig) Waldie and Lynne (Bobby) Stone; grandchildren, Kevin Waldie and Scarlett (Jacob) Byrne. Great grandchildren Violett and Max.
No services will be held at this time. Jane, like her husband Art, donated her body to the University of Louisville Medical School. Gibson & Son Funeral Home is assisting Jane's family with her final wishes. In lieu of flowers, donations to the Lewisport Baptist Church Food Pantry would be greatly appreciated. Share your memories and condolences with her family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: 'Grit and Merit': Kiefer Hendricks Releases Inspiring Debut Album
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Kiefer D. Hendricks, of Hawesville, has just released his first album titled 'Grit and Merit,' on December 25th, 2024. He is the previous Webmaster for The Hancock Clarion, and…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer Kiefer D. Hendricks, of Hawesville, has just released his first album titled 'Grit and Merit,' on December 25th, 2024. He is the previous Webmaster for The Hancock Clarion, and produced the album with his good friend, Eli Holmes. There are eleven tracks on this phenomenal blues/rock album, and every song is a treasure to listen to. No matter what style of music you normally prefer, you will enjoy it, and Kiefer made sure everyone can do just that because it is free to listen to! Kiefer said his favorite song is the first track. It's called 'You to Thank,' and he wrote it about his mom, Julie Embry. 'My mom has always been there for me,' he said, 'even in the roughest times I've ever known, and I've been through some rough ones. She's always been there, ready to give from her heart saying, 'What do you need? How can I help?' She's always there to help me. She's always there to prop me up, and she's always going to love me. You'll never find that in another person. You'll only get it from your mom.' He wrote all of the songs in one year. He played all of the guitar tracks and sang all of the vocals on the album. His friend, Eli, played all of the drum tracks and did the production. They worked on it together, remotely, for three years, and Eli surprised him by completing the production on Christmas Day. Eli currently lives in Los Angeles. They've known each other since they were teenagers, and have been collaborating on music since then. He was aware that Kiefer had taken the time to write some amazing songs, and sent him equipment so they could work together and get them recorded. Kiefer said that the process was challenging but a lot of fun, and very rewarding. 'I worked very hard on this album for years, and I'm very proud of it. I tried to bring a message of hope, God, and positivity to this record and I'm so glad its message is being heard,' he said. 'This album has a recovery theme, and a redemption theme, and a theme of serving God too…We live in a wayward world, and if you can bring a little light in it, then you really accomplish something, I think.' He's been playing guitar since he was 10-years-old, and just recently took up playing the banjo as well. He said his taste in music is very eclectic. 'I like everything from Ben Folds, to Frank Sinatra, to older rap, to just about anything…I grew up in a really musical family. My mom pretty much gave me my taste in music from what she listened to when she was younger,' he said, 'and I just took the ball and ran with it. From there, I decided I wanted to start playing at a very early age. I had a little Flintstones ukulele when I was a baby that I used to play. When I got to be about 10 or 11, they said, 'Let's get him a guitar!'' The album has already been getting a solid amount of traction since its release, just a few weeks ago. In his 34 years of life, Kiefer has gained a lot of wisdom to impart to others in his songs, and his listeners can feel that. 'While I was writing it and recording,' he said, 'I was picky with the tracks because I always felt like, 'Are they any good?' Every artist is never satisfied with their own work. I didn't choose the title of the album, Eli chose it. I thought that it spoke to the recipe for a great comeback. I started off down a really rough path. I've seen some things that have just changed me, fundamentally. And I realized that if I wanted to change at all, I had to make some promises to myself. One of them was getting an education, and one was treating all the people around me better. You've got to have goals.' In December of 2023, Kiefer earned his Associate's Degree in Applied Science and Computer Programming at Owensboro Community Technical College (OCTC). He is also a CompTIA A+ certified computer technician, and is currently working on a Bachelor of Science in Information Technology degree through Western Governors University, which he will likely complete by the end of this year. He was recently hired at OCTC as an adjunct faculty member, and began teaching CIT-105, Introduction to Computers, on January 13th. I asked Kiefer if he had any advice for someone reading this, who would like to record their own album, or start learning an instrument. He said, 'The truth of the matter is, I've started with so many different instruments over and over again. The thing is, it's never too late to learn, and you will LOVE it. Music is the best outlet that there is out there. It's the greatest hobby I've ever found. As far as getting into recording your own music, just start writing. Do it stream of conscious if you have to but just start writing, and you'll get something that you like…Don't give up. You can achieve your dreams. When I started this, these were things that I never thought possible, and now I'm doing them.' Kiefer is a Christian, and one of his main goals was for the album to have an overall theme of the importance of serving God. 'My relationship with God didn't come until I got older,' he said. 'I kind of made the mistake of thinking, 'How can there be some all-powerful being?' Well, the thing is, the human mind wasn't meant to comprehend it, at all. And the fact of the matter is, there are just too many 'coincidences' in this world for there not to be a God. And I believe that Jesus is the Lord and Savior.' Along with his position as Webmaster for The Clarion, for many months Kiefer would also come to the office on his days off and help the previous owner and publisher, Donn Wimmer, with any computer issues that needed to be resolved. He was a huge blessing to the newspaper, and is greatly missed in the work environment. 'I just want to tell the readers how appreciative I am of them,' he said, 'not only for reading The Clarion, and for listening to my music but for always being there for us and helping us provide for our families.' Kiefer's mom, Julie, lives in Hawesville. She works from home, and is a medical coder for Norton Healthcare. His step-dad, Tony Embry, works at Commonwealth.
The album, 'Grit and Merit,' is available for anyone to listen to for free. Just go to: kieferdhendricks.pro. He said a physical copy of the album is currently in the works. His best friend, Scott Richards, of Nebraska, has a son who is a very talented artist, Chance Richards, and he has already been commissioned to do the artwork for the album cover.
You can also go directly to SoundCloud and enjoy listening to it at: https://on.soundcloud.com/ fV5R5UL4UajLvwgv7 .
This is a very positive and uplifting album, and I highly recommend that you take the time to listen to it. I guarantee that it will put you in a cozy, feel-good mood.

title: From Muddy Gut to the World: Veronica Taylor's Grand Adventures
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Veronica Taylor, of Lewisport, has visited Europe many times. Last August, she and three of her friends flew to the Netherlands, and enjoyed a wonderful river cruise that took them…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer Veronica Taylor, of Lewisport, has visited Europe many times. Last August, she and three of her friends flew to the Netherlands, and enjoyed a wonderful river cruise that took them on a tour of Amsterdam, and then on to Germany, Austria, Hungary, and Czechia. When they are not going on adventures together, she and her friends play bridge regularly. Veronica's traveling companions on this trip were Julie Burg, Nancy Wilson and Kathi Redfern, all of Owensboro. They left on August 26th, 2024, and returned three weeks later on September 16th. Over the years, Veronica has made trips to Iceland, France, Wales, India, Costa Rica, Peru, and Belize, once each. She has visited Italy, Scotland, England, and Northern Ireland, each twice. And she has traveled to the Republic of Ireland six times!
'I've also visited 46 of the U.S. states,' she said. 'I'm missing Hawaii, Idaho, North Dakota, and Rhode Island. I'll get to those before I die. I've had great times everywhere, and would go back again to visit any of them!…I'm a little girl from Muddy Gut, and I've been all of these places.' She and her friends absolutely LOVED the Grand European River Cruise they went on together, and they also enjoyed a lovely train ride through Slovenia. 'It was a really great trip. We had so much fun talking to people in airports, and just around. You find out so many things, and you run into such interesting people,' Veronica said. 'My friend tells me that I've never met a stranger, and she's probably right. I talk to everybody, and I think my life is richer for it. Talk to the locals, and talk to the people around you; That's my advice. And always be courteous. I have never had anyone be discourteous to me, ever. I'm always courteous to them first. You respect them and their lifestyle in their country, and they will pay you back tenfold.' They had booked three extra days to go sightseeing in Amsterdam when they first arrived, before beginning their cruise. They visited the Van Gogh Museum, dedicated to Vincent Van Gogh, and took a canal boat ride. 'Amsterdam is, basically, a canal city; It's not unlike Venice, but they have more streets and more ground than Venice,' she said. 'Most everyone gets around on a bicycle, so there are bikes everywhere.' They went on a really nice walking tour of Amsterdam as well, and their guide was a very informative young man, she said, who told them tons of interesting facts about the city. They also took a train to The Hague, and drove by the International Criminal Court building, an international tribunal. 'We did not get to go in the building,' she said. 'That was interesting to see because that's where all of the war crimes were tried for from WWII, and they're still tried there. While we were at The Hague, we went to see the 'Girl with a Pearl Earring.' What's fun about it, is it took us 30-40 minutes to figure out how to get our train tickets…One of the things I learned from international travel is don't be afraid to ask, and almost everyone speaks English. If the first person you talk to doesn't speak English, the second person you talk to will. And most of them are really friendly. Also, the thing that I learned from having a deaf employee was that you can pantomime almost anything. You don't have to use words; you can act out what you need to ask. We finally got our train tickets, and had a really nice trip through the countryside, going to The Hague.' When they boarded the boat to begin their cruise, they first headed to Kinderdijk. 'It was a Viking Cruise. They are on their toes to be courteous, helpful, and friendly,' Veronica said. 'Everyone smiles all of the time, and wants to give you help all of the time. Our boat took off, and went down to Kinderdijk, where we saw the windmills, bunches of them. They told us lots of stories about why there were windmills. We got to go into one where people actually lived. They're not that big; I can't imagine raising a family in one, but people did. I learned that the windmill not only spins with the wind, but it rotates around the building. That was one of my favorite things, was learning about the windmills.' They were traveling on the Rhine River, and the next stop was in Cologne, Germany. 'We made eight stops in Germany, going down the river,' she said. 'They all have wonderful cathedrals and castles, and all of that is amazing and interesting to walk through. The best part is the food, the beer, and the people though. When we got off the boat, everywhere they provided a guided walking tour of the city or town wherever we were.'
After visiting Koblenz, Germany, they were headed out on the Main River, a right tributary, and the longest tributary of the Rhine. They stopped at Miltenberg, Wurzburg, Bamberg, Nuremberg, and Regensburg. 'At Wurzburg,' she said, 'that's where we started seeing lots of vineyards, and that's where they grow the grapes for the Riesling wine. The vineyards in that area looked very different from the vineyards in Italy for some reason. They were all on a hillside. All of the hillsides are covered with vineyards.' They stopped at Passau, in Lower Bavaria, and then the boat started on the Danube River. She said most of the travel was during the nighttime, so they usually arrived in a new town in the morning. 'Some of the travel was in the daytime. When it's in the daytime, it's really nice just to sit out on the deck and watch the world go by. These cruises are really slow moving. If you're wanting to race around and run, this is not the trip for you. It's just a very calmly paced vacation,' she said.
Next was Austria. When they arrived, they first stopped at Melk, then Krems an der Donau, and then Vienna. 'Vienna is one of the most beautiful cities I have ever seen,' Veronica said. 'I would go back to Vienna in a heartbeat. It was clean, friendly, easy to get around – they had trams and subways and I used both of them, and it was easy to do. I wish that I had paid to go see the Lipizzaner stallion facilities. I did get to see a Lipizzaner stallion. A few of them were being evaluated for whether or not they could continue in the school or go be regular horses. Lipizzaner stallions are the horses that perform an exercise called 'airs above the ground.' It's a trained exercise that they have to do, and they're beautiful, all white horses.' She and her friends also enjoyed a tour of the Schönbrunn Palace, while in Austria. And during the trip to Vienna, Veronica met up with a friend that she had worked with in Washington, D.C. 'We met at the opera house. I met her sister and her mother. We went out to eat, and had a pleasant time. They were bicycling the same stretch of the river. It was fun to meet up with her,' she said. 'There is so much to see in Vienna.'
On the ship, the kitchen staff always tried to make cultural foods from the area where they were docked. Most of the walking tours started in the morning, and they had the choice of coming back to the boat and having lunch, or having lunch wherever they were. There was usually a bus available for them to travel back and forth from the boat as well. 'My favorite thing in all of the Germanies was the food and drink; It was all so good. And the food on the boat was outstanding,' she said. 'You could eat a buffet breakfast, or you could order a special breakfast. Lunch and dinner you ordered from a menu, and there were at least eight entrees to choose from.' The next stop on their tour was Budapest, the largest city of Hungary.
'I learned that Budapest is actually two cities, Buda and Pest. Buda is on one side of the river, and Pest is on the other side. My favorite thing in Budapest was the market,' she said. 'It was in an old railroad station. It was HUGE. They had everything – fruits, vegetables, fish, chicken, meat, and alongside of that were souvenirs, clothes, etc. It was two stories, and there was an Aldi in the basement, which I thought was funny.' She said she's not much of a shopper, but did purchase five different kinds of paprika in Budapest to take home, and some beautiful Christmas ornaments in Prague to bring back. She mainly bought local, craft dark beers to enjoy while there, along with some delicious dark chocolate she purchased in Vienna. 'I did not take lots of pictures either, but what I always do when I travel is I send myself postcards,' she said. 'As much as I can, I make sure I use the local postage. I either address it to myself or to one of my animals. Right now, I have four cats. I address it to one of the cats, and it usually says, 'Really miss you, be home soon,' or some silly thing. Then I have a picture of someplace where I've been before, and I have a stamp. I have a stack of them from lots of different places. I also try to send postcards to little kids I know.' She said the crew on the ship were teasing her because she was sending out so many postcards. She mailed out around 13 from each country. 'The crew on the ship made us feel like we were safe. They made us feel like they wanted us to have a good time,' she said. 'The waitstaff called the four of us either 'The Spice Girls,' or 'Charlie's Angels.' We thought it was funny. We were so proud that we had nicknames.' She said they really enjoyed the crew, and talked with them a lot. And with that, she offered another tip for your future travels. 'Engage the people around you in conversation,' Veronica said, 'even if you have a hard time talking to each other. Ask them about their lives, and talk to them about your life. Learn something from each other. We got to know the people pretty well. It just made it more interesting. There were two women from New Orleans, and some from Chicago, Wisconsin, Tennessee, all over.' They had an activity every evening on the boat. Sometimes it was the cruise director telling them what they were going to be doing the next day, or the chef announcing something special that he was going to cook for them. They also played short videos about the area they were floating through. When they were approaching Vienna, dancers came onboard the boat one night to show them The Viennese waltz. 'They had little competitions – trivia competitions, etc. And there was a music one, and that was the most fun,' she said. 'You could get up and dance and sing, and watch everybody, and join in. They just did a good job of entertaining. We won the last competition. My partner who they partnered me up with and I were pantomiming Sonny & Cher.'
When they arrived in Budapest, they took a train to Prague, and she said that was another highlight of the trip, and fun taking the train across. She said viewing the countryside, and just watching people board the train was interesting. During the train ride, they also went through Slovenia. 'Unfortunately, when we got to Budapest the temperature dropped out and it started pouring down rain,' she said. 'We did venture out in the rain to go see the astronomical clock, and we also took a ride in an antique car through Prague. It's amazing that the clock still works! It is this one clock in the middle of town. It has the positions of the sun and the moon; it has a calendar. It has six of the apostles that come out periodically. On an hourly basis they come out, like a cuckoo clock, but it's the apostles. It's just an amazing sight to see.'
She said they are trying to plan a trip to Spain and Portugal in the next few years. And Veronica is currently planning a trip to Antarctica! 'I am trying to find somebody to go with me and everybody says, 'It's too cold!' You have to book it at least a year ahead of time, so I'm a little behind in booking,' she said. 'It usually involves a flight down to Argentina, and then boating in the stretch between Argentina and Antarctica is some of the roughest waters in the world…I will be taking more pictures in Antarctica.' Her next trip is going to be here in the U.S. though, and she'll be traveling to Jazz Fest 2025, in New Orleans, Louisiana. 'I'm going to go down to Memphis and hit Graceland and Beale Street. I'm going to drive through Mississippi and maybe visit some more blues clubs,' she said, 'and then go to the Jazz Fest. I'll drive back up on the Natchez Trace, hit Tupelo and visit Elvis's birthplace. Then I'm going to top it off at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center, in Huntsville.' Veronica was born and raised in Lewisport, and grew up on Muddy Gut Road. She is a 1971 Hancock County High School graduate, and daughter of the late Joe & Catherine Taylor. She moved back to Lewisport in 2020. She is one of two newly elected Hancock County Board of Education members, and serving for Educational District 2. She'll be sworn-in at the first monthly meeting of the year, on January 23rd. 'Lots of things will happen at the first board meeting,' she said. 'We will approve the new officers, and approve the budget. It will be a very active meeting.' Veronica is also Co-Founder of Hancock County Community Kitties, established in February of 2021.
'We haven't set the date yet for the next clinic,' she said. 'We change partners periodically but I think we are going to be sticking with Friends of Butler County Animals. The last clinic, we took 50 cats, and we try once a year to have a free clinic. We are approaching 600 cats we've spayed or neutered in Hancock County, and that's since we started this. We'll try to have a Facebook page up and running by the first clinic this year, and we post flyers up all over the county.'

title: Vastwood Lake Now Stocked With Rainbow Trout!
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer It was announced last week that Vastwood Park Lake has been added to the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR) Trout Stocking Program for 2025. The first…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer It was announced last week that Vastwood Park Lake has been added to the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR) Trout Stocking Program for 2025. The first stocking took place on Friday, January 17th, and the lake received one thousand rainbow trout. Vastwood Lake is also scheduled to receive one thousand rainbow trout in October, and one thousand in November of this year. Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts said, 'We (the Hancock County Fiscal Court) originally requested that Kentucky Fish and Wildlife stock Vastwood Lake with trout a few years ago. There was some concern regarding the size of the lake (approximately 20 acres). We were persistent to just give it a chance to see how it goes. They agreed, and we are very excited. We think it gives our community members a unique opportunity to enjoy Vastwood Park throughout the winter.'
As you may remember reading in previous Clarion articles, KDFWR crews have periodically come to Hancock County to check the size of the fish in the lake. In the fall of 2023, the Fisheries Program Coordinator for the Northwestern Fishery District of the KDFWR, Jeremy Shiflet, and his team were checking the largemouth bass population, using electrofishing equipment that temporarily stuns the fish so they can be quickly netted up, placed in the live well, measured, and then immediately released back into the lake. They captured 57 largemouth bass that fall, ranging from 5 to 19 inches. Shiflet said they saw many bluegills, channel catfish, and a couple of grass carps at the time as well. The largest fish they captured was 3.5 pounds.
Shiflet also explained why there are a lot of smaller fish in the lake. He said that is because of the shallow, clear water, and how aquatic vegetation tends to grow in those areas. The county has to have the lake treated once or twice a year to keep that under control. When you have the clear water, you have low productivity and excessive, really thick vegetation, and that leads to slower growth. It is a constant battle, and Shiflet and his team regularly work with the Hancock County Parks crew to promote faster growth of the fish, adding bigger fish, and taking care of the structure of the lake near the shore where the fish are partial to, providing them with a place to feed and hide, and also bringing them closer for anglers to have the opportunity to try and catch them. Per the Memorandum Of Understanding on agreement with Hancock County to help manage the lake, the KDFWR has stocked catfish on an every-other-year basis. They stocked those in 2022, and again in 2024. Anglers do not need a trout permit to catch and release trout! However, a trout permit IS required to harvest those fish. Trout permits may be purchased at any in-person license vendor. There is no minimum size, and anglers may harvest eight fish per person, per day. The KDFWR covers 14 counties, from Union County all the way to Larue, Hardin and Meade County along the Ohio River. Like and follow the KDFWR Facebook page to see regular posts with updates.
Happy Fishing!

title: James W. 'Jim' Cummings

content:

James is survived by his daughter, Kelli Cummings; sons, Todd Cummings and Mack (Becky) Cummings; grandchildren, Michal Cummings, Nolan Cummings and Natalia Cummings; siblings, Betty Brown, Patsy Littlepage and Don Cummings along with several nieces and nephews.

title: Steven A. Mason
description: Steven A. Mason, 64, of Hawesville, passed away on Wednesday, February 19, 2025 at Owensboro Health Regional Hospital with his family by his side. He was born in Owensboro, Ky on March 22, 1960 to…
content:
Steven A. Mason, 64, of Hawesville, passed away on Wednesday, February 19, 2025 at Owensboro Health Regional Hospital with his family by his side. He was born in Owensboro, Ky on March 22, 1960 to Thomas and Kay Mason. Steve was a member of Hawesville Baptist Church, where he was on the Building and Grounds Committee and was retired from Domtar after 38 years of service. Steve had many interests and hobbies throughout his life; riding dirt bikes, '71 Chevelle's, '78 Dodge pick-up trucks, building cars and participating in demolition derbies. He enjoyed raising a vegetable garden, golfing, fishing, hunting, bowling, cooking, going on cruises, boating, water skiing, raising chickens and collecting eggs. He celebrated life. Steve was preceded in death by his father, Thomas Mason and stepfather, Pascal Powers. Survivors include his wife of 46 years, Paula Spencer Mason; daughters, Jaclyn (Reat) Haynes and Leslie (Andrew) Clark; grandchildren, Shealyn Mason, Lainey Myers, Bailey Myers, Trace Haynes, Oliver Haynes, Mason Clark, Preston Clark, Spencer Clark and Charlotte Clark; Mother, Kay Powers; stepmother, Martha Mason; step siblings, Martina (Chuck) Billings, Brian (Lisa) Greer, Ruth (Rick) Grant and Glen Powers; brother in law, Steve (Rita) Spencer; aunts, Mary Jane (Johnny) Owens and Carolyn Cassady; uncle, Wendell (Beverly) Richardson along with several nieces, nephews and cousins.
Services will be held at 2 p.m. on Monday, February 24, 2025 at Hawesville Baptist Church with burial following in Mt. Eden Baptist Church Cemetery. Steve's family will be greeting friends on Monday at the church from 10 a.m. until service time at the church. Memorial contributions may be made to the Hawesville Baptist Church Building Fund. Share your memories and condolences with his family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Lady Hornets off and running with three run rule victories!
description: Madison Higdon rips a shot for the Lady Hornets. Higdon hit a home run during a win over McLean County Tuesday at Vastwood Park. Dwayne Wroe's Lady Hornet softball team was back in action after…
content: Madison Higdon rips a shot for the Lady Hornets. Higdon hit a home run during a win over McLean County Tuesday at Vastwood Park. Dwayne Wroe's Lady Hornet softball team was back in action after winning 18 games in 2023. Hancock County began their 2024 campaign with a 16-1 win over the Owensboro Knights on Monday at Vastwood Park. The game was called after four innings due to the 15-run rule. Ella House had a big day at the plate for HCHS as the senior hit a 3-run home run in the third inning. Hancock County began the game with Lily Roberts on the mound. The senior was back after a long layoff from knee surgery. She wears a brace now, but her performance was as impressive as ever. Roberts pitched three innings and struck out every batter she faced. Baylee Estes put the Hornets on the scoreboard in the bottom of the first when she led off with a double and later scored on a passed ball. Kylie Westerfield and House followed with base hits and Layni Roberts later singled. Carolina Jones came in as a pinch runner and the score was 4-0 after one frame. Lily and Layni Roberts both smacked RBI doubles in the second and Westerfield scored on a hit by House. House smashed her 3-run shot to left field in the third inning and the score was 10-0. Layni Roberts later stroked another RBI double in the same inning. Owensboro Christian scored their lone run in the top of the fourth off 8th grade pitcher Jordyn Waltrip. Hancock County added five more runs in the home half of the frame off six base hits. The game ended when Westerfield crossed home plate. Lily Roberts got the win on the hill with 9Ks and three perfect innings pitched. Waltrip allowed one run on three hits, with one walk. House was 4 for 4 at the plate with the homer and six RBI. Layni Roberts was 3 for 3 with two doubles and two RBI. Westerfield was 2 for 2 with four runs scored. Lily Roberts was 2 for 3 with a double and two RBI. Estes was 2 or 4 with a double. Aubree Mosby was 1 for 1 with one RBI. Waltrip and Madison Higdon both went 1 for 2, and Ava Riggs was 1 for 3. McLean County game 1 Hancock County flexed their muscles during a doubleheader sweep of McLean County here Tuesday. The Lady Hornets won 10-0 in five innings during game 1. Lily Roberts gave up her first base hit of the season when Sophia Frailey led off the game with a single to right field. That was the only hit the star pitcher allowed all evening. The Lady Hornets took a 1-0 lead in the second on a sacrifice fly by Waltrip. The girls broke the game open with eight runs in the third. Estes and Westerfield led off the inning with base hits. Lily and Layni both walked before Riggs and Emmalynn Higdon followed with singles. Estes got another hit when the girls batted around the line up. Ansley House came on to pitch the fifth and she did fine. After walking the first batter Hancock County got a double-play. House struck out the next batter. Ella House ended the game with a walk-off, RBI single in the bottom of the fifth. Lily got the win while allowing no runs on one hit, with eight Ks and no walks over four innings. Ansley had one K and one walk in one inning of relief. Emmalynn Higdon was 2 for 3 with two RBI. Ella, Baylee and Ava were all 2 for 3 at the plate with one RBI each. Westerfield was 2 for 4. Waltrip had two RBI and Lily and Layni had one RBI each. Estes had three stolen bases and Ella House stole two. McLean County game 2 Madison Higdon hit a home run and Emmalynn Higdon stroked two doubles as the Lady Hornets plated 19 runs in four innings during game 2. Hancock beat McLean 19-4. The Lady Hornets scored two runs in the first inning, eight in the second, seven in the third and two in the fourth. Waltrip got the win on the mound. She allowed four runs on three hits, with four Ks and two walks over 3.1 frames. Ansley got the final two outs. She walked one. Emmalynn was 3 for 4 with three RBI. Estes was 2 for 3 with three RBI. Waltrip was 2 for 4 with a double and one RBI. Jones was 2 for 2 with one RBI. Riggs was 1 for 1 with one RBI. Madison Higdon was 1 for 4 with three RBI. Mosby and Ansley House had one RBI each. Audrey Carnes scored two runs. By Steve Wimmer

title: Dennis Johnson, Jr.
description: Dennis Johnson, Jr., 83, of Reynolds Station, KY, went to his Heavenly Home on Friday, March 8, 2024, with his wife and children by his side.
content: Dennis Johnson, Jr., 83, of Reynolds Station, KY, went to his Heavenly Home on Friday, March 8, 2024, with his wife and children by his side.
