title: Willow & Pine Market shares important lessons for at-home chefs
description: 'One of the most important lessons a cook learns is 'everything in its place' – to streamline organization and enable efficiency, says Anne Higgins, owner of Willow and Pine Market.' 'Seamless…
content: 'One of the most important lessons a cook learns is 'everything in its place' – to streamline organization and enable efficiency, says Anne Higgins, owner of Willow and Pine Market.' 'Seamless integration of carefully selected everyday essentials will ensure an at-home chef is set up for success in the kitchen' Kitchen organization Anne says just the thought of spring gets her excited to organize spaces and get creative…especially in the kitchen! 'As a military family, we've moved a lot and I've had to organize a variety of kitchen spaces…small, large, and everything in between,' Anne said. 'I tend to be a bit of a maximalist. I love kitchen gadgets, tools, and utensils! Let me share with you some of my spring cleaning tricks to help keep my kitchen tidy and functional. I begin by sorting through every single drawer and cabinet…throwing away broken and damaged items…eliminating unnecessary duplicates…and paring down to only those items that I really use.' Durable utensils 'A good way to reduce clutter in your pantry and kitchen is to buy utensils and appliances that serve dual functions. Another best practice is to buy quality products that won't have to be replaced quickly. Dreamfarm is one of my favorite brands. Their utensils are durable and can be used for multiple tasks.' Kitchen towels 'Don't hang on to faded, old towels when there are so many pretty options available! Quality towels make all the difference when cooking, baking, and cleaning up. They can also add a touch of color and personality to your kitchen. Our Geometry towels are made from recycled materials, are super absorbent and are fast drying! I absolutely love these, they are my 'go-to'. Crown Linen Designs hand towels are beautifully embroidered and made from high quality linen.' Showcase your special things 'Once you have cleaned out and organized the kitchen, move everything off the countertops, give them a good cleaning, and then begin to add your seasonal touches. Before purchasing anything, try decorating with your favorite serving pieces instead. Prop up your favorite platter in the corner…fill a mixing bowl with fruit…display candles and other small items on a special cake stand. I have so many wooden utensils (because I'm a maximalist!) that I store them next to my cooktop in a larger planter! Be creative and showcase your special things'! Workshop Classes Willow & Pine also offers special workshop classes to help you with entertaining family and friends! vimeo.com/812876867 For everyday kitchen essentials, visit Willow & Pine Market in downtown Owensboro, located at 126 West 2nd Street.

title: HC School District traveled to Spring Job Fair for WKU Students
description: Pictured h
content: Pictured here, attending the Spring Job Fair at WKU are (l to r): SHES Principal Jennifer Howe, HC Schools Assistant Superintendent of Instruction & Assessments Robin Poynter and Director of District Programs Joey Minton. Superintendent Robby Asberry, Assistant Superintendent Robin Poynter, South Hancock Elementary School Principal Jennifer Howe and Director of District Programs Joey Minton attended a Spring Job Recruitment Fair for Western KY University students at WKU, hosted by Green River Regional Education Cooperative (GRREC) on Friday, March 15th. The Job Fair is held twice a year during fall and spring semesters at WKU in an effort to help their school partners with the growing shortage of teachers. The Student Teaching Recruitment Fair offers a platform for school districts to promote their districts to WKU students. A recruitment video was played for potential teacher candidates at the Job Fair, and had very positive testimonials from current teachers at NHES and SHES, saying that they love teaching in Hancock County and that it's not just a school district, it's a 'family'. Some teaching positions may open soon at the elementary schools in Hancock County, and the recruitment video was first played at the HC Board of Education Meeting on Thursday, March 14th for the Board and all in attendance before the aforementioned group of individuals left for the Job Fair the next day. 'We have put a lot of time and effort into this,' Superintendent Asberry said. The video also had positive testimonials from literacy coaches who've traveled all across the state of Kentucky, saying that HC Schools are doing a 'fabulous' job, and thanking the district and teachers for all of the time and effort they've put forth in training and implementing IMSE (Institute for Multi-Sensory Education) Science of Reading instruction in the classrooms 'seamlessly'. IMSE Co-Founder Visits NHES & SHES On Thursday, March 21st, IMSE Co-Founder Jeanne Jeup is flying in to observe at NHES and SHES and meet the teaching staff. 'One hundred percent of our teachers and most of our teaching assistants have been trained through IMSE the Science of Reading approach to teaching our students to read,' Asst. Superintendent Poynter said. 'It has been a 2 year process that will make a huge impact on our students learning to read for many years to come! We will start the day at South Elementary School at 9 a.m. for classroom walkthroughs, then lunch at The Patio to discuss future steps for teacher support, and then on to North Elementary School at 12:30 for more classroom walkthroughs. At 3 p.m., we will have a reception for North, then a reception for South at 4 p.m. for teachers to meet Jeanne Jeup personally, and Jeanne will provide feedback to the teachers.' By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Husband and wife team start new flooring company in Owensboro
description: Matt and Amanda Wilson Matthew (Matt) Wilson's been in the flooring business for 22 years. He and his wife, Amanda, purchased Wilson's Custom Flooring almost 3 ye
content: Matt and Amanda Wilson Matthew (Matt) Wilson's been in the flooring business for 22 years. He and his wife, Amanda, purchased Wilson's Custom Flooring almost 3 years ago, and work together as a stellar team providing the very best custom flooring, marble, granite and quartz countertops, ceramic tile showers and more. 'I worked on my own with a guy, and that's where I learned,' Matt said. 'Then I went out on my own and worked for another store for about 10 years and did mostly new construction. I did my own thing once I got real busy. After I did that for about 5 years, the previous owner stopped at a job site and wanted to know if I'd be interested in buying him out. I went home and talked to my wife, Amanda. She was co-owner of a salon. She decided she was ready for a change so we went in together and bought the store. She helps everybody design when they come and pick stuff out, and I'm out in the field with the guys making sure everything stays up to par – like everybody expects us to do. We do all types of floor covering – ceramic tile or porcelain tile, natural stone, and we also do hardwood (unfinished or prefinished). We don't do as much hardwood as we used to because luxury vinyl has kind of taken over the world of wood- look floors. We do a lot of unfinished hardwood because we also have a sand and finish crew and so we're able to extend existing floors out into the rest of your house, sand the whole thing and we can make it a perfect match so that it looks like it has always been there.' Hardwood Flooring If a customer has hardwood flooring that is aging, he said he and his crew can make it look like new again. 'If the finish is coming off or it's had water damage, or if the customer just wants it in more rooms, we can weave it into the existing floor like it was all laid at once, and then sand the whole floor. We then put 3 coats of finish on. We can stain it if they want us to before we do the finish. A lot of people, these days, use the natural finish. We'll do water base or oil base depending on the type of species it is, or the personal preference of the homeowner.' We also sale and install prefinished Harwood. And have a huge selection to choose from in our showroom. Luxury Vinyl We have a huge selection of luxury vinyl flooring in all colors. It has become a very popular option for previous hardwood customers. With a real wood look and feel people like the fact that this product is waterproof. So they can break out the steam mop or spin mop. Not having to worry if kids or pets are messing up the flooring with wet paws or feet. Everything we carry is a 20 mil wear layer and 5mm thick. Embossed and registered so what you see if what you feel. So if there is a knot whole or chatter marks you don't just see it you can feel it. Porcelain tile We made our name on installing custom showers and bathrooms. From a 12×24 Porcelain tile with any pattern, to a 24×48 and bigger. We are also certified to install large gauge Porcelain panels 120×60 and they are becoming quite popular with minimal grout lines. We also do a lot of Kitchens, backsplashes, and fireplaces, really a one-stop shop. If you can dream it, we can help you design it and make it a reality. Carpet 'Carpet isn't as popular as it once was,' said Matt. But people still want it in bedrooms, living rooms, and some outdoor areas. With our Shaw pet perfect, you get a 20-year warranty against stains, pet or people related, no bleach warranty and wearing or high traffic spots. Really they have you covered! If your one of the people who likes to step out of bed onto Carpet you can do that and still have an amazing warranty. They also have some amazing patterns to make that floor a statement piece in your home.' Husband & Wife Team with Large Crew 'Amanda works in the store and helps design,' Matt said. 'Customers come in and pick a wood or vinyl for most of the house, and then a carpet, a tile for the bathrooms and the kitchen, and Amanda does the styling – she styles it and we'll tile it. That works out really well. It's been great. She loves doing it. We have 9 crews that install everything from tile, hardwood, and LVT and carpet.' Amanda (41) and Matt (47) are blessed with 2 children. They've been married 17 years. Their youngest daughter attends Owensboro Innovation Academy, and their son is attending college in Nashville, TN. Wilson's Custom Flooring is located at 1811 West Ninth Street in Owensboro. The phone number is (270) 683-0029. To reach them by email: wilsonscustomflooring1811@gmail.com . Check out their website at: www.wilsonscustom.com .

title: United Way Diamond Celebration – Artist Call Deadline is April 30th
description: United Way of the Ohio Valley (UWOV) is hosting The Diamond Celebration to celebrate 75 years of Caring. The event will be held at the River Park Center in Owensboro on Friday, August 23rd and will…
content:
United Way of the Ohio Valley (UWOV) is hosting The Diamond Celebration to celebrate 75 years of Caring. The event will be held at the River Park Center in Owensboro on Friday, August 23rd and will begin at 6 p.m.
Barrels of HeART – Artist Call Barrels of HeART will return for this event, and was adopted last year from Louisville-based, non-profit Bourbon With HeART. UWOV will have 14 bourbon barrels to be painted and sponsored. They are actively looking for artists who are interested in painting one of the unique bourbon barrels for this event. Artists can apply by April 30th , at: uwov.org/barrels-of-heart/.
Artists can apply by April 30th, at: uwov.org/barrels-of-heart/. There will be a special-invite VIP Happy Hour starting at 5 p.m. The Diamond Celebration will be a night of celebration, appreciation, achievement awards and recognition of everyone and everything that has made UWOV continue to be a pillar of the community for many years. There will also be live music, a cash bar and the unveiling of the locally painted bourbon barrels.
Speaker Bracken Darrell The event will feature keynote speaker Bracken Darrell, Owensboro native and President & CEO of VF Company, which produces popular brands like Vans, North Face and Timberland. Darrell has more than 30 years of experience in business leadership and brand management with global consumer companies.
UWOV Director of Resource Development & Marketing Savannah Daniels said, 'We want everyone who has been involved with United Way in any fashion – donors, CEOs, volunteers and non-profit employees to attend the Diamond Celebration, and anyone who wants to learn or connect more with United Way to come and see what we're all about! This is to honor all people who helped United Way make a difference and grow in our old and new relationships.'
Tickets On Sale May 31st through UWOV
Tickets are $75 in honor of the 75th anniversary and will go on sale May 31st. You can purchase your tickets at UWOV.org or at the UWOV Office located at 403 Park Plaza Dr. in Owensboro. Sponsorships are still available, reach out to sgatton@uwov.org for information. See UWOV FB Page, as well as their Instagram Page @unitedwayohiovalley for more details.

title: Elderly woman Saved from apartment Fire in Lewisport
description: Seen here are Local Heroes (l to r): Angela Bottoms, Jerrad Morris and Leslie Tindle. These resi
content:
Seen here are Local Heroes (l to r): Angela Bottoms, Jerrad Morris and Leslie Tindle. These residents of Poplar Grove Apartments, as well as Angela's husband, Richard, all worked quickly to make sure that their elderly neighbors were gotten safely out of their burning apartment. Jerrad & Leslie carried the elderly woman out of the apartment successfully just before the oxygen tanks inside exploded!
An apartment fire happened in the early morning hours of Monday, April 1st at Poplar Grove Apartments in Lewisport. Pam & Ron McEntire, elderly residents, barely escaped. Thankfully, their neighbors heard their calls for help and were able to lift Mrs. McEntire from her hospital bed and out of the apartment just before the oxygen tanks inside exploded!
Jerrad Morris and his girlfriend, Leslie Tindle, live upstairs on the right hand side, and Mr. & Mrs. McEntire's apartment is downstairs on the left hand side. Jerrad said he woke up at 6:40 a.m. with stomach cramps that morning. 'I heard, ‘Help! Help!' I wasn't sure what I had heard so I paused for a second and then heard it again,' he said. 'I looked at Leslie and she went to the door to listen. We heard it again and she went out the door to see what it was.
I stepped out and saw my neighbor outside and I smelled smoke so I got the fire extinguisher. My neighbor saw me with the extinguisher and stopped me and said, ‘That's not going to do it' (the fire was too big at that point).
I put the extinguisher away and ran back down to the apartment and tried going in two times. I made it into the living room. I had to go back out because I was choking (from the smoke). I couldn't see and went upstairs to grab my phone for a flashlight. It didn't do any good; I couldn't see. I went back out, choking from the smoke again. On my third attempt, I heard Leslie scream, ‘She's in here! Come get her!'
When I got her out, she just looked at me and was in shock and disbelief. Leslie said if I hadn't gotten there the lady would have died. She had already tried to get her out of the apartment 3 times. That was her last breath and she had given up trying to do it herself. It was a scary situation.
Our neighbor across from us (Richard Bottoms) went in 5 times and his wife (Angela Bottoms) went in twice to try and get Mrs. McEntire out of the burning apartment. They didn't see her or know where she was at.
Leslie told me that when she had went into the apartment, she saw Mr. McEntire grab a walker and push it out of the way. She asked him where his wife was and he told her. She went in there with the lady and he exited the building (to get to safety).
There was even a teenager over there and he couldn't get her out. I was the only one who could get her out. As soon as I pulled her out of the apartment, the oxygen tanks they had in there exploded.'
Leslie was remembering all that had transpired saying, 'I heard her holler and when I opened the door I smelled the smoke. I ran down the stairs and ran into their apartment. The door was open. A neighbor (Angela Bottoms) went in first.'
Angela said, 'I tried to get the lady out, but I could not lift her. There was fire everywhere. The smoke was thick. My husband, Richard, went in about 5 times and couldn't find her. He couldn't handle the smoke. Then, Leslie came and she went in after her and I believe she got trapped.'
Leslie said the smoke was really thick and that Mrs. McEntire was falling off of her hospital bed. 'I just kind of cradled her fall and then was helping her take breaths through a shirt,' she said. 'I hollered out because I felt like I was getting ready to pass out and that's when Jerrad heard me. He was able to find me and he picked her up and carried her out.'
Leslie still managed to carry Mrs. McEntire's feet while Jerrad carried her by the waist and the two got her out just in time before the oxygen tanks exploded. 'Leslie sat with her in the grass until the firefighters got here,' Jerrad added.
The elderly couples' apartment is boarded up and currently being renovated after the fire. They have been temporarily moved into another apartment until theirs can be repaired. They may be displaced at the moment, but they are alive thanks to their brave and caring neighbor heroes!
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Fiscal Court Provides Update on Splash Pad; All HC Fire Departments will require new air packs by December
description: The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday evening, April 22nd, and approved the comprehensive list of surplus property for the Hancock Coun
content:
The Hancock County Fiscal Court met on Monday evening, April 22nd, and approved the comprehensive list of surplus property for the Hancock County Surplus Auction on Saturday, April 27th at 10 a.m.
The City of Lewisport, City of Hawesville, HC Public Libraries and the HC School Board will all have surplus items at this sale as well as the HC Fiscal Court. Hancock Real Estate & Auction, Inc. along with Dixon & Dixon Auction Services will be holding this very large auction at the HC Fairgrounds, located at 1430 State Route 1389 in Hawesville.
Splash Pad Construction Begins Soon As reported in the Clarion, $200K was secured in 2022 from the Land & Water Conservation Fund grant for the construction of a Splash Pad (Spray Park) at Vastwood, through the partnership with Hancock County and GRADD. Domtar has generously donated $25K toward the project, and Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts said Commonwealth and Southwire have agreed to donate to the project as well.
The Splash Pad design is mostly completed, and construction could begin as soon as late spring or early summer. It will be located between the parking lot in front of the beach house and tennis courts, just south of the lake. The small building with equipment room and new bathroom facilities will be located right next to the Splash Pad, and a little closer to the tennis courts.
The Court had talked with the architect of the Splash Pad and GRADD, and it was recommended that they rebid for the general contractor with itemization to see what each contract costs, one for the Splash Pad and one for the building, which required the new bid to be out for 7-21 days again.
The general contractors all had the Splash Pad itself subbed-out to a company in Cincinnati. The bids submitted were: Lanham Brothers-$1,382,394, Danco -$1,387,000, and GN Excavating -$1,209,684.24. The Court approved the lowest bid from local Gary Nugent of GN Excavating as the general contractor.
Roberts said, 'This will be done with a combination of County funds, grant funds and private donations from some of our largest companies. The maximum the Splash Pad holds is about 2,700 gallons but it recirculates from a holding tank.
We're using city water but we're recirculating that. We're not just using runoff water, which would be an astronomical cost. We don't want any un-needed waste regarding the water. It isn't a flow-through system, the water will be retreated and used again. It costs a little bit more up front for a recirculation system, but we'll recoup some of those costs on the back end of that.
We will have a pre-construction meeting and get some things in order. After that, we'll be ready to start. Hancock County doesn't have a Splash Pad or public pool. We are the only county GRADD serves that doesn't have a Splash Pad. I think our youth will be excited for that. We're looking forward to being able to start the project and finish it.'
Fire Dept. Report Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards reported, 'We were informed by High Tech Rescue (Drager) on March 22nd, the vendor we use to service all of our SCBAs (Self Contained Breathing Apparatus) at the station, and they advised of the first notice from Honeywell, the parent company of Survivair Honeywell Air Packs, that they are discontinuing production and certification. They will no longer support the service of our air packs.
The notice is effective as of December 16th of this year, and they cannot support the service of any SCBAs – those that are used by all 4 departments in the county. We all 4 have the same manufacturer of our SCBAs.'
All 4 Hancock County Fire Dept. Chiefs or representatives met last week and discussed this potential replacement of SCBAs. Currently, there are 48 in service with the county fire departments that will need to be replaced before the deadline in December – HVFD has 15, LVFD has 15, Dukes Fire Dept. has 8 and South Hancock Fire Dept. has 10.
'Our packs we have in-house were purchased 17 years ago,' Richards continued. 'The cylinders all have a 15-year service life. We replaced all of our cylinders in 2021. We believe Lewisport replaced all of theirs in 2020; they were a little older than ours. Dukes and South Hancock have not reached their life expectancy on their bottles yet. Every 5 years they're tested, but in 15 years they're done.
The need in the County is approximately 48 air packs to cover everything we have with the standards with ISO, etc. It essentially is 4 air packs per engine, or 1 per seat. Ideally, in Hawesville our two county trucks are 5-seat cabs so we'll need 5 for each one. Our city truck is a 2-seat cab, but it will require 4 air packs, to meet ISO ratings. ISO ratings are what sets our insurance standards for homeowners in our jurisdiction. That will be countywide.'
The quotes from companies that Richards submitted to the Court for the 48 basic replacement units were: $332,276.16 at $6,897.37 per unit from High Tech Rescue (Drager), and $367,200.00 ($7,650 per unit) from FDSAS (MSA). The MSA quote is only good through May 30th, 2024.
'These are the basic air packages,' he said. 'We have until December to figure out how to replace all of them in the county. We've looked at grants. We do every year. The AFG (Assistance to Firefighters Grants) grant is open right now. Dukes has an application in right now and they are waiting to hear back. If awarded, it will be sometime in late 2025. Dukes applied last year for 10. We've applied for different things at our station every year. We've gotten one AFG Grant in 20 years. We'll continue to apply for them.
All of the manufacturers now are starting to cut deals. MSA, at the International Conference in Indianapolis this past weekend, they were cutting trade-in deals on their packs. The numbers we've gotten from those are only good until the end of May, and then that price goes up. Once word starts getting out and it gets rolling, supply and demand will take over.
Owensboro Fire Dept. and a lot of Daviess County's departments use MSA already. State Fire Training uses MSA, and Aleris and Commonwealth's fire brigades use MSA. Everything in our county has been Honeywell as long as I've been a part of it, and that's been 31 years. We've upgraded a couple of times in that 31 year time. There was no precursor to this. We got notice just this month.
We haven't heard anything so far from the Fire Commission as far as any kind of assistance that's out there. One of the things we've looked at is the Fire Commission's loan programs. The problem with ours in Hawesville, is it's tied up for 3 more years with our engine. That was our low interest loan and we can't get another one until that's paid off. Dukes has a loan out right now as well on their station and won't be able to get one either. We'll have to come up with something.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Darrell Wall Sworn-In as Lewisport Magistrate
description: Darrell Wall is being sworn in by Judge Daniel Boling at the Hancock County Judicial Center Friday. Wall is the new magistrate
content:
Darrell Wall is being sworn in by Judge Daniel Boling at the Hancock County Judicial Center Friday. Wall is the new magistrate for Lewisport District 1. Wall was appointed by Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear following the resignation of former magistrate John Garner. Joining Wall is his daughter Rebecca Boling, holding grandson Leyton, and daughter Anna Wall.
Darrell Wall was sworn-in Friday as the new Lewisport (District 1) Magistrate. Judge Daniel Boling gave the oath and Wall will serve until the election on November 5th.
Former District 1 Magistrate John Garner resigned to serve as School Resource Officer at North Hancock Elementary. The Hancock County Democrat Party selected Darrell Wall as their candidate at their executive meeting.
Wall will hold office, as the Governor appointed candidate, until a candidate is elected at the General Election on November 5th, 2024. The newly elected individual in November will take office immediately and fill the unexpired term.
HC Republican Party The Hancock County Republican Party has not yet selected their candidate to run against the Democrat candidate in November. They will meet again on Tuesday, April 23rd, as the executive committee needs more time to interview the candidates and they will also be electing new officers. content:

Service (cooperation, helpfulness, responsibility, etc.),

title: Free breakfast & lunch approved for ‘24/'25 school year by Board of Education
description: At the Hancock County Board of Education Meeting on Thursday, April 25th, the HCHS Future Business Leaders of America Students were recognized for their exceptional Regional and State Competition…
content:
At the Hancock County Board of Education Meeting on Thursday, April 25th, the HCHS Future Business Leaders of America Students were recognized for their exceptional Regional and State Competition winnings, which were featured in the 4-18-2024 edition of The Hancock Clarion. Congratulations HCHS FBLA Students!
2 New SROs Recognized at Meeting
The 2 new HC Schools School Resource Officers (SROs) were also recognized at the meeting: Cody Axton and Mitch Brown. As reported in The Clarion, Cody Axton will serve as the SRO at South Hancock Elementary, and Mitch Brown will serve as SRO at Hancock County Middle School. John Garner will serve as SRO at North Hancock Elementary, and Mark Powers will serve as SRO at Hancock County High School.
2024/2025 NHES Principal It was announced that Dr. Jacob Bryant was hired as the new North Hancock Elementary School Principal for the new school year (2024/2025), beginning in the fall. Current NHES Principal Kelly Moore is retiring after this school year. She announced her retirement this year, after over 30 years in education.
Dr. Bryant currently serves as Assistant Principal at HCMS, and PhD Candidate Assessment Director for University of the Cumberlands. He has served as Assistant Principal, Gap Coordinator, RTI/MTSS Chair, Athletic Director and Middle Grades Teacher at College View Middle School in Daviess County.
He and his wife, Laura, and their 2-year-old son live in Owensboro. He said he is looking forward to working with the dedicated staff, engaged parents and supportive community in helping all students reach their limitless potential.
CEP Pilot Approved at Meeting
A district-wide Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) Pilot was approved by the Board at the meeting. CEP is a non-pricing meal service option for schools in low-income areas. 'That is going to be free breakfast and lunch for all students in Hancock County next year,' Superintendent Robbie Asberry explained. 'All students K-12 will have free breakfast and lunch next year. This is a full year's commitment. We will look at it again at this time next year for the ‘25/'26 school year.'
Regardless of income or status, every student in a participating school gets this free meal service through the program. The success is determined by participation, i.e., students eating breakfast and lunch at school.
Scherrer explained, 'This will be at no cost to the district because it's based on reimbursement from the federal rate. If for some reason our revenue did decrease a little and we did have a negative impact, we have a contingency balance in our food service account. That is a credit to Mr. Boling and all of the work he's done for the past several years, along with Pam Ramsey, who retired. They built up that account to the point where we can take a little bit of a hit during the CEP Pilot, if it comes to that.
I'm pretty confident that once we explain to parents that their students get free breakfast and lunch every single day and they don't have to worry about any money, it could be a couple thousand dollars in savings for families that have multiple children in the district, that we'll see our participation numbers increase dramatically.'
Hornet Mascot for All HC Schools The Board approved Hornets as the 2 elementary schools' mascot for the new school year in the fall and going forward at the meeting, which will make the Hornet the mascot of all of HC Schools.
'We're going to be changing, and all of our schools in the district will be Hornets,' Asberry said. 'We surveyed the staff of NHES and SHES and two thirds of the teachers were in favor of the change to Hornets.'
Early Kindergarten Entrance Policy 'This is just an update of, if someone is wanting to go to kindergarten and they're not quite of age yet,' Asberry said, 'there is some testing (to determine if they can attend early).' The policy outlines how that will be specifically handled in those situations and was approved by the Board.
Financial ' Trey Anderson, our new CFO, is cleaning up a lot of old projects,' Asberry said, 'to where we have some money that we can now use for construction. It's not something we'll be using right now but it will be there for us to use, and if we didn't go through that process then we couldn't use it. It is from old construction, going all the way back to NHES. There was some money left over in that construction and it was just sitting there because you have to finalize it to be able to then use it later. Some of it has gone back a long time.'

Anderson read aloud the financial report for the Board to approve, which was: Total Receipts for the month -$763,128.53, Total Expenditures -$1,518,863.72, and Balance at the close of the month -$5,304,883.84.

title: 20 Cherry Trees planted during Hawesville Clean-Up Day
description: The City of Hawesville held the 2nd Annual Clean-Up Day on Saturday, May 4th. Volunteers met at Hawesville City Hall and brought landscaping tools from home to work together in cleaning up Main…
content:
The City of Hawesville held the 2nd Annual Clean-Up Day on Saturday, May 4th. Volunteers met at Hawesville City Hall and brought landscaping tools from home to work together in cleaning up Main Street, as well as planting 20 ornamental trees between the road and sidewalks on each side.
'We had 20 trees put in,' Hawesville Mayor Robbie McCormick said. 'We had about a couple of dozen great volunteers that care about Hawesville, and we've had several great compliments on them already.'
The cherry trees that were planted are configured in a red and white pattern, and going up and down Main Street to give the City some beautiful color, he said.
'City Manager Jake Powers headed all of this up,' McCormick added, 'and he did a wonderful job in putting it together, with our new Clerk, Amy Roberts. Our goal is to keep Hawesville moving forward. Sometimes it may be little things, like these trees that add beauty to our town.
Bright Star Nursery provided the trees at a VERY special price. These trees are normally anywhere between $175-$200 a piece, and we got them for $50 a piece. They'll get about 8-10 feet tall.'
Thank You! The City of Hawesville expresses gratitude to all of the volunteers who participated in the improvement of Main Street in Hawesville, with sidewalk cleanup and planting of trees. A big THANK YOU to: Paula & Fred Gray, Karen & Steve Robertson, Jacob Cantlin, Nathan Powers, Josh Roberts, Ashtyn Gray, Jake Powers, and especially Eli McCormick, for their hard work. Also, a special thanks to Bright Star Nursery for their exceptional assistance in selecting the trees!

title: Nancy's Notes: The Old Victrola
description: When Grandma passed, Granddaddy moved in with us. He had his own room across the hall from the rest of the family. In the far corner of the room stood an old Victrola. It was made of heavy stripped…
content:
When Grandma passed, Granddaddy moved in with us. He had his own room across the hall from the rest of the family. In the far corner of the room stood an old Victrola. It was made of heavy stripped oak and stood taller than me. It had a large speaker in front and a crank handle on the right side we had to turn the turntable on top. I had to pull up a chair to stand on it to open the lid to play our records. They were thick and about 12 inches round -78s.
We only had a few records but we played them on that old Victrola often. It kept my sister and me occupied for hours while Granddaddy was away. I was about 7 and my sister 4.
Some records were orchestras. I remember the Blue Danube Waltz. Mama would come to the room and dance like an angel floating across the floor with her bare little feet.
We played Al Jolson. Mama had seen him on the theater screen when she lived near Chicago before she met Daddy. 'Mammy, how I love you. How I love you my dear old Mammy,' he'd sing in the most beautiful voice. Granddaddy would cry when he heard it. That is what his and Grandma's kids called them when they were young – 'Mammy' and 'Pappy'.
Eddy Arnold sang 'Won't you ride in my little red wagon'. That made me want one so Santa brought me one for Christmas. In the summer, I delivered watermelons and cantaloupe in town and made a little spending money.
Dina Shore sang about 'Buttons and Bows'. I liked it because it sounded like horses trotting to the music. I always thought of my clothes. Mama made almost all my clothes and they always had a lot of buttons and bows, especially the big bow made by a long wraparound sash.
On the flip side of the record was Dina singing 'The Surrey with the Fringe on Top'. Before Grandma passed, Old Doc came to our house to treat her in a fringed surrey pulled by a pretty bay horse.
Roy Acuff sang on a record that made me and my sister act like we were flying through the sky in the room. It was 'The Great Speckled Bird'. It was not until many years later I learned the song was not about a bird. The Great Speckled Bird is actually the Bible and mentioned in the Bible itself.
Hank Williams sang 'I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry'. I really didn't like that one. It reminded me of laying in the bed at night and listening to the old train make its way through the valley where we lived.
I would crank up that old Victrola as much as I could, jump in my chair and put the record on. It would play the voices normally for a few minutes, the record would get slower, the voices get lower, and I'd have to jump off the chair, wind the crank up and climb back up to hear the rest of the record.
I can still hear the music, but I can't hear the voices.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Leona Whitworth
description: Leona May Whitworth, age 92 of Hardinsburg, KY passed away May 19, 2024 at her residence. She was born in Hardinsburg on August 1, 1931, daughter of the late Jesse and Minnie Wheatley Clark. She was a…
content:
Leona May Whitworth, age 92 of Hardinsburg, KY passed away May 19, 2024 at her residence. She was born in Hardinsburg on August 1, 1931, daughter of the late Jesse and Minnie Wheatley Clark. She was a member of Goshen Baptist Church. Leona worked at IMS Sewing Factory for many years. Her passion was being a mother, grandmother and homemaker. She enjoyed being outdoors, mowing her yard, raising a garden, canning and cooking for her family. She was a wonderful seamstress who made beautiful clothes, quilts and embroidered items. Her family was made of five generations of love and they were very important to her.
In addition to her parents, she was preceded in death by her husband Loyd Whitworth, son Darrell Whitworth, daughter Anna Lee Whitworth, grandson Brian Whitworth, granddaughter Kalyn Whitworth, brother James Earl Clark and sister Anna Belle Butler.
Leona is survived by 7 children: Eugene (Cindy) Whitworth, Jimmie (Lou Ann) Whitworth and Donnie (Paula) Whitworth of Hardinsburg, KY; Doris (Dwight) Raymer and Byron (Connie) Whitworth of Leitchfield, KY; Carolyn (Rusty) McGee of Falls of Rough, KY; Michael (Michelle) Whitworth of Balltown, KY

title: Healthy Habits: Natural Tick Repellent
description: There are many essential oils that are very effective in deterring ticks. Choosing pure, organic, therapeuti
content:
There are many essential oils that are very effective in deterring ticks. Choosing pure, organic, therapeutic-grade essential oils as an alternative to chemical bug sprays is a wise decision.
If you don't believe essential oils can get the job done, then consider this: geranium oil has been shown in studies to be as effective as DEET! Chemical bug sprays are toxic and those toxins are absorbed into your bloodstream when applied to the skin. Think about choosing a pre-made natural bug spray, such as Herbal Armor Brand, or creating your own.
Here is a list of some of the best essential oils for keeping the ticks off this year:
oregano,
cedarwood,
clove bud,
citronella,
red thyme,
lavender,
lemongrass,
geranium,
eucalyptus,
lemon and neem seed oil. Oregano and cedarwood essential oils both have a component called cedrol, which has been proven in a study to kill 100 percent of the unfortunate pestering ticks that come into contact with you!
Oregano oil must be diluted with a carrier oil, such as organic extra virgin olive oil, jojoba oil, or unrefined, fair trade coconut oil and shea butter. Only 5 to 6 drops of undiluted, pure organic, therapeutic grade oregano essential oil are needed per one ounce of carrier oil to make a great natural tick repellent. (*See my column on oregano oil that details more of its health benefits in the 11-12-2020 edition of The Clarion.)
Carvacrol is another component in oregano oil, as well as in red thyme oil, and is highly effective in killing the bacteria that causes Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi). This makes oregano oil a 'double threat' because it not only kills the ticks it comes in contact with, it also kills the bacteria they carry that causes this terrible disease.
Dilute pure essential oils with a carrier oil and do a patch test on your skin first to make sure that they don't cause any irritation. If you have sensitive skin, you may want to dilute more than what is recommended. A general recommended dilution ratio is: 3 to 12 drops of therapeutic grade essential oil per one ounce of carrier oil.
Essential oils such as oregano, citronella, clove, lemon and lemongrass can be very intense and may need to be diluted more than others to prevent skin irritation. Others like lavender essential oil (Lavandula angustifolia), you may find that they don't require quite as much dilution with a carrier oil.
Essential oils can be placed directly onto the outside of clothing, shoes, hats, etc., without diluting them first. Choose clothing items that you don't mind getting stained a little with these oils. They can also just be treated for stains in those areas before you wash them.
There are hundreds of varieties of ticks out there. Those of us who have hiked and hunted in Kentucky know all about 'seed ticks' or 'turkey mites' and how they are almost impossible to avoid in the deep woods. They are ticks in larvae form, are less than a millimeter in size and have 6 legs instead of eight. Female ticks hatch them onto a host and then they fall off once they've grown.
In these deep woodsy areas, I recommend that you cover yourself from head to toe in your choice of one or more of the aforementioned essential oils diluted. Also, wear long sleeves and pants that are covered with the undiluted essential oils. And, make sure to wear a hat! They can drop from trees onto your head as well.
Check yourself immediately when you come in from the woods. Have someone check your back as well. If you've been in deep woodsy areas, you may want to also get out a magnifying glass and check to make sure that no seed ticks have latched onto you. Carefully remove the entire tick with tweezers and treat the infected area with antiseptic, such as organic tea tree oil.
Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennfier Wimmer

title: Planning & Zoning in Hancock County; What it Could Mean to You
description: The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission met on Monday evening, June 3rd, to review and approve the new budget for the next fiscal year. At the last meeting, commission members voted to replace…
content:
The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission met on Monday evening, June 3rd, to review and approve the new budget for the next fiscal year.
At the last meeting, commission members voted to replace the unexpired term of Thomas Hunt as Commission Vice Chairman, and Adam Hunt was voted in to fill that term. Some members also discussed the need to expand zoning in the county last month due to increased growth, and Julie Vogt, of Lewisport, was voted in as a new board member.
Overview of Commission
Overview of Commission HC Urban Planning Commission Administrator Jeff Dame explained, 'The HC Urban Planning Commission is responsible to oversee rezoning and development plans. That's basically it. The zoning ordinance covers several things, including building permits.
We really don't have much on the agenda usually, unless somebody wants to rezone a property, or if we have a new cell tower come in, etc. We have to meet at least every other month, six times a year.
The Planning Commission is a regulatory agency. We don't enact things. The government bodies – the fiscal court and the 2 cities are the ones that enact it. They enact the zoning ordinance and we enforce it.'
Expansion of Zoning
Expansion of Zoning Dame continued, 'About a third of the County is zoned now. When you're talking about expanding the zoning beyond what we have, it would be up to the Hancock County Fiscal Court to do that. The Planning Commission cannot do that.
Some of the members have talked about approaching the fiscal court and expressing their concerns about wanting that to happen. The Planning Commission has no power to do that.
I think there may be a misconception that the Planning Commission enacts laws or expands zoning, and we don't have that power. The only power that we have is to change the zone if it meets conditions, or when somebody wants to change it.
Some people think we can change it, and we can't. The property owner has to initiate that process. We are a regularity commission. Each member is appointed by one of the government bodies.
As far as expanding the zoning, the cities would not be involved in any zoning expansion because they're already located in a zone. It would be totally up to the Fiscal Court on whether or not they wanted to do that. And, they would have to initiate it.
If some of the Planning Commission members went to the Court and expressed their concerns, they would be treated as a group, as the Planning Commission, but no different than any other citizen of Hancock County.'
Building Permits
Building Permits Dame also explained that building permits are required outside the cities, and that it depends on what you are building. 'The misconception that I've run into is that building permits are only required within the city limits of Hawesville and Lewisport,' he said. 'That's not really true. They are required in the zoning part, which is about a third of the County. Some people don't realize they need them. Most people call in, but there are some that still don't realize that.'
HC Board of Adjustment
HC Board of Adjustment 'The Hancock County Board of Adjustment is a completely different board, and that meeting is a call meeting,' Dame said. 'We don't have a meeting unless we actually have something come up. The Board of Adjustment is in charge of dimensional variances and conditional use permits.'
Planning Commission Members
Planning Commission Members The HC Urban Planning Commission Chairman is Tim Cecil, new Commission Vice Chairman is Adam Hunt, Commission Administrator is Jeff Dame, Commission Attorney is T. Tommy Littlepage, and Commission Secretary is John Ogle.
Commission Members representing Hancock County are: Tim Cecil and Dan Allard. Commission Members representing Lewisport are: Thomas Turner, Tim Turner, Duane Potts, and newest member Julie Vogt. Commission Members representing Hawesville are: Adam Hunt, John Ogle and Roy Butler, with one seat open to be filled.
Board of Adjustment Members
Board of Adjustment Members Tim Cecil is the temporary Chairman of the Hancock County Board of Adjustment (Thomas Hunt was the previous Chairman). Board Administrator is Jeff Dame, and Board Attorney is T. Tommy Littlepage.
Board of Adjustment Members representing Hancock County are: Tim Cecil and Joe Hagman. Board Members representing Lewisport are: Wesley Pate and Roy White. Board Members representing Hawesville are: Joan King and Josh Powers.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Lady Hornets fall to Daviess in regional final
description: Layni Roberts celebrates after ripping a double during the 3rd Region title game at Ohio County Friday. Daviess County won 5-0 to claim the championship. The Lady Hornets had their season come to an…
content:
Layni Roberts celebrates after ripping a double during the 3rd Region title game at Ohio County Friday. Daviess County won 5-0 to claim the championship.
The Lady Hornets had their season come to an end after a 5-0 loss to Daviess County in the championship game of the 2024 3rd Region Fast Pitch Softball Tournament held at Ohio County Friday. Hancock County finished as region runners-up, Class 'A' state runners-up and 11th District champs. The team's final record was 29-10.
'With (Kamryn) Timmons on the mound I knew runs were going to be a premium to come by and we were going to have to play error free and a good solid game all around. We just didn't do it,' HCHS coach Dwayne Wroe said. 'But I wouldn't trade my girls for anybody. They took us on a great ride this year.'
Both teams had solid pitching and played well defensively through the first two scoreless innings until Daviess County (28-6) plated a run in the top of the third. Out fielders Kylie Westerfield and Baylee Estes both made catches on line drives in the second.
An error allowed Kylie Clark to reach base and she later scored on a single by Annie Newman to give the Lady Panthers a 1-0 lead.
A diving catch by Estes in left field during the fourth inning brought Hancock County fans to their feet. Third baseman Ava Riggs made a nice play for an out, and after a walk and an error by the Lady Hornets, pitcher Lily Roberts got a pop up and Jordyn Waltrip made the catch for the third out.
Sadie Morris bunted for a base hit to begin the fifth inning. She stole second then advanced to third base on a sacrifice. A fly ball hit by Callie Smith allowed Morris to tag up and score.
Trailing 2-0, the Lady Hornets needed some offense and Layni Roberts came through with a shot to the gap in right-center field. A 1-out double by the senior catcher gave life to Hancock County.
DCHS pitcher Kamryn Timmons got a strike out and Emmalynn Higdon later hit a soft liner that was caught by the first baseman to end the threat.
Daviess County began the sixth with a walk and a base hit. A run crossed home plate on a ground out to make the score 3-0.
Roberts got a strike out, but an error by the Lady Hornet defense allowed another run to score. Waltrip led off the bottom of the sixth with a hit, but Timmons got the next three batters out on strikes.
Smith tripled to right field in the seventh and later scored on a wild pitch. Audrey Carnes caught a line drive at first base for the third out.
Hancock County went down 1-2-3 in the last of the seventh and Daviess County celebrated with their fifth consecutive 3rd regional title.
'We played good, but against a quality team like this you really have to bring your 'A+' game. We didn't have it tonight so you take your hat off to Daviess County and coach John Biggs. He's really got it going over there,' Wroe said.
Timmons got the shutout win on the mound. The freshman allowed no runs on two hits, with 12 Ks and no walks over seven innings. Roberts took the loss while allowing five runs (three earned) on five hits, with three Ks and four walks.
Roberts completed her high school career as the school's all-time leader in strike outs. She was 26-7 on the hill with 328 Ks.
Layni Roberts was 1 for 3 at the plate with the double. Waltrip was 1 for 2.
The HCHS program says goodbye to five seniors in Emmalynn Higdon, Ella House, Layni Roberts, Lily Roberts and Kylie Westerfield.
'These seniors have accomplished a lot and what they've meant to the program is unmeasurable. I'm really going to miss them,' coach Wroe said.
'The future is still bright for Hancock County softball, we just gotta get to work.'
Semifinal
Semifinal The Lady Hornets reached the title game of the 3rd Region Fast Pitch Softball Tournament by defeating Ohio County 7-1 in the first semifinal game played last
Thursday at Hartford. Daviess County beat Meade County 1-0 in nine innings during the second semifinal game.
The Lady Hornets came ready to play and jumped all over the home standing Lady Eagles in the top of the first inning.
Baylee Estes led off the game with an infield hit and promptly stole second base. Ella House and Lily Roberts drew walks and the bases were loaded for Layni Roberts. The senior took a 1-0 pitch and drilled it down the first base line for a 3-run triple.
The Lady Hornets were celebrating and Ohio County made a quick pitching change.
Emmalynn Higdon got a ground out RBI and the girls led 4-0.
Lily Roberts was on the mound and she set down Lady Eagle batters in order in the bottom of the frame. Roberts got two strike outs in the second and three in the third as the score remained 4-0 in favor of the Lady Hornets.
Ava Riggs delivered a 2-out double in the fourth and Jordyn Waltrip drew a base on balls before Madyson Higdon came to the plate.
The 8th grader they call 'Boom' was true to her nickname as she sent a 2-1 pitch over the fence in left-center field. A line drive, 3-run home run that made the score 7-0.
Ohio County had no immediate response as Roberts struck out six batters over the next 2.2 innings before Talynn Clark wrecked a no-hit bid with a solo home run in the sixth inning.
Roberts did not appear fazed and she finished the game with a strike out in the seventh. She earned the win while allowing one run on three hits, with 15 Ks and two walks over seven innings. Addyson Graves took the loss for the Lady Eagles. Estes was 2 for 4 at the plate with a run scored and two stolen bases. Layni Roberts was 1 for 3 with the triple and three RBI, and Madyson Higdon was 1 for 3 with the homer and three RBI. Lily Roberts was 1 for 2 with a run, Riggs was 1 for 3 with a run, Audrey Carnes was 1 for 4 with a double, Ella House was 0 for 3 with a run scored, and Emmalynn Higdon was 0 for 3 with one RBI.
Clark was 1 for 3 with the solo home run to lead Ohio County at the plate.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Ultrasonic water meters discussed at Hawesville Council Meeting
description: The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, June 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-Owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided an update on projects. Sales Representatives from Fortiline Meter Company…
content:
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, June 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-Owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided an update on projects. Sales Representatives from Fortiline Meter Company also presented to the Council.
There was lengthy discussion on the possibility of the City purchasing new water meters that are ultrasonic and much more accurate at reading. Mayor Rob McCormick said discussion will continue at the next meeting. All of the City's current meters (drive-by tech meters) are out of warranty.
The new meters would make for huge cost savings on manpower, fuel, and catching water leaks quicker, etc. The manual readings the City's crewmen have to do monthly wouldn't be necessary, as the new system has software that sends out a cellular signal, reads the meter once an hour, stores the data and 3 times a day sends a text message that is logged to a webpage assigned to the City's Admin. It generates the billing data and provides access to the meter readings directly to the water customer; They can log directly into the portal and see what their meter readings are.
Budget Amendment
Budget Amendment The second reading of the City's Budget Amendment (02-04) was completed. McCormick asked the Council to look the numbers over and notice that they haven't changed since the last reading. The Amendment was then accepted, and the next step in the process is to publish it.
New Budget
New Budget The first reading of the New Budget was completed for Fiscal Year July 1, 2024 – June 30, 2025, estimating revenues, resources and appropriation funds. Details of the budget proposal have been reviewed by the Council and it is has been adopted. The Special Meeting was set for Tuesday, June 18th at 6:30 p.m. to pass it after the second reading.
City Manager's Report
City Manager's Report Hawesville City Manager Jake Powers said, 'For our Land and Water Conservation grant for our project, we have recently had a survey done on that. As soon as we get the findings from that we'll pass that along to GRADD and they will instruct me on how to move forward with the start-up.
We started our Phase 1 site visits today. We had the environmentalist working with us with the Brownfield Project and to look at our 2 Main Street properties. They said that normally those will go for about $5K. And this is coming at no cost to us. We had about $10K worth of work done today, at no cost to the City.
We also visited the 2 properties and had Phase 1 site assessments for those as well. We also need to start looking at scheduling our next Brownfield Town Hall Meeting. Shane Barton (Downtown Revitalization Coordinator with CEDIK) is working with us on this. He's really happy with how it's going so far.
At the blue house downtown, the side door was stuck open. They immediately said, ‘We're not going in there.' They said that it is coming down, basically.
The Presbyterian Church, they were pleased with that structure. There were some minor household EPA type issues that they mentioned briefly. They said it will definitely have potential to be revitalized. We're going to get reports on all of this; that way we'll have all of their direct comments.'
Police Report
Police Report Hawesville Chief of Police B.J. Burton was absent and McCormick read his report saying, 'May was a healthy and exciting month for everyone. I know here, as Chief, it was eventful and significant. Citations were: two stop signs, 4 improper passing speed, 10 warrants – 9 served in city limits, 1 civil citation and 15 traffic stops without citation. I made contact with 25 vehicles and it does not include roadside assistance, nuisance complaints or calls taken within the City. The HCHS students that needed some hours, we've painted the side of the street and some parking spaces coming up the street to mark for parking.'
McCormick said, 'I feel like B.J. is doing a very good job for us. He's carrying on with some of the past practices that our chief had, who is here tonight (former Chief of Police Cody Axton).'
Fire Dept. Report
Fire Dept. Report Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards reported, 'The totals for the month of May are 39 different calls, 35 of those were fire, the rest were rescue. That takes our yearly total up to substantially higher than last year's.
We received our new pagers with the upgrade to the new digital system. We're finishing up on the boat to put it into service. Right now, several different upgrades in the station – LED lighting, etc. This weekend was State Fire School. We didn't send anybody this year. We'll continue with our in-house training at least twice a month.'
McCormick asked if they have found any avenues for possible funding for the new air packs they need. Richards said they are still looking and haven't yet. 'We're trying to find some things also,' McCormick said. 'Jake's been working diligently on that.'
Storm Water Project
Storm Water Project Matt Curtis reported, 'Several months ago, we had to increase the budget for the Storm Water Project. That request to FEMA has been approved. In the meantime, GRADD has been working on the matching funds to take care of the City's portion of that, and 5.2 percent was the low match. The new budget number of $3.35M took it up $174K.
We've gotten word that the City will have a zero cost facility. We're expecting to see the Local Match Participation Program Grant, which is the grant for the City, after the start of the fiscal year on July 1.
The next steps on it is mechanical design, the structure and all mechanical and electrical components of it, including the force mains (pipelines) going up over the levee area are going to be completely gutted. When it's done the bones are still going to be there but all of the mechanical equipment and electrical components are going to be brought up 7 decades from when it was first put in (the current plant was installed in the early 50s).
The electrical design is just getting started. That's one of the requirements for the Army Corps of Engineers. We have to meet their electrical standards before we have our next process. Once that takes place, we're looking to try to bid this late 3rd quarter into the 4th quarter of this year.'
Phase One of the entire project will be the sluice gate, he said. That will be the top priority of the contractor who's bid is accepted later in the year. In the meantime, other equipment will be used to raise the gate until the plant is fully built. 'When the river comes up,' he said, 'we can shut the sluice gate and then we can pump. Right now, we have to have other equipment means to raise that gate until this thing is fully built.'
Cleaner Water Program
Cleaner Water Program 'The state has come out with the Cleaner Water Program (Bipartisan Infrastructure Law New Funding 2022 to improve drinking H2O & wastewater). State legislature reorganized how the grant funding will come in. Previously, it came down to KIA (KY Infrastructure Authority) and then they would come to the local officials and determine what the priorities were in the community and then it was dispersed.
Now, the state legislature has gotten involved and KIA is going to rank them. Those rankings are going to go to state legislature and then next spring the legislature is going to [divvy those out]. That is a funding source that we're looking at for several future projects for the City of Hawesville.
We'll be looking at a project award knowing that we're getting funding in April 2025. That window is open right now but the state hasn't provided an application to submit. That window closes August 15th, 2024. We know what we've got to do and we'll get that taken care of.'
Contact State Reps
Contact State Reps Curtis said this is an opportunity for City officials and citizens of Hancock County to contact local state representatives, state senators, etc., and tell them that this is a HUGE priority for the City of Hawesville to get this funding.
Regional Water Plant
Regional Water Plant He continued saying, 'The Hancock County Regional Water Plant ranked Second in the entire state of KY for the drinking water project. That project will be funded this round of revolving funds. How that money is coming down, 100 percent loan or a percentage of it being up for forgiveness, we don't know at this point until the Intended Use Plan comes out. I was talking with KIA today and they're thinking that it will be at the end of summer before that plan comes out. As more details come up about that we will come back and make sure you guys are updated.'
Future Projects
Future Projects He added, 'With future projects for the City of Hawesville, one of the things we were meeting about was talking about the regional water plant and making sure that we've gotten some of the problems as far as what is out there in your distribution, where they are having to go and make repeated repairs over and over again, and closing the system up by creating more loops so you don't have dead end lines.
This is so they are not having to flush water and put water on the ground – all measures to get you to the point of – if and when you decide to become a non-producer and if you're purchasing water that you're able to sell every drop of water that you possibly can instead of putting it out on the ground.
There are 3 projects that we're working on with Superintendent Brian Patterson and GRADD to get those in and apply for funding. There are 2 water system improvements. Phase One has a bunch on lines in areas we have issues in distribution. The Center Booster Station has been an issue with piping failures, and [correcting issues] on Harrison Street, Main Cross, etc., and also creating some loops out on KY 69 and Old Hartford Rd.
Phase 2 is with the pump station- here recently, the Cities had tanks inspected. The inspector told me that we might as well count on interior and exterior minor structural repairs. There are the 2 unused tanks on Hawes Blvd. and Fred Hodges, and there's the Donna Lou Ln. Water Main that we've had issues with.
One other, is the Windward Heights Lift Station. It is something that Brian and the crew are having issues with. It's not in a good location. One solution we've talked about is moving it away from the intersection down into that grassy field area, to where an accident wouldn't cause damage which has happened before.'
Force Main Project
Force Main Project 'The KYTC (KY Transportation Cabinet) Force Main Project (conveying wastewater from a lower to higher elevation) – we've been working with the KY Finance & Administration Cabinet. It was put out for bids. There were zero bids received on May 30. Their process is a nightmare to work with is my guess why there were no bids. If you don't do things a certain way it kicks back. They have put it back out to private quotation through KYTC. We provided names of several contractors that we're familiar with that we feel would be a good fit for this project. We're waiting for those bids to come in.'
Regionalizing
Regionalizing The amount of funding for regionalizing is huge right now, McCormick said. Curtis explained why saying, 'I've been talking with (GRADD Executive Director) Joanna Shake and Blake Edge at GRADD and this was the highest ranked project that they've ever had come out of the counties they serve.
The reason for that is last year Hawesville was not listed in that project profile. It was 101st ranked in the state last year. This year, there was a discussion about Hawesville interconnect – a stand alone plant that both cities would be purchasing the water from and there was more of that regionalization talk and then it went from 101st to 2nd. It is HUGE. The state put a ton of money in what they are calling ‘generational projects'. If you check certain boxes, they are throwing money at them.
They're looking at multi-million dollar projects to try to get all these small communities, as many of them as they can, to compliance with what is coming down with the regulations of the emerging contaminants, which are PFAS (plastic chemicals). These have to be removed from drinking water and eventually will have to be removed from wastewater and, all the while, the manufacturing of those chemicals is still occurring. Removing something that is continuing to be produced – you're never going to be able to get it out of the water systems, but that's where the EPA is going and we will have to all follow suit.'
McCormick said, 'They are really pushing hard for regionalization and we've all talked. I don't want to regionalize east at all. We definitely don't want to regionalize west or south, into Daviess County, etc. If we do, we want to within our County to where we're all getting the funding and can have better opportunities, but before we buy a single drop, these lines will be replaced as infrastructure, these worst places. That is going to give us the opportunity to get the money to do the infrastructure by tacking it onto a regionalization.
We've not committed to anything. All we're doing is saying we're interested. We are willing to take a look at it but if we were to do it tomorrow, we'd spend twice the money that we're spending right now on the water because you're buying the water then, you're not producing.'
Curtis said, 'There are multiple costs associated with what the fee is for the thousand gallons that you all would be purchasing. The whole premise in all of the discussions we've had of here and in Lewisport is that it is equal for both communities.
The regionalization – they're pushing it along with the emerging contaminants. There was a push for OMU (Owensboro Municipal Utilities) to come east and at that time (25-30 years ago), it was $15M-$16M then. To give you a point of reference, OMU just spent $50M in that range. They are getting ready to go ahead and go back and put another $30M into that plant to meet PFAS regulations.
The technology has been looked at. For Lewisport's plant it's been taken care of from day one. We're not going to have to go back. The cost of the emerging contaminants are staggering. It's not a one time you build it and it's done. You have to go back and replace your filter every so many years. It is never ending.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Local Band Ole 60 Breaks Friday After 5 Record
description: The local band Ole 60 played at Owensboro After 5 last Friday and broke the 28 year attendance record at the venue! There were a lot of Hancock Countians cheering them on in the crowd. Two of the…
content:
The local band Ole 60 played at Owensboro After 5 last Friday and broke the 28 year attendance record at the venue! There were a lot of Hancock Countians cheering them on in the crowd. Two of the members, Ryan Laslie and Jacob Young, are from Hancock County. The other members are from Owensboro, Ohio County, and Tell City.
Ole 60 hit Number One on the Apple Country Music Album Charts with their debut EP 'Three Twenty-Four' earlier this year. The 5-piece band are: rhythm guitarist Tristan Roby, bassist Colby Clark, lead vocalist & guitarist Jacob Young, drummer Aden Wood, and lead guitarist Ryan Laslie.
The band started with Jacob and Tristan practicing in a shed in Maceo. The two joined with Ryan Laslie and began playing together at the Galaxy Pizza & BBQ Restaurant, which is owned by Ryan's brother, Bradley.
Jacob and Ryan were both employees at the Galaxy at different times and hadn't yet met until Bradley introduced them. They decided on naming the band 'Ole 60' because that was the route that Jacob took to Tristan's house when they first started jamming together.
Three Twenty-Four was released last August, and the band began playing shows in January of this year. They have signed with Grey Area Sound in Nashville, as well as joining with Nashville's United Talent Agency for booking assistance.
Website & Social Media
The Band's website is: https://www.ole60music.com/. The full list of their upcoming gigs are listed there, along with your chance to purchase tickets. They are selling out fast so order soon! All of Ole 60's social media links are listed at: https://linktr.ee/ole 60
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Leslie White's Children's Book 'Tommy the Tidy Tiger' doing well
description: Leslie Cooper White has very recently published her children's book titled 'Tommy the Tidy Tiger', and it has already been picked up...
content:
Leslie White wrote & illustrated her new children's book: Tommy the Tidy Tiger
Leslie Cooper White has very recently published her children's book titled 'Tommy the Tidy Tiger', and it has already been picked up by 100 book platforms nationwide!
She self-published her beautiful children's book via Spines Online Publishing Platform on June 6th, and it is about a playful and adorable little tiger named Tommy who teaches children the importance of keeping themselves and their surroundings clean.
Leslie is the daughter of Leon & Sarah Basham Cooper, of Hancock County. After over 30 years at Dart Polymers, Inc., she retired and currently works from home and travels in Contract Logistics with Disaster Resource Group, one of the largest suppliers of turnkey-based services in the U.S., and based in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. She has a Master's Degree in Supply Chain Management & Logistics from Michigan State University.
Leslie and her husband, Tommy, live in Lewisport and are blessed with 2 grown children: Ashley and Jacob, both Hancock County High School graduates.
Tommy the Tidy Tiger is available for purchase in paperback now on Amazon.com, for example, as well as many other platforms.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Kentucky nursing-home industry says Biden staffing mandate ‘impossible' to meet
description: The nursing-home industry is pushing back against a new Biden administration rule that sets minimum staffing requirements
content:
The nursing-home industry is pushing back against a new Biden administration rule that sets minimum staffing requirements for federally funded long-term care facilities and will require many of them to hire more nurses and nurse aides.
Morgan Jemtrud, director of communications for the Kentucky Association of Health Care Facilities and the Kentucky Center for Assisted Living, told Kentucky Health News in an email that the staffing mandate is not attainable for several reasons, including the health-care workforce shortage.
'The staffing mandate is impossible. CMS estimates it will cost around $300,000 per building (AHCA estimates more), but there is no funding to support the implementation of the rule,' said Jemtrud. 'Also, the required staff are simply not available. RNs are in demand across all health-care sectors, and no pipeline is being built to produce the number of RNs this rule requires.'
Jemtrud was referring to an analysis from the American Health Care Association, a nursing-home lobby, that says meeting the mandate would require nursing homes to hire more than 100,000 more nurses and nurse aides at an annual cost of $6.8 billion. The analysis also says 94% of nursing homes were not meeting at least one of the proposed staffing requirements.
New staffing requirements
The Nursing Home Minimum Staffing Rule requires all nursing homes that receive Medicare or Medicaid payments to provide 3.48 hours of direct nursing care per resident per day, including a defined number for registered
nurses (0.55 per resident per day) and nurse aides (2.45 hours per resident per day).
'This means a facility with 100 residents would need at least two or three RNs and at least 10 or 11 nurse aides as well as two additional nurse staff (which could be registered nurses, licensed professional nurses, or nurse aides) per shift to meet the minimum staffing standards,' says a White House fact sheet about the rule.
It will also require facilities to have an RN onsite 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to provide skilled nursing care.
The new staffing requirements will be phased in over three years, except at rural facilities, which will get up to five years. The law allows for some 'limited, temporary exemptions' for facilities in areas with workforce shortages that demonstrate a good faith effort to hire the required staff.
Within two years, most homes must provide an average of at least 3.48 hours of daily care per resident. About 6 in 10 nursing homes are already operating at that level, according to a Kaiser Family Foundation analysis. But the analysis says only 19% meet the defined number of hours required for RNs (.55) and nurse aides (2.45) that is required under the full implementation ofthe law.
'When facilities are understaffed, residents may go without basic necessities like baths, trips to the bathroom, and meals – and it is less safe when residents have a medical emergency,' said the fact sheet, noting that it will also 'ensure that workers aren't stretched too thin by having inadequate staff on site.'
Brice Mitchell, spokesperson for the state Cabinet for Health and Family Services, told Kentucky Health News in an email that the administration is reviewing the federal rule and its impact.
'Medicaid funds 70% of all long-term care in the state and there is ongoing work to expand a nurse career ladder to help increase recruitment,' Mitchell said. 'At this time, we are unable to determine the number of Kentucky nursing homes that don't meet the new federal rules.'
Good first step, says nursing home ombudsman
Denise Wells, executive director of the Nursing Home Ombudsman Agency of the Bluegrass, said her group was 'very pleased' with the 24-hour RN requirement, but didn't think the minimum hours per resident per day went far enough.
She said the 24/7 RN requirement is important because the acuity level of patients has increased over the years, meaning patients need more assistance with their activities of daily living than ever before. And, she said, 'Medical emergencies don't just happen for eight hours of the day; they can happen 24 hours a day.'
Wells said they were disappointed in the hours per resident per day only being 3.48 because research shows that the minimum care that an average resident needs is 4.1 hours per day.
'And that is simply to avoid negative health outcomes,' she said. 'It's not to live their best lives, it's not to have the greatest quality of life, it's just to have that minimum care provided.'
Wells called the new staffing rules a 'good first step.' 'We are trying to make sure that the message is that this is not the ceiling; that it's a floor,' said Wells. 'It's the absolute minimum, but facilities should be staffing higher than this. . . . Nursing homes are required to staff to sufficient levels to meet resident needs, and so if they have residents that their care plan indicates that they need more than the 3.48 hours per day, then the facility needs to staff to meet that need.'
Can nursing homes afford more staff?
Jemtrud with KAHCF and KCAL was asked about the financial impact of the rule. She said Kentucky nursing homes are already financially strained and there are no funds to help meet the new requirements.
'Before this rule, 79.9% of Kentucky facilities are in distress or at risk of financial distress using the Altman Z-score,' Jentrud said, citing a formula used to determine a company's risk of bankruptcy.
'CMS estimates the total cost of the final rule at about $4.3 billion per year, but AHCA continues to estimate the cost above $6 billion per year,' she said. 'There are no funds from Medicare, Medicaid, or other payers to increase payment rates to providers for any of the rule requirements.'
Wells, asked how facilities can address the health-care workforce shortage, said her group prefers to call it a 'job quality crisis' caused by low pay, poor conditions and little support. She pointed to reports from the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care that have showed how nursing homes hide profits, and saif there is not enough transparency in how Medicaid and Medicare dollars are used these facilities.
KFF Health News Skeptical
KFF Health News also points to researchers who are 'skeptical that all nursing homes are as broke as the industry claims or as their books show. A study published in March by the National Bureau of Economic Research estimated that 63% of profits were secretly siphoned to owners through inflated rents and other fees paid to other companies owned by the nursing homes' investors.'
In a lengthy statement from the American Hospital Association, Stacey Hughes, AHA executive vice president, said, in part, 'CMS' one-size-fits-all minimum staffing rule for nursing homes creates more problems than it solves and could jeopardize access to all types of care across the continuum, especially in rural and underserved communities that may not have the workforce levels to support these requirements.'
The American Health Care Association issued a statement in opposition of the mandate and said the industry will keep pressing Congress to overturn the regulation.
'While it may be well intentioned, the federal staffing mandate is an unreasonable standard that only threatens to shut down more nursing homes, displace hundreds of thousands of residents, and restrict seniors' access to care,' Mark Parkinson, CEO of the AHCA, said in a statement. 'Issuing a final rule that demands hundreds of thousands of additional caregivers when there's a nationwide shortfall of nurses just creates an impossible task for providers. This unfunded mandate doesn't magically solve the nursing crisis.'
The mandate also implements stronger transparency measures to ensure nursing home residents and their families know when a nursing home is using an exemption, according to the fact sheet.
U.S. House Republicans at a House Energy and Commerce health subcommittee voiced their concerns about the new staffing mandate. The subcommittee chair, Republican Rep. Brett Guthrie of Kentucky's 2nd District, said he was 'extremely concerned' about the mandate along with the 80/20 rule which requires agencies that provide home- and community-based services to spend 80% of their Medicaid payments on compensation for workers who directly provide care.
Guthrie said both rules 'threaten access to long term care services for Medicaid beneficiaries by setting arbitrary staffing and pay standards. . . .This approach simply won't work.' He added later, 'These rules come at a time where we have seen more than 500 nursing home facilities close since the start of the pandemic and where we have 150,000 fewer long-term care workers than we did before 2020.'
By MELISSA PATRICK, KENTUCKY HEALTH NEWS
