title: Legislative Update- Representative Scott Lewis
description: Legislative Update Representative Scott Lewis Educating Kentucky children Education remains the General Assembly's top priority this session. Last session, we provided our K-12 education system with…
content: Legislative Update Representative Scott Lewis Educating Kentucky children Education remains the General Assembly's top priority this session. Last session, we provided our K-12 education system with historic investments included in HB 1 and HB 6 and provided schools with stronger strategies to improve student performance in mathematics through the Numeracy Counts Act (HB 162, 2024). This session, there has been no shortage of bills filed related to our education system ranging from efforts to help schools recover from the severe weather we have faced this winter to legislation addressing the administrative burdens our teachers face in the classroom. Several education-related measures have cleared committee and/or the full House this week, including: Addressing the healthcare workforce shortage through scholarships: HB 305 aims to address the healthcare worker shortage in the commonwealth by extending healthcare training scholarships funded by the Kentucky healthcare workforce investment fund, established in HB 200 from the 2023 Regular Session, to physician assistants, dietitians, and nutritionists. HB 305 passed the House of Representatives 92-0 and is on its way to the Senate for consideration. Establishing college credit transfer pathways for high-demand degrees: HB 427 would establish college credit transfer pathways for high-demand degree pathways between KCTCS and 4-year institutions ensuring that college credits earned are applied to a student's degree. This legislation passed the House 93-0 and is on its way to the Senate for considerations. Establishing performance standards for higher education educators: HB 424 would establish a performance and productivity evaluation for employees at public higher education institutions, administered at least every four years. This legislation would permit universities to remove employees who do not meet performance or productivity standards. Improving school safety: HB 14 continues the work the General Assembly has done to improve school safety. It would allow school districts to employ an enhanced security system that includes a wearable alert alarm system and direct the Center for School Safety to establish the Wearable Panic Alert Grant Program to support districts as they seek access to these devices. Reducing red tape in education: HB 48 removes administrative burdens placed on teachers, schools, and school districts that do not improve their ability to educate students. Promoting advanced coursework in schools: HB 190 would require school districts to establish an advanced coursework pathway policy with automatic enrollment for high potential students who are distinguished for grades 4-12. Supporting school districts through severe weather: HB 421 would allow school districts to shift their calendar model from 170 instructional days to 1,062 instructional hours. This would allow schools to extend school days to offset lost instructional time due to school closures. Additionally, this legislation would allow the Commissioner of Education to grant up to five disaster relief days for alterative student instruction and waive up to five student attendance days to school districts that would be unable to achieve 1,062 instructional hours with an extended schedule by June 4, 2025. HB 421 passed the House 82-7 and will move on to the Senate for consideration. Identifying and supporting low performing schools: HB 298 would require the Department of Education to annually review schools to determine CSI status. This would allow KDE to provide support to more school districts. Federal law requires CSI identification every three years. As always, I can be reached anytime through the toll-free message line in Frankfort at 1-800-372-7181. You can also contact me via email at Scott.Lewis@kylegislature.gov and keep track through the Kentucky legislature's website at legislature.ky.gov.

title: Updates Given by Engineer Matt Curtis at Hawesville City Council Meeting
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, February 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided updates on projects. Regionalized Water Plant Curtis…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, February 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided updates on projects.
Regionalized Water Plant Curtis began with an overview of the status of the Hancock County Regional Water Treatment Plant project in the City of Lewisport, and presented data on what regionalization and an agreement between the two cities would look like in the future if Hawesville decides to partner for that.
As reported in The Clarion, the City of Lewisport has been working on a Regionalized Water Plant project for Hancock County, in order to supply local needs. Both cities have older water plants that need to be upgraded or replaced, which was the main factor in moving forward with plans for a new plant in the City of Lewisport, that would also have an interconnect for the City of Hawesville. Lewisport City Administrator Jason Roberts said the initial talks with Bluegrass Engineering were solely about the condition of the 2 existing water plants, and that it was time for a new plant in Lewisport. They began searching for funding to regionalize, with the main goal always being to keep the water plant local (no outsourcing). The main focus was always to prevent Lewisport from having the need to tie-on to Owensboro Municipal Utilities, or for Hawesville needing to tie-on to Hardinsburg Municipal Utility, for example. The Reverse Osmosis Pilot Study began in Lewisport, and during that study the realization was made that the Environmental Protection Agency had changed the standards on PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). They found that the project was then considered 'Generational,' and would qualify for millions in funding. Generational projects are focused on getting small communities into compliance with PFAS regulations. And, with the original goal of this being a stand-alone plant for the whole county, that regionalization discussion brought the project from 101st to 2nd on the list for grant funding. The number one spot has been forfeited since then, making the Hancock County Regionalized Water Plant project the number one project of its kind in Kentucky. 'There was $8M given towards the project from the state, and of that $8M, $6.3M is grant, principal forgiveness. I've never seen them give that large of a percentage to one project,' Matt Curtis said. '$8M was the cap for funding year/Fiscal Year 2025. They're pursuing a state line item, obviously that will be next fiscal year. There is a potential, based upon what some state reps are saying, that there's some money there that they could allocate toward the project during this session. We'll see what happens with that. Also, there is KISRF (KY Infrastructure & Economic Development Fund), and whatever they can't get elsewhere, they can go back for a second round of funding from KIA (KY Infrastructure Authority). There's also the federal line item from Congressman Brett Guthrie's Office that they've requested, of $2.5M. At this point, we don't have all of the money that we need for it but things are progressing to where we're pretty much getting prodded to go ahead and get design started.' The week of Feb.10th-14th was the tentative start date, weather depending, for the test well to be drilled on the site, located adjacent to the Lewisport Library. Curtis said transmission mains have already been designed, which include ones that run into Vastwood Park, and with a master meter to serve Hawesville.
'KIA's part, when they're doing underwriting,' he continued, 'they come back with some questions. This was the same that occurred here for the City of Hawesville on the sewer plant when we got KIA funding for it. They are just wanting to get through some particulars. One of the biggest ones that they pushed for was an MOA (Memorandum On Agreement) or MOU (Memorandum Of Understanding) between the sister cities. It doesn't lock anybody into it, but what they want to know is if the governing body of Hawesville is in agreement that they would like to purchase water from this regional water plant, the same that Lewisport would. It would be a simple agreement that says: 'We agree that this is what we want to pursue at this point, and it makes the most sense for both entities.'' Public Meeting The initial regionalization agreement will be reviewed by both mayors and city councils in the next couple of months. And, as you may have read in a previous edition of The Clarion, Lewisport Mayor Chad Gregory announced his plan to organize a Public Meeting in April to provide an opportunity for answering residents' questions on the project. An exact date and time have not been set for that, but Gregory said it may be held at North Hancock Elementary School. Curtis explained the importance of regionalization to Hawesville Council members, and also said that there is possible funding that may be available for the City of Hawesville's current projects. 'The state has always wanted, and has tried to persuade as many utilities as they can to regionalize where they can,' he said. 'The thought process is that there is an economy scale of savings when you regionalize. Also, with these immerging contaminants, PFAS, plastics, that's becoming a big driving force. The PFAS regulations are there for drinking water, and they're going to start being enforced. This technology, with the reverse osmosis, removes PFAS. It's one of the 2 treatments that are known to remove PFAS from drinking water, that and granulated, activated carbon. It's a big expense to remove those PFAS. The funding, as far as regionalization goes, that's what moved this project. Generally, the state will get $35M for drinking water, $35M for cleaner water – sewer, and once they run out of money, you're below the money. When GRADD went through and finessed the narrative of that project and included Hawesville in it, it jumped to the second project. There is a pot of money at Frankfort for regionalization projects; We're trying to get some more of that to make this project more viable and least costly to Hawesville and Lewisport. One of the things we're doing, with each municipality having their own treatment plant, there's a cost of production and cost of delivery of water. You're pulling water out of the ground, treating it, and there's a cost associated with delivering it to each of your all's meters. We're looking at that from both cities. We're looking at the audited financial statements, and pulling out those treatment expenses. The treatment plant has specific line items in that budget: chemicals are all at the treatment plant, most of your electrical expense is at the treatment plant. We're looking at those usable expenses and deducting those out to derive what the cost of delivery is for each utility. We're looking at the cost of production of the new plant, and then marry those two together to get a point of what those rates will ultimately look like, long-term. Whatever it's costing Hawesville, per thousand gallons, will be what it's going to be costing Lewisport.' Curtis explained how the rates would be calculated. There will be a cost to the treatment plant, and that is based on the production numbers and water usage, and how many gallons each city purchases; It is not a flat fee. This will be disproportionate because Hawesville purchases more water than Lewisport. Currently, it is 60-40. According to the monitored 6-year average, production is 900,000 gallons a day for both cities, with the Hawesville plant producing 60 percent of that, and Lewisport producing 40 percent. Those numbers, of course, fluctuate. If they start as soon as possible, the regionalized plant could be operational in as soon as three years from now. 'That plant, starting out, if both sister cities come together with it, we're going to be looking at sizing that for 1.5 million (gallons),' he said. 'There will be 600,000 gallons per day, with excess that will be there for future growth. If an industry comes in, there won't be a big cost added on, on the backend of the project where we've got to upsize the plant because of them. Now if a major water user comes in, obviously that's a game changer in it but they can pay their way just the way that everybody else would…I know I'm in a delicate situation working for both of you (Hawesville and Lewisport). Looking at it, I've talked to Mayor McCormick about this, and let's ignore regionalization as an option. What does Hawesville have to do to get to the point where it has PFAS removal, and we bring everything up to a new plant and those costs?…The thought about that is from a public's perspective: Is it going to cost us more to hook into them? And it's not. We looked at those numbers. The likelihood of you getting a grant to do it, is slim to none. With regionalization, you bring in that possibility. The best-case situation, and I'm not saying that this is going to happen but it's a realistic possibility, that we could get this almost 80 to 90 percent principal forgiveness of grant. There are things in motion about funding. There's a very good chance we could be looking at that, for this size project, and $20M is what this will ultimately cost.' Council members discussed the potential of these 'forever plastics' (PFAS) causing cancer, and that citizens are concerned. Also, there are already a number citizens in Hawesville who are struggling to pay their water bills, and there is concern about those customers being able to pay those bills, especially if the price is raised in the future. 'I don't have a problem saying it's a carcinogen, at some level,' Curtis said. 'It's two grains of sand in an Olympic sized swimming pool; it's such a minuscule sample size…That's the trigger point on the NCLs (National Contaminant Limits). My other issue with it is we're not removing manufacturing of these products. We're continuing to manufacture them, so we're continuing to reintroduce them into the environment that we're removing them from. And there's really only one industry that is getting hit with it, and that's the drinking water industry. So, that's my editorial on it. If you're going to remove it, let's quit manufacturing and consuming these products…It's in your toothbrush, clothes, everywhere, plastic drinking bottles, etc…' Hawesville City Manager Jake Powers and Matt Curtis have put together a project profile. The most important and immediate focus is to get Hawesville's system at its very possible best. 'If you're having to now buy water, you're paying for it whether you sell it or not,' Curtis continued. 'The goal is, we've got to tighten up the distribution system within Hawesville. We've got a project that is going through the same funding sources as the plant, and we could tie the two together to try to get that as well, in that funding package. That includes water main replacements – Harrison Street, Main Cross, these known areas they've been tracking where there are repeated repairs done. Let's get it out of the system; let's tighten it up.' McCormick said, 'I stress sternly that unless our infrastructure can be rebuilt, and I think some of you know that, we will not have any interest in tying-on to Lewisport, or the regional plant at all. Because there's no sense in us doing like we have, a city to our east that is buying water from the city on to their east, and they're buying 2 million gallons a month, and selling about 800,000 gallons a month. I can't put the city in a fiduciary manner that we'd be paying for water that we're not selling. Now, at least we're in control of that cost. Unless this infrastructure goes through, and Matt and Mayor Gregory, in Lewisport, know this…unless this infrastructure is rebuilt, I'm not onboard because we're not going to have done to us like what's being done up the road.' Curtis said, 'We've got to get that tightened up and cleaned up. And that project is about $2.1M – painting the tanks (in Hawesville) is near a million dollars, when you paint all three of them, roughly.' McCormick added, 'I think we want to look at that as sister cities instead of another entity eventually trying to gather us up…He was talking about how we had excess gallons to use. Domtar has reached out. I've been in discussion with Jeff Durbin. They're talking to us about hooking on to our water system, which we are providing water on Skillman already. We're within distance there to make it feasible for them. This would be strictly for potable water. It will not be for production.'
Storm Water Lift Station The Storm Water Lift Station was discussed next, and Curtis said the final design plans with electrical, mechanical, structural, etc., have been submitted to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. 'We reviewed those about 10 months ago,' he said. 'We're doing the final review now. Once we get their blessing, we can move that project to bid…That project is moving forward.'
Force Main Project Bluegrass Engineering has been working to finalize the Force Main Project in the City of Hawesville, with the KY Transportation Cabinet (KYTC). The project will start in the next couple of weeks. Curtis said, 'All that's left to do, essentially, at the library there's a manhole. Somewhere between that manhole and where it ties into the gravity sewer line, it's busted up. We believe it was caused by the force main and the grout that came from that pipe penetration got in there, lodged and did whatever. We had it in our plans to remove that manhole, dig up on the other side where the gravity sewer is, cut out both sections, slip joint a pipe in there, fill it full of stone, blacktop the driveway, and done.' McCormick said, 'Mr. Dixon will be happy that his driveway will be back (in good order) like it always was for years.' 'The contractor said he didn't include it in his bid, he missed it,' Curtis added. 'It was on those plans.' 'The work they did was about $6K,' said McCormick. '$89K was what the bid was. There wasn't that much to do. That's the bureaucracy that we've had to deal with…'
Fire Dept. Update Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards gave the summary for the month of January: 52 total runs, 16 EMS assists, 7 motor vehicle accidents, 8 fire alarms, 1 brush fire, 2 residential structure fires, 1 vehicle fire, 1 water rescue (a new one for the fire department, he said), and 16 miscellaneous, which are false alarms, etc. 'We added one new member in January,' Richards said. 'Our membership is also working on the Second Annual First Responders Day. We did that last year in May. The date is set for Saturday, May 17th for that, which is county-wide.'
Annual Firefighters Banquet Richards also announced the date for the 2025 Firefighters Banquet. It will be on Saturday, March 22nd. Like and follow the Hawesville Fire Department Facebook page for more details on this year's banquet.
Operation of Golf Carts in City Limits Ordinance 01-25, concerning the rules and regulations for operating golf carts in Hawesville city limits, was introduced. The regulations are in accordance with KRS 189.286. If passed, this would permit the operation of golf carts on public roadways under its jurisdiction, and for the safe and regulated operation of golf carts on certain designated public roadways within the city. 'This ordinance was built off of an ordinance that Lewisport uses,' McCormick explained. 'It has all of the verbiage that theirs has in it.' He asked the council members to take the ordinance home, review it thoroughly, and bring any concern to the next meeting so that amendments can be made before the second reading and potential passing of it.
Ordinance 03-25 The first reading was given of this ordinance, which proposes adjustments to water or utility bills in the case of leaks, and offers relief to customers with unusually high charges due to such occurrences. 'Our staff pulled East Daviess County's procedures and Lewisport's, and built this ordinance off of them. It's very solid,' McCormick said. 'There are certain stipulations here for the eligibility for leak adjustment…They have to show that they've done their due process; It's written in here. There will be an application form available from the City of Hawesville.' The price of water does fluctuate, depending on the cost of water treatment chemicals, etc., and adjustments will reflect what the cost is at the time of the leak. Water rates are set according to the costs to produce it for customers.
'Our superintendent (Brian Patterson) did a very good job in bidding out chemicals,' McCormick said. 'There are some months we're paying a little bit more for chemicals and some now that we're paying less. So, it is fluctuating in costs. The manpower, that fluctuates because it depends on if we have a water issue what the manpower is to do, such as with a major leak. We've had a couple recently that were very major. I think this is fair.'

title: Baby Miya Bill Sponsored by Representative Scott Lewis
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Kentucky House Bill 574, aimed at further protecting children who are neglected and abused, was introduced on February 14th. Representative Scott Lewis was the primary co-sponsor of…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer Kentucky House Bill 574, aimed at further protecting children who are neglected and abused, was introduced on February 14th. Representative Scott Lewis was the primary co-sponsor of the bill, which will be called the 'Baby Miya Bill,' in honor of the late eight-month-old Miya Rudd, of Ohio County, who was found deceased and hidden in her family's home in Reynolds Station in June of last year. 'The bill has to go to the house floor,' Representative Lewis explained, 'then to a senate committee, and then the senate floor. So, it has still got a way to go. I'm hoping we will get it through. It's to put guardrails in place; There were some procedural errors, not on purpose or anything like that. I think with this new bill, with the procedures and guidelines that we have in there, it may keep this from happening again. Of course, bad people do bad things and no matter how many laws we make some of them will still be broken. I do think that some of the stuff we've put in here is really good. The other part of it is that Baby Miya will live on through this bill. It's named after her, and it will always have that name. That's special to me.' A summary of KY HB 574 is as follows: 'Amend KRS 620.030 to require any person with reasonable knowledge of the matter to notify the local law enforcement agency or the Department of Kentucky State Police (KSP), the Cabinet for Health and Family Services or its designated representative, the Commonwealth's attorney, or the county attorney that a child has been born to a parent who has another child in the care, custody, or control of the cabinet or other person as a result of removal pursuant to KRS Chapter 620; amend KRS 620.040 to require [those entities] or the local law enforcement agency…to be notified a child has been born to a parent who has another child in the care, custody, or control of the cabinet or other person as a result of removal pursuant to KRS Chapter 620; establish a rebuttable presumption that a child born to a parent who has another child in the care, custody, or control of the cabinet or other person as a result of removal pursuant to this chapter is in immediate danger of dependency, neglect, or abuse; amend KRS 620.050 to require the Cabinet for Health and Family Services to investigate when it receives notice that a child has been born to a parent who has another child in the care, custody, or control of the cabinet or other person as a result of removal pursuant to KRS Chapter 620; amend KRS 620.060 to establish that ex parte emergency custody order may be issued when a parent or other person exercising custodial control or supervision has another child in the care, custody, or control of the Cabinet for Health and Family Services or other person as a result a removal pursuant to this chapter, creating a rebuttable presumption that the child is in immediate danger of dependency, neglect, or abuse; amend KRS 620.080 to establish a rebuttable presumption that the child would be dependent, neglected, or abused if returned to or left in the custody of his or her parent or other person exercising custodial control or supervision if the parent or other person exercising custodial control or supervision has another child in the care, custody, or control of the Cabinet for Health and Family Services or other person as a result a removal pursuant to this chapter; provide that the Act may be cited as Baby Miya's Law.'
Representative Lewis released a letter to the public last week on social media. He wrote: '…This bill intends to put procedures in place to protect all of our precious children. This bill is to honor her.' To provide more context and further explain why the bill is worded in such a manner, Miya's parents had other children that had been removed from the home prior to her birth. We at The Clarion have been providing ongoing updates on Baby Miya's heart-breaking and tragic death. At the time when original details were released, Miya's cause of death was yet to be officially determined, and the investigation is still ongoing. The report from the state medical examiner revealed that the cause of death is still undetermined, however the autopsy report showed that meth was in her system, according to the results returned from toxicology testing. A missing child investigation began on June 6th, 2024. When KSP first questioned Miya's parents, Tesla N. Tucker (29) and Cage C. Rudd (30), at their residence in Reynolds Station, they stated that they had not seen her for a month. KSP had opened the missing child investigation after a search warrant and welfare check was conducted. Tucker and Rudd were arrested at that time. Both were charged with Possession of Controlled Substance 1st Degree (Fentanyl), Possession of Drug Paraphernalia, and Abandonment of a Minor. Rudd was also charged with Possession of Controlled Substance 1st Degree (Methamphetamine). The parents were detained at Daviess County Detention Center. A search was conducted by KSP on Friday, June 14th, 2024, and that's when Baby Miya's body was found in the residence, where it had been hidden in a concealed manner, under debris and wrapped in a blanket. After processing the scene, her body was determined to be in a state of decomposition, and was taken by the Ohio County Coroner's Office, then transported to the KY Medical Examiner's Office in Louisville. Miya's parents, as well as Miya's grandfather, Ricky J. Smith (56), and Brodie C. Payne (28), were each charged with: Abuse of a Corpse, Tampering with Physical Evidence, and Failure to Report the Death of a Person. Tucker and Rudd were additionally charged with: Trafficking in Controlled Substance, 1st Degree (Greater than 2 grams-Methamphetamine), Trafficking of Legend Drugs, Trafficking Marijuana, Child Abuse 1st Degree, and Engaging in Organized Crime. KSP Troopers later charged Payne for his role in the illegal drug operation held at the Rudd residence, where he had been residing for approximately 6 months. Payne was charged with Trafficking in Controlled Substance, 1st Degree (Greater than 2 grams-Methamphetamine), Trafficking of Legend Drugs, Trafficking Marijuana, Engaging in Organized Crime, Possession of Paraphernalia, and Wanton Endangerment – 1st Degree. The Daviess County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit had begun a drug trafficking investigation on Payne months prior.
Tucker, Rudd, Smith, and Payne have been charged with murder and child criminal abuse in connection to Miya's death. These four have all been indicted, and the last court date was on February 3rd, at the Ohio County Judicial Center, where they were set to have their arraignments. Tucker, Smith and Payne appeared virtually, and all entered pleas of 'not guilty.' Rudd did not appear virtually. His lawyer said he will be at the next court date, which is the pre-trial hearing, and is set for March 4th, in Ohio County. Tucker is currently detained at Ohio County Detention Center. Rudd, Payne and Smith are detained at Davies County Detention Center.
The investigation has been ongoing by KSP, Ohio County Coroner's Office, and the KY Medical Examiner's Office.

title: Hancock County Farm Supply It's More Than Just A Farm Store… It's an Agribusiness
description: On Monday, February 24, the Agricultural Communications class from Hancock County High School visited Hancock County Farm Supply in Hawesville. Gordon Gaynor, manager of The Farm Store, explained the…
content:
On Monday, February 24, the Agricultural Communications class from Hancock County High School visited Hancock County Farm Supply in Hawesville. Gordon Gaynor, manager of The Farm Store, explained the ins and outs of the business's success story and how it has become a 'one stop shop.'
Humble History
In the early 1900s, Shelby Davis opened the first farm store on Main Street in Hawesville. This store sold your basic hardware and other small farm necessities. Several years later, the store was bought by Billy and Elizabeth Stephens, the owners of Bill's IGA. The business began to expand beyond the building's capacity, so the store was moved to a plot of land on Highway 60 next to where the current Independence Bank is located. This relocation provided 6,000 square feet of warehouse space and storefront. In 1959, ownership changed to Raymond and Dorothy Lamar. During this period, bagged fertilizer was added to the inventory and stored at the fairgrounds.
In 1979, the current 12,000 square foot building was constructed to accommodate the business's growing size. The former building was then repurposed as a warehouse, which remains in use today. Later, additional buildings were built to store lumber, plumbing and concrete supplies, plus a shop for machinery and equipment maintenance.
Truly a One-Stop-Shop
For over half a century, Hancock County Farm Supply has been the happy home for all of your home & garden, outdoor, appliance, and farm supply needs. Originally, Hancock County Farm Supply was a 'jack of all trades' establishment, offering washers, dryers, and appliances for a variety of needs. With the pricing and inventory of a big-box store, and the warm welcoming feeling of a local small business, this store appeals to a large array of people.
Today, the Farm Supply is well versed in everyday needs on the farm and in the home; offering hand tools, bulk and bagged fertilizer/seed, equipment rental, plumbing and electrical supplies, septic systems, and so much more. The store supplies our local schools, county road department, and several factories and businesses with equipment and tools, as well as our general community. Driving past, the gas pumps may have stood out to you as well, which were added to increase the appeal of the store on the corner.
Continuing the Legacy
Following in the footsteps of the previous owners and managers, the current set of 7 full-time and 2 part-time employees strive to supply the community with everything they could ever need. Randy Atherton, the former manager, added lumber, which was described as a much needed 'business-saver,' allowing it to grow into the store we know and love. Lumber is still a top selling commodity, as well as fertilizer during the spring and summer months. The availability of these items save the people of Hancock County a trip out of town; instead, thanks to Hancock County Farm Supply, we've got everything we need here at home.
Gaynor stated 'I can't say what, but stay tuned for big changes in the coming years', which left many students wondering what could be in store for what we know as 'The Farm Store'

title: Across the Kentucky Color Line – Lee Durham Stone's First Book
description: Historian Lee Durham Stone, Ph.D., author of Across the Kentucky Color Line: Cultural Landscapes of Race from the Lost Cause to Integration. Muhlenberg County native and Historian Lee Durham Sto
content: Historian Lee Durham Stone, Ph.D., author of Across the Kentucky Color Line: Cultural Landscapes of Race from the Lost Cause to Integration. Muhlenberg County native and Historian Lee Durham Stone, Ph.D., has published his first book – Across the Kentucky Color Line: Cultural Landscapes of Race from the Lost Cause to Integration, which focuses on filling in many important missing pieces of racial interaction in the historical literature of Western Kentucky, specifically from the post-Civil War to school integration in the 1960s. The book was named '# 1 New Release' on Amazon for 6 weeks since its publication in December of 2023. It is currently ranking highly in several categories, and has received many outstanding reviews. Lee cites all sources within the book, making it especially helpful to educators, students and researchers. 'Most histories of Kentucky focus on Louisville and, particularly, the Bluegrass area because a lot of the professors are at Lexington, and those are the 2 main cities,' Lee said. 'And, now there's a whole lot being written about Appalachia. So Western Kentucky has just been ignored in so many ways. I moved back to KY in 2011 and started reading about the history of KY and noticed that there was a gap in the historical literature on Black history in Western KY. Then, I read this quote by Toni Morrison, saying that if there's a book that you really want to read but it has not been written yet, then you must be the one to write it. I had this epiphany when I read that. I thought, ‘Oh my God, maybe I'm the one that needs to write this book.' I came to this realization that if nobody has written a better Black history of Western KY, that maybe I was the one to do it.' In the prologue, Lee describes an experience of going on a school trip in 1957 to see The Ten Commandments, directed by Cecil B. DeMille, at a movie theater in Central City, joining segregated school children and witnessing the heartbreaking, unequal treatment. He describes on page 13, the irony of watching a movie about a freed people, while his African American peers were still suffering. He wrote: 'These Black schoolchildren, their teachers, and the nationwide Black movie-going public vicariously witness an indelible social irony in that living moment. They watch a freed tribe – the Israelites – finally reach their Promised Land. Conversely, however, 1950s Black Americans dwell in a precarious position. Symbolically, they are waiting in Pharaoh's Land on the far shore of the Red Sea. Alternatively, perhaps they are closer, undergoing the trials in the desert – the wandering antecedent stage to reaching their ‘home over Jordan.'' Lee describes the 'otherness' that was experienced as 'segregated felt space' on page 14. Those children were already struggling with confidence like their peers at that age. What a challenge to overcome! It would take much more grit and tenacity to uplift and encourage themselves. It was a definite road block at that point in their lives, as they would be moving into adulthood soon. Would they be able to muster enough self confidence to achieve their goals in life? This unequal treatment posed a clear disadvantage to any of them that did not laser focus on maintaining a positive mindset. These challenges could only be met successfully by having an unwavering faith in God, just as the reverend and civil rights leader Martin Luther King, Jr. encouraged in his sermons, and in his most famous speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in 1963. It is extremely important to include these left out accounts in order to heal the psyche from the trauma of it all and establish the understanding that is necessary to produce compassion. Compassion is demanded for renewal and assurance that history will not again repeat itself. Prevention requires a full exposure so that racism cannot just become more covert and continue to thrive, as John Howard Griffin so perfectly illustrated in Black Like Me, published in 1961. Along with Jim Crow education and local resistance to school integration in 1963, Lee examines in his book the trial and 'legal lynching' in 1907, the secretive Possum Hunters of 1914-1916, as well as Black businesses and African Americans in coal mining. His many years of research and interviews have made this a must-read, as well as a must-include on the shelves of libraries, schools, museums and archives of every county, especially in the Western KY counties, which includes Hancock. Lee earned his PhD in Geography Education at Texas State University, a Masters in American History at Gettysburg College's graduate program associated with the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, a Bachelors at University of Kentucky in 1970 (during which time he played some walk-on, non-scholarship basketball during his freshman year in 1965), as well as a Mining Reclamation degree at Madisonville Community College. In '77 & '78, he was a state strip coal mine inspector. Before beginning his teaching career, he served in the Peace Corps in Jamaica for 3 and a half years. He taught high school social studies for over 20 years, five of those in Hopkinsville, and is now retired and resides in Franklin, KY. His youngest brother, Mark Stone, is the current editor of their family newspaper, the Times-Argus, in Central City, and was 2021 KY Farm Bureau Communications Award Winner. Across the Kentucky Color Line is available for purchase only on Amazon. If you would like to invite Lee to speak at your school, county museum, library, etc., you can email him at: leedurhamstone@yahoo.com. See his author's page for more information at https://kentuckyhistorybooks.wixsite.com/stone. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Updates on projects provided at Hawesville City Council Meeting
description: The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, March 12th, and Mayor Robbie McCormick announced that only what can be matched of the Land and Water Conservation Fund Grant that was awarded in th
content: The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, March 12th, and Mayor Robbie McCormick announced that only what can be matched of the Land and Water Conservation Fund Grant that was awarded in the full amount of $161,500 for a new playground in downtown Hawesville will be applied. 'Any monies that match that is what we will use on the playground,' McCormick said. 'We do have a major contributor already. I can assure you that we will not spend this money unless we have the matching funds to take care of it. We're not going to go back in debt on this type of project.' Storm Water Lift Station FEMA (Fed. Emergency Mgmt. Agency) has approved the budget increase application for the Local Match Participation Program to go toward the City's Storm Water Lift Station. The district has been working with KY Emergency Management, resulting in FEMA approving the increase of the grant from a little over $700K to $3.015M. The City will have a percentage of that to pay – around $174K. There are grant applications submitted through GRADD that could possibly result in the City's percentage being totally paid for. Fire Dept. Update Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards said there were 37 total monthly runs for February. 'We're in the middle of brush fire season (Feb. 15-April 30) and haven't been real busy yet, thankfully. Rain is incoming, so that is good.' He added that there is an exemption for agricultural burning of brush piles to clear off for crops and that someone is with them at all times and they are following those exemption rules. Exemption to Unfreeze Funding The releasing of state funding has been frozen/withheld from the City because of past incompliance with audits. 'We've found a possible law that would help us move forward,' McCormick explained. City Attorney Jamie Stephens added, 'It's an exemption and, thankfully, it doesn't require the audits to all be caught up. It only requires us to have a financial statement done in the even numbered years and the audits done in the odd numbered years. Our KIA (KY Infrastructure Authority) funding and other grant systems are going to require yearly audits but to get the funds unfrozen we don't have to have all of the audits completed. We reached out to DLG (Dept. For Local Government) and a couple of different offices for direction on funding that's frozen and how much is there. It is a program for a one-time ever exemption to have frozen funds released, and audits have to be finished. 2019 -2023 Municipal Road Aid has been frozen at over $71K. There are $6,500 of back bills they have not paid that we could get released; we managed to locate that so far. We're waiting to find additional ones. There are several months of KLEFPF (KY Law Enforcement Foundation Program Fund-DOCJT) payments as well.' Stephens said she's also doing research and found that the City may be missing out on some of the Coal Severance Tax Funds, and is continuing to find out how much funding is out there. They were sent a list of processes to go through, and a project resolution to comply with in order to get this one-time release of funding. An affidavit must then be signed by the mayor addressing several areas, and one is what records they've been unable to locate and what steps they've taken to reconstruct those. A lot of hard work has been put in and they are hoping to get the funds released so they can start pulling those monies in and even if they don't spend them, they can be added to the CDs where more interest can be drawn than what currently is now, McCormick said. Monthly Financial Statements City Clerk Amy Roberts recently compiled the information for the council to know exactly what is in every one of the City's accounts and all of the balances. 'I think this is an added help,' McCormick said. 'I know it is to me and I feel like to you as well, to know where we have money at. There are certain things that these monies can be spent on in some of these categories, as you know. We talked about, on our financials, we want to continue to draw this money so we have to continue to keep our audits and everything caught up, but we will be able to choose where the money is pulled from. Let's say we have a water issue on Harrison St., we can go back and see if that falls under line maintenance, etc. We've got ‘Repair & Rebuild of Infrastructure' (category) and we can pull money from that for those types [for example] and hopefully that will protect our General Fund and our Water & Sewer. We do have some big things to tackle coming up. I am really pleased with Amy going above and beyond in pulling this information for you guys.' Equipment & Tool Purchases 'Today our crew was cleaning out the ditch here,' Councilman Wayne Herndon said. 'They told me they really appreciated this backhoe. It makes their job easier.' McCormick added, 'We had to make a decision; we had no choice. We had a backhoe that was down and it was going to cost us about $4-5K to fix it. It was going to be down for weeks. Councilman Herndon, Councilman Justin Basham and I discussed it, and I made the executive decision to get the backhoe. It's $2K a month, but we had to have it.' They will also be purchasing tools that are much needed, and will save the City money going forward. City crewmen are doing a tool inventory now to see exactly what they have and what is needed. The council plans to furnish both of the City's service trucks with the tools they need. Bluegrass Engineering The newest employee at Bluegrass Engineering, Scott Coon, introduced himself to the council. He's spent almost 40 years in waste water management and mostly has pumping and controls experience, he said. 'I've switched from the sales side to the engineering side, and am looking forward to learning all about your system and how we can help you. I've already performed a first in Hawesville. After 36 years I finally dropped my phone in your sewer station,' Scott said, comically. 'Hawesville has already broken me in.' McCormick said, 'He's going to work great with us, as Matt Curtis and Bryan Lovan have (Co-Owners of Bluegrass Engineering). We have a great extension with Scott.' Resolution Approval A Resolution for the City of Hawesville was read aloud and approved by the council, authorizing Mayor McCormick to execute any documents which are deemed necessary by DLG (Dept. for Local Govt.) to carry out projects and to act as the correspondent for projects, and apply for the KY Local Match Participation Program (LMPP) – a Project Proposal Grant application for up to $174,200 for the City's Storm Water Pump Station Upgrade Project. The City of Hawesville desires to carry out flood planning and mitigation activities on behalf of the residents of the City by supporting this project and it is recognized that LMPP monies available for those purposes, pursuant to KRS 147A.029, impose certain obligations and responsibilities upon the City and will require, among other things, approval of a satisfactory application transmitted to DLG for approval and other obligations in connection with receiving the LMPP Grant of monies for that purpose. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Don't Stress
description: Relaxation, a healthy/positive mindset and quality sleep are essential for a healthy lifestyle, no
content: Relaxation, a healthy/positive mindset and quality sleep are essential for a healthy lifestyle, not just during designated calendar dates such as Spring Break but on a regular basis. We've all heard and know it's true that stress is a 'killer'. It lowers the immune system and allows disease to set up camp, so don't stress! Staying Calm I remember our youth leader at church saying often, 'It's no real, real problem.' He would say that when, for example, we were freaking out because we had to perform our play for another church and someone was sick and couldn't play their part. We were complaining and scrambling around. We were adding unnecessary stress to ourselves and others, and he knew that. He would get us all to take a deep breath and realize that it was easily solved and that the drama was not helpful in any situation – not for little problems or for 'real' problems. There are 'real problems' that occur, and not even then would stressing out be helpful. You wouldn't want an EMT or firefighter to show up at your house in an emergency and be carrying on about how bad the problem was would you? It is counterproductive during emergencies as well as with every day smaller problems. Focus on the solution and remain calm. Remember what Christ Jesus said in the Sermon on the Mount – Matthew 6:27 (KJV): 'Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?' Sleep Getting a good night's rest every night is key for good health. Did you know that studies have proven that if you are sleeping between the hours of 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. that you'll be getting the most health benefits? Why? Because during these hours is when your body's beneficial human growth hormone (HGH) is released for overall healing, along with others. So it is best to try to get to sleep before 10 p.m. each night. Also, children need more sleep than adults because they are still growing. It is recommended that newborns (0-3 months) have 14-17 hours of sleep a day. Infants 4-11 months need around 12-15 hours. Toddlers age 1-3 should get 11-14 hours of sleep, and preschoolers (3-5 years) should get 10-13. For children ages 6-13, 9-11 hours of sleep each night is recommended. Teens (14-17) require around 8-10. Adults ages 18-64 should strive for 7-9 hours. And, adults over 65 should be getting 7-8 hours of restful sleep each night. Positive Thinking You can really add to your stress levels by thinking negative thoughts about yourself and others. Practice positive thinking and uplift yourself, and then you will easily be able to uplift others with positive words as well. Stress is harmful for all aspects of health – body, mind and spirit. Don't stress, be blessed – 'Casting ALL your care upon Him; for He careth for you.' 1 Peter 5:7. Be Well and God Bless You. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Lyday rescues Hornets with ninth inning double
description: Carter Lyday takes a mighty cut during the Hornet's win over Henderson County Tuesday. The sophomore delivered the game winning hit to beat Tell City Monday. Carter Lyday knocked in the game winning…
content:
Carter Lyday takes a mighty cut during the Hornet's win over Henderson County Tuesday. The sophomore delivered the game winning hit to beat Tell City Monday. Carter Lyday knocked in the game winning run and the Hornets defeated Tell City 5-3 in nine innings during a varsity baseball game played in southern Indiana Monday. 'Carter smashes one to left-center field and gets us a run in the ninth and chaos broke loose from there,' HCHS coach Brad Keown said.
The game was tied at 3-3 through eight innings when Carson Clark was hit by a wild pitch to begin the ninth. Clark later stole second base and was in scoring position when Lyday came to the plate with one out. Lyday jumped on a 1-2 pitch and smacked a fly ball to left-center field. The ball fell in for a double and Clark scored to give Hancock County a 4-3 lead. Dec Lewko later drilled a line drive base hit to knock in Lyday. Kolby Keown made the catch on a bases loaded line drive to end the game in the home half of the ninth. Clark helped put Hancock in extra innings when he hit a 2-run base hit with two outs in the sixth frame. Lewko got the win in relief while allowing no runs on four hits, with 10 Ks and three walks in 4.2 innings. Jordan Payne allowed three runs (two earned) on five hits, with nine Ks and three walks over 4.1 frames. 'Jordan threw a great game. He threw his heart out and Dec came in with a long stretch and was able to finish it off. We had two great pitching performances,' the coach said. Lewko was 3 for 5 with a double and one RBI, Clark was 1 for 3 with two RBI, Jack Roberts was 1 for 2, Lyday was 1 for 4 with a double and one RBI, and Jacob Shultz was 1 for 4. Brock Tindle had one RBI. Kaiden Casebolt had four hits for Tell City. C. Stiff took the loss on the mound. Owensboro The Owensboro Red Devils scored two runs in the seventh inning to win a close, 5-2 contest against the HCHS Hornet varsity baseball team here last Wednesday, March 20. Errors hurt Hancock County when Owensboro plated two unearned runs in the first inning. Jordan Payne led off the second with a double and later stole third base. Dylan Mucker drove in Payne with a line drive to left field and the score was 2-1. Brock Tindle was on the mound for HCHS and the senior held down the Devils long enough for the Hornets to tie the score at 2-2 in the fourth. Again it was Payne who crossed home plate. The senior singled, stole second, advanced to third on a base hit by Tindle and scored on a single by Carson Clark. The Hornets had runners at second and third base when Owensboro recorded the third out. The Red Devils went back in front 3-2 in the fifth on an RBI double by Blake Kimbrell. Owensboro later plated two runs on a hit by Brady Benjamin in the seventh. Dec Lewko doubled with two outs in the bottom of the seventh but was left stranded when OHS made a 6-3 put-out to win the game.
Payne was 2 for 3 at the plate with a double, Tindle was 1 for 2, Clark and Mucker were both 1 for 3 with one RBI and Lewko was 1 for 4 with a double. Tindle allowed five runs (three earned) on five hits, with six Ks and four walks over 6.2 innings. Kolby Keown allowed one hit and struck out one batter in 0.1 innings of relief. Muhlenberg County Muhlenberg County had 14 hits and 14 RBI during a 15-1 win over the Hornets in five innings at Vastwood Park last Thursday.
The Mustangs scored eight runs on six hits in the first inning and later plated seven runs in the fourth. Hancock County's lone run came in the third when Kolby Keown scored on a fly ball hit by Jack Roberts. Keown allowed eight runs (seven earned) on six hits, with two Ks and one walk in one inning pitched. Lewko allowed no runs on two hits, with three Ks and one walk over one frame. Louden Fluharty allowed five runs on three hits, with one K and two walks in 1.1 inning, and Noah Keown allowed two runs on three hits, with one K and three walks over 1.2 innings. Roberts was 2 for 2 at the plate and Clark was 1 for 2. Eli DeBoer had three hits and five RBI and Colton Carver had four RBI. By Steve Wimmer

title: Total Solar Eclipse Path Runs Near Hancock; 90%
description: The path of totality for this year's total solar eclipse on Monday, April 8th runs through 13 U.S. states from 1:30 p.m. to 2:40 p.m. CDT. In the path are Paducah, Evansville, Indianapolis and other…
content: The path of totality for this year's total solar eclipse on Monday, April 8th runs through 13 U.S. states from 1:30 p.m. to 2:40 p.m. CDT. In the path are Paducah, Evansville, Indianapolis and other fairly nearby cities in relation to Hancock County. If viewing in Evansville, for example, the eclipse will be visible right at 2:05 CDT. This will be the last major eclipse to cross North America for 20 years. Pilot Warning The Hancock County Airport has reported that more incoming plane traffic than usual is scheduled for the big day. The Federal Flight Assoc. has issued a statement warning pilots to prepare for operational changes and a greater volume of traffic at airports along the path of totality. One must physically be on the strip of land called the path of totality to fully experience all of the viewing phenomena talked about, and our area is just slightly off that choice viewing path but not far! Almost 32 million people will be inside the path, according to sources. HC Schools Hancock County Schools are all provided with viewing glasses for staff and students by the district. Permission slips were sent home and students with parent/guardian signatures will have the chance to view the eclipse. Hancock County Middle School Principal Traci Sanders said the science teachers will be covering lessons throughout the week before Spring Break so that when students return, they'll be ready for viewing and know what to look for. All HCMS classrooms will be going outside in the afternoon to catch a view. HCHS Principal Ginger Estes said if it is in the curriculum, students (with permission) will participate, but there isn't a whole school event planned. All North and South Hancock Elementary students with permission slips signed will have an opportunity to go outside for a view during the school day. The Path of Totality The prime viewing time in Indianapolis is estimated at 3:10 EDT. Just before that, it will be visible in Bloomington, IN at 3:05 EDT. The path runs through Dallas, Texas, Little Rock, Arkansas, Poplar Bluff, Missouri, and then Paducah, KY, which is right on the very far edge of it. Next, it runs through Indianapolis, Dayton & Cleveland, Ohio, and up through Buffalo, NY, Burlington, VT, parts of Maine and into Canada. Tens of millions will be watching this event and striving to get to the nearest area that is inside that sweet spot. There is a viewing event happening at the Indianapolis Zoo, and viewing glasses are included with the general admission price. There are amazing views that can only be seen from earth in the path of a total solar eclipse during 'totality', when the disc of the moon obscures the disc of the sun, including 'Baily's Beads' for instance, which are the mountains of the moon visible along the perimeter of the sun. You can actually see those jagged edges and they look like glowing beads. By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Meade pulls out 2-1 win over Lady Hornets
description: Jordyn Waltrip winds up to deliver a pitch for the varsity girls at Vastwood Park. Meade County scored twice in the seventh inning and pulled out a 2-1 comeback victory over Hancock County Lady…
content:
Jordyn Waltrip winds up to deliver a pitch for the varsity girls at Vastwood Park. Meade County scored twice in the seventh inning and pulled out a 2-1 comeback victory over Hancock County Lady Hornets during a varsity softball game played at Brandenburg Tuesday. Baylee Estes led off the game with a base hit and later scored on an RBI hit by Lily Roberts. The game was a pitching duel between Lily Roberts and 8th grader Veronica Roberts for most of the game. The Lady Hornets brought in their 8th grade pitcher, Jordyn Waltrip, in the fifth inning.
Waltrip set down the Lady Waves in order. Meade County got a 2-out double and a base on balls in the six, but Hancock County got out of trouble without allowing a run. The Lady Hornets had a chance for an insurance run when Layni Roberts led off the sixth inning with a base hit, but the Meade pitched followed with two strike outs and the score remained 1-0 heading to the seventh. The Lady Waves' batter led off the final frame with a double and advanced to third on a ground out. The next two batters drew a base on balls before Danica Love delivered a walk-off, 2-run hit to end the game. Lily Roberts allowed no runs on one hit, with seven Ks and three walks over four innings. Waltrip was charged with the loss. She allowed two runs on three hits, with three walks over 2.1 frames. Veronica Roberts got the win while allowing one run on three hits, with 11 Ks and two walks in seven complete innings. Estes was 1 for 2 at the plate, Lily Roberts was 1 for 3 with one RBI, and Layni Roberts was 1 for 4. Apollo A 5-run fifth inning propelled Apollo High School to a 7-4 win over the Lady Hornet softball team during a varsity game played in Owensboro last Thursday. The E-gals led 1-0 through four innings until Hancock County's Jordyn Waltrip belted a 2-run home run in the top of the fifth inning. The 8th graders shot scored Ava Riggs and the Lady Hornets led 2-1. Apollo's Mallory Velotta answered with a 2-run homer in the home half of the same inning and the E-gals' Tyler Hall added another 2-run bomb later in the frame to make the score 6-2. Apollo plated one more run in the sixth before Hancock County rallied in the seventh. Waltrip got a base hit and Aubree Mosby stroked a double. Both players eventually scored before Apollo recorded the final out. Lily Roberts allowed five runs on four hits, with six Ks and five walks over 4.2 innings. Waltrip allowed two runs (one earned) on one hit, with one K and two walks in 1.1 innings. Waltrip was 2 for 3 at the plate with the home run and two RBI. Mosby was 1 for 2 with a double and
one RBI, Ava Riggs and Ella House both went 1 for 3 and Kylie Westerfield was 1 for 4. By Steve Wimmer

title: Grand Jury Report
description: Comes the grand jury, by the foreman, and reports to the court that they met in session on the 22nd day of December 2023 to consider all pending matters at that time. After having heard testimony from…
content: Comes the grand jury, by the foreman, and reports to the court that they met in session on the 22nd day of December 2023 to consider all pending matters at that time. After having heard testimony from various individuals, a total of 7 True Bills and zero No True Bills were returned. The remainder of the cases referred to the grand jury by the Hancock District Court and not addressed by this grand jury shall be referred to the next Hancock County grand jury. This the 22nd day of March 2024. Curtwrights indicted in three cases By Ralph Dickerson The Hancock County grand jury indicted Hawesville resident Michael R. Curtwright on a total of four charges in two separate cases. In the first case Curtwright stands accused of possession of a handgun by a convicted felon, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The grand jury accused Curtwright of possessing a 9 mm handgun, and 25-.25 handgun, a 45-.45 handgun, a .308 caliber rifle, a .22 caliber rifle, a .223 caliber rifle, and a 9 mm rifle in one case. He stands accused of committing these offenses in January of 2024. In the other case, Curtwright stands accused of theft by failure to make required disposition of property $10,000 or more when he failed to deliver the materials to build a home. He also stands accused of criminal trespass in the first degree for unlawfully remaining in a building. He stands accused of committing these offenses in October of 2023. The court set his bail in the amount of $10,000 in each case. He faces arraignment in both cases on 4-26-24 at 10 am. In the companion case, Jadah K. Curtwright stands accused of theft by failure to make required disposition of property $10,000 or more for the failure to deliver the material to build a home. She also stands accused of criminal trespass in the first degree for remaining unlawfully in a building. The court set a bail of $10,000 for her. She faces arraignment on the charges on 4-26-24 at 10 am. Taylor indicted for strangulation and other offenses The Hancock County grand jury returned a three-count indictment against Lewisport resident Michael Taylor. He stands accused of committing the offense of strangulation in the first degree, assault in the fourth-degree domestic violence minor injury and terroristic threatening in the third degree. He stands accused of committing these offenses in November of 2023. The court set his arraignment on the charges for 4-26-24, at 10 a.m. The court also set a bail of $10,000. Laslie indicted for sex related offenses The Hancock County grand jury returned a three-count indictment against Hawesville resident Justin L. Laslie. He stands accused of sexual abuse in the first degree-victim under 12-years-of-age, attempted rape in the first degree-victim under 12-years-of-age and attempted incest-victim under 12-years-of-age. He stands accused of committing these offenses in February of 2022. The court set his arraignment on the charge for 4-26-24 at 10 a.m. The court also set a bail of $50,000. Neether indicted on theft charges The Hancock County grand jury indicted Hawesville resident Ian A. Neether on three theft related charges. He stands accused of theft of identity, fraudulent use of a credit card and unlawful access to a computer in the first degree. He stands accused of committing these offenses from August 2024 to November of 2023. The court set his arraignment on the charges for 4-26-24, at 10 a.m. The court also set a bail of $10,000. Stewart indicted for harassment The Hancock County grand jury returned a charge of harassment-no physical contact against Hawesville resident Kenneth A. Stewart. He stands accused of committing the offense from April of 2023 to October of 2023. The grand jury also returned a no true bill on a charge of sexual abuse in the first degree, meaning no indictment on that charge. The court set his arraignment on the charges for 4-26-24, at 10 a.m. The court also set a bail of $500.

title: Farmer's Market Begins June 15
description: The first Lewisport Farmer's Market of 2024 is set for Saturday, June 15th at Chapman Park Pavilion in downtown Lewisport.
content: The first Lewisport Farmer's Market of 2024 is set for Saturday, June 15th at Chapman Park Pavilion in downtown Lewisport. The time has not yet been set, but may be from 10 a.m. to noon. As the date gets closer, there will be more solid details for each market in The Clarion. Expecting Bigger Turnout The City of Lewisport Collections & Administrative Assistant Megan Simpson is the organizer and said that she is expecting a bigger turnout this year. 'I have been in contact with new vendors and people have already been planning bigger gardens,' she said. 'I hope anyone who even has extra vegetables plans to show up! It is still free to the public, and free to set up!' Tentative 2024 Market Dates The tentative dates for this year's Lewisport Farmer's Markets, all held at Chapman Park Pavilion in downtown Lewisport, are: June 15th & 24th, July 8th, 13th & 22nd, August 5th, 10th, & 19th, September 2nd, 14th & 30th, and October 12th. The very first Lewisport Farmer's Market was held on Saturday, July 1st, 2023 and there was a good turnout. Local homemade items, local honey and homegrown produce are some of the many wares that are sold and purchased at the market. Call Megan Simpson at Lewisport City Hall in advance if you'd like to participate, so that your items can be advertised before each market. The number is (270)295-3324.

title: Unfreezing of Funds is Hopeful for City of Hawesville
description: The releasing of state funding has been frozen/withheld from the City of Hawesville because of past incompliance with audits, and there is a way to possibly unfreeze this funding. Hawesville Mayor…
content:
The releasing of state funding has been frozen/withheld from the City of Hawesville because of past incompliance with audits, and there is a way to possibly unfreeze this funding.
Hawesville Mayor Robbie McCormick explained at the Hawesville Council Meeting on Tuesday, April 9th, 'It's a resolution for records lost, damaged or destroyed – records per KRS 65.037. This will allow the City to file for a one-time forgiveness to receive our funding that the state has been freezing.
I have to sign an affidavit for this stating that we are doing everything on here that we're saying. It includes being under contract with a CPA firm, and we have included every single thing on this resolution that we needed to file, City Attorney Jamie Stephens has. Is it pretty good odds that we're probably going to get forgiveness, Jamie?'
Stephens answered, 'I think so. The resolution is nothing that is binding. It is not the equivalent of an ordinance. It's simply a requirement of the program that allows us to have that funding unfrozen, and sets forth in there reasons why we have struggled with that and what records that we've had trouble finding or locating, or audits being behind and that sort of thing. It gives them an idea of what barriers we've had and what we have to overcome in order to get these audits completed.'
McCormick continued, 'This will help us tremendously, because our Municipal Road Aid funds will be unfrozen. Our funds that we're charging the state road dept. will be forgiven. We've got coal and mineral funds out there that are coming in; It's substantial.'
Stephens added, 'There are still at least four vendor accounts that they have not gotten any balances from that remain frozen; we're unsure about how much of those. I think we have found at least $73K so far that was frozen, but there's considerably more. We just don't know what those final figures are until they give access again.'
McCormick said, 'If at any time doing this we fall out of compliance on this, with my affidavit signed it's on me. We have to stay within our guidelines with what we're doing.'
Fire Dept. Report Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards provided the March run reports from the station. There were a total of 54 runs for the month. 'Eight of those were rescue calls,' he said, 'and 46 were fire calls. That puts it at a total of 134 for the year so far; That is 3 months in. We've had 17 rescue calls so far for the year.
The radio upgrades are coming in. They're doing a lot of testing on our radio systems. Hopefully, that should get our sirens working better as well.'
County Emergency Services Day – June 15 'One of the big things we're working on right now with all of the County Emergency Services, including the County Emergency Services Association,' Richards continued, 'is the planning for Emergency Services Day. It's going to be at Vastwood on June 15th. Mark your calendars for that. There will be a lot more information as we get closer to that date. Hopefully, we can get some community involvement with that.'
Firefighter of the Year – Jason Mattingly 'We want to thank those that attended the Annual Fireman's Banquet in March,' Richards said. 'We recognized our Firefighter of the Year – Jason Mattingly, and our Junior Firefighter of the Year – Nolan Veach . We definitely appreciate the work they're doing.'
Junior Firefighter of the Year – Nolan Veach. We definitely appreciate the work they're doing.' New Members 'There were 2 new members added last month,' Richards announced, 'One of them is Coben Capps, and Jeff Gray was reinstated off of retirement as a member as well.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hawesville to Raise Sewer Rates; Truck Traffic to Close on Town Hill
description: Hawesville Mayor Robbie McCormick announced at the City Council Meeting Tuesday evening that the City's sewer rates will be raised saying, 'The average increase on the sewer rate will be between $8…
content:
Hawesville Mayor Robbie McCormick announced at the City Council Meeting Tuesday evening that the City's sewer rates will be raised saying, 'The average increase on the sewer rate will be between $8 and possibly $12 monthly.'
There were rate increases put into ordinances every year that weren't enforced during the previous administration, council members stated, and now it is necessary to enforce the raised rates. 'We don't want to do this,' McCormick said, 'We have to do this to meet our debt. If we don't, we're out of compliance. This will generate the amount of money it takes to pay the $15K payment per month.
This is not for a limited time. This is not a surcharge that we're putting on to pay for a waste water pump. This also covers our cost to treat the water and our cost to employ and actually pay the debt that we owe. This whole ordinance covers everything that it costs for residents, small businesses, commercial and industrial.
Without passing this ordinance, we're not going to be able to stay liquid as a City, and it's my job to make sure this City is run in a fiduciary manner. That's the way we're running it. I hate increases; we all do. It is set up on a 20-year note.
These increases will all be dedicated to go for the payment of that plant but this is not a surcharge line. This is an actual bill. I do feel like there was a lot of hard work put in this ordinance. Councilman Wayne Herndon helped. Councilman Justin Basham had some ideas. Councilman Tracy Johnson has asked [pertinent] questions. Councilman Danny Doyle and I have talked. I would like to get a sponsor for this first reading.'
Special Meeting – April 16 Councilman Herndon made a motion to sponsor the first reading. City Attorney Jamie Stephens read a first reading of Ordinance 4-16. 'We will be having a special meeting next Tuesday (April 16th) at 6:30 p.m.,' McCormick continued, 'to have a second reading of this ordinance.'
City Controller Report City Controller Jake Powers said, 'I went to the (free) Brownfield Bootcamp again last week, as well as August last year. I got some good information and brought that back. I was able to start it rolling with the kickoff meeting and the Town Hall meeting. We had our Forum with the high school students.
Shane Barton (UK's Community & Economic Development of KY Downtown Revitalization Coordinator) sat in on that. It went really well. We got some good feedback from sophomores, juniors and seniors (at HCHS).
We had about 190 survey responses, from the surveys we sent out. Those are like investments that we're making on this plan. Shane is helping us develop a plan. That's what we'll use to tie-in to these block grants and other grants. We're getting this free of charge from Shane to develop a really strong plan. It's the community that wants these things, not just our mayor, etc. We're talking to the community and finding out what is wanted and what's needed. It's helping build a good economic plan.'
Culvert Flood Councilman Danny Doyle alerted the council members and mayor about a citizen that had asked about a culvert flooding and running back toward his house. McCormick said, 'As soon as Brian and crew get the time, they're going to go over and open it up. Our superintendent said the water is not backing up; The flow to it is a little slow because of that side. We have other things taking a little more priority right now, getting into compliance with everything. I told him we'll take care of it when we can.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

content:
The HCHS Hornets varsity baseball team battled from behind and lost 6-3 to the Red Devils in Owensboro Monday. OHS added their final run in the sixth before recording the last out in the seventh inning. Payne allowed three runs (none earned) on no hits, with two Ks and one walk in one inning pitched. Keown allowed two runs on five hits, with three Ks and four walks in four innings pitched. Fluharty allowed one run on one hit, with one K and no walks in one inning of relief. Trevor DeLacey got the winfor the Devils. Roberts was 2 for 4 with a double and one RBI. Mucker was 1 for 2, Shultz was 1 for 3 with one RBI, Lewko, Fluharty and Tindle all went 1 for 3. description: Breckinridge County plated three runs in the sixth inning to win 5-2 over the Hornets during a varsity baseball game played in Hardinsburg Thursday. Hancock County grabbed a 2-0 lead in the second…
content:
Breckinridge County plated three runs in the sixth inning to win 5-2 over the Hornets during a varsity baseball game played in Hardinsburg Thursday.
Hancock County grabbed a 2-0 lead in the second inning. Carson Clark reached base on an error and Louden Fluharty laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance the runner. Jordan Payne then singled to left and the Hornets had runners on the corners. Lane Dixon entered as a pinch runner for Payne and promptly stole second base.
Two batters later Kolby Keown came to the plate with two outs and the sophmore hit a 2-RBI line drive to right field. The Hornet defense allowed a run in the home half of the frame and the score was 2-1.
Breck's Camden DeWitt led off the third with a triple and Conner Willis singled him home to tie the score.
Payne was on the mound and he and the Hornet defense held the Tigers at bay until the sixth when errors cost Hancock County.
Three consecutive errors by Hornet infielders followed by a base hit and a hit batsman and Breck now led 4-2.
Lewko got a strike out but a walk allowed the fifth run to score. The Hornets eventually got out of the inning with a 6-4-3 double play, but went down 1-2-3 at the plate in the seventh.
Payne allowed two runs (one earned) on five hits, with two Ks and two walks in 3.2 innings pitched. Lewko allowed three runs (none earned) on one hit, with one K and one walkd in 2.1 inning of relief.
Tristan Wicker got the win for Breck County.
Payne and Keown both went 1 for 2 at the plate.
Breck County Breck County scored nine times in third inning during a 13-3 win over the Hornets in five innings Friday at Hardinsburg.
Playing as the visitors, the Tigers plated two runs in the top of the first inning. Hancock County got a 4-6-3 double play and a strike out by Brock Tindle to end the frame.
Dec Lewko led off the home half of the inning with a base hit and Dylan Mucker followed with a single to right field. Louden Fluharty delivered the go-ahead run with an RBI hit to right field.

title: Seeking Music at Maple Mount participants for reunion – June 7-9
description: The Greater Owensboro Music Camp, better known as 'Music at Maple Mount', was popular with many young people from Hancock County during...
content:
The Greater Owensboro Music Camp, better known as 'Music at Maple Mount', was popular with many young people from Hancock County during its run from 1975-2005. There is a Reunion happening for all the participants on Friday- Sunday, June 7th- 9th. The first Greater Owensboro Music Camp, which most everyone eventually called Music at Maple Mount, began in 1975. Young people from across Kentucky and elsewhere gathered on the campus of the Ursuline Sisters of Mount Saint Joseph for a two-week camp to learn from some of the finest music instructors in the country. The Music Camp reunion is part of the celebration recognizing 150 years since the Ursuline Sisters of Mount Saint Joseph arrived in what is now known as Maple Mount. Had the music camp continued, this year would have been the 50th one. Everyone who participated in the camp through 2005 is invited back to share remembrances and, of course, music. The reunion will occur Friday through Sunday, June 7-9, 2024. It will begin with a meet and greet on Friday evening in Owensboro, then continue with many events at Maple Mount, located at 8001 Cummings Road, on Saturday and Sunday, concluding with a concert on Sunday afternoon. Full Schedule & Registration A full schedule and a link to registration can be found at: www.ursulinesmsj.org/music-at-maple-mount-reunion.
