title: Tindle throws 1-hitter in Senior Night win over Grayson County
description: Brock Tindle, Kolby Keown and the Hornet baseball team celebrate a 7-1 win over Grayson County on Senior Night at Tommy Keown Field. Brock Tindle pitched a 1-hitter and the Hornets scored six runs in…
content:
Brock Tindle, Kolby Keown and the Hornet baseball team celebrate a 7-1 win over Grayson County on Senior Night at Tommy Keown Field.
Brock Tindle pitched a 1-hitter and the Hornets scored six runs in the fifth inning to win 7-1 over Grayson County at Vastwood Park's Tommy Keown Field Friday.
'Tonight was all about the mound. Brock took command the whole game, and we were able to produce runs,' HCHS coach Brad Keown said.
Jack Roberts walked and scored on a passed ball to give Hancock County a 1-0 lead in the first. Tindle and the Hornet defense held the Cougars at bay for the next six frames. Jordan Payne and Carson Clark put back-to-back hits together in the fourth, but the visitors managed to get out of the inning unharmed.
The Hornet offense busted out in the fifth. The inning began innocent enough with a walk and a ground out, but then another walk followed by base hits from Dylan Mucker and Dec Lewko and home team led 3-0.
Louden Fluharty had an RBI ground out before Tindle ripped a line drive to center field. When the dust settled the Hornets held a commanding 7-0 lead.
Tindle walked to the mound in the seventh with a no-hitter in play. The senior got a strike out and a ground out, but Grayson's Jake Bratcher wrecked the no-no with a single up the middle. Tindle was unfazed and promptly recorded the final out on a fly ball to Payne.
Tindle allowed one unearned run on one hit, with five Ks and two walks over seven innings pitched. Levi Rogers took the loss for the Cougars.
Payne was 1 for 2 at the plate for HCHS. Tindle was 1 for 3 with two RBI, Clark was 1 for 3, Lewko was 1 for 4 with two RBI, and Mucker was 1 for 4. Roberts walked three times and scored two runs. Kolby Keown also scored a run.
'We're a young team and we're going to have some errors, but we're getting a little better every game. I told them the focus is all about getting ready for district play at the end of the year,' the coach said.
Whitesville Trinity Dylan Mucker had four hits and Dec Lewko ripped two triples when the Hornets out hit Whitesville 16 to four during a 13-5 win for Hancock County Thursday at Trinity.
Mucker got the ball rolling with an RBI hit in the top of the first inning. He later scored and the Hornets led 2-0. Hancock added four more runs in the second off hits by Clark, Tindle, Jacob Shultz and Lewko.
Lewko's 2-run triple in the third made it 9-0 before Trinity managed three runs in the fifth. The Hornets led 13-3 in the seventh. The home team got two runs across in last before the contest ended. Payne got the win on the mound. He allowed three runs (one earned) on four hits, with three Ks and two walks over six innings. Keown allowed two unearned runs on no hits, with two Ks and two walks in one inning of relief.
Mucker was 4 for 5 with two RBI, and Lewko was 3 for 4 with the two triples and three RBI. Payne, Tindle (RBI) and Shultz all went 2 for 4, Roberts was 1 for 2 with one RBI, Clark was 1 for 3 and Fluharty 1 for 5.
Ohio County The Hornets and the Ohio County Eagles played to a 2-2 tie when their game was called due to rain after four innings Monday at Tommy Keown Field.
The Eagles led 2-0 after scoring a run in the second and third innings.
Wild pitching aided Hancock in the third when Roberts and Mucker were both hit by a pitch. Fluharty singled in a run and the score was 2-1.
Kolby Keown got a couple of strike outs as the Hornet defense set down the visitors 1-2-3 in the top of the fourth.
Two walks and a single by Shultz left the bases loaded for Roberts in the bottom of the inning. Roberts hit a hard grounder that the Eagles' short stop couldn't handle.
Brock Tindle scored and the game was tied.
Moments later the game was called for rain after four innings.
Keown allowed two runs on no hits, with two Ks and seven walks over four frames. OCHS pitcher Owen McConnell allowed four hits.
Fluharty was 2 for 2 at the plate with one RBI. Roberts was 1 for 2 with one RBI, and Shultz was 1 for 2.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Estes hits two inside-the-park, Waltrip smashes grand slam
description: The Lady Hornets offense was in full display during a 16-1 win over Breckinridge County in a varsity softball game played in Hardinsburg on Wednesday, May 1. An RBI single by Ella House put Hancock…
content:
The Lady Hornets offense was in full display during a 16-1 win over Breckinridge County in a varsity softball game played in Hardinsburg on Wednesday, May 1.
An RBI single by Ella House put Hancock County ahead 1-0 in the first inning. The score was unchanged until the third.
A home run, four triples and a double later and the score was 10-0. Baylee Estes got it all going with a triple, then finished off the inning with an inside-the-park homer.
Jordyn Waltrip belted a grand slam home run in the fourth and Estes followed with another inside-the-park home run. The score was 16-0 when Breck County plated their lone run in the home half of the inning. The game was called via run rule.
Lily Roberts got the win on the mound while allowing no runs on no hits, with six Ks and no walks over three perfect innings. Bella Bryant allowed one run on two hits, with two Ks and one walk in one inning of relief. Ashlyn White took the loss for Breck County.
Estes was 4 for 4 with two home runs, a triple and three RBI. Waltrip was 2 for 3 with the slam, a triple and five RBI. Layni Roberts was 2 for 3 with a triple and two RBI, Ella House was 2 for 4 with one RBI, Emmalynn Higdon was 1 for 2 with a triple and one RBI, Audrey Carnes was 1 for 3 with a double and one RBI, and Lily Roberts was 1 for 3 with one RBI. Carolina Jones, Ava Riggs and Aubree Mosby all scored a run. Bryant had one RBI.
Tell City Lily Roberts had 14 strike outs and the Lady Hornets won 7-2 over the Lady Marksmen at Tell City last Thursday.
Higdon singled a run home in the first inning when Riggs scored from third base.
Roberts struck out the side in the first two innings. Lily then doubled in a run in the third before Layni Roberts followed with an RBI double to make the score 3-0.
Two Lady Hornet errors set the table for a 2-run double by B. Hayko in the fourth. Roberts pitched her way out of trouble with two more strike outs.
Bryant delivered an RBI hit in the sixth that made the score 4-2. Hancock County plated three insurance runs in the sixth before Higdon recorded the final out in right field in the seventh. Roberts got the win on the mound while allowing two runs (none earned) on four hits, with 14 Ks and two walks over seven frames. H. Mechels took the loss for Tell City.
Lily Roberts was 2 for 4 with a double and two RBI, and Layni Roberts was 1 for 2 with a double and one RBI. House and Estes were both 2 for 4, Waltrip and Bryant (RBI) both were 1 for 2, Higdon was 1 for 4 with one RBI, and Riggs scored a run and knocked in a run.

title: Brooklyn Porter Chosen as Delegate to the Congress of Future Medical Leaders
description: HCHS Junior Brooklyn Porter was chosen as a Delegate
content:
HCHS Junior Brooklyn Porter was chosen as a Delegate to the Congress of Future Medical Leaders.
Hancock County High School Junior Brooklyn Porter was chosen as a Delegate to the Congress of Future Medical Leaders, a very selective program for high school students with academic honors who have decided to study to become physicians or go into medical research fields after graduation.
HCHS Health Science Instructor Tiffany Carnes nominated Brooklyn for this prestigious program. Carnes is HOSA-Future Health Professionals Chapter Advisor at HCHS, and selected Brooklyn to participate in the program because of her genuine interest in the medical field.
Brooklyn said she appreciates Mrs. Carnes for instilling in her a love of healthcare, as well as supporting her in all of her classes and HOSA. She also greatly appreciates her mom, Kimberly, for making this amazing opportunity possible. 'She's always pushing me to follow my dreams,' she said.
She was accepted into the Early College Program this year to pursue her Associate's Degree in Science, and says she plans to explore her options in specialty nursing. Next school year, she will be taking all of her high school credits at OCTC, such as English 101, College Algebra and General Psychology, as well as Anatomy and Physiology classes.
This summer, she will be attending a 3-day Congress along with students from all around the United States. National Medal of Science recipients and Nobel laureates will be discussing medical research and the students will have an opportunity to hear miracle stories told by patients, get advice from medical school deans, learn about medical technology, leading medical advances and more.
Brooklyn is the daughter of Kimberly & Ryan Porter, and has 2 brothers, Jayden and Mason. Her mom is a 2nd Grade Teacher at South Hancock Elementary.
She has played percussion in the Hornet Concert Band, as well as being a color guard member in the Hornet Marching Band. She also participates in HCHS Theatre and Choir.
For years, she's been very active in Theatre Workshop of Owensboro, Shadowcasts with River Park Center, Owensboro Dance Theatre and Bluegrass Children's Theatre, and recently accepted the opportunity to attend the Giordano Dance Summer Intensive Workshop in Chicago again this year.
'I am looking for sponsors to help pay the expenses for both of these special opportunities, as both are very expensive,' Brooklyn said. 'I have to pay tuition, travel, lodging and food for both trips.'
Fundraiser & Sponsorship
Fundraiser & Sponsorship She is selling Texas Roadhouse peanuts as a fundraiser for the 2 trips she'll be taking this summer. If you would like to contribute to her fundraiser or sponsor her, please contact her mom by email at: kimberly.porter@hancock.kyschools.us. A direct contribution can be made by check to: The National Academy of Future Physicians and Medical Scientists, with Brooklyn's name on the memo. Donations of gift cards to help with lodging and meal costs would also be greatly appreciated.
Brooklyn has been assistant teaching her own Pre-K Class at the dance studio, where she has studied dance for 14 years now. She's also been working summers at Holiday World, and has gone on 3 international mission trips to Honduras.
She worked in Comayagua and El Ayundante building pilas (above ground water basins) and latrines, painting a school, installing water filtration systems and sharing the gospel to the families at each work site. Her 3rd trip, she went to Tela and worked with a new start-up mission reaching out to the community, helping with Beach Vacation Bible School and painting a school.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Urban planning and more zoning discussed at Monday's meeting
description: The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission met on Monday evening, May 6th at the HC Administration Building in Hawesville, for a special meeting to make up for their missed meeting during the…
content:
The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission met on Monday evening, May 6th at the HC Administration Building in Hawesville, for a special meeting to make up for their missed meeting during the ‘23/'24 fiscal year. Members discussed the continued growth of Hancock County, which will require further zoning.
The discussion began with Greg Wettstain addressing the fact that with continued growth in the County, there is a need for more zoning. Tommy Turner also expressed his concerns about areas throughout the County that are still yet to be zoned.
New member Julie Vogt, of Lewisport, was sworn-in by Commission Attorney T. Tommy Littlepage. The Lewisport City Council made the approval for Vogt to serve on the City's Planning & Zoning Board in March of this year, as reported in The Clarion.
Chairman Tim Cecil, Administrator Jeff Dame and members also discussed the election of a new Commission Vice Chairman to replace the unexpired term of Tommy Hunt.
A History of the Urban Planning Commission
The Hancock County-City Planning & Zoning Commission, as it was first named, was established in the late 1960s. One of the important realizations that inspired the forming of the commission, was that it is essential for the county to receive grants and loans for infrastructure projects in the county, such as sewer projects in Lewisport and Hawesville.
Those who served on the commission in 1969 were: Brinton Wiles, Chairman; James S. Pell, Joe C. Pell, Jim Fallin, George Allard, John Emmick, Ralph Boling, Billy Taylor, Otto Keown, J.C. Adams, Delbert Boyd and Robert Feltner.
These individuals worked diligently to set up the overall planning and zoning program that would take several years to fully establish. Interim zoning regulations were outlined, with regulations that were completed in the span of approximately one year.
At their March meeting in 1969, Feltner briefly outlined the work that had been done to date by the commission to develop the program for the welfare and potential of the county saying, 'One of the most important things is that everything needs a plan before it can be properly developed. Planning and zoning is needed in this county.'
Many of the commission's regular meetings during the late 60s and early 70s were sponsored by the Hancock County Chamber of Commerce. One such meeting was held on Thursday, June 4th, 1970, which was a Public Forum at the RECC building in Hawesville, open to all citizens interested in the future of Hancock County and the purpose of planning and zoning.
The meeting was led by Feltner, Commission Vice Chairman at the time. Mr. Henry Hodges from the department of Economic Development, Frankfort, was also present at the meeting to discuss the state's role in the project. Then Chamber President, Randy Shultz, vocalized the extreme importance of the commission as well.
It was in January of 1970 that new members had been elected. That regular meeting was held at the Lewisport Community Center. Brinton Wiles was re-elected Chairman; Robert Feltner-Vice Chairman, and William Taylor was re-elected Secretary-Treasurer.
iles, Taylor and John Emmick were selected as a new committee to study the candidates for Zoning Inspector at this early commission meeting. In addition, a committee of Robert Feltner, Jim Fallin and J.C. Adams was appointed to draft recommendations for administering the zoning code, building permit fees, and the other matters pertaining to county-wide zoning.
It was also announced at this meeting that the permanent code was expected to be established in that year (1970). Other business discussed, was that Sheriff Ralph Boling's seat on the Planning Commission would be filled by R.M. d'Oliveira, Manager of Southwire's Rod & Cable Mill, and Robert Feltner would replace Otto Keown.
In the following meetings that year, a committee was appointed by County Judge Joe Pell to make adjustments in zoning where applications varied with the code.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: County Storm Shelters discussed at Hawesville Council Meeting
description: The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, May 14th. Councilman Danny Doyle had brought up the question about storm shelters in Hancock County at the last council meeting. Hawesville Fire…
content:
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, May 14th. Councilman Danny Doyle had brought up the question about storm shelters in Hancock County at the last council meeting. Hawesville Fire Chief Shane Richards researched since then, and reported that there are zero FEMA certified shelters in the county's response area.
'There are 2 housing-only shelters,' Richards said. 'One is the Hawesville United Methodist Church and the other one is the Hancock County Senior Citizens Center. Those are the 2 shelters we have listed with Emergency Management. Those are the only ones we have in our area.'
Councilman Danny Doyle said, 'Thank you, Shane. You all do a good job. I'd like to start making people aware where those places are. We failed to do that over the years. I'd like to see us stay on top of that.'
Richards added, 'The FEMA certification on those – there's a lot of things that go along with those as far as being able to do that certification. Most of that will go through Emergency Management, but we can work with them and see if we can get something rolling in that direction. It is a project that we will take on.'
Fire Dept. Report
Fire Dept. Report Richards continued with his monthly report saying, 'For the month of April, total calls were 52 runs for the month; the majority of those being 18 good-intent calls, which were, essentially, anything that was cancelled on. There were 15 EMS calls. Breaking down those totals – there were 39 total for the fire runs and 13 total for the rescue calls. Our grand total for the year is at 186 calls so far.
We got the boat back from the county today with the new Hawesville striping on it. As of right now, it's going to be housed at the top of the hill until we can free up some space.
We have the Forestry grant we're working on. We're processing all the equipment for it. It's a 50/50 split grant for us, for different forestry equipment. Some changes have been made to that; It's gearing more toward brush fires and forest fire type equipment.
We have an application in with the National Volunteer Fire Council for a PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) Grant. There are 12 grants for 4 sets each, nationwide. We're trying to get those, if at all possible.
We went to the fiscal court evening meeting last month and I presented them with a fact sheet. I have copies for you if you would like. We were, basically, told by our vendor on our air packs that Honeywell is getting out of the air pack business; all parts and services are going out on Dec. 16th, 2024. Those will no longer be a viable option for use.
We're in the process of figuring out what we're going to do to replace all of them. We went to the county first because all 4 departments in the county have the same model and style packs. We're going to have to replace everything in the county. It's totaling out right now at 48 air packs. In Hawesville we've got 15. We're looking at how to replace those.
We are working with different vendors. They're offering pricing breaks right now. We're trying to find the funding for it. The ballpark figure for the county was $330K for all 48 packs. Our 15 packs in Hawesville would total approximately between $103K – $113K.'
Mayor Robbie McCormick said, 'We see what the fire department is facing. One thing I've done is I have reached out to Owensboro on their emergency truck that you all are wanting. They are willing to work with us. I'm trying to keep it from going to auction. So we're trying to do an inner-city transfer. I'm in hopes that will work out but I can't make any commitment to that now.'
Richards said, 'That plan is, hopefully, to replace our squad 202 truck, our smallest truck we have, that was built in-house several years ago. We want to replace it with an actual service-built rescue truck. We're in the process of doing that as well.'
City Manager's Report
City Manager's Report The Domtar 2K Your Way program began last year, providing $2,000 for assistance with a variety of areas where it can be applied, at each recipient's choice. City Manager Jake Powers said, 'We're going to use the Domtar 2K Your Way grant for the reimbursement of the trees and everything that we used for the tree planting along Main Street. We had submitted that application to Domtar to fund the tree planting and Clean-up Day we hosted. We're still waiting to see if we were awarded on that.'
City Maintenance
City Maintenance Superintendent Brian Patterson provided an update. Todd Adkins has officially retired, and Patterson is the new Hawesville Superintendent. He's working on getting his new structure, he said, and has one person dedicated for the water plant, one for the sewer plant, one for maintenance, and 2 individuals focused on mowing, weed eating and trash pick-up for the City.
Budget Amendment
Budget Amendment The first reading of the city's budget amendment was read by City Attorney Jamie Stephens. McCormick explained, 'This budget has been gone through thoroughly. I've gone through it. Councilman Wayne Herndon has gone through it. There are several adjustments on this because we are now working off of facts. We've gotten far enough along that we can work off of facts. Next year, this budget will not be written like this. The budget will have line items like our sister city (Lewisport) is using to where we can track that. We need to emulate some of the good things they do and that is one.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Feeling 'Chosen' by Angel Studios
description: Jamie D. Taylor at Angel Studios in Utah. When my late husband, Dave Taylor, passed away on September 5, 2022, I knew I was also entering a fight for my life. I knew my spiritual life and soul
content:
Jamie D. Taylor at Angel Studios in Utah.
When my late husband, Dave Taylor, passed away on September 5, 2022, I knew I was also entering a fight for my life. I knew my spiritual life and soul was at stake. See, our souls are the most precious commodity in existence, and I knew I needed to fall into God's arms more than ever before, if I was going to survive.
I made the decision to be even more cautious about the environment I was in. This meant only listening to Christian music, watching positive and uplifting tv shows, movies, and reading books with these qualities.
It was at this time I finally decided to begin watching 'The Chosen'. I'd heard many great things about it, but I hadn't made an effort to watch it. Once I did, I couldn't stop.
I was eager to find out about the next season and other productions from the same company which led me to the Angel Studios website. It was there I found the opportunity to invest in 'His Only Son', which would become their first theatrical release in March 2023.
I've always loved movies and just about any form of entertainment, even participating in productions as a stagehand during my childhood, taking improv classes as an adult, performing stand-up, and being a co-host on a successful podcast. Unfortunately, the older I got and the closer to God, the less comfortable I felt in the entertainment industry.
Finding the opportunity to participate as an investor in a Christian film and have my name in the credits meant everything to me! I didn't realize it at the time; this investment came with a free six-month membership to something called the 'Angel Guild'. The Angel Guild is the vetting body for all projects produced or distributed by Angel Studios and only projects that pass can become Angel Studios productions. To join the Guild, you had to have been an investor. This changed in October of 2023, and now you can pay a small fee to join on a monthly or annual basis.
Since joining the Guild in March of 2023, I have become the number one ranked Guild Member of about 300,000. This has given me the opportunity to participate in internal streams as well as being asked for my opinion on changes within the Guild. Earlier this year, I found the opportunity to participate as an extra in Season Five of 'The Chosen' which was filming in Goshen, Utah. This is only thirty minutes South of Provo, Utah, where Angel Studios Headquarters is located.
A week before my scheduled days of filming, I was emailing one of my Angel Studios contacts and mentioned I would be in Utah soon and he insisted I stop by the offices! After two twelve-hour days of filming on April 29-30, I stopped by Angel Studios on May 1st, where I was treated like a celebrity! Apparently, my name had been brought up several times in corporate meetings as the number one Guild Member and even the President made sure to meet me while I was visiting!
It was during this visit I was invited back the following week to attend 'Illuminate', the Angel Studios big annual event where the previous year's successes are discussed, upcoming projects are announced, and awards are given.
I returned May 6th and was able to attend a screening for the upcoming 4th of July release 'Sound of Hope: The Story of Possum Trot', as well as 'Illuminate', where I was given VIP access and even helped present the awards to this year's winners in front of all the directors, producers, executives, actors, and financiers of Angel Studios productions.
It was an amazing and spectacular experience, and I am forever grateful for God's unceasingly remarkable and unexpected blessings!
For information regarding being an extra on 'The Chosen' visit comeandseefoundation.org. For information regarding joining the Angel Guild, visit angel.com.
By Jamie D. Taylor

title: Healthy Habits: Castor Oil
description: Castor oil has been used in home remedies for centuries. The oil is extracted from the c
content:
Castor oil has been used in home remedies for centuries. The oil is extracted from the castor seed, botanically named ricinus communis, which is said to have antiviral, antibacterial, antifungal, anti-parasitic and anti-inflammatory properties.
Castor oil has many topical and internal uses, but I will be focusing on topical remedies here. It can be helpful in stimulating the immune system and in treating skin conditions, urinary problems, pain & inflammation, infections and digestive/gastrointestinal challenges.
A pack can be applied topically for an effective way to strengthen the lymphatic system, increase lymphatic flow and promote lymphatic drainage. There are high levels of ricinoleic acid in the castor seed, a special fatty acid with healing qualities. Ricinoleic acid has the ability to penetrate through the top layer of skin to the dermis, and can break up scar tissue and congestion, i.e. boils, acne, etc.
Hundreds of years ago, the castor seed plant was named 'Palma Christe' because the leaves, people said, looked like the hand of Christ Jesus. The plant is native to India, and is used worldwide for its medicinal properties.
Castor Oil Pack A 'pack' can be made by soaking cloths in organic, unrefined castor oil and then wrapping them over a specific area of the body. For example, to boost lymphatic drainage, wrap the castor oil cloths around your midsection, cover with dry towels and plastic wrap, and apply heat for up to 2 hours.
Castor oil packs can be used for:
balancing hormones,
reducing pain,
minimizing inflammation,
bringing down swelling,
detoxing,
promoting the healing of internal organs,
soothing & calming the nervous system,
strengthening the immune system and
relieving PMS & cramping. These packs are said to effectively treat endometriosis, fibroids, liver congestion, ovarian cysts, swollen lymph glands, acne and more. Always do your research and/or talk with your health practitioner before trying any home remedies.
There are some contraindications to consider. For instance, it can be useful during labor and birthing, but it should not be used during the pregnancy because it could cause induced labor, or cause the mother to experience dehydration and other symptoms that could be possibly harmful to the baby.
Treating Acne There are several different recipes you can try with organic castor oil to treat acne. It can be applied to the effected areas as a compress, and can be paired with one or more of the following: organic jojoba oil, turmeric powder, tea tree oil, and organic therapeutic grade essential oils such as juniper berry, clary sage and sandalwood.
Hair & Scalp Treatment Castor oil can be massaged into the scalp to relieve dryness and stimulate hair growth. A deep conditioning hair treatment that is also said to strengthen the hair fibers can be easily done at home by first dampening your hair and gently towel drying out the extra moisture.
Apply the castor oil to your damp hair and scalp and cover with a shower cap. Wrap a hot towel over the shower cap and allow to sit for at least 30 minutes before washing out. These hair treatments can be applied once a month or more often. You can also add a few drops of organic rosemary essential oil to the castor oil before applying it.
Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Dorothy Nutt
description: Dorothy Hayden Nutt, age 86, of Nicholasville, Kentucky, died May 25, 2024 after a short illness. She was born April 12, 1938, in Daviess County, Kentucky, the daughter of the late Loyd Russell and…
content:
Dorothy Hayden Nutt, age 86, of Nicholasville, Kentucky, died May 25, 2024 after a short illness. She was born April 12, 1938, in Daviess County, Kentucky, the daughter of the late Loyd Russell and Dorothy Mae Allgood Hayden. She was preceded in death by her brothers, Larry Lee Hayden and William Michael Hayden and her sister, Mackey Jo Hayden.
Survivors include her husband, Michael James Nutt, of Nicholasville; two sons, Stephen Gerald Ayres (Danielle) of Nicholasville, and Bradley Lloyd Ayres (Jimena), of Estero, Florida. Sisters: Sherry Hayden Pulliam of Owensboro, Kentucky, and Becky Hayden LeRoy (John), of Las Cruces, New Mexico. Four grandchildren: Dexter Ayres, Nicholasville; and Lauren, Madeline, and Katherine Ayres of Jupiter, Florida. Nephews: Scott, Todd, and Jeff Pulliam, Owensboro, Kentucky; and Robbie Hazelrigg, Tell City, Indiana. Nieces: Ginger Fleming, Hawesville, Kentucky; Susan Hazelrigg, Las Cruces, New Mexico; Lee Ann Chappell and Donna Bland of Lewisport, Kentucky; Renee Hayden, Marietta, Georgia; and Elizabeth Hudson, Umatilla, Florida. And, twenty-four great nieces and great nephews.
Dorothy retired in 2001 from International Paper Company in Memphis, Tennessee, after 11 years of service. She had previously retired from General Electric Company, Owensboro, Kentucky and Portland, Oregon, after 26 years of service.
She was a member of the Lewisport United Methodist Church, and her family and friends were her enjoyment in life. She loved traveling with her special friends Pat, Martha, and Mary Maude.
Services will be held on Friday, May 31 at Gibson & Son Funeral Home in Lewisport, Kentucky. Family visitation will be from 10:00am – 11:00am, public visitation from 11:00am – 1:00pm. Funeral service will begin at 1:00pm and immediately following will be the graveside service at Lewisport Cemetery.
The family requests that in lieu of flowers, expressions of sympathy may take the form of donations to the Lewisport Methodist Church or Church/Charity of one's choice.

title: Healthy Habits: Coconut Water
description: The fresh juice of green, 'young' coconuts is what is referred to as coconut water, not to be confused with coconut milk, which is an emulsion of coconut water blended with the freshly grated inner…
content:
The fresh juice of green, 'young' coconuts is what is referred to as coconut water, not to be confused with coconut milk, which is an emulsion of coconut water blended with the freshly grated inner flesh of mature coconuts.
Fresh organic coconut water is wonderfully hydrating and replenishes electrolytes. It is a choice alternative to sports drinks, juice drinks and sodas that can be loaded with sugar, artificial colors & flavors and preservatives.
Here are some of the many health benefits that coconut water can offer:
boosts hydration,
assists in optimal digestion,
aids metabolism,
helps with weight loss & healthy weight management (helps reduce food cravings),
destroys intestinal parasites,
prevents kidney stones,
calms urinary tract infections,
replenishes electrolytes,
promotes healthy skin,
reduces blood pressure,
improves heart health,
improves cognitive function/memory,
increases energy levels naturally,
helps reduce joint pain, cools the body/regulates body temperature,
and helps regulate blood sugar. (*The natural sweetness of coconut water can satisfy sugar cravings as a healthy alternative for those on low sugar diets.) One cup of coconut water contains approximately sixteen percent of our daily recommended potassium, which assists in keeping fluid and electrolyte levels balanced. One cup of coconut water also provides: about 56 mg of calcium, 60 mg of magnesium, 10.4 g of carbs, 0.5 g of protein & manganese, and only 44 calories, with zero fat and cholesterol.
I recommend unflavored Harmless Harvest Brand Organic Coconut Water. I'm sure there are other good brands out there, but this one just stands out above all others I've tried. It has a great taste, it's naturally sweet but not too sweet, and the company seems to have the highest standards for quality.
It is interesting to note that the consistency of coconut water is similar to the liquid inside our red blood cells. There is a myth that coconut water is identical to plasma. It is not. There are, however, reported emergency cases where IV fluids ran out in remote areas or weren't available at all, and pure, fresh coconut water was used successfully as an alternative.
Contraindications
Contraindications If you have a health condition that requires limiting potassium or sodium, then coconut water may not be a good choice for you. Along with the aforementioned amount of potassium in the water, it also contains around 101 mg of sodium per each 8 ounce serving. With any suggestion that I make in my columns, please always do your own research and/or talk with your doctor before trying.
Hydration
Hydration While coconut water is a great alternative to sports drinks, sodas and other drinks loaded with cane sugar, it isn't meant to replace water. Coconut water is over 90 percent water itself, but make sure you are still drinking plenty of filtered water daily. It is recommended that adults drink eight 8-ounce glasses of water a day.
Some warning signs of dehydration are: headache, dizziness/lightheadedness, fatigue, confusion, and dry mouth, eyes and lips. The human body is 60 percent water. Losing even 2 percent of our body's water content can hinder memory, clarity, mood, etc.
Staying hydrated decreases the risk of kidney stones, relieves/prevents constipation, reduces headaches, improves physical & mental performance, and according to studies can provide migraine headache relief, just to name a few. So stay hydrated!
~Be Well and God Bless You.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Bluegrass Engineering gives updates on projects for City of Hawesville
description: The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, June 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-Owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided an update on projects. st
content:
The Hawesville City Council met on Tuesday evening, June 11th, and Matt Curtis, Co-Owner of Bluegrass Engineering, provided an update on projects.
Storm Water Project
Storm Water Project Curtis said, 'Several months ago, we had to increase the budget for the Storm Water Project. That request to FEMA has been approved. In the meantime, GRADD has been working on the matching funds to take care of the City's portion of that, and 5.2 percent was the low match. The new budget number of $3.35M took it up $174K.
We've gotten word that the City will have a zero cost facility. We're expecting to see the Local Match Participation Program Grant, which is the grant for the City, after the start of the fiscal year on July 1.
The next steps on it is mechanical design, the structure and all mechanical and electrical components of the projects, including the force mains (pipelines) going up over the levee area are going to be completely gutted. When it's done the bones are still going to be there but all of the mechanical equipment and electrical components are going to be brought up 7 decades from when it was first put in (the current plant was installed in the early 50s).
The electrical design is just getting started. That's one of the requirements for the Army Corps of Engineers. We have to meet their electrical standards before we have our next process. Once that takes place, we're looking to try to bid this late 3rd quarter into the 4th quarter of this year.'
Phase One of the entire project will be the sluice gate, he said. That will be the top priority of the contractor who's bid is accepted later in the year. In the meantime, other equipment will be used to raise the gate until the plant is fully built. 'When the river comes up,' he said, 'we can shut the sluice gate and then we can pump. Right now, we have to have other equipment means to raise that gate until this thing is fully built.'
Cleaner Water Program
Cleaner Water Program 'The state has come out with the Cleaner Water Program (Bipartisan Infrastructure Law New Funding 2022 to improve drinking H2O & wastewater). State legislature reorganized how the grant funding will come in. Previously, it came down to KIA (KY Infrastructure Authority) and then they would come to the local officials and determine what the priorities were in the community and then it was dispersed.
Now, the state legislature has gotten involved and KIA is going to rank them. Those rankings are going to go to state legislature and then next spring the legislature is going to [divvy those out]. That is a funding source that we're looking at for several future projects for the City of Hawesville.
We'll be looking at a project award knowing that we're getting funding in April 2025. That window is open right now but the state hasn't provided an application to submit. That window closes August 15th, 2024. We know what we've got to do and we'll get that taken care of.'
Contact State Reps
Contact State Reps Curtis said this is an opportunity for City officials and citizens of Hancock County to contact local state representatives, state senators, etc., and tell them that this is a HUGE priority for the City of Hawesville to get this funding.
Regional Water Plant
Regional Water Plant He continued saying, 'The Hancock County Regional Water Plant ranked Second in the entire state of KY for the drinking water project. That project will be funded this round of revolving funds. How that money is coming down, 100 percent loan or a percentage of it being up for forgiveness, we don't know at this point until the Intended Use Plan comes out. I was talking with KIA today and they're thinking that it will be at the end of summer before that plan comes out. As more details come up about that we will come back and make sure you guys are updated.'
Future Projects
Future Projects He added, 'With future projects for the City of Hawesville, one of the things we were meeting about was talking about the regional water plant and making sure that we've gotten some of the problems as far as what is out there in your distribution, where they are having to go and make repeated repairs over and over again, and closing the system up by creating more loops so you don't have dead end lines.
This is so they are not having to flush water and put water on the ground – all measures to get you to the point of – if and when you decide to become a non-producer and if you're purchasing water that you're able to sell every drop of water that you possibly can instead of putting it out on the ground.
There are 3 projects that we're working on with Superintendent Brian Patterson and GRADD to get those in and apply for funding. There are 2 water system improvements. Phase One has a bunch on lines in areas we have issues in distribution. The Center Booster Station has been an issue with piping failures, and [correcting issues] on Harrison Street, Main Cross, etc., and also creating some loops out on KY 69 and Old Hartford Rd.
Phase 2 is with the pump station- here recently, the Cities had tanks inspected. The inspector told me that we might as well count on interior and exterior minor structural repairs. There are the 2 unused tanks on Hawes Blvd. and Fred Hodges, and there's the Donna Lou Ln. Water Main that we've had issues with.
One other, is the Windward Heights Lift Station. It is something that Brian and the crew are having issues with. It's not in a good location. One solution we've talked about is moving it away from the intersection down into that grassy field area, to where an accident wouldn't cause damage which has happened before.'
Force Main Project
Force Main Project 'The KYTC (KY Transportation Cabinet) Force Main Projects (conveying wastewater from a lower to higher elevation) – we've been working with the KY Finance & Administration Cabinet. It was put out for bids. There were zero bids received on May 30. Their process is a nightmare to work with is my guess why there were no bids. If you don't do things a certain way it kicks back. They have put it back out to private quotation through KYTC. We provided names of several contractors that we're familiar with that we feel would be a good fit for this project. We're waiting for those bids to come in.'
Regionalizing
Regionalizing The amount of funding for regionalizing is huge right now, McCormick said. Curtis explained why saying, 'I've been talking with (GRADD Executive Director) Joanna Shake and Blake Edge at GRADD and this was the highest ranked project that they've ever had come out of the counties they serve.
The reason for that is last year Hawesville was not listed in that project profile. It was 101st ranked in the state last year. This year, there was a discussion about Hawesville interconnect – a stand alone plant that both cities would be purchasing the water from and there was more of that regionalization talk and then it went from 101st to 2nd. It is HUGE. The state put a ton of money in what they are calling ‘generational projects'. If you check certain boxes, they are throwing money at them.
They're looking at multi-million dollar projects to try to get all these small communities, as many of them as they can, to compliance with what is coming down with the regulations of the emerging contaminants, which are PFAS (plastic chemicals). These have to be removed from drinking water and eventually will have to be removed from wastewater and, all the while, the manufacturing of those chemicals is still occurring. Removing something that is continuing to be produced – you're never going to be able to get it out of the water systems, but that's where the EPA is going and we will have to all follow suit.'
McCormick said, 'They are really pushing hard for regionalization and we've all talked. I don't want to regionalize east at all. We definitely don't want to regionalize west or south, into Daviess County, etc. If we do, we want to within our County to where we're all getting the funding and can have better opportunities, but before we buy a single drop, these lines will be replaced as infrastructure, these worst places. That is going to give us the opportunity to get the money to do the infrastructure by tacking it onto a regionalization.
We've not committed to anything. All we're doing is saying we're interested. We are willing to take a look at it but if we were to do it tomorrow, we'd spend twice the money that we're spending right now on the water because you're buying the water then, you're not producing.'
Curtis said, 'There are multiple costs associated with what the fee is for the thousand gallons that you all would be purchasing. The whole premise in all of the discussions we've had of here and in Lewisport is that it is equal for both communities.
The regionalization – they're pushing it along with the emerging contaminants. There was a push for OMU (Owensboro Municipal Utilities) to come east and at that time (25-30 years ago), it was $15M-$16M then. To give you a point of reference, OMU just spent $50M in that range. They are getting ready to go ahead and go back and put another $30M into that plant to meet PFAS regulations.
The technology has been looked at. For Lewisport's plant it's been taken care of from day one. We're not going to have to go back. The cost of the emerging contaminants are staggering. It's not a one time you build it and it's done. You have to go back and replace your filter every so many years. It is never ending.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: The Tree House
description: When I was a little girl I always wanted to build a tree house, but there was never a tree available. Then, when my kids were young they wanted one. Movies portrayed tree houses as a place where kids…
content:
When I was a little girl I always wanted to build a tree house, but there was never a tree available. Then, when my kids were young they wanted one. Movies portrayed tree houses as a place where kids could get away from their parents and hang out with friends. They take big trees with long strong branches. Our trees were always too small.
My kids are always doing something special for my birthday. This year my son called and said, 'I've found a tree house. It's big enough for a party.' He sent me pictures and, sure enough, there up in the trees sat a cabin. It was in the town where he lives – Horse Cave, KY, not that far from Hancock County. My son rented it for the weekend of my birthday.
When we arrived at the tree house and climbed the 3 flights of steps to get there, I found a dream come true, a fully furnished kitchen with everything we'd need to cook a meal, nice living room, bedroom with primitive log bed, bath and upstairs loft with two queen beds. The outside deck provided a gas grill, table, chairs and lawn furniture in the tree tops. I had the best birthday ever. I felt like a kid again.
The tree house is part of KOA Campground. Also available, there are covered wagons and teepees where families can stay. Across from the campground is Kentucky Down Under. This is a park where one can see the animals of Australia. The kids took me there for my birthday last year. I got to walk among the kangaroos and wallabies and pet them. I was thrilled to see a mama kangaroo with a baby joey peeking out of its mother's pouch.
We went shopping at the many gift and collectable shops near Cave City. My favorite is Hippy Joe's where one can purchase 50s and 60s clothing and memorabilia. This is all part of the tourism around Mammoth Cave, Cave City and Horse Cave. I always enjoyed the small caves with their stalactites and stalagmites, the beautiful crystal onyx, and the massiveness of Mammoth Cave.
My kids loved Dinosaur World with its life size dinosaurs. They love Topsy Turvy World where they make water run uphill. They came out of there disoriented, sometimes unable to walk without staggering. Funtown Mountain was once Guntown Mountain. It is an old western town. It has been closed this year for the making of a western movie. It should open up soon.
These are just some of the entertainment possibilities. Why travel long distances when you can find this close to home? I have really enjoyed visiting this area.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: An Essay By HCHS Graduate Alexis Gay
description: Hancock County, a small county located along the Ohio River in the Owensboro Metropolitan Area. The county was formed in 1829 by...
content: Hancock County, a small county located along the Ohio River in the Owensboro Metropolitan Area. The county was formed in 1829 by taking parts of Breckinridge, Daviess and Ohio counties. From its beginnings to its evolution into a center of industry, Hancock County has had a significant amount of economic growth and change over the years. Prior to plants and mills, Hancock County consisted of small farming communities, logging and timber, and small shops and inns. Agriculture has always been a fundamental part of the economy, being that it is an ideal place with fertile soil and a temperate climate. The potential for agriculture opportunities was quickly recognized, and staple crops such as tobacco, corn, and wheat were grown. Another important factor to the growth of Hancock County's industry is its geographical location along the Ohio River. This location of the county was well-positioned and ideal to take advantage of the growing trade along the river. Not only was the county ideally geographically located for trade and commerce, but there was also an expanse of people that was eager and willing to fulfill the job in new industries that the 1960s would bring. With the revolution of industry in the 1960s came plants and mills. Among these, included was paper, aluminum, and power. These industries have powered the economic health of our community. With these facilities, over 2,500 manufacturing jobs are supporting the community and providing good wages and benefits to those who hold them. These jobs provide reliability and dependability to those in the community. The paper industry started in the mid 1960s with a brown paper mill called Wescor. They made brown corrugated paper for the center of boxes. Then, in the late 1960s, because of the great location to resources, an expansion of sorts for the paper industry was created with the addition of a fluff pulp mill named Western Kraft. They made bleached pulp for other paper mills throughout the country for paper creation. In the late 1970s early 1980s another expansion was completed under the new paper mill owners Willamette Industries. They added a paper machine that took the bleach pulp already produced on site and turned it into uncoated free sheet, what we know as copy paper. And then again in the mid 1990s another upgrade to the site was completed, adding another paper machine called H2. It was the widest paper machine at the time, also producing uncoated free sheet for the paper market. This mill over time stimulated the workforce, not only creating hundreds of jobs at the paper mill but created jobs for truckers bringing chips and sawdust to the mill; Truck drivers that delivered paper to end users that the mill produced. The mill also used the railroad system to deliver paper and pulp to other areas of the country for use. Also, in the 1960s, the Aluminum industry was attracted to the county because of the same resources and geographical location. Companies like Martin Marietta, now Commonwealth Rolled Products, NSA, now Century Aluminum, and Southwire company. These corporations all had ties to each other. Century provided some of the purest aluminum made in the world. NSA supplied Martin Marietta with pure aluminum so they could make alloys to sell to industries such as the defense department, mobile home sector, and the trucking industry to make semi-trailers. NSA also provided pure aluminum to the Southwire corporation to make aluminum cable that carries electricity throughout the community of Hancock County. These industries have thrived in Hancock County for decades and have helped shape the economy, landscape, and livelihood of the business and residents of not only Hancock County but many surrounding counties as well. There have been small business startups associated with supporting these big industries throughout Hancock County and our region of Kentucky. Small businesses such as restaurants, insurance companies, welding contractors, and electrical contractors to name a select few. These industries are still shaping Hancock County today with new technologies they bring to the community. High school students get exposure to these industries early in their lives due to their parents or grandparents that have worked at one of these industries. The industries have sought out these kids to help them make career decisions for their future through co-op programs that expose what types of jobs exist at each place. The industries have also been key in donating time and or money to special projects within the community and school such as sports and clubs. It is hard to say how much the history of these industries have impacted the county, the people, and the region to date. It is unimaginable what Hancock County would be like if we didn't have this rich industrial history.

title: School Board freeing-up funding for future project
description: The Hancock County Board of Education meeting was held on Thursday, June 20th. They have been going through the process to free-up funding that can be applied to a future project. 'We have old…
content:
The Hancock County Board of Education meeting was held on Thursday, June 20th. They have been going through the process to free-up funding that can be applied to a future project.
'We have old construction projects that were never closed out,' Superintendent Robby Asberry said, 'and so there is money sitting in there. Trey Anderson, when he took over as CFO (Chief Financial Officer/Treasurer), has been working to close all of those old ones out to where the money could be spent on a future construction project.'
The Board approved closeouts in May and again at this month's meeting. The process to free-up these funds is as such: the Board approves one to be closed out, it is sent to the KY Dept. of Education, and then the KDE brings it back and the Board sends the next.
'We actually have another step,' Asberry said. 'We will be closing out some projects in July. Some of the projects were in the negative and some of them were in the positive. Overall, it was a net positive. One of the old projects closed out was the building of NHES from '04/'05. These are all of the different construction projects throughout the school system that were never closed out for some reason.
The big thing that we're still thinking about is the construction of the new middle school. That is something we're still working towards. With construction costs that keep going up, we're not there yet. We want all of that to go toward that future funding.'
KSBA
Every year, the Kentucky School Board Association requires that the schools' policies are upgraded accordingly with all new laws. KSBA does this for every school district in the state.
Asberry explained, 'KSBA takes the new KY revised statutes enacted during the last legislative session and makes sure that all of our policies coincide with the new laws. The only changes we had were any revisions that had to be changed because of any new laws that were passed.'
KSBA requires that the National Motto 'In God We Trust' be displayed in a prominent location in each elementary and secondary school in the Commonwealth, for example, per KRS 158.195.
The most notable change approved by the Board, per these new laws, is to display on the district's internet landing page the percentage of students scoring Proficient and Distinguished in reading and math, as well as at the top of each page of the district's website in a banner format, along with a web link to the detailed results of the district's performance on the most recent Summative Assessment.
HCHS Fees
The Board approved a list of fees for the '24/'25 School Year at Hancock County High School. Those are as follows: Math Department-$10, Agriculture Dept.-$25 (an increase of $5), Choir-$10 (new fee), and Art-$10 (new fee). 'There really were no significant changes,' Asberry said. 'These school fees, usually, are those consumable things for the student (products or items the student will use up completely).'
Pledge of Collateral
As required by the KDE every year, the Board completes a Pledge of Collateral with their bank, First Financial Bank. This measure certifies that their bank has enough cash collateral above the FDIC insurance, and that the money that HC Schools puts into the bank is protected.
Treasurer's Bond
The Board approved a $500K bond for HC Schools Treasurer Trey Anderson. This bond of insurance is required by the KDE of every school district annually, and is a protective measure for any financial fraud or errors.
Auditor's Contract
The HC BOE is audited annually, as all districts are, and the Board approved Patrick & Associates for this year's audit which will begin in August and is due on November 15th, 2024.
Hancock County native, Kris Kemp, partner at Myriad CPA Group, has presented the audit for the last several years. The firm is under time constraints and can only do so many school districts this year, which is why they could not do HC Schools audit. 'A lot of auditors can only take so many school districts,' Asberry said, 'so we'll be going with a new auditor this year.'
CPA Tammy Patrick, partner at Patrick & Associates, he said, will likely be the one presenting the audit at an upcoming HC BOE meeting this year.
Preschool Program
An increase in days for the Preschool Instructional Assistant Program and Bus Monitor Positions was approved. All preschool students will now receive 5 days of instruction. Asberry said, 'We feel this was a better schedule for the parents of preschool students. This change will also increase the Preschool Instructional Assistants to 173 days, and our Preschool Bus Monitor to 180 days.'
CEP Pilot-Complete Forms
As reported in The Clarion, a district-wide Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) Pilot was approved by the Hancock County Board of Education during their April meeting. CEP is a non-pricing meal service option for schools in low-income areas and will be implemented for one year beginning in fall, and then reviewed again for approval for the '25/'26 school year.
Asberry said that free and reduced lunch forms must still be completed by the parents/caregivers of all students. 'That paperwork is the reason why we're able to do the free breakfast and lunch for all students,' he said. 'People call it 'free lunch forms' but it's so much more than that. There are so many more things that we use that information for.
That's the reason we're able to do the CEP, because of how many free and reduced lunch students that we have. It's VERY important for parents/caregivers to fill that out. It will be with the student enrollment forms. It is online registration.'
Families will be receiving those forms sometime in July, he said. Regardless of income or status, every student in a participating school gets this free meal service through the program, and success is determined by participation.
The program will be at no cost to the district because it's based on reimbursement from federal dollars, and will provide free breakfast and lunch to all students at HC Schools. Applications for free or reduced-price meals are at www.hancock.kyschools.us, and on the parent portal account under the More & Meal Benefits section.
Treasurer's Report
Treasurer Trey Anderson reported that the balance on-hand at the start of the month was $5,085,507.15. The total receipts for the month were $2,288,947.14. The expenses for the month were $1,268,930.24, and the balance at close was $6,125,791.99.
Superintendent Closing Statement
Asberry said, 'I am thankful to close out another great school year. We're looking forward to improving the next school year, like we do every year. That's what we'll be doing this summer. We want to keep moving forward and keep improving every year.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Donn Wimmer, longtime Hancock Clarion editor and publisher, passes at age 89
description: Family and employees of The Hancock Clarion mourned the passing of Donn Wimmer, who died on Monday, June 24. He was the editor of The Hancock Clarion for 65 years and publisher for more than 50 years.
content:
Family and employees of The Hancock Clarion mourned the passing of Donn Wimmer, who died on Monday, June 24. He was the editor of The Hancock Clarion for 65 years and publisher for more than 50 years. He died at the age of 89.
Donn worked closely with many family members throughout the years, including his grandfather, R.I. Downs, his mother, Bernice Downs Wimmer, his sister Patricia Engle, his daughters Linda Dillon and Jennifer Wimmer and son Steve Wimmer.
His late wife, Juanita Wimmer who also assisted the newspaper when needed, passed away in 2022, while their first born, Suzanne Wimmer, passed in 2018.
Donn is considered by many to be a legend in the newspaper business, as he is believed to have been editor and publisher for longer than any other in Kentucky history.
He was honored by the Kentucky Press Association in 2006 when he was presented the prestigious Lewis Owens Award in recognition of 'Distinguished Service' to his community.
Donn running the press with his daughter, Linda. He talked about his time at the Clarion recently.
'I've lived a long 89 years and have accomplished lots of things. My involvement with the Clarion has been a great experience. It's had many challenges, but overall I loved every minute of it.'
He began his newspaper career at the The Hancock Clarion in the 1950s, working under then editor Roscoe Downs as a printer. His mother Bernice took the reins for a time before Donn became editor in the early 1970s.
Donn with his mother, Bernice. Donn's accomplishments
Some of Donn's many accomplishments include his tireless effort in getting the new airport built in Hancock County. He served as chairman of the Airport Board during its inception in realization in 2007. He continued as a board member until his death.
Donn played an integral part in forming the Industrial Foundation in Hancock County. He continued his involvement through stories and photos in the Clarion and as a board member. Donn was well known throughout the state, not only as a newspaper man, but also as a photographer and pilot.
He was the first to publish a photograph in the Clarion and later became a respected and sought after aerial photographer. He documented the construction of all the industry in the county and entertained his readers with his aerials of farms and properties throughout the county. Donn loved to fly.
He and his friend Stu Spindel teamed up to win first place in the Kentucky Air Derby in 1985. Later that same year Donn was named 'Pilot of the Year' by the National Race Pilots of America.
Donn with Stu Spindel
Donn served on many other boards and was a past member of the Jaycees, Lions Club and the Hancock County Historical Society.
He also loved to play golf and was a charter member of Windward Heights Country Club. A photo he made of the club's signature hole still hangs in his office at the Clarion.
He received many accolades over the years, including being named Hancock County Citizen of the Year.
He was also very proud of his time as Boy Scout leader. He remained in close contact with his scouts up until his death. Many of his scouts gathered recently for a dinner and reminisced about their time together.
During his later years Donn began writing a column – Remembering Stories from the past. His writings included stories about interesting past articles from the Clarion and also about growing up on a farm in Virginia.
Donn loved his family, his community and the Clarion. He will be remembered for many years to come.

title: Betty Morris
description: Betty Ford Morris, 85, of Hawesville, beloved wife, mother, Ganny and sister passed away peacefully into the arms of her Father on July 12, 2024 after having a wonderful Life. She was born on June 14,…
content:
Betty Ford Morris, 85, of Hawesville, beloved wife, mother, Ganny and sister passed away peacefully into the arms of her Father on July 12, 2024 after having a wonderful Life.
She was born on June 14, 1939 to the late Henry and Thelma Lanman Ford in Tell City, IN. A strong lover of her family, she was a wonderful mother, an amazing grandmother and such a blessing to her great grandchildren. She loved spending time with them and kept her 'goody cabinet' stocked and ready for a visit. She was preceded in death by her husband Wilford Morris, sisters Nancy Peter, Mary Marchand, Thelma Wolf, Velma Taylor and brother Henry Ford.
She is survived by her loving children, Kenny (Donna) Morris and Kevin (Jamie) Morris; grandchildren, Tori Morris, Duane Morris, Adam Morris and Tabatha Morris; 18 great grandchildren along with many nieces and nephews.
Betty worked in production at GE for 29 years and retired on July 1, 1994. She had a passion for meeting the needs of others and family was always a top priority. Every visit she made was with full of snacks for people and animals alike.
A member of Blackford Baptist Church, she loved participating in her Sunday School class and had a great relationship with those ladies. Her Class of Ruth purchased quilts and other things for those in need.
In her final moments, she was surrounded by her loving family.
Our Mom, Betty, and Ganny's memory will live on in our hearts and stories as she is now celebrating in Heaven with her Lord Jesus Christ.
Funeral Services will be held at 10 am on Monday, July 15, 2024, at Blackford Baptist Church with burial following in the church cemetery. Betty's family will be greeting friends from 3 pm until 6 pm on Sunday at Gibson and Son Funeral Home, Hawesville Chapel and from 9 am until service time at Blackford Baptist Church. Memorial contributions may be made to her Snday School Class at Blackford, The Class of Ruth. Share your memories and condolences with her family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com.

title: Parade of Homes features 15 houses in July; one in Tell City
description: Parade of Homes The 66th annual Parade of Homes begins July 20 featuring 15 newly built homes by 11 homebuild
content:
Parade of Homes
The 66th annual Parade of Homes begins July 20 featuring 15 newly built homes by 11 homebuilders.
The event will start this weekend on July 20-21 and continue the following weekend, July 27-28. Houses will be open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturdays and 1 to 5 p.m. Sundays.
Admission is free, and there will be giveaways.
'It's the most homes to be featured on the tour in five years,' says Adam Hicks, executive officer of the Green River Building Industry Association, formerly the Homebuilders Association of Owensboro. The tour includes a broad spectrum of homes in different price ranges.
Hicks stated there will be townhouses to condominiums, and two big-time homes in The Preserve, all being new builds. 'I'm excited about the variety of homes available to tour, including the parade's first venture into Indiana, with a house in Tell City included.
The Parade of Homes not only offers prospective homebuyers with a look at options available, but gives the builders an opportunity to show what sets them apart in a highly competitive industry. The Parade of Homes is a testament to the continued strength of the region's homebuilders.
'There are a lot of really good builders that build solid homes for every level of income,' said Hicks. 'So, it's just being able to show what they can do, compared to what the others can do for potential homeowners. Before a home can be in the parade, the houses must be finished, so a lot of it is just timing. A lot of the builders this year wanted to participate, so they timed their homes accordingly.'
Hicks says the Parade isn't just for those thinking about a new home. If you're not looking to build a brand-new home, but might be looking to update your current home, this tour will give you great ideas.
By Linda Dillon

title: Hawesville Moving Forward with Water Meter pilot
description: As reported in The Clar
content:
As reported in The Clarion in June, the Hawesville City Council were given a presentation by sales representatives from Fortiline Meter Company. The decision was made to go forward with a pilot/test run of 20 of those new water meters since then, as all of the City's current meters are out of warranty. At the July 9th meeting, updates were provided on how that ultrasonic system is operating.
'These meters are much more accurate on their readings,' City Manager Jake Powers said. 'In our 20 pilot order, we ordered 10 dual and 10 quad. The dual meters pick up off 2 different cell phone towers; If one of the signals isn't as strong as the other it will use the stronger signal reading.
For the quad meters, there are 4 cell towers that it can get a signal from. We had a proximity test and our signal is really good so if we can get by with just the dual meters [moving forward], then that's what we'll do because it's a little bit cheaper than the quads.'
The new meters would make for huge cost savings on manpower, fuel, and catching water leaks quicker. The City of Hawesville has lost thousands of gallons of water when leaks were not caught immediately. In the last year, there have been 21 leaks with a recorded loss of 700,400 gallons.
The manual readings the City's crewmen have been required to do monthly with the older drive-by tech meters wouldn't be necessary any longer if the decision is made to completely switch over to the new system, and would free up time for them to tend to other important work.
The software with the Fortiline meters sends out a cellular signal, reads the meter once an hour, stores the data, and sends a text message 3 times a day that is logged to a webpage assigned to the City's administration. It generates the billing data and provides access to the meter readings directly to the water customer; They can log directly into the portal and see what their meter readings are.
Superintendent Report
Hawesville Superintendent Brian Patterson reported that along with the amount of rain as well as some challenges with the City's mowing tractor, the crew has struggled with completing some of the mowing.
'I've been working with our new mapping system [on the new water meter pilot],' Patterson said. 'We've had a couple of water lines that have gotten hit. I had to go back and adjust the maps where the lines were supposed to be. This new mapping system adds the water lines and where they are exactly located.
We're working on trying to get our meters put on this map so that we know where they are. We put water drops on it and have added photos that we take. Every time we dig a water line up, we put it on there so that whoever looks at the map can look at the picture and it tells exactly what was placed in that area.'
Powers added, 'We can pull up a picture of what the repair looked like and track the water loss in that time period, and how long it was going on, how long it took to repair it, the parts, everything. We're going to use this pilot period to see the past usage rate readings compared with the new meters. The new meters are much cheaper than the old meters already. If we can get cost savings out of the meters and then it pay dividends in the long-term, then that's definitely something we're interested in doing.
It will also help on meter readings as more of these meters get implemented. Right now, about 40 percent of the old ones aren't reading the way they should; We're having to manually read meters. This will solve that and open up more man hours for our workers.'
Mayor Rob McCormick said, 'That's why this is valuable. It's really good information that they were able to add to this map. Brian is able to add where the line actually is now. You can take pictures once a line is broken and download them into the portal so they can keep track of where these breaks are, with the address, and that shows what's going on. It's excellent; This is working very well.
With the pilot, they had everything but the lids (which are ordered and coming in soon). I think that's $10,042, for the 20 meters. Brian is doing a wonderful job in tracking and keeping our water. The City is being kept up better than ever.'
Windward Heights Line Rehab Fund
McCormick spoke on the Windward Heights Line Rehab Fund saying, '$99,552.56 is in that fund and has to stay there because the loan was set on 20 year's only payment, in 2016 (previous administration). We cannot pay that until we can pay it in full, or we have to continue to pay interest on it.'
New U.S. Flags
The City purchased 50 new U.S. Flags to display downtown for Memorial Day through July 4th. Those were totaled at $1,648. City Clerk Amy Roberts has submitted an invoice to the HC Fiscal Court for those, as they have agreed to reimburse them for the cost, and McCormick said that is greatly appreciated.
Ad Valorem Tax
The first reading of the Ad Valorem taxation rate for the Fiscal Year beginning July 1st, 2024 and ending June 30th, 2025 was read and approved. The rate is set at 39.40 cents per $100 of assessed valuation on real property; 75 cents per $100 of assessed valuation on personal property; and 41.28 cents per $100 of assessed valuation for motor vehicles. The second reading will be at the August meeting.
'It was supposed to have been in effect in July,' McCormick said. 'We had 30 days after for the first reading of this. Of course, nothing changed on here. It's all the same.'
City Manager Report
City Manager Jake Powers reported, 'We've been doing a cyber security workshop. I've had a few Microsoft team meetings here. They were getting a grasp on our disaster reaction plan. If, for example, a tornado took out City Hall, would we have a place to go to operate our billing from, payments and generating the bills, and making our payments, etc.
They sent us a box that we've plugged into our server that's running tests on it to determine the strength [for a precaution against an actual cyber attack]. It will send the report back and they will review that to see what successes and failures it has and generate that report to give to us to let us know our strengths and weaknesses.
This is all free. They offer a template on what our plan should look like if we wanted to adopt one that they had. What they find out from the regional report for GRADD generates funding for everyone within the GRADD district to get cyber security funding.'
Town Hall Meeting
Powers said they are looking forward to the next Town Hall Meeting scheduled for Monday, August 12th, at 6:30 p.m., and held at the Hawesville Methodist Church Hall. A large public attendance is greatly encouraged.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hancock County Fair Starts Today!
description: Make sure you get out to the Hancock County Fairgrounds in Hawesville, and don't miss the award winning 2024 Hancock County Fair! The HC Fair is Wednesday, July 31st,
content:
Make sure you get out to the Hancock County Fairgrounds in Hawesville, and don't miss the award winning 2024 Hancock County Fair!
The HC Fair is Wednesday, July 31st, Thursday, August 1st, Friday, August 2nd, and Saturday, August 3rd. There will be carnival rides, tons of delicious foods, competitive events, exhibits, pageants, motor sports, livestock & animal shows, and more.
Wednesday
There is Free Admission on Wednesday at the Fair, and the County Wide Church Service Night begins at 6:15 p.m. Exhibits entries start at 2:00 p.m., and you're encouraged to bring your produce, canned & baked goods, crops, and all other entries! There is a Raffle for a chance to win $100 – for youth and adults, and you get a raffle ticket to place in the box for each entry!
Rides
All of Casey's Rides are Free with the $10 Gate Admission on Thurs., Fri. & Sat. Children 2-years-old and younger have Free admission. Rides open on Thursday & Friday at 5:00 p.m., and on Saturday at 2:00 p.m. *On Saturday, August 3rd, Rides will be open from 1:00 p.m.-2:00 p.m. for Special Needs Riders ONLY, organized by Autism Advocates of Hancock County.
Thursday
On Thursday, baked goods entries are due at 8 a.m., Laser Tag is at 4 p.m., and an OPEN Livestock Show this year at 5:30 p.m., open to Hancock County and ANYONE in surrounding areas. Pony Cart Racing begins at 5:00 p.m., and the Annual Talent Show starts at 6 p.m. At 7:00 p.m., there will be an ATV/UTV/Side by Side Timed, Obstacle Course Event (practice laps, 5-6 p.m.), a Pony Pull, and Zach Jennings Band will be performing! The Miss Teen & Hancock County Fair Queen Pageants will kickoff at 7:30 p.m., at the Pavilion Stage.
Friday

Saturday
