title: School Board frees-up almost $200K for Future Projects
description: The Hancock County Board of Education met on Tuesday evening, July 30th, and Superintendent Robby Asberry said the total amount that has been freed-up from all previous construction projects at HC…
content:
The Hancock County Board of Education met on Tuesday evening, July 30th, and Superintendent Robby Asberry said the total amount that has been freed-up from all previous construction projects at HC Schools is $197,371. These dollars will stay in a Construction-Restricted Account, he said, and will be available to use with the next construction project.
The main goal, he said, would be for that funding to go toward construction of the new Hancock County Middle School. The Board added to the agenda for this month's meeting, approving BG5 closeout form reference # 2355, and also BG5 closeout form reference # 2365. This is the very last of those close-outs of old projects, and that leftover construction funding can now be used in future construction projects.
Purchase of Van
The Board purchased a new van, and split the cost in half with the District Food Service. District Food Service will be using the van to deliver meals to the Hancock County Alternative Program (HCAP), located in Lewisport, and it will also be used for the Summer Food Service Program. The school district will be using the van to transport South Hancock Elementary students to any afterschool extracurricular activities that they participate in, such as track and field at HCHS, during those seasons.
New Position
A new position was approved for Bus Monitor/Food Service. 'This is going to be a permanent Bus Monitor and a Cook/Baker,' Asberry said. 'That person will deliver the food to our alternative school (HCAP), and also transport those South Hancock students to the HCMS/HCHS Campus for extracurricular activities, as needed.'
During other seasons, when transportation isn't required for those SHES students, they will fill in/substitute for bus monitors that are out or were added to a different bus. Now that the new position has been approved by the Board, it will be posted, and then they can hire.
Asberry added that they have been able to fill most of the positions vacated due to retiring staff, etc. They do, however, still have a position open in the district for Special Education, as well as a position for an instructor to teach classes for the new Plumbing Career Pathway offered at HCHS this year. They are still looking for a couple of custodians in the district as well.
Pilot Program – Free Meals
The pilot program set up for this school year with free breakfast and lunch for all students in the district is good to go, Asberry said. 'We are for sure going to be able to do it for this '24/'25 school year. We feel like it's going to be a success and we're hoping to be able to continue it every year. We still need parents to fill out the income part of school registration. That is the big factor on us being able to keep it. Also, we need participation to be up. I think that participation will increase with it being at no cost.'
Approvals
The Board approved the Owensboro Innovation Academy agreement for the new school year, which is done annually. Nothing has changed on the agreement from last year.
Also approved, was the Special Education Procedure Amendments, done annually, and amended to be compliant with any new regulations.
Policy and Procedures updates were approved at the June meeting, and a second reading was done at this month's meeting. No changes were made except for the Kentucky School Boards Association (KSBA) recommendations that correspond with any new revised statutes enacted during the last legislative session. When the legislators pass new laws, the Board is required to change policies to match those new laws.
All school districts hire KSBA to go through school policies to make sure they are matched with any new laws. One of those changes for this year was a requirement for posting the KY Summative Assessments test scores for reading and math on the district website. Those have already been posted. Overall District Proficient & Distinguished Scores are: 49 percent in Math, and 45 percent in Reading.
The Board approved the '24/'25 Mental Health Services Contract as well, the same agreement that is approved every year.
In addition, the new school year's Code of Acceptable Behavior & Discipline Handbook was approved. 'This year we did have our Board Attorney, Regina Jackson from ELPO Law (English, Lucas, Priest & Owsley, LLP), review our handbook and she was able to take some things out that were no longer applicable,' Asberry explained. 'Every year we keep adding to the handbook, according to any new KRS, but sometimes we have to have an attorney look at it; We don't like to take things out unless an attorney tells us it's o.k. to do that.'
The KSBA approves the new Handbooks before each new school year, makes sure they correspond with any new KRS laws enacted during the last legislative session, and then the Board approves those.
Emergency Substitute Certs
The Board approves Emergency Substitute Certifications every year in July to ensure all substitute teacher and classified substitute certifications are up to date. 'If any of them are in emergency basis,' Asberry said, 'we have to approve those to be able to substitute for this school year. If someone was working on getting their substitute credentials, and they didn't have all of those completed at the time, we can emergency certify them if we really need them before they finish those.'
Food Service
The Food Service inactive account debt was approved for payment. If there is a debt owed to Food Service, per federal regulations, it has to be removed from the Food Service Account at the end of each fiscal year. The total debt owed to Food Service was $1,246.80. Food service is a separate account because it is using federal dollars and kind of acts as its own business; It's under the district umbrella but is separate.
ARC
The Board approved ARC (Admissions and Release Committee) and 505 Chairs. Each year they approve training for the ARC in Special Education at each school. They have certain individuals each school has trained, and approve that list each year. The Chairperson runs the 504 meetings, and one example of a '504' would be a medical diagnosis that impedes education.
Treasurer's Report
Director of Finance Trey Anderson reported that the balance on hand was $6,125,791.99, total received for the month was $1,046,736.71, and total expenditures for the month were $2,858,077.97, with a balance at the close of the month totaling $4,597,587.62.
Closing Statement
Superintendent Asberry closed the meeting saying, 'We've had a good summer. We've wrapped up another good year. We're making improvements and we want to continue, each year, to be the best school district in the state of Kentucky. We're working on that. We're glad for the extra time that we've had before the school year to be able to get everything accomplished before school starts.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Young man suffers Mini Heart Attack from Vaping
description: Jacob Temple (26) began vaping at age 15, and was doing so daily for about 12 years straight. A few years ago, he began experiencing severe...
content:
Jacob Temple (26) began vaping at age 15, and was doing so daily for about 12 years straight. A few years ago, he began experiencing severe lung challenges, and said he did not link those health problems to vaping. He thought it was safe and continued for 2 more years after that, until he suffered an anterior myocardial infarction, or 'mini' heart attack.
'I had my esophagus split from coughing so much,' Jacob said. 'I went without sleep for about 3 weeks because I would cough so much during the night.'
The damage caused to Jacob's esophagus resulted in an air bubble forming, and it was pressing on his heart.
'I went to the hospital for the fifth time,' he said, 'and finally the doctor who was taking care of me told me, 'I've seen you in here too much. I don't think it's asthma. I'll try to look at some other options.''
The doctor returned with a diagnosis called EVALI, which stands for: E-cigarette or Vaping product use-Associated Lung Injury (originally called vaping-associated pulmonary injury), and told him that he had to quit vaping immediately so his lungs could heal.
Jacob said he managed to quit, and that his lungs did heal up a little bit but the addiction was very strong and he started up again about 6 months later.
'I re-ripped my esophagus in the same spot, and an air bubble formed again,' he said. 'I went back to the hospital and they hooked me up to an EKG because my blood oxygen level was below 70, and I had a mini heart attack. I had it while I was hooked up to the EKG. That was probably the worst it was.'
Since then, Jacob has quit vaping for good but says he still has extreme lung challenges.
'I can't really breathe well anymore,' he said. 'I can't run after my kids like I used to. I have to take a pretty slow pace at work a lot of the time just because of how bad it is. It's like permanent asthma; It's always ongoing. I don't have asthma attacks but my lungs don't work at 100 percent anymore. I've done so much damage to the small airways of my lungs, that they will never open back up. I, basically, have half my lungs. . .All that from vaping.'
He said he was vaping Delta-8 CBD (sourced from hemp and legalized), along with vaping tobacco, and that the doctor told him people who vape both of those products daily are the ones who mostly suffer the same injuries he sustained, and diagnosed with EVALI.
'Most of the people that get EVALI do both,' he said, 'However, they can get it from just vaping [one product], and some people have died from it. Vape settles, it doesn't rise like smoke, and so it stays in your lungs longer. I'm lucky I didn't have to be put on oxygen. I do have to have a permanent emergency inhaler now.'
When he looked up the study, he said he found that any type of vape pens are toxic. However, choosing a ceramic coil vape can minimize the damage to your lungs. Unfortunately, the SMOK Brand devices that he was vaping with on a daily basis had metal coils.
'You can buy certain vaping coils,' he said. 'I was buying a vape that you would replace (disposable), with the coil in, not the gas station ones, and I thought I was safe. It turns out I was buying the ones with the metal coils, instead of the ceramic coils that are safer. I didn't realize it. You do get the option for ceramic on some of them. They have said in every vape shop that I went into that ceramic is safer because it doesn't release all of that stuff when it gets too hot. Any time a metal coil vape gets too hot, it releases a lot of harmful stuff.'
When vapes had first hit the market in his area, Jacob said he began vaping as a teenager.
'I was a football kid at Apollo,' he said. 'I smoked cigarettes and dipped, and did all the dumb stuff.'
He was 24 when he quit vaping the first time, he said, and then started back up before turning 25.
'It's too easy to just get it out and vape and put it back into your pocket,' he said. 'You don't have to go outside and smoke a cigarette. You don't have to run off and disappear at a function. It was way simpler, and I do miss it sometimes but I know that I will be in a world of serious hurt if I touch one again. The small airways at the bottom of my lungs are completely wrecked. They have closed up and will not open back up ever. It's been about a year since I touched a vape now. I still have a lot of trouble. It still isn't getting any better. I am coughing quite often.'
Jacob has a message for anyone who is vaping, especially young people. He is a parent, he truly cares about young people, and wants them to know the dangers of vaping.
He said, 'I thought I knew everything. My parents tried to tell me. I thought I knew it all. I kept buying vapes, and I got hooked. Here I am, and I almost died. I had a heart attack at 25-years-old. I can't even do the sports I used to do, or play with my children because I do not have the lung capacity to do it anymore. I breathe heavy just from walking, and I'm not a big person; I weigh 150 pounds. It's not like my body takes that much effort to move. It shouldn't be that much of an effort but it is. I ruined a lot of stuff for myself because I didn't listen. I wish I had. So kids, listen to your parents when they tell you something might be dangerous. Take it into account, and do some research because the more research you guys do on these things, the more you'll see that we do know they're dangerous; we just act stupid about it.'
Jacob and his wife, Kaila, live in Owensboro. They are blessed with 2 children. Jacob was raised in McLean County, and Kaila is from Daviess County. He is a painter with John Allen Painting, and Kaila works at South Central Bank.
Jacob's step-dad is Josh Henderson. Josh lived in Hancock County for a number of years with his family when he was a youth, and attended Hancock County High School. Jacob's mother is Jennifer Temple, of Owensboro. Everyone in his extended family that lived in Hancock County has moved away over the years, he said. His family name is Dennisons.
By Jennfer Wimmer

title: Nancy's Notes: Lost
description: I first met her when I had a yard sale. She said she and her husband lived in a camper. In the winter, they had no electricity and about...
content:
I first met her when I had a yard sale. She said she and her husband lived in a camper. In the winter, they had no electricity and about froze. I gave her all the warm comforters and clothes I had. She was sweet and friendly. We sat in the yard and talked for awhile. I could tell there was a problem. She spoke like a child, 'My mom called me Evvie so that's my name. I'm going to call you Millie. We can be friends.' She stopped occasionally to talk after that. The last time she called me 'Ma Ma' and hugged me goodbye.
I moved a year and a half ago and had not heard from her since, until my daughter sent me this: Gold/Silver Alert Endangered Missing Adult – Evelyn Blake, 64-year-old female – white shirt – tan shorts – Last seen July 21, 2024 – 4000 block of Old Railroad Rd. – Breckinridge County (this is not far from the Hancock County line). If seen call (270) 276-6266.
I am very concerned about Evelyn. It was reported she has dementia. Being alone and confused in the woods and brush could be very dangerous with the wild animals. But think of the mosquitos and ticks, and all the rain and storms. As of Sunday, she had not been found. A family member said they were still searching with horses, mules, and 4 wheelers but hope is fading that she may be found alive. A new question arises. What if she has been kidnapped and kept for her monthly check? She would not know or understand what is happening. If anyone has any information, please contact officials.
Dementia or Alzheimer's should be of concern to all of us. 6.2 million Americans have been diagnosed with it. Life expectedness is 3-11 years. It causes the brain to shrink to one third of normal size. It causes 50,000 deaths a year in the United States.
People with healthy lifestyles are 60 percent less likely to have the disease. I think it's time we take a look at how we are living. We need to give up bad habits like smoking, drinking and drugs, get up and start exercising, and pray to God it's not too late, not just for ourselves but for our families.
By Nancy Marlow Moffett

title: Braving the Battle: Emily Mclevain's Journey Through Breast Cancer
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Emily Mclevain (36) was born and raised in Hancock County. She is a lo
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Emily Mclevain (36) was born and raised in Hancock County. She is a loving mother and wife, and is in the middle of a very brave battle against breast cancer.
She and her husband, Jalen, are working together to win this, and get her well. She is dedicated in being positive, and keeping an upbeat attitude, especially to encourage their children during this very tough time.
'I just did my fourth chemo treatment,' Emily said. 'The first 4 were bi-weekly. The next 12, I'll do weekly. After I finish chemo, in 4-6 weeks, they'll remove whatever is left of the cancer. Next, I'll do radiation, and then I'll be on an anti-estrogen pill for 5 years.'
She said it is very important to her to encourage women to do self-exams monthly and if they find a lump, like she did, to go to the doctor immediately and not hesitate.
'Right when I felt the lump, if I would have went and called the doctor the next day, it might have not went to my lymph nodes,' she said. 'I had put it off for 6 weeks. Do not put it off, because I'm at Stage 3, Grade 2. If my underarm hadn't started hurting, I would not have gone.'
Emily is a believer, and said she truly believes that God, so amazingly, has put all the right people in her life to help her take on this very serious health challenge.
'My Grandma (Carol Estes), my mom's mom, was always stern that we grew up in church,' she said. 'When I found out I had breast cancer, it made me open my eyes to so much. It makes you aware of what's really important in life. It just makes you look at life differently when something tragic happens to you…The doctors say my survival rate is very high.'
She said that she doesn't want women to be afraid to go to the doctor when they find a lump, and to realize that getting tested right away to find out for sure, could save your life.
'I needed a biopsy,' she said. 'It doesn't hurt at all. The shot to numb it didn't really hurt at all. My husband and grandmother went with me, and held my hand.'
Her grandmother asked the doctor to call her with the results of the tests, if he couldn't get in touch with Emily. Carol received the results, and delivered the bad news to them in-person in the last week of June.
'I sat on the couch and I started bawling, and I looked at her and said, 'I have cancer, don't I?' And, she said, 'Yea.' The doctor said that we could do a lumpectomy but, right now, we're waiting for me to see a genetics counselor and find out if it's a possibility that I might get it again. If so, that will determine if I'll get a mastectomy. I prayed that night; I stayed up crying. I said that I was going to wake up a newer person and just remain positive, and I have. It's been hard financially, emotionally, and physically, but I have a good support system around me.'
Next year, once the chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation are complete and Emily is cancer-free, the plan is for her to also have a hysterectomy, because the cancer is estrogen-based.
'I'm still learning about it,' she said. 'I have had thyroid disease since I was around 7. They have to watch that closely. I just really encourage people to get themselves checked yearly at the doctor, and check themselves once a month. It can really save a life. I could still be going around having cancer, and not even knowing it if I had never checked myself. It was God prompting me to go to my left breast and check it.'
Emily's best friend and classmate at Hancock County Schools, Diamond White, was diagnosed with breast cancer and, very sadly, passed away 11 years ago. She was a mother of two.
'She had two babies. . .That's one of my biggest fears. Everybody asks me now how I'm doing. Most days, I feel like I'm at peace. I was talking to my friend about that, and she said, 'You know that's God, right?' Because, the hardest part was the confirmation that I have cancer, and telling my kids.'
She said another hard part of this has been the chemotherapy, how it has made her feel, and losing her hair.
'I can't even look at myself in the mirror,' she said. 'Right now, I just take it one day at a time, and I just try to remain positive for my kids. I want them to see me positive. My friend, Kara Kellems, told me that if you remain positive through cancer that it will help your body heal faster.'
Emily said that the chemotherapy treatments make it so that she's unable to do much of anything sometimes, and that her husband is right there to help. She is so thankful for his help, she said, because it is so needed right now, especially for their children.
'I'm ready to get to the next step; Chemo is rough. It's been very helpful for him to be at home. He's the main one that actually takes care of the kids right now,' she said.
Emily expressed that so many people have helped and reached out that she won't be able to name them all here. She wishes to thank Everyone who has been so supportive through this, and extends a special Thank You to: Carol Estes, Robert & Rebecca Blanton, Preston Blanton, Bailee & Jeremy Hodges, Linda Bolin, Natasha Paulsen, Barb Birgy at WBKR, Christy Dunn, Ifeanyichukwu & Jessie Ude, and Gina Berry & her church family at Owensboro First Church of the Nazarene.
Owensboro Health Mitchell Memorial Cancer Center is where Emily is receiving treatments, and she would like to also thank her treatment team doctor, Dr. Hodskins, Melissa Hoegg, and Dr. Chris Glaser, MD, FACS, Surgeon.
Fundraiser
'Emily's Fundraiser' has been organized to help raise funds for Emily and her family during this very challenging time. It is scheduled for Saturday, October 19th, at Panther Creek Park Lakeview North Shelter, located at: 5160 Wayne Bridge Rd., in Owensboro, and starts at noon. There will be a Gift Basket Auction, soups, hot dogs, hamburgers, chips, drinks & desserts. The Food Tray is only $5.
Go Fund Me Page
To donate to the Go Fund Me Page set-up to help Emily and her family as they are faced with financial struggles, please go to: https://gofund.me/d1f24141.

title: Bernard Allen Wethington
description: Bernard Allen Wethington, 66, of Lewisport, KY passed away peacefully in the loving arms of his Lord and Savior on October 11, 2024, at his home surrounded by his loving wife and four daughters.
content:
Bernard Allen Wethington, 66, of Lewisport, KY passed away peacefully in the loving arms of his Lord and Savior on October 11, 2024, at his home surrounded by his loving wife and four daughters. Bernard was born January 14, 1958, in Cloverport, KY at his home, the son of the late Maurice and Sally Dukes Wethington. Bernard worked many different jobs throughout his life. He was a farm hand, deck hand, mechanic, and construction worker. Bernard married Margaret Ford on July 4, 1975. They have spent every day since in love and enjoying each other's company. They have four daughters, thirteen grandchildren, and 7 great grandchildren with more on the way. Bernard was an avid outdoorsman. He enjoyed hunting, fishing, and watching the elk of Eastern KY. He especially enjoyed spending time with his family, passing on his love for the outdoors to his grandchildren. Bernard loved to watch John Wayne films, McLintock being one of his favorites and woodworking with his wife. Remaining to cherish Bernard's memory are his loving wife of 49 years, Margaret Ford Wethington; four daughters Laura (Todd) McCollam, Amanda (Robert) Scott, Edna Cooper, Sue (RJ) Simpson, 13 grandchildren, Keaton McCollam, Trey Shaffer, Colby Stagner, Donald and Wyman Scott, Tyler (Amber) Cooper, Arthur (Kirsten) Cooper, Emilee (Jeffery) Bernardi, Maggie (Dakota Kennedy) Cooper, Shelby Cooper, Ryan, Peyton, and Jase Simpson, 7 great grandchildren, two brothers Ed (Marcella) Wethington, Charlie Wethington, one sister Betty Mangum, a special sister-in-law Kathleen Dawson and her children, Matt Thrasher, Brittany Neihaus, Emma Burgess and several nieces and nephews. Preceding Bernard in death his parents Maurice and Sally Wethington, a brother Paul Wethington Sr., and a sister Nancye Wells, a son-in-law James Cooper and a great-grandson Alex Cooper.
A private memorial service will be held by the family. Gibson & Son Funeral Home has been entrusted with care. Share your memories with his family at www.gibsonandson.com.
The family would like to send a special thank you to the members of the Hospice organization for their care and support.

title: Eddie Price Featured in National Humanities Magazine for Cane Ridge Revival Program
content: Hancock County author Eddie Price appears in the Fall 2024 quarterly magazine Humanities published by the National Endowment for the Humanities. Amy Lifson, assistant editor at Humanities was writing an article on the Cane Ridge Revival which took place in Kentucky in August 1801, and came across one of Price's taped presentations online entitled 'What I Saw at Cane Ridge.' Price presents the program across the state of Kentucky and beyond for the Kentucky Humanities Council which he has been affiliated with since 2012. Price says, 'Amy Lifson called out of the blue from Washington DC and interviewed me for almost an hour. She had been writing about the Cane Ridge Revival and wanted to know about my experiences presenting the program as 'an eyewitness to the revival.' I shared several experiences and research on the revival and its long-lasting impact. The Humanities article starts with one of my quotes and includes the fact that I got the material while writing my first novel Widder's Landing.' The article also includes an ending quote about the time Price was presenting a program at Crofton Chris tian Church. Price mentioned that for a hundred fifty years at most brush arbor sermons, tent revivals, and camp meetings the opening prayers ended with 'Lord, make it like you did at Cane Ridge!' At that moment little old lady stood up and shouted, 'They used to say that at our revivals in the 1950's!'

title: Pure Country Friends Bring the Gospel to Local Nursing Homes
author: Jennifer Wimmer
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Bill Cooper (74) is Pastor at West Point Baptist Church, in Reynolds Station. He is a seasoned gospel and country music singer and guitarist, and he and others formed the band Pure Country Friends years ago. For 23 years now, they have traveled to many local nursing homes to play gospel music, minster to and fellowship with people.
'I go to Heartland Villa and Oakwood twice a month,' Bill said. 'Once a month, I take my guitar and play some gospel songs, and lead a little church service, and preach just 15 minutes or so. Then, I go back with 2 or 3 of my friends that play other instruments. I play flat top, and I sing most occasions.'
He said the people they visit really enjoy the music, and appreciate the fellowship.
'They are lacking in attention from the public, and even from families,' he said. 'So, when I started playing, I was invited to come and play for the pleasure of playing and I had a great time, but it's come to be that these folks have such a need for a connection with other people. If I say, 'Does anybody need a hug?' I guarantee every head in the place is nodding 'yes.' So, that's why we're there. They need some attention from family, friends, and neighbors, and so we give them a little.'
He said, at one time, they were getting out to 11 different nursing homes. Along with Heartland Villa, and Oakwood, they've traveled to Chautauqua and Calumet Trace, to name a couple. The members of the band, over the years, have been from Hancock, Ohio and Daviess Counties.
'It's just a shame that some of the folks that have played with me over the years are not able to now,' he said. 'There are still about 4 of us: myself, Linda Farmer, Betty Brown, and Joanne Jones. Barry Stout, the harmonica player, due to health reasons hasn't been able to play for quite awhile. George Winchester (former Pastor at West Point Baptist Church) passed away about a month ago. He was 89 when he passed, and he hadn't been able to sing with us for awhile. George and I played music together all of those years. We were a duet on Gospel music.'
He said they usually always end their Gospel shows with 'Will the Circle Be Unbroken,' and they invite everyone to sing along.
'I like the hymns,' he said. 'Especially at the nursing homes and even the jails, they lean towards the peppy stuff. I've learned the best thing to do is you can sing one that will make you bow your head and get a tear, and then follow it up with something that is almost a toe-tapper that is uplifting, like 'I Saw the Light' or 'I'll Fly Away,' that sort of thing, and they just love it.'
Bill said many musicians have contributed to the group over the years, and that there are too many to name them all.
'A faithful member was Dale Bradbury,' he said. 'He played the fiddle with me. He has moved back to Oklahoma to be near family. He's still in good health, but he's 83 and wanted to be close to family. Once in a while, we may have a guest come in and play with us, but it doesn't happen often. Another member that's been playing ever since I have is Floyd Stewart. Linda and Betty attend my church, and some of the others do on occasion.'
Bill has been pastoring at West Point Baptist for 2 and a half years. He said he studies hard, and preaches from the Bible. He has not pastored at any other churches. When George Winchester was pastor at West Point Baptist, he needed some help, and Bill first became an associate pastor.
'I worked with Brother George for a number of years,' he said. 'I was a Sunday School teacher for 20 of those years, and then I became Associate Pastor. I filled that job until George felt like he needed to give it up. They took 6 or 8 months to canvass some possibilities, because I had first told them that it would be better if they found a younger preacher, maybe. But, when they came and asked me would I take it, I accepted it.'
He has been the Song Leader at West Point Baptist for 15 years, and continues to lead the praise and worship music, as well as pastoring and teaching the Adult Sunday School class.
For 12 years now, Bill has also been traveling to Breckinridge County Detention Center, and playing Gospel music and ministering there.
'I go there and do several shows in December, at Christmas time,' he said. 'That's what I was really looking for. When I asked to be ordained, it was because there are some that can't go to church – the ones in jail, and the ones in the nursing home certainly can't get out, unless somebody comes to them, and there are some shut-in at home, and I want to reach those people. That was my reason for being ordained, more so than pastoring. It's been great for me to pastor too.'
He said his calling into the ministry was a little nontraditional, and that he had felt the Lord calling him to preach, but that did not happen until he retired from his job at Commonwealth, and began to drive the school bus during the weekdays. Then, his weekends opened up and he was able to start.
'I got involved in preaching some, and the nursing homes, and that sort of thing,' he said. 'Also, I went to church every Sunday from that time on, when it was available to me. Through the years, I was baptized at Roseville Baptist Church, within 3 miles of the church I go to today. The next one I was a member of for years was Zion Baptist, a few miles down the road. I came from there to West Point Baptist.'
When he and his wife, Brenda, were first choosing a church home, he said they had aimed at visiting different small churches in the area and checking them all out. They chose West Point Baptist because it was close to their home, and they have family members who attend there.
'It's been great,' he said. 'We still visit other churches. We play music in other churches. West Point feels like home. We're comfortable in this small church. We know every body. I feel good about my service there.'
Bill graduated from Fordsville High School. He worked at Commonwealth for many years, and served as a union representative for 30 years (USW Local 7325 at the time). He served as Vice President, Financial Officer, Negotiator, Food Bank Trustee, and on the Grievance Committee.
He and his wife, Brenda, have been married for 32 years. Brenda is a United States Army Veteran, and served 4 years. They are blessed with 5 children: Dale, Rene, Melonye, Natalie, and Steven. They are also blessed with 10 grandchildren: Aaron, Kene, Chaz, Hannah, Cameron, Hailey, Caitlin, Christian, Eric, and Babii, as well as 7 great-grandchildren: Kylan, Jude, Paislie, Adelyn, Harrison, Kennedy, and Tucker.
'Brenda is my biggest support,' he said. 'She sings some with us when we do a show. And, we've done several funerals, where she came up and sang with me. Being a pastor's wife might have been kind of a surprise for her. It was for me, becoming a pastor in the first place. She carries a good load at the church. People rely on her. She at least semi-chairs or chairs every committee, and she's our Financial Secretary. She has kitchen committee, and takes care of the flowers when we have people out, and all kinds of things. She makes the arrangements for all of the extra devotionals we have. We have a music service once a month, and she takes care of the fellowship hall and all of the food, etc. I told the people when they were interviewing me for the job as pastor, they asked me a question about her, I said, 'Well, I want you to check me over good because I can be iffy, but my wife will be the best pastor's wife you can imagine.''
West Point Baptist Church is located at 3033 Pellville Rd., in Reynolds Station. Sunday School is at 10:00 a.m. Sunday Worship is at 11:00 a.m. Sunday Evening Service is at 6:30 p.m., and Wednesday Bible Study is at 6:30 p.m. The phone number is: (270) 233-4622. title: Donna Marsch Receives U.S. Dept. of Ag Lifetime Achievement Award
description: Donna Marsch received the United States Department of Agriculture Lifetime Achievement Award, on October 29th, in Washington, D.C. Donna is originally from Livermore, and graduated in 1986 from McLean…
content: Donna Marsch received the United States Department of Agriculture Lifetime Achievement Award, on October 29th, in Washington, D.C. Donna is originally from Livermore, and graduated in 1986 from McLean County High School. In 1989, she earned a Bachelor's of Science in Agricultural Business, with a minor in Business Administration. She and her husband, Scott Marsch, met after attending four classes together, and married in 1992. After graduating, she started working as Loan Officer for USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA), in Hartford. She later transferred to Hardinsburg, and became the loan manager in 2006. Donna now covers Breckinridge, Meade, Grayson and Hardin Counties. Farm Service Agency's loan program offers financing for farm real estate purchases, equipment, livestock and annual operating funds. Collaborating with other lenders and state programs, FSA can often offer financing that allows first-time buyers a chance to start their own operations when they can't meet the rates and terms of conventional lending institutions. As a Farm Loan Manager, she oversees the lending practices of her staff, completes environmental reviews for new operations, monitors loan security and repayment, and currently serves as a trainer for new employees. Donna will retire next July, in 2025, and has worked under 6 presidents. She currently lives in Hawesville with her husband, Scott, where they farm beef cattle.

title: Gerald Buckley Ayres
description: Gerald Buckley Ayres, age 94, formerly of Lewisport Kentucky passed away peacefully on November 4, 2024. He was born August 28, 1930 in Lewisport. To family and friends, he was known as 'Jerry' and…
content:
Gerald Buckley Ayres, age 94, formerly of Lewisport Kentucky passed away peacefully on November 4, 2024. He was born August 28, 1930 in Lewisport. To family and friends, he was known as 'Jerry' and was one of eight children of the late Samuel C. Ayres and Katy Lou (King) Ayres. He was preceded in death earlier this year by Samuel C. Ayres Jr., his oldest brother and also Dorothy Hayden Nutt his former wife, mother of his two children. Survivors include his two sons Stephen Gerald Ayres (Danielle) of Nicholasville, Kentucky and Bradley Lloyd Ayres (Jimena), of Estero, Florida. Jerry is also survived by his siblings Phillip, Betty Boltinghouse, Peggy Parsons, Henry (Gail), Mary Buck (Dan), and Charlotte. He has six grandchildren – Dexter Ayres, Nicholasville; and Lauren, Madeline, and Katherine Ayres of Jupiter, Florida, Isabella Buenaver of Miami, Florida and Maria Pombo of Orlando, Florida. Jerry lived most of his life in Lewisport growing up from a boy to a young man in the Adair community where he helped with the family farm. He started school at The Linton School, a one-room schoolhouse on Adair Road and then attended the 'new' Lewisport Grade and High School when it was built. He graduated from Lewisport High School in 1948 and right after graduation Jerry continued to work on the family farm. In 1951, he enlisted in the US Navy. During his time of service, he was a Damage Controlman aboard two naval destroyers – the USS Putnam and USS Wood until his discharge in 1955. After returning home from service, Jerry took a job with Kelly & Wilmore operating a forklift and backhoe on various utility trenching projects along Kentucky's roads. During off times from Kelly & Wilmore, Jerry helped Tommy Emmick with his gas station in Lewisport. Desiring steady work closer to home in order to raise a family, Jerry took a job at American Olean Tile in 1959 where he worked as a supply manager until his retirement in 1992. Jerry was a member of The Lewisport Methodist Church, sang in the choir for a number of years and helped with fundraising activities such as church concession stands at the county fair and town festivals. In the 80's Jerry was active in The Lewisport Lions Club. He was selected as Lion of the Year in '87 and during local events where the Lions Club was involved, he could be found spraying and turning chickens on the barbeque pits at the Lewisport Community Center. He helped coach little league baseball teams in which his sons Bradley and Stephen participated. After he retired from the tile plant in '92, Jerry was a daily fixture around Lewisport riding his bike or driving and making his rounds – checking on his mom, visiting with friends at gathering places like Eli's and Bennio's and spending summer afternoons watching barges at the Lewisport Boat Ramp before settling in for the night watching sports on TV. And yes, Jerry was an avid sports fan and he considered the University of Kentucky Wildcats 'his' team. In 2021, Jerry moved to Nicholasville to live with Stephen and Danielle, son and daughter-in-law where he made his home there until his passing.
Services are at 1:00 pm Friday November 9, 2024 at Gibson & Son Funeral Home, Lewisport Chapel with burial Following in Lewisport Cemetery. Jerry's family will be greeting friends from 10:00 am until service time. Online condolences may be left for Jerry's family at www.gibsonandsonfh.com. In lieu of flowers, the family would like to request expressions of sympathy as memorial contributions in Jerry Ayres' name directed to The Lewisport United Methodist Church, 450 4th St, Lewisport, KY 42351.

title: Honoring 50 Years of Lady Hornet Basketball: Alumni Join in the Celebration

title: Heartland Villa Celebrates 30th Years of Care & Community
content:
Heartland Villa Nursing & Rehabilitation Center in Lewisport is celebrating 30 years of service to the community in December. The facility has new ownership, and was purchased in February of this year by Encore Health Partners.
David Curry has served as Heartland Villa Admissions and Marketing Director for 3 years now, and said upgrades to the facility have recently been implemented, such as roof repairs. There are also plans for more upgrades with construction in the near future.
In addition to new ownership, there have been some changes in leadership roles. The new Heartland Villa Director of Nursing is Jackie Harper. She began as a CNA at Heartland Villa, and has also served as Assistant Director of Nursing. During her time there, she has continued her education to become an LPN, a RN, and an Infection Control/Skin Health Nurse. Long-term care is Jackie's passion, and she is excited to be working with the outstanding team.
The new Heartland Villa Administrator is Josh Piper. He was Activities Director for almost 2 years, and has spent the majority of his career in long-term care (LTC). He is a Western Kentucky University graduate, and earned a Bachelor's in Health Care Administration, with a focus in LTC. Josh is dedicated to making a positive impact in the residents' lives.
'Hancock County is super important to me,' Josh said. 'I went through college while working full-time here at this facility, and everybody has just been so kind and really amazing to me during this transition time in my life. It is an honor to serve as the Administrator of Heartland Villa center. I have worked in communities across western Kentucky and southern Illinois over the last 10 years, and have never seen such community involvement in a long-term care facility. From community advocates like Hancock County Senior Services providing transportation to churches like Lewisport Baptist Church or Immaculate Conception, and caring for our residents' spiritual needs, the community of Hancock County shows up for our residents. We are beyond proud to have such a great community. Thank you all for your continued support.'
30th Anniversary Celebration
The Hancock County community is invited to Heartland Villa to help in celebrating their 30th year of service on Tuesday, December 3rd, starting at 8:00 a.m. There will be coffee, and donuts from Rolling Pin Pastry Shop.
'We'd love to have anybody attend who can show up,' Josh said. 'We're just trying to have everybody out to have a good time, stop by, say hello, and enjoy themselves, and celebrate being a standard in the community for the last 30 years, and growing the leadership that we currently have.'
Staff with Extensive Service
'We have a few employees that have been here since the beginning,' David said. 'Rhonda Wheatley (Kentucky Medication Aid) has been here with us for 30 years. Tanya Hester, our Business Office Manager, has been here for 29 years, almost 30. Anissa Riley is a nurse here, and has been here for 25 years.'
Tanya is Hancock County native, and the daughter of Marvin & Dorothy Embry. She is a 1991 Graduate of Hancock County High School.
The Therapy Team
'Our Therapy Team has been around for a long time as well,' David added. 'They have over 51 years of combined experience, which I think is an important testament to our facility. They have a number of success stories, as far as with rehab to home services, and just keeping people independent as much as they can. That's one of our strong areas within the skilled nursing facility.'
The Therapy Team members are: Director of Rehabilitation Trent Schraner, Physical Therapy Assistant Michelle Kratzer, and Speech Language Pathologist Carrie Wright.
Two members of this amazing team are Hancock County natives. Michelle is the daughter of Judy & Don Steiner, of Hawesville. She is a 1991 Graduate of HCHS. Carrie Wright is the daughter of Sheila & Mike Ogle, of Hawesville, and a 2004 Graduate of HCHS.
Generations of Residents
'I think it's amazing that we get to take care of generations of different residents,' David said. 'I think that's been a key part of satisfaction for me. It's a small-town community; I enjoy that aspect of it. Our focus is keeping locals, local. It is an important piece to keep Hancock County natives in Hancock County. It's a total win for everyone.'
Holiday Dinner
Heartland Villa is also hosting a Holiday Dinner for residents and their guests (limit 2 guests per resident), on Thursday, December 12th, at 5:00 p.m. Please call Cindy or Andrew at (270) 295-6756 to RSVP by November 22nd.
Contact Information
Heartland Villa Nursing & Rehabilitation Center is located at 8005 US Hwy 60 West, in Lewisport. The phone number is (270) 295-6756 . Like and Follow the Facebook Page for updates!

title: Lienthal Earl White
description: Vietnam Veteran, U.S. Air Force Sergeant passed away at the age of 81, on Monday, January 20th, 2025 in Fort Worth, Texas. Lienthal, affectionately known as Len, grew up in Hancock County, Kentucky.…
content: Vietnam Veteran, U.S. Air Force Sergeant passed away at the age of 81, on Monday, January 20th, 2025 in Fort Worth, Texas. Lienthal, affectionately known as Len, grew up in Hancock County, Kentucky. He was born in Owensboro, KY, on April 6th, 1943. He proudly served as a Sergeant in the United States Air Force, valiantly serving in the Vietnam War. He lived a life filled with dedication to his family and service to his country. His military service was a testament to his character, showing his commitment and bravery during a challenging time in history. Len is survived by his beloved wife of 56 years, Rosie White; daughter, Melissa Aguillard; son-in-law, Mark Aguillard; and three cherished granddaughters, Morgan, McKinley and Madelyn Aguillard. He also leaves behind his brothers Joel White, Roy White, Larry White, and John Mark White, as well as his siter, Sharon White Johnson. Len's legacy extends to many nieces, nephews, and friends whose lives he touched with his kindness, story-telling and uncanny sense of humor. He was preceded in death by his parents, Earl & Opal White, as well as his infant son, Paul Stewart White; and his niece, Kara White. Also remembered are his sister-in-law, Paula White, and countless friends who enriched his life over the years. Len was a faithful Christian, and his family and friends are comforted in knowing that he is now peacefully resting in the arms of his Lord and Savior, Christ Jesus. Len's impact on those around him will not be forgotten, and his spirit will live on in the memories shared by all who knew him. Family and friends are invited to celebrate Len's life with visitation to be held on Friday, January 31st, 2025, from 1:00 p.m.-2:00 p.m., at the Emerald Hills Funeral Home & Memorial Park, located at 500 Kennedale Sublett Rd., in Kennedale, TX, followed by a funeral service beginning at 2:00 p.m. Interment will take place on the same day at 3:15 p.m. In lieu of flowers the family requests that donations be made to The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research at: michaeljfox.org.

title: Man Arrested after High-Speed Chase and Shooting in Hawesville has been Indicted
author: Jennifer Wimmer
description: By Jennifer Wimmer Carl Newhard, of Lewisport, appeared before the Grand Jury on February 28th, and has been indicted. He had a warrant out for his arrest in Daviess County, and evaded arrest on…
content:
By Jennifer Wimmer
Carl Newhard, of Lewisport, appeared before the Grand Jury on February 28th, and has been indicted. He had a warrant out for his arrest in Daviess County, and evaded arrest on January 14th. This led to a high-speed chase from Lewisport to Hawesville. The chase ended with Newhard crashing his truck into the Hancock County Museum caboose on River Street in Hawesville. He was then shot at when he pointed a weapon at the arresting officer, and while a Hancock County School bus was in the vicinity with children onboard. The Grand Jury charges are as follows: Count 1, Fleeing or Evading in the First Degree, when with intent to elude of flee, knowingly disobeyed a direction to stop, given by a police officer, thereby creating a risk of serious physical injury or death to others while operating under the influence; Count 2-22, Wanton Endangerment in the First Degree by wantonly engaging in conduct which created a substantial danger of death or serious physical injury to another person; Count 23-24, Wanton Endangerment in the First Degree by engaging in conduct which created a substantial danger of death or serious physical injury to a police officer; Count 25, Disregarding Stop Sign, failed to properly stop at clearly marked stop sign; Count 26, Operating a Vehicle Under the Influence of Alcohol or Drugs; Count 27, Disregarding Traffic Light, failed to properly stop at clearly marked traffic light; Count 28, Possession of a Controlled Substance in the First Degree, knowingly and unlawfully possessing a quantity of methamphetamine; Count 29, Possession of Drug Paraphernalia, knowingly and unlawfully had in possession items used for the distribution and ingestion of controlled substances; Counts 30-32, Criminal Possession of a Forged Instrument in the First Degree, with knowledge that it was forged, and with the intent to defraud, deceive or injure another, a counterfeit $100 bill; and Counts 33-34, Criminal Mischief in the First Degree, intentionally damaged property causing pecuniary loss of $500 or more. Bond was set at $50,000. The Arraignment is scheduled for Friday, March 7th at 10:00 a.m. Conditions of the bond are: no use of alcohol or drugs; no new arrests or violation of law; no use/possess of firearm or other weapon; no possession of police scanners; must pay $25 bond fee and $40 Sheriff's services fee before release; must sign a waiver of search and seizure; must pay all jail fees before release; no contact with victim or their family; pay current child support; curfew from 6 p.m.-6 a.m. except for employment, court appearances, meetings with attorney, or medical emergencies; maintain employment; and must submit to weekly drug tests at defendant's cost if requested. As reported in The Clarion, Newhard, 60, was evading arrest and had speeded out of Lewisport toward Hawesville on the afternoon of January 14th. Hancock County Sheriff's Deputy Jeff Hendrick observed the truck passing him at the intersection of Big River Road and River Road, and initiated his emergency equipment in an attempt to stop him.
He continued speeding eastbound on River Road, making no attempt to stop. Deputy Aaron Emmick setup at the intersection of Main Street and Adams Street with spike strips. Those were successful in rendering 3 of Newhard's tires flat. Nonetheless, he continued through the City of Hawesville on Main Street at 70 MPH, and ran through the stop sign at the intersection of Harrison Street and Main Street, as well as the traffic light at the intersection of Madison Street and Main Street. Deputy Hendrick advised that the truck made an attempt to cross the bridge into Indiana, before coming off the roadway and returning to the roadway on Bridge Street. Once on Bridge Street, the truck came off the roadway again, nearly striking the bridge pillar. After passing the pillar, Newhard crashed into the red caboose attached to the Hancock County Museum. Deputy Hendrick utilized the front of his vehicle to pin Newhard's driver door shut, to prevent further fleeing action. Newhard brandished what appeared to be a firearm out of the driver's side window, and pointed it at Deputy Hendrick, who then retreated to the rear of his vehicle before opening fire on the truck and striking him with two rounds. Newhard dropped the weapon and placed his hands out of the window. Deputy Emmick arrived on scene and helped remove him from the truck. They then found another firearm in the floorboard that had been between Newhard's feet. The deputies provided medical treatment until EMS arrival. Newhard was then taken in an ambulance to Owensboro Health Regional Hospital. Both deputies, thankfully, were unharmed. Newhard has been held at Breckinridge County Detention Center, with post-arrest complaints pending of: Fleeing or Evading Police, Disregarding Stop Sign, Wanton Endangerment – 1st Degree, Attempted Murder of First Responder (Peace Officer), and Operating a Motor Vehicle Under the Influence of Substance (189A.010(1C) – 1st (AGG CIR). When the incident happened, a Hancock County School bus was in the vicinity. Bus Driver Mary Lou Brake, Bus Monitor Katie Hanks, and 13 students from various grades were onboard. Mary Lou and Katie removed themselves and the students from the area, and they deserve the ultimate praise for their actions, as do the students for being very compliant, and following instructions. HC Schools Superintendent Robby Asberry and Assistant Superintendent Nick Boling immediately visited all of the schools, and ensured that they have the mental health resources available for the students.
Kentucky State Police were called to investigate. Hancock County Sheriff's deputies canvassed the area in an attempt to locate security camera footage. Possession of footage was captured from 105 River Street. Deputy Emmick was assigned to the case for further investigation.

title: Lady Hornets have 24 wins as district tourney approaches
description: Audrey Carnes makes the catch at first base just before the runner reaches the bag. The Lady Hornets softball team won and will compete in the district tourney next week. Baylee Estes had four hits,…
content:
Audrey Carnes makes the catch at first base just before the runner reaches the bag. The Lady Hornets softball team won and will compete in the district tourney next week.
Baylee Estes had four hits, Emmalynn Higdon belted a home run and Ella House and Aubree Mosby combined to produce five runs during an 8-3 win for the Lady Hornets over Owensboro here Thursday.
Hancock County scored a run in the first inning then added five more in the second. Layni Roberts led off the second with a double before Mosby, Baylee Estes and Audrey Carnes hit back-to-back-to- back two baggers. House followed with an RBI hit and girls were off and running on Senior Night. Higdon connected for her homer in the third and the score was 7-0.
Ellington Embry put OHS on the scoreboard in the fourth when she smacked a 3-run home run. The Lady Hornets added an insurance run off the bat of House in the home half of the fourth. The HCHS defense, behind pitcher Lily Roberts, held down the visitors the rest of the way.
Lily got the win while allowing three runs on seven hits, with 13 Ks and four walks over seven innings. Alyssa Rhineburger took the loss for OHS.
Estes was 4 for 4 with one RBI, Carnes was 3 for 4 with a double and one RBI, Layni Roberts was 2 for 3 with a double, House was 1 for 2 with three RBI, Higdon was 1 for 2 with the homer and one RBI,
Mosby was 1 for 2 with a double and two RBI, and Jordyn Waltrip was 1 for 3.
Lyon County Hancock County out hit Lyon County 13 to 6 during a 10-2 win for the Lady Hornets during a tournament at Daviess County Friday.
Estes walked and scored on a hit by House in the second inning and Kylie Westerfield later scored to make it 2-0 Hancock.
Waltrip ripped an RBI triple in the third and the Lady Hornets led 4-0 after Waltrip scored. Lyon County closed the gap to 4-2 in the fifth frame then HCHS took care of business with six runs in the sixth. Eight Lady Hornet players hit safely during the big inning.
Ava Riggs went 3 for 4 at the plate and House was 2 for 4 with two RBI. Lily Roberts was 2 for 3 with one RBI, Layni Roberts was 2 for 4 with two doubles and one RBI, Waltrip was 1 for 2 with the triple and one RBI, Mosby was 1 for 2, Carnes was 1 for 4 with a double and two RBI, and Higdon was 1 for 3 with a double and one RBI.
Roberts got the win on the mound while allowing two runs (one earned) on six hits, with six Ks and three walks in seven innings pitched.
Holy Cross Audrey Carnes hit a homer and knocked in five runs during a 12-2 win over Holy Cross during the Daviess County tourney.
Holy Cross grabbed a 2-0 lead in the top of the first inning, but it didn't last long. Carnes tied the score when she hit a 2-run home run to center field in the same frame. Riggs delivered an RBI hit and the score was 3-2.
Hancock County banged out seven hits during a six run third inning and the rest is history. Lily Roberts got the win on the mound. She allowed two runs (one earned) on four hits, with two Ks and two walks over four innings. Bella Bryant allowed no runs on two hits, with one K and no walks in two innings of relief.
Carnes was 4 for 4 with a homer, double and five RBI. Riggs was 3 for 4 with one RBI, Estes was 3 for 5, House was 2 for 3 with one RBI, Waltrip was 2 for 3, Layni Roberts was 1 for 2 and Lily Roberts was 1 for 3. Bryant was 1 for 4 with two RBI, Higdon was 1 for 4 with a double and one RBI, and Madyson Higdon was 1 for 1.
Elizabethtown Elizabethtown scored two runs in the fourth inning then held on to win 2-1 over Hancock County on Monday at E-Town.
Hancock took a 1-0 lead in the first inning when Estes singled and later scored on a defensive error. Lily Roberts was setting down Panther batters and the HCHS defense was doing a job.
An E-Town player reached base on an error in the fourth and Taytum Spiers tied the score with an RBI single. Spiers later scored on a wild pitch.
A double by Riggs gave Hancock a chance in the fifth, but the sophomore was left stranded. Estes reached second base in the sixth, but again the offense was unable to score. Lady Hornet batters went down on strikes in the seventh.
Lily Roberts took the loss while allowing two runs (none earned) on two hits, with eight Ks and no walks through six innings. Spiers struck out 15 to earn the win.
Estes was 1 for 2 at the plate. House, Layni Roberts and Riggs were all 1 for 3.
Heritage Hills Heritage Hills won a 15-9 slug fest on Saturday during the Team Lauren Cancer Awareness tournament at Daviess County.
Riggs went 2 for 4 at the plate with a double and one RBI for the Lady Hornets. Emmalynn Higdon was 2 for 4, Estes went 2 for 5 with one RBI, Bryant was 1 for 2, Layni and Lily Roberts both went 1 for 3 with one RBI each, and Carnes was 1 for 4 with one RBI. Waltrip was 0 for 2 with one RBI.
Bryant pitched three innings, allowing seven runs (six earned) on nine hits, with two walks. Waltrip allowed four runs on three hits, with two walks in 2.1 innings, and Ryleigh French allowed four runs (one earned) on three hits, with one walk over 1.2 innings pitched.
District tournament The Lady Hornets have amassed the most wins of any 3rd region team with 24 victories this season against nine losses. The girls will compete in the 11th District tournament to be held at Brandenburg beginning next week. Hancock County plays Breck County at 5pm Monday. The winner plays Meade for the title on Tuesday.
By Steve Wimmer
