title: City of Lewisport preparing for Heritage Fest
description: At the Lewisport City Council meeting on Thursday evening, May 16th, Mayor Chad Gregory announced, 'We applied for funding to help...
content:
At the Lewisport City Council meeting on Thursday evening, May 16th, Mayor Chad Gregory announced, 'We applied for funding to help with the new water plant. It was $2M in federal funding, from Congressman Guthrie, and we are now in the top tier. Hopefully, later on in the year we'll find out if we got it.'
Lewisport Heritage Festival
Lewisport Heritage Festival The City is gearing up for the 35th Annual Lewisport Heritage Festival held in downtown Lewisport on Thursday, May 30th through Saturday, June 1st. City Administrator Jason Roberts reported that everything is going well in preparation for the festival. Three summer employees have been hired by the City and will begin working a week before the festival on May 28th.
'We have 16 food vendors right now and 4 different beverage vendors,' Roberts said. 'I talked to Superintendent R.J. Simpson about the tractor pull coming up this week. Next week's an off-week, so everybody is going to be looking for a pull. We had a huge turnout last year. A lot of people didn't come because they didn't like the sled we had, but now we have a different sled so R.J. said there will be a lot of people interested; It's going to be a really big pull.'
Thursday
Thursday On Thursday, May 30th, the festival will kick-off at 5:30 p.m. with words from Mayor Gregory and a Flag Ceremony by Hancock County VFW Post 5186 at Chapman Park. The Opening Prayer by Bro. Brian Adkins is at 5:45 p.m., and the Heritage Festival Pageant (Princess, Miss Teen & Miss Lewisport) is at 6 p.m. Rides open at 6:30 p.m. ($20 Arm Bracelet). Possum Pickers bluegrass music is from 7:30-9:30 p.m.
Friday
Friday Rides open at 5 p.m. on Friday, May 31st, and the Heritage Festival Pageant (Tiny Miss/Mister, Little Miss/Mister & Junior Miss) at Chapman Park begins at 6 p.m. Dan Hall and Blackford Creek Band country/rock music is from 7:30-10 p.m.
Saturday
Saturday On Saturday, June 1st, there will be food and events all day long. Sunshine Circle Homemakers Breakfast at the Lewisport Community Center is from 8-10 a.m. The 5K Run/Walk on 4th St./Market St. is from 8-10 a.m. The Baby Contest at Chapman Park begins at 9 a.m. Kids Games are from 9-11 a.m. The Fire Dept. Open House is 10 a.m.-1 p.m. The Antique Tractor Pull begins at 10 a.m. at the Community Center. The Antique Tractor Show/Drive is at 11 a.m., with Judging at 3 p.m., and Tractor Drive at 4 p.m. The Pet Show at Chapman Park begins at 3 p.m. The Craft Show begins at 4 p.m., as well as the Car Show/Cruise In. Josh Merritt Band will play from 4-6 p.m., and the Talent Contest begins at 6:15 p.m. Cody Lohden plays from 7:30-10 p.m. Fireworks will begin at 9 p.m.
Free bird house building kits will be available for pick up at City Hall. Bird houses for the Kids' Bird House Building Contest can be turned in at the HC Farm Museum on Saturday, June 1st by 3 p.m. Judging with prizes will be at 4 p.m. at the Farm Museum. *Please see the full Heritage Festival Schedule on the City's official flyer in The Clarion.
Police Report
Police Report Lewisport Chief of Police Greg Linn provided an update on new officer Nick Jarboe who was injured during his academy training last year saying, 'Nick came back to work last Monday. We've had, since the last meeting, 34 calls for service. Everything is going well and we are gearing up for the festival now.'
Councilwoman Mary Margaret Hawkins asked about extra security for the Heritage Festival. City Admin. Jason Roberts responded, 'We're going to hire somebody to come out. We're getting some quotes on multiple people.'
Fire Dept. Report
Fire Dept. Report Lewisport Fire Chief Troy Roberts informed the council that the vendor of the air packs used by all of the county's fire departments (Honeywell) has informed that they are leaving the air pack business. Those air packs, as of December, will no longer be a viable option for use and will need to be replaced.
'We were trying to do a group rate for the county,' Roberts said. 'It was going to be approximately $313K for 48 air packs (county-wide). We have 15. Hawesville has 15. On our side, for just our 15, you're looking at $127K and change. The old ones were purchased over 15 years ago. The price is going up. The county requested the inventory of what we all had.' (*As reported in The Clarion in coverage of the April Fiscal Court meeting.)
Roberts also informed the council that one of the flat bottomed boats formerly utilized by the HC Rescue Squad has its new striping and is at the Lewisport Fire Station for use as a rescue boat. He also said that teaching fire safety at the schools, such as fireplace safety, is something that he and the crew are focused on. They have received some donations from businesses in the community on remodeling a unit for taking to the schools and teaching those upcoming fire safety classes.
Treatment of City Employee
Treatment of City Employee Councilwoman Mary Margaret Hawkins expressed her disappointment at the meeting that a City employee of 10-15 years was fired without notice. It was stated that this employee had to go on maternity leave and that her family members had even offered to fill-in for her in her absence.
City Administrator Jason Roberts countered the complaint by stating, 'We had to fill the position.' He added that her family members who offered to fill-in for her absence were not insured.
Councilwoman Hawkins said that it was handled poorly and not the way the City does things, and that the position should have only been filled temporarily so that the woman could return to her position.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Lady Hornets beat Breck 12-2 in district; Roberts records 1,000th strike out
description: Lily Roberts and the Lady Hornets softball team celebrated Lily's 1000th career strike out following the team's 12-2 win over Breckinridge County in the district tournament at Brandenburg Tuesday.…
content:
Lily Roberts and the Lady Hornets softball team celebrated Lily's 1000th career strike out following the team's 12-2 win over Breckinridge County in the district tournament at Brandenburg Tuesday.
Lily Roberts recorded her 1,000th career strike out and the Lady Hornets won 12-2 over Breckinridge County during opening round action of the 11th District Softball Tournament Monday. The event is being held at Meade County.
'Yes, we want to win the district, but we needed to win this game to advance to the region (tournament). So now we just have to win three games and do something that hasn't been done in history at Hancock County, and that's go to state in fastpitch softball,' HCHS coach Dwayne Wroe said.
Hancock County took the lead in the first inning on an RBI grounder hit by Ella House. Baylee Estes singled and scored.
The Lady Tigers got a leadoff double by Skyler Henderson in the second inning, but the Lady Hornet defense left her stranded on base after three strike outs by Roberts.
Hancock County blew it open in the home half of the second.
The inning began innocently enough when Layni Roberts lead off with a single. Emmalynn Higdon walked and Ava Riggs laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance the runners. Jordan Waltrip lined out to the pitcher and there were two outs.
The first run came home on a ground ball RBI hit by Bella Bryant and the score was 2-0. Estes then came to the plate and the speedy junior hit an inside-the-park home run that gave HCHS a 5-0 advantage. Three more runs crossed home plate before the third out was finally recorded and the Lady Hornets led 8-0.
Breck County plated two runs in the third before Roberts struck out the side in the fourth.
Back-to-back doubles by House and Lily Roberts resulted in another run for Hancock County. A fly ball by Waltrip brought in two more runs and the score was 11-2.
Lily recorded her milestone strike out in the fifth and the game was called via run rule when House doubled home Estes in the bottom of the inning.
Roberts allowed two runs (none earned) on three hits, with 10 Ks and one walk in five innings pitched. Ashlyn White took the loss for Breck.
Layni Roberts was 3 for 3 at the plate and Estes and House both went 3 for 4 with three RBI each. Lily Roberts was 2 for 3 with two RBI, Audrey Carnes was 1 or 4 with a double. Riggs was 0 for 1 with one RBI.
Other HCHS team members who contributed are Kylie Westerfield, Aubree Mosby, Ryleigh French, Madyson Higdon and Ansley House.
The Lady Hornets played Meade County in the title game Wednesday after the Clarion went to press.
Owensboro Christian The Lady Hornets softball team closed out the regular season with a 15-0 win over Owensboro Christian last Thursday. There were numerous notable performances, including a no-hitter thrown by Lily Roberts and a home run hit by Emmalynn Higdon.
Roberts struck out the side in the first inning and the Hancock County offense went to work. Baylee Estes began with a base hit before Audrey Carnes and Ella House followed with RBI doubles. Layni Roberts connected for a double then Higdon smashed a 3-run home run to make the score 6-0.
The Lady Hornets added four more runs in the second inning and five more in the fourth when the game was called due to the run rule.
Lily Roberts got the win on the mound. She allowed no runs or hits, with 11 Ks and one walk over four innings. K. Percy took the loss for OCA.
Layni Roberts was 3 for 3 at the plate with two doubles and one RBI. Carnes was 3 for 4 with a double and two RBI. Ava Riggs was 2 for 3 with a double and two RBI. House was 2 for 3 with a double and one RBI. Higdon was 1 for 1 with the homer and three RBI. Carolina Jones and Ryleigh French both went 1 for 1 with one RBI. Bella Bryant was 1 for 1. Ansley House was 1 for 2 with one RBI. Estes and Audree Mosby were both 1 for 2.
By Steve Wimmer

title: Newman – Serving their country from the American Revolution until now is a family tradition
description: Homer Newman stands next to the grave marker of his great grandfather who served in the American Revolution. United States Ar
content:
Homer Newman stands next to the grave marker of his great grandfather who served in the American Revolution.
United States Army Veteran Homer Newman (74) was recently elected as Commander of the local VFW Post 5186 of Hancock County. Scott Padgett, of Lewisport, was the previous Commander.
'We have about 10 active members,' Homer said. 'It should be triple that. We've got the veterans in this county. Anyone that has been in service of any type is welcome at the VFW.' (*Hancock County Post 5186 meets at 200 Main Cross Street in Hawesville, on the second Tuesday of each month at 6:30 p.m.)
Homer added, 'A war veteran who didn't serve in the war but served in the service, if he has anything that comes back service related, like an accident or PTSD, whatever, we work with them free of charge. We try to get them medical help if it doesn't involve compensation for their injury. We have a new service officer.
Leroy Lamar was the old one and did a great job, but he thought it was time to hand the baton off, so he handed it off to Wayne Stephens. He is doing a great job for the members and people. He's taking it very seriously and doing an awesome job. He's had it for about 8 months and the cases he's been involved in, he's won every one of them. And, it's free.'
Veteran Assistance
Veteran Assistance Even if you're not active in the VFW, you can still get this assistance, Homer said. 'As long as you're a veteran, if you need some help call Wayne Stephens or myself,' he said. 'My phone number is (270) 922-8785. And, Wayne's phone number is (270) 929-6256.'
DAR
DAR Homer expressed his appreciation for the Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) saying, 'As many of you know, the DAR have organized in Hancock County and are doing a fantastic job. They have researched and brought forth information on members of families of those who've served. DAR is a great institution. They are very respectful.
My great-great-great-great-great grandfather was Edmond Newman. He is buried up here at Hawesville Cemetery. He served in the Revolutionary War.
I got to checking the facts and there's been a Newman in every war of this country since the Revolutionary War up to today, other than Afghanistan and Korea. My father served three and a half years in WWII, overseas. His name was Homer. He was in food service.
My wife, Joan, was a member of the DAR and they had a presentation at the graveyard in memory of my grandfather, Edmond.
It was awesome. Everybody was dressed in Revolutionary War attire. They were giving out a flag to the closest kin. This gentleman in the Guard had a flag folded and handed it to me and said, ‘You are the nearest descendant of Edmond. This is from a heartfelt country in service for your granddad. We want you to have this.''
Vietnam
Vietnam Homer enlisted in the U.S. Army when he was only 17-years-old, right out of high school. 'My mom had to sign for me to go in,' he said. 'Norman Arnold and I went in together and signed up the same day. We went through basic training together, up to 6 weeks of basic in Fort Knox.
They got us out and ran us in our skivvies at 3 o'clock in the morning in October and I came down with pneumonia. I had to go to the hospital for 2 weeks so that separated me and Norman from each other. He had gone on and graduated and I had started all over again. Norman is a friend I'll love forever.
My first assignment was Fort Detrick, Maryland, in chemical warfare. I went up there for a year and then I got orders for Vietnam. Everybody was getting drafted back then in 1967, unless you went to college. I was lucky to get out of high school. I had no aspirations of going to college whatsoever so I knew I was going to get drafted.
I went and volunteered to try to stay out of an infantry unit. Well, it worked the first year and then after a year, almost to the day, I got orders for Vietnam and I went to Vietnam and flew into Cam Ranh Bay on a commercial airliner. I got there and stayed overnight and they sent me up to the 90th Replacement Battalion (near Long Binh, Vietnam, between Bien Hoa and Saigon).
I was an E-4, Specialist Fourth Class, Spec 4 they called it. I had been in a year and went up to Spec 4. I went in as a Private. My job was supposed to have been food service, but I did everything. Over there, everybody did everything. Mostly I filled sandbags to put around our tent so if we had an attack, maybe we'd live through it. I drove a truck in convoy over there. I worked out at the mess services. I worked in supply for awhile.
Wherever they needed somebody, that's where they put you. I never argued. They knew I was easy. I just didn't care; I just wanted to get my year over with there and live through it.
When I got to Bien Hoa, they had one of the biggest attacks, a mortar was on Bien Hoa and they'd shut the airport down even. There was no incoming and no outgoing because the mortars on the compound. They said, ‘Tomorrow, you're going up north.' I said, being a 17-year-old kid, ‘What's up north?' They said, ‘Well you're going up 8 miles from North Vietnam.' I was 8 miles from the DMZ (Vietnamese Demilitarized Zone).
Down south, you would have the Viet Cong soldier, which was a farmer by day and at night would attack you. When you got up north though, it was the hardcore North Vietnamese, well-trained, well disciplined fighting machines. So that's what we dealt with. I'm proud to say I went through a year in Vietnam and never got a scratch. The Good Lord was watching over me.
I know of 3 times I should have been dead. One time, I was in a three quarter ton truck and I was headed back to the base and picked up some supplies in it, and I got halfway up on a rice patty dam, like a little dirt bridge across the rice patty, and this armor plated 2 and a half ton truck on the other side started coming across.
He hit me and knocked me off that dam and I flipped 3 to 4 times. What was really bad about it, I had just picked up a hitchhiker that was going back to his base. He was in the back of the truck when it flipped. I wasn't hurt. It shook me up good. It scared me. First thing in my mind was, ‘What about him?' Did it roll on him, or kill him? I was very concerned about him.
Luckily, all he got out of it was it threw him a way and he broke his left arm, a compound fracture. I was so concerned over him, even though it wasn't my fault; I had the right of way. I went to the hospital to see this young man and I really didn't know how to approach him because here I had broken his arm and I felt bad about it.
I got to the hospital, he saw me and came up and hugged me. He said, ‘Thank God for you. This arm is broken and I'm going on a one way ticket to Japan. I'm out of Vietnam!' For some reason in Vietnam your bones don't heal right. I don't know if it's the heat or what. I really felt better about that then.
The second time, I was sitting on a sandbag on top of a bunker on the perimeter line to keep anybody from trying to take us over. A shot went off and the bullet hit about 3 inches over from where I was sitting. It hit the sandbag and put a hole in it. So, that was twice.
Then, we had an attack one night of mortars and rockets. Where I had been, we had a tent that had a dirt floor. That was all we had, if we were lucky. Sometimes we slept out in the jungle. It was during Tet Offensive, the worst disaster of Vietnam; I was right in the middle of it. During that, I had been right outside 10-15 seconds earlier. It was a direct hit by mortar where I had been standing just seconds earlier. I had seen it was getting bad and had ran to the back of the tent and jumped in an underground bunker. That's 3 times I should've been dead.
I was 18 at that time, during Tet Offensive. I spent 3 years in the military. After Vietnam, I went to gate duty, right on the ocean at Virginia Beach for a year. Of course, after Vietnam, anything is going to be good. It was good duty. I had a good sergeant over in E-7.
I was so disillusioned with the whole process of Vietnam and everything else and didn't even want to talk about it. For 30 years, I wouldn't even speak about it. I wanted no part of the Army or the military. I put my 3 years in and I did my duty honorably. I just wanted out of it.
I divorced after I came back from Vietnam. I left Vietnam about 30 days earlier than what I should to put in my year, because of a family dispute. I got with the Red Cross and the Chaplain and they sent me home a month early. Everything happens for a reason. Two weeks after I left to come home, my unit went up Hamburger Hill – a blood bath up in the A Sau Valley where the North Vietnamese had concrete bunkers built. It would have been a wonder if I had lived through that. By me getting sent home early, I bypassed that. The Good Lord was watching over me again.'
Homer married a second time. He and Joan 'Jo' spent many happy years together. 'She passed away 4 years ago in February,' he said. 'She passed in 2020. She was 68. We think it was a massive heart attack or stroke. She never had a heart problem in her life.
It's funny how things work around. I thought it was the worst thing in the world to divorce. That's something you didn't do. As It turned out, it's probably the best thing that ever happened to me. For one thing, I married Joan and she was such a sweetheart.
I went to work when I first went out of the military. It was rough on jobs; you couldn't find a job. My mom called Billy Stephens, Old Man Bill. He always called her ‘Genie' because her name was Eugenia. And, she said, ‘Bill, this boy of mine needs a job.' He said, ‘Well, Genie, have him down to Brown & Root Monday morning at 7 o'clock, and he's hired.'
I worked there until the end of construction, which was about 8-9 months. I tried to get on at NSA. I don't know what it was; I just couldn't get on there. I went to 2 people that basically got me a job at NSA, one was Dr. Smith and one was Bernice Wimmer. I worked at The Clarion when I was a kid. I enjoyed it. I worked around good people. I have been blessed in my life to be around good people.'
Homer's brother-in-law, Tony Gray, who was in the U.S. Army Reserves, encouraged him to sign up several years later. 'I was in the 100th Division U.S. Army Reserves. I stayed 17 years; Nobody told me to leave. With those 17 years and my 3 years, I picked up on a full pension. I've been blessed.
The camaraderie of the Vietnam Vets kind of flows along with the camaraderie of the VFW. You take care of your buddy and your buddy takes care of you. You've got each other's back. I've got 4 buddies. One is outside of Raleigh, NC, and he's a Baptist minister. I've got one in Connecticut. I have one in Michigan. And, the rest of them have died, I'm sad to say.
My buddy in Michigan, Jim Duncan, he and I were like the bobsy twins. Me and him and Charles Collie, if you've seen one of us, you've seen the other one of us, like the Three Stooges. Such good friends. If you want to have a good friend, you make a friend in combat and you'll never forget it. They wanted to get back home safe and sound. But, they wanted me to get back home too, so we watched out for each other.
I had visited Michigan twice. Jim Duncan had been down here twice. His wife called me up and said, ‘Homer, Jim has had brain surgery for cancer. He's not doing good. He's more or less comatose. Is there any way you can come up here? He wants to see you before he dies.'
I told her, I said, ‘Pam, it's going to take me about 9 hours to get there. I'll see you in 10 hours.' So, I called my son, Norman, and told him I was going to Michigan and asked him if he could watch the dogs. He said, ‘Nah, you're not going to Michigan by yourself, Dad.' He took 3 days vacation from Century Aluminum and took me up there.
I got there and walked in, and he was more or less comatose. She went up to his ear and said, ‘Jimmy, Homer is here.' The biggest smile you ever seen went across his face. I asked the family if they would leave the room and I could have a couple of minutes private with my buddy. I just got up to his ear and told him, ‘Jim, it's o.k. I know you are a believer in God. It's o.k. to go on. I appreciate you being my friend and watching over me in Vietnam.
The Good Lord has given both of us over 50 years since Vietnam. We have no regrets. We've lived good lives. We've raised children. Now, you go on to Heaven and, Buddy, I'll see you when I get there.' He died in my arms, when I was holding him.'
Homer has one daughter, Laraine, and one son, Norman. 'Two blessings,' he said. They have multiplied the blessing by giving him 6 beautiful grandchildren. He says he loves being a grandpa and is so thankful to have made it home from Vietnam.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: HC Schools Retirees Recognized
description: The 13 retirees
content:
The 13 retirees from Hancock County Schools were recognized and presented with a gift at the Board of Education meeting last week. This year's retirees are: Michelle Gregory, Shelly Gray, Heather Miller, Mary Price, Pam McCaslin, Denise Roach, Charlena Williams, Theresa Feldpausch, Laura Szefi, Danny Gray, Bob Daniels, Melanie Adkins and Kelly Moore.
Hancock County Schools Superintendent Robby Asberry said, 'We thank you for all your years of service. I am very pleased with our turnout tonight. In the past, we've honored our retirees in July and I think that it works much better in May so I'm so glad to see the turnout. I love hearing their speeches and what it means to them to be working in our school system. I just really appreciate them.'
The retirees who were in attendance at the meeting spoke about how they will greatly miss teaching at HC Schools. Retirees who were unable to attend for the group photo and receive their award in person were: HCMS Instructional Assistant Denise Roach, HCMS Science Teacher Theresa Feldpausch, Maintenance & Computer Tech Bob Daniels, NHES Principal Kelly Moore and HCMS/HCHS Choral & Theatre Director Melanie Adkins.
Retirees Speeches NHES 2nd Grade Teacher Michelle Gregory said, 'It's just been a great honor to be a teacher at Hancock County Schools. It's the only school system that I've ever taught in. I started off 29 years ago at Lewisport Head Start as a preschool teacher. I moved over to Hawesville Elementary and taught second grade until that school was closed, and then started at the new school at North Hancock.
I have a lot of memories. It's really surreal that this is happening right now – just seeing former students that I've taught, like Lacey Mosby. She was in that first 2nd grade class that I had at Hawesville Elementary and now she's our Family Resource person. I not only have been gifted to teach the kids in HC, but now they are some of my co-workers. I'm very blessed. It is bittersweet.'
NHES K-1 Teacher Shelly Gray said, 'I started 27 years ago. I was at Hawesville Elementary and taught Title I for a couple of years and then Reading Recovery. My home at Hawesville, we called ‘the shack out back' because we were in the old BOE building for awhile. They put up the trailer units when they started to condemn part of the building and then I was able to teach my youngest one. She was a student in the last class at Hawesville and was in my kindergarten class. Then we moved to the new building. It's been a privilege to teach where I've grown up and to teach kiddos here in my own community. I'm very thankful for that.'
Art Teacher Heather Miller said, 'I taught 28 years of art in Daviess County and the rest in Hancock County. I was very gifted to be able to teach all those years. Not only did I get to teach just a few kids, but I got to teach every kid that came through the school. I felt like I was very blessed to get to know and touch all of those kids' hearts. They all gave back to me and so I felt like I was blessed back. I'm just thankful for all of the time I got to teach. I appreciate it. Thank you.'
Special Ed Assistant Teacher Mary Price said, 'I'm probably the oldest one here that's retiring and the one that's been here the least amount of time. I have 2 degrees but am retiring as an assistant because I was able to work with the special needs children pretty much one on one like I always wanted to do. It was only 5 years I was here. It was great. I'll miss everybody.'
HCMS Guidance Counselor Pam McCaslin said, 'I'm just grateful that I had the opportunity to spend my career here at HC Schools, 28 and a half years coaching and teaching. I started out in math and stepped into guidance counseling. It's been an honor, a treat and a pleasure. HCMS is a special place and I'm very blessed and grateful to be there.'
HCMS Special Ed Teacher Charlena Williams said, 'Hancock County was here for me whenever I needed to get home closer to my parents. I was able to be here during their final years. I realize that God has a plan and it's a great plan. Kentucky is a wonderful state to teach in. In a small system like this, you know your kids. You know their parents and you can contact them. You know that everything is o.k. and you're going to get through it because you've seen their parents get through it and you've weathered the storms. I want to thank each and every one of you here for allowing me to be a part of this wonderful system.'
HCHS Media Center Teacher Laura Szefi said, 'As an elementary education major and someone who added secondary library science on as an endorsement last minute, I never thought I'd spend 27 years in the high school. I'm very grateful to have been here. I'm grateful to have had administrators that have let me branch out and take my position in different directions and learn new things. I'm very appreciative and excited about my next challenge.'
HCHS Guidance Counselor & Athletic Director Danny Gray said, 'This building is my life, since 1987. I really enjoyed it. I'm blessed to have a family that was willing to let me make this building my life. I wouldn't have changed it for the world. I've loved it.
I feel like I'm leaving it better than I found it; That was one goal of mine. I've been blessed. I want to thank HCHS Principal Ginger Estes, Superintendent Robby Asberry, Assistant Superintendent Nick Boling, Director of District Programs Joey Minton and Assistant Superintendent Robin Poynter. They brought my love back for this building. Those guys gave us an opportunity to lead and believed in us. When we told them we could do something they said, ‘Show us you can do it.' Now we have a new football field and new track. I'm very thankful. Most of all, I'm thankful for my wife. She gave up a lot, but she was also excited about it every step of the way.'
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Big Rivers donation helps HC Animal Shelter
description: In spring of 2021, Big Rivers donated $20K to the Hancock County Shelter Supporters toward a quarantine building at the Hancock County Animal Shelter. The much needed building is now completed and…
content:
In spring of 2021, Big Rivers donated $20K to the Hancock County Shelter Supporters toward a quarantine building at the Hancock County Animal Shelter. The much needed building is now completed and sits by the shelter in Lewisport, at 305 Gene Hayden Rd.
Tuesday morning, May 28th, Director of Communication & Community Relations for Big Rivers Electric Jennifer Keach and Judge-Executive Johnny 'Chic' Roberts visited the shelter to see the building. Shelter Director & County Dog Warden Ronnie York completed the heating & air and a drainage system in the building to equip it for isolating rescued dogs.
Keach said, 'When Big Rivers closed our Coleman Station and dismantled it and had the demolition, we decided that we wanted to give back to the community, because it's very important to support our community. We went to Judge Roberts and asked for his opinion on two worthy causes in this county. The Shelter Supporters donation I am particularly happy about, being a dog enthusiast; I rescue them myself. We're very proud of what they're going to do with this. I'm impressed with the building, for sure.'
Big Rivers donated $20,000 to HC Shelter Supporters, as well as $20,000 to Hancock County Repair Affair in Hawesville, as was recommended by Roberts. HC Shelter Supporters is a non-profit group that supports the HC Animal Shelter.
Roberts said, 'We are very thankful for the generous donation from Big Rivers and what it means to the Hancock County Animal Shelter. Ronnie York, Galena Murphey, and the staff out here do a great job. None of this is possible without the volunteers. The HC Shelter Supporters took the donation that Big Rivers gave and maximized that amount. We're very thankful for what they do.'
Shelter Supporters President & Rescue Coordinator for the HC Shelter Galena Murphy said, 'We knew what we wanted to do with the money – to build a quarantine/isolation building, but it took us this long to come up with something.'
The new quarantine building was a kennel that an Amish family had built for their breeder dogs. The gentleman developed terminal cancer and the family needed money for his medical care. Shelter Supporters decided to purchase the kennel from the family, and then Ronnie York made all of the modifications it needed.
'Ronnie has done an absolutely beautiful job with it,' Galena said. 'He has really modified it to suit what we need at the animal shelter. We are all so proud of it; We are so proud of Ronnie.'
Dogs taken in at the shelter will now have the quarantine building to stay in until they are treated for any diseases they have, and then they can be assimilated into the kennel at the shelter as space is available. The new building is not intended for overflow. The maximum capacity at the HC Animal Shelter will remain at 16 dogs. There are always dogs there that need good homes, and the shelter is currently full to capacity. Please consider adopting one today!

title: HCHS Teacher Volunteering this summer in Moldova with Ukrainian Refugees
description: Seen here is HCHS History Teacher William Fogle giving his first guest lecture at Aristotle University in 2016. He will be guest lecturing again in Greece this summer, as well as volunteering in…
content:
Seen here is HCHS History Teacher William Fogle giving his first guest lecture at Aristotle University in 2016. He will be guest lecturing again in Greece this summer, as well as volunteering in Moldova to help support Ukrainian refugees.
Hancock County High School History Teacher William Fogle will be traveling to Moldova this summer and volunteering for 3 weeks in July to help support Ukrainian refugees at the Chabad Lubavitch Jewish Community Center in Kishinev.
'I have a good friend who is a Lubavitch Rabbi who runs the Jewish Community Center in Kishinev, Moldova,' William said, 'and they've processed more than 35,000 Ukrainian refugees through the center. I'm going to do a volunteer stint with them. I'll be doing whatever they feel best serves them. They don't turn anyone away. Whoever comes through from Ukraine, they take in.
While I'm in Moldova, for part of one day I'll be going to a country that exists but does not exist. I've been there before. It's a little place called Transnistria. It is a Russian enclave that they did not give up after the fall of the Soviet Union. It's between Moldova and Ukraine.
It's an interesting place. The people are mostly Moldovans and very friendly. There are Russian troops everywhere in Transnistria. My Rabbi friend in Kishinev services the Jewish community through the capital of Transnistria, and I'll travel with him.'
Greece William has been affiliated with the METAdrasi Organization in Greece for many years, and traveled to Thessaloniki, Greece last summer to work with refugee children at a center there in art therapy. He said it went really well. 'I was paired up with some very good, experienced psychologists from Aristotle University,' he said. 'I have nothing but good things to say about that. The art therapy certainly helped them to express things that they are prevented from expressing due to language barriers.
Most of my refugee work I do this year will be done in Kishinev. In Thessaloniki, I will be doing a guest lecture series on the American Presidency at Aristotle University. I have a friend who is the Dean of the College of Political Science, Statistics and Psychology; It is a conglomeration of colleges in one.'
In 2016, he guest lectured at the university and is excited to have been invited back. He is making 2 separate trips to Greece this year. William travels to Thessaloniki regularly, and has since he was 19. He says it's like a second home to him, and that he has tremendous support and a friendship network there that he's had for more than 40 years through a very strong and active Jewish Community. It is referred to as a 'Jerusalem of the North'.
Kosovo During his trip to Greece last year, he traveled north into Ferizaj, Kosovo to speak at an elementary school named after his dear friend, the late Afrim Abazi, who was murdered in the 1980s. He and William met many years ago while he was studying in Switzerland. He will be traveling back to Kosovo this summer as well to speak at the school Afrim attended as a boy again, and to gather more details from Afrim's family and ask for permissions for a book he's writing about him.
Ireland Before he sets out on those journeys, on Saturday, June 1st, William and his wife, Dee, are traveling to Ireland. This will be their second trip there since he suffered a massive stroke in 2018. 'This trip is basically a victory lap for me because that was the first place I went after I got out of my wheelchair and wanted to celebrate walking again,' he said. 'When I was there last time I was confined to a cane and I hobbled all over Dublin and everywhere else Dee and I went. Ireland is always nice. I have improved a bit more. I can go up and down stairs freely without depending on a rail. Who knows if full usage is ever going to come back, but you do what you can.'
He has begun rebuilding his strength by returning to practicing Krav Maga martial arts last year, and will add Judo, he said, in the fall of this year. It was a long recovery process after his stroke, with the help of physical therapy. It has taken much determination on his part to get to where he is today.
'We're just going to be in Ireland about a week,' he said. 'Our base is going to be in Dublin. We're going to go to see the Cliffs of Moher. I highly recommend Limerick. It is right out of the book almost. It is a fairy tale in itself; it is so scenic. The Book of Tales at Trinity College is definitely number one on the list. The Long Room at Trinity College is something I'm fascinated with. It is the one library room in the world that has the most books in it, more than 200,000. I have to go and hang out there for a bit.
The nice thing about Ireland is that it's a small enough island that you can get to wherever you want to go within a few hours. We are free wheeling it on this trip. We're just going to kind of sit down and decide what we want to do when we get there this time. We're going to stay in the Republic. The weather will be nice; we won't have to worry about rain.
We're going to get to fly first class to Dublin because when we were supposed to go during Spring Break, the plane was shut down for maintenance so the airline said they'd make it up to us this way. We'll be in first class, which will be nice, from Charlotte to Dublin.'
William has been teaching for over 20 years in Europe and in the U.S. He began teaching at HCHS in 2022, and said he loves it. In the fall, he will be teaching U.S. Government and dual-credit Political Science. He sponsors the HCHS Chess Club and will be hosting the Second Annual Dreidl Championship this year. He says he's excited about sponsoring a Mock Trial Team this next school year as well.
He earned his first degree at Lycee-College des Creusets in Sion, Switzerland, and his Bachelor's in Political Science & History at Indiana State University, with multiple minors. His Spanish Degree and teaching credentials, he earned at University of Southern Indiana, and his first Master's at Western Kentucky University. He's currently completing an Education Specialist Master's Degree with Principal Certification through University of the Cumberlands.
He has served on the Advisory Board for the U.S. Servas National Board for 3 years, and has been involved with them for 40 years. For a few years now, he has also volunteered as a mentor at the International Center of Owensboro.
William's bestselling book, A Stroke Survivor's Tale: A Survivor and Caregiver's Resource, was published by AR Press in 2022, under his pen name, Liam Bernard, and he'll be working on a second edition soon. He's currently working on his first novel that will be completed by the end of autumn. After that, he'll be writing ‘Teacher Tales', he said, a reflection on his experiences in teaching on both sides of the Atlantic.
William & Dee live in Owensboro. They are celebrating 25 years of marriage this year.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Healthy Habits: Marine Collagen
description: In last week's edition of The Clarion, I wrote about the health benefits of grass-fed
content:
In last week's edition of The Clarion, I wrote about the health benefits of grass-fed beef gelatin, a great source of bovine collagen – which mainly offers types 1 & 3 collagen. One of the best ways to get the full benefit of types 1 & 2 collagen is through consuming the skin and scales of fish, like cod. Since that is not a very appetizing venture, a marine collagen powder can be taken daily.
Marine collagen is a great alternative to bovine collagen, especially for those with certain allergies or diets. It can also be taken in addition to bovine collagen/grass-fed beef gelatin, because it will give you more of the benefits of type 2 collagen.
Vital Proteins Marine Collagen Brand is made with integrity. It is sourced from fresh, wild-caught, non-GMO cod, and is highly assimilable/absorbable. Marine collagen peptides are small and easy for our bodies to absorb and utilize. As I always advise, please do your research and/or check with your doc before taking any new supplements to make sure they are right for you.
Here are some of the many health benefits that marine collagen offers:
antibacterial,
great source of protein,
slows/reverses aging,
assists in healthy weight management,
strengthens hair & nails,
tightens loose skin,
'plumps' skin naturally,
decreases fine lines/wrinkles,
is said to reduce cellulite,
helps reduce joint pain,
supports optimal digestion/improves gut health,
helps maintain cardiovascular health,
assists in a healthy weight loss regimen,
helps with stabilizing blood sugar levels,
increases skin elasticity,
improves thyroid health,
helps with muscle repair
can help prevent injury, and can potentially prevent and even reverse arthritis symptoms. We may be including fish in our diets, but some of the parts that we don't usually consume provide the most collagen. There are around 28 types of collagen, with types 1, 2 & 3 being the main ones that make up the majority of all collagen, which is the most abundant protein in our bodies.
The most common type of collagen, type 1 or CI, makes up 90 percent of hair, skin, nails, organs, bones, ligaments and tendons. Type 3 collagen (CIII) partners with type 1 to support skin & bone health, as well as promoting the optimal health of our muscles, blood vessels and the arterial walls of our heart. It is most commonly found in tissues with elastic properties.
Type 2 collagen (CII) is what makes up most of the protein molecules in our cartilage, as well as the connective tissue protecting our bones at the joints, in our eyes and in our spinal disks. It can help reduce joint pain through its effect on the immune system, alleviating osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, and also promotes skin health.
The brand of marine collagen powder I've recommended is 'unflavored'. Three tablespoons of this powder has 12 grams of collagen. It can be stirred or blended into whichever liquid you choose to add it to. You can add it into smoothies, shakes, juice and even your morning cup of coffee. I have read that many people add it into warm/hot beverages such as coffee and hot cocoa, and I can see why; It really doesn't dissolve very well in cold liquids.
A tip for those who do not like the taste of marine collagen powder or grass-fed beef gelatin – I have discovered that chocolate beverages mask the slight flavor really well. If you are not a chocolate lover, then try adding them to something savory such as a cup of warm, organic chicken broth.
Be Well and God Bless You.

title: Families enjoy KY 4-H Passport Kitchen
description: Zaden, Brantley and Tobi Sharp showing off the Nigerian fried rice they made together with their parents, Krystal
content:
Zaden, Brantley and Tobi Sharp showing off the Nigerian fried rice they made together with their parents, Krystal & Shelby Sharp, as part of their participation in KY 4-H Passport Kitchen over the last several months.
Lisa Hagman, Hancock County Extension Agent for 4-H Youth Development, began offering a 5-month program called Passport Kitchen earlier this year that is now almost complete. The free program provides an in-home culinary adventure for children ages 9-18 to enjoy with their families.
Hancock County 4-H had 10 families participate and all received 5 kits, one for each month featuring a different country. Krystal & Shelby Sharp, of Hawesville, and their 3 children, Zaden, Brantley and Tobi, are one of the families in the community that enjoyed Passport Kitchen together.
Hancock County Middle School Eighth Grader J.D. Powers participated in the program as well, with his father and grandfather. They had fun and learned a lot about cooking by completing the kits together.
HCMS Student J.D. Powers and his grandfather, Franklin Powers, learned to cook together through the free KY 4-H Passport Kitchen program. They are seen here measuring flour for their Irish soda bread.
'I provided a recipe and kitchen item each month in their kit,' Lisa said. 'The coolest thing has been happening. Franklin Powers, his son Jason Powers, and his son J.D. Powers get together each time and cook together. None of them knew how to cook and are learning through this program.
There is one more kit and country left that they will be covering during Passport Kitchen featuring Poland (this month). The Kentucky 4-H Passport Kitchen program is intended to provide young people from Kentucky with the opportunity to experience the food cultures of different countries in a self-paced experience.'
Beginning in January and through May, participating families in the community received one kit a month with a corresponding dish to prepare at home for each featured country. The countries and dishes were: Japan -Okonomi yaki, Ireland -Irish soda bread, Nigeria: Nigerian fried rice, Ojibwe -wild rice soup, and Poland -perogies & gingerbread cookies.
Each Passport Kitchen kit included a recipe card for a local dish from each featured country, a link to a cook-along YouTube video, information about the country, cards with phrases in the country's language, a 'passport', one ingredient, and kitchen utensils such as measuring spoons.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: New Choral & Theatre teacher – Kenneth Basham
description: Kenny Basham, the new HCMS/HCHS Choral & Theatre Teacher, and his wife Sarah. Kenneth 'Kenny' Basham will be the new Hancock County Middle and High School Choral & Theatre Teacher beginn
content:
Kenny Basham, the new HCMS/HCHS Choral & Theatre Teacher, and his wife Sarah.
Kenneth 'Kenny' Basham will be the new Hancock County Middle and High School Choral & Theatre Teacher beginning in fall for the ‘24/'25 School Year. The current teacher, Melanie Adkins, has worked for 20 years in the public school system and 5 years in the private school system, as well as teaching private voice and piano for 13 years. After 38 years of teaching music, she said she has decided it is time to retire.
Kenny grew up in Hawesville and is the son of Gerald & Kristine Basham. He graduated from HCHS in 2010, and then earned his Bachelor's in Music Education at Kentucky Wesleyan College (KWC), with an emphasis in Vocal Performance, and a minor in Piano.
'Melanie was my music director and was the one that started my career in music, aside from my parents,' Kenny said. 'My dad was really the ignitor on that, but she's the one that cultivated the talent and it went from there. I cannot remember a time that my family and I weren't doing music. My dad, my brothers, myself, and my sister sometimes, we would all go around and play at several churches.
We played just in the back yard as well. That's where I started learning guitar. I sang duets with my brother, Anthony. We started learning piano together. It really wasn't just one person that started it, it was the whole family, and then Melanie cultivated it.
Our home church was Safe Harbor in Pellville, and we played a lot there (Larry & Monie Sosh are pastors there). That's where I cultivated my drumming skills and played piano with Larry. He's an amazing pianist.'
For the last 10 years, Kenny has been an elementary school music teacher, at Sorgho Elementary and West Louisville Elementary, in Daviess County. 'I've done countless programs,' he said. 'I've had 100s of students and I have loved every minute of those 10 years, but it's time for me to move back home and take over for the music teacher that started it all for me.
I have big shoes to fill. Melanie Adkins has carried this program for 20 years and has really built it into something special. It's my intention to take that something special and make it even better. Moving back to Hancock County means moving closer to my family. I'm really excited about furthering what I do now and bringing my talents back home.'
Kenny was very active in musicals while attending HCHS, and said that he carried that love of theatre over to college. He was in 3 musicals while at KWC, specifically with Theatre Workshop of Owensboro (TWO). He plays piano for TWO and has continued to be actively involved with them every year since.
'I started taking piano lessons from Carolyn Kinsey,' he said, 'the music teacher at Breckinridge County. I really excelled when I got to college and started taking piano lessons from Dr. Diane Earl, the Professor of Music at KWC. She has played in countless countries. She's just a fantastic pianist. She plays for the (Owensboro) Symphony Orchestra. She was my instructor for 5 years. I took private voice lessons in college, and also taught piano lessons and private voice lessons.'
He is on the Worship Team at his church, Pleasant Valley Community Church, in Daviess county, and plays piano, guitar and has helped out with the youth program there for awhile now. He was also the Youth Director for a middle & high school program at Ignite 360 Church for 8 years.
'I might not have directed any theatre programs necessarily, other than the ones in elementary school,' he said. 'I have written most of the ones for my elementary school programs. I will say that I absolutely love putting on programs for people and making them happy. I do all of the technical side. I'm very involved in the technical side for our church and school – sound, lighting, video editing, all of it.
It is my intention to get Hancock County known in the community, farther than just a concert. I'll be recording most of the songs that we do, that we might not perform, so that parents and families can listen to ALL of the amazing things that they're doing in the classroom – more than just at concert night.'
He said that his style of teaching is very energetic. 'I'm just really excited about it,' Kenny added. 'I'm anxious to get started. I've already started packing up and moving stuff over there. I build a lot of relationships with the kids and we have a lot of fun.
To me, music is both challenging and fun. Kids don't go to choir to be bored; They go to choir because they love singing songs that they love. So it's my goal when I take over the program, to do challenging music that ignites their creative spirits and minds, but also to do fun music that the audience will enjoy, that my students will enjoy, and that I will enjoy.'
Kenny and his wife, Sarah, will be moving closer to Hancock County soon. She is a Loan Officer at US Bank, in Owensboro, and they'll likely be moving to Maceo, he said, so that they will still be close to her work and also be near to his new job at HCHS. They also run a DJ business together – K & S DJ Services, based in Owensboro, and have DJed many elementary school dances. He said they are hoping to DJ some school dances in Hancock County, and other functions soon.
By Jennifer Wimmer

title: Hornets fall to Meade in district tournament
description: The Hornet baseball season came to an end with an 8-0 loss to Meade County in the 11th District tournament he
content:
The Hornet baseball season came to an end with an 8-0 loss to Meade County in the 11th District tournament held at Brandenburg Monday. 'It definitely wasn't the season we wanted, but we have a young team and we knew that coming in,' HCHS coach Brad Keown said. 'We had good pitching all year and they were able to keep us in games, but we weren't able to put the other two parts together.' Meade County (19-17) scored three runs in the first inning, two in the second and two in the fourth. The Hornets best chance was in the fifth when Brock Tindle led off the inning with a base on balls. Jacob Shultz advanced Tindle to second base on a sacrifice bunt and Kolby Keown followed with a base hit to left field. Keown stole second and the boys had runners at second and third with one out. Tindle tried to steal home but was thrown out at the plate. Dec Lewko then singled and Keown advanced to third. He was stranded there when the third out was recorded. Jack Roberts led off the sixth with a single to right field, but courtesy runner Lane Dixon was thrown out trying to steal second. The next two batters went down on strikes. The Green Wave added one more run in the sixth. The Hornets went down 1-2-3 in the seventh. Tindle started on the mound. He allowed five runs (four earned) on six hits, with three Ks and no walks in 1.1 innings pitched. Porter Hay allowed two runs on six hits, with four Ks and two walks in 2.2 innings of relief. Jordan Payne allowed one run on one hit, with one K and three walks in one inning of relief. Roberts and Keown both went 1 for 2 at the plate for HCHS. Lewko and Dylan Mucker were both 1 for 3. Aiden Bratcher was 2 for 2 with a double and two RBI to lead Meade County. Hancock County finished the year with a record of 6-20. By Steve Wimmer

The Hornets best chance was in the fifth when Brock Tindle led off the inning with a base on balls. Jacob Shultz advanced Tindle to second base on a sacrifice bunt and Kolby Keown followed with a base hit to left field. Keown stole second and the boys had runners at second and third with one out. Tindle tried to steal home but was thrown out at the plate. Dec Lewko then singled and Keown advanced to third. He was stranded there when the third out was recorded.
Jack Roberts led off the sixth with a single to right field, but courtesy runner Lane Dixon was thrown out trying to steal second. The next two batters went down on strikes.
The Green Wave added one more run in the sixth. The Hornets went down 1-2-3 in the seventh. Tindle started on the mound. He allowed five runs (four earned) on six hits, with three Ks and no walks in 1.1 innings pitched. Porter Hay allowed two runs on six hits, with four Ks and two walks in 2.2 innings of relief. Jordan Payne allowed one run on one hit, with one K and three walks in one inning of relief.
Roberts and Keown both went 1 for 2 at the plate for HCHS. Lewko and Dylan Mucker were both 1 for 3.
Aiden Bratcher was 2 for 2 with a double and two RBI to lead Meade County.
Hancock County finished the year with a record of 6-20.
By Steve Wimmer
